pieces.title: How index strategies can be an effective vehicle for loan market exposure
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that index-based strategies can now give investors representative, low-cost beta exposure to leveraged loans, a market historically dominated by active management, because growing volumes, electronic trading (rising from under 1% to over 6% of trading between early 2024 and mid-2025) and portfolio trading have eased the barriers that once made indexing impractical. The firm explicitly promotes its LVLN ETF, which tracks the S&P USD Select Leveraged Loan Index and uses sampling and a monthly rebalance to control costs, and it concludes that loans are poised to become as accessible to index investors as high-yield bonds.

pieces.title: How are investors repositioning portfolios?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Portfolio Insights team reports, based on 12 months of average category allocations, that investors are gradually moving away from long-leading areas such as Large Value and Large Growth, and from core fixed income and high yield, towards mid- and small-cap equities, international (particularly emerging market) equities, short-term and multisector bonds, and thematic and alternative strategies such as inflation-protected bonds, technology funds, long-short equity, systematic trend and commodities. The firm views the diversification into international and alternative exposures as productive, but argues that alternatives should be sized deliberately as accents that complement, rather than replace, the core portfolio anchors, and suggests that developed international value is an underappreciated complement to emerging markets.

pieces.title: Outlook for 2026
pieces.summary: KKR's 2026 Outlook argues that, with the economic backdrop still favourable but the credit cycle maturing, investors should "High Grade" their portfolios by upgrading holdings, capital structures and counterparties towards resilience, quality and capital efficiency, a step KKR says is currently cheap to take. It frames the environment as a "Regime Change" of higher-for-longer rates, geopolitical friction and more discriminating credit markets, and favours quality and scale in public equities, operational-improvement and carve-out opportunities in private markets, Asian equities and collateral-based cash flows, while avoiding apparently cheap assets with weak competitive positions or fragile capital structures. KKR's bottom line is to own less beta and more alpha, sourced through structuring, governance and active ownership.

pieces.title: The 2026 Global Equity Playbook
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that investors entering 2026 face a scarcity of growth, capital and certainty, and recommends anchoring portfolios in highly profitable companies, diversifying across regions and styles, and actively reducing volatility. Its explicit views are that the US gap versus other markets could narrow (it does not expect sustained structural US underperformance), that AI exposure is necessary but should be selective and diversified to manage crowding risk, and that quality companies with durable profitability offer attractive long-term opportunities, having lagged in 2025 when speculative growth stocks rallied.

pieces.summary: Schroders argues that US retirement savings, held mainly in 401(k)s and IRAs, act as a large and steady source of equity demand, with about $980 billion of gross contributions in 2024 and an estimated $480 billion going into US equities. Its key risk is an AI-driven rise in unemployment among high earners, who disproportionately fund these monthly flows; the piece models unemployment reaching 10% in an AI-boom scenario and states that the resulting fall in contributions could be material for equities. Schroders supports this with the 2022 episode, where pension buying was the only meaningful bid for US stocks and may have cushioned a 20% fall, though it cautions that the figures are not a like-for-like decomposition of demand.

It cites Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's projection that US data centre direct water use could roughly double to quadruple by 2028 from 2023 levels, and examples from Chile and Arizona where water concerns altered or halted projects. pieces.title: Take Two: Stocks rise ahead of Middle East peace deal - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's weekly market roundup reports that global stocks hit record highs on hopes of a US-Iran peace deal, with oil prices falling and inflation concerns easing, even as the Federal Reserve held rates at 3.50%-3.75% and signalled a possible hike before year-end. It also covers the Bank of Japan's rise to 1%, the Bank of England's hold at 3.75%, weak Chinese retail sales, and the case for gold as a hedge against economic and geopolitical shocks as central banks diversify away from the US dollar. The piece offers no explicit investment call; its main stated view is that gold will likely remain a useful hedge against shocks.

pieces.title: Sports bettors: Don’t gamble with your taxes
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors warns sports bettors that winnings are taxed as ordinary income while losses can only be deducted as itemized deductions up to 90 per cent of winnings under recent US tax law changes, and notes that state-level taxation also varies. The firm argues that bettors should maintain detailed records of all wagers and consult tax advisors, particularly given the increased accessibility and frequency of sports betting.

View from the markets: Why have emerging market tech stocks been so volatile? - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris reports that emerging market semiconductor and technology hardware stocks have fallen about 28% from their July peak, though they remain up 47% year to date, and he attributes the volatility to wide disagreement over the economic and profit impact of artificial intelligence. The firm argues that this uncertainty, shown by the sharp rise in forecast dispersion for EM tech hardware (from 10 to 82, against a steady five for non-tech), makes earnings forecasts highly sensitive to new information. Its explicit view is that, for longer-term investors, earnings growth over the next two years should still be significantly positive, with forecasts near 90%, and that the precise outcome matters less than the direction.

pieces.title: Solvency II: What 2027 securitisation reform means for insurers
pieces.summary: Invesco argues that the 2027 Solvency II recalibration, effective 30 January 2027, materially reduces spread-risk capital charges for selected senior securitisations, notably AAA non-STS (including AAA CLOs), senior STS ABS and RMBS, and BB senior non-STS, giving European insurers a timely reason to reassess an asset class they have historically underweighted. Its illustrative model of a €10 billion insurer credit portfolio suggests capital release of about €57 million with broadly unchanged income, or extra annual income of roughly €5 million to €6 million at similar capital consumption. Invesco stresses, however, that lower charges do not remove the need for collateral analysis, diversification, due diligence and monitoring, and that AAA CLOs are not a cash substitute, since prices can fall in risk-off markets even when credit impairment remains remote.

pieces.title: Great expectations - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that investor sentiment is bullish and that US macro expectations have improved, with 2026 GDP consensus at 2.4% and AI investment supporting resilience, though it warns of AI-linked inflation pressure and of markets being stretched. It sees the Fed's policy stance as close to neutral, questions the 45 basis points of 2026 cuts priced by markets, and prefers high-yield credit to duration, given the flat yield curve and near-record-low credit spreads. Its explicit caution is that extreme positioning could amplify even minor shocks.

pieces.title: Yahoo Finance: Mike Downing
5 Key Questions with ’27 in Sight
pieces.summary: PGIM's weekly view, dated 5 October 2026, addresses the question investors are asking ahead of 2027 of whether a "one and done" Fed scenario is plausible, arguing that the Fed could pause in October but is not finished hiking. PGIM points to still-strong U.S. demand (real consumption near a 4% annualised pace and post-pandemic-high private domestic demand) and to increasingly structural constraints in energy, trade, labour, technology inputs and food. It concludes that lower rate sensitivity in the economy does not justify easier policy, and that if tightening is transmitting less effectively the Fed may need to tighten more forcefully rather than stop.

pieces.title: Investment News: Understanding Equity-Linked Notes and Alternative Income
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, via portfolio manager Natasha Sibley, explains how equity-linked notes generate income from equity volatility rather than interest rates or credit spreads, and distinguishes stability notes from autocallables, which carry different risk and return profiles. The piece cautions that higher headline yields come with distinct risks, so the source and sustainability of yield must be understood, and it presents an ETF structure as a more accessible way to gain exposure to these strategies. The firm's explicit position is that these notes are a differentiated alternative income source, though its stance is framed as explanatory rather than a firm recommendation.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that UK tax and spending levels are not excessive by international standards, that the UK's public finances are risky but far from the most concerning among developed economies, and that its projected narrowing budget deficit should st

pieces.title: PERE UK Roundtable
pieces.summary: PGIM convenes a roundtable discussion on UK real estate against a backdrop of economic and geopolitical uncertainty, including post-Brexit positioning challenges, a new Labour government struggling with debt and productivity, and global tariff volatility. The piece reports that this uncertainty has prompted investors, businesses and consumers to pause capital decisions, which will dampen real estate demand, and argues that UK business leaders must play a role in helping the country redefine its global position.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: What BDC Markets Are Signaling About Private Credit Valuations
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that BDC equities are lagging their bonds because equity investors doubt the credibility of reported net asset values, while BDC loan marks remain elevated relative to the broadly syndicated loan market, and the valuation reset has yet to begin in earnest. It notes that the new-deal spread advantage over leveraged loans has shrunk from more than 300 bps in 2017–2018 to under 100 bps by Q1 2026, leaving BDCs with less differentiated economics. PIMCO's explicit view is that private and public credit valuations are likely to converge, possibly slowly, so further pressure on BDC equity valuations remains a meaningful risk.

pieces.title: The Middle Market Niche: The Investment Opportunity for the Middle Market
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that the core middle market, companies with roughly $25–100 million of EBITDA and $150 million–$1 billion enterprise values, offers a differentiated direct lending opportunity with less competition, the ability to hold whole loans rather than syndicate them, and a portfolio with less overlap with other lenders. Andy Frank, Global Head of Origination at Fortress, contends that this positioning, sitting beneath the broadly syndicated loan market and above the lower middle market, matters because it delivers real structure, documentation and pricing, along with direct relationships with management teams.

pieces.title: Megatrends for insurance investment tech
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that insurance companies face mounting complexity across investment management—from private markets and digital assets to regulatory reporting and climate risk—requiring unified technology platforms rather than fragmented legacy systems. The firm contends that a consolidated investment management system serving as a single source of truth across public and private markets, asset-liability management, and analytics would enable insurers to improve operational efficiency, regulatory compliance, and strategic differentiation. BlackRock positions its Aladdin platform as the solution to transform technology infrastructure from an impediment to innovation into a competitive advantage.

pieces.title: ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management reports that European UCITS ETFs drew a record €125 billion in Q3, taking year-to-date inflows to almost €350 billion, already above the €327 billion recorded for all of last year. Global equities led the flows, with a sharp rise in all-country exposures, while Europe rebounded and emerging markets recovered, and Chinese equity ETFs saw continued outflows. The firm's Head of ETF Research, Daniel Dornel, also highlights strong fixed-income inflows despite rising yields and says the continued growth of active ETFs "highlights investors' appetite for new strategies"; the piece offers no explicit market call beyond this reading of flows.

Sharesify podcast with James Thom
pieces.summary: Aberdeen promotes a 12-minute Sharesify podcast in which James Thom, co-manager of Aberdeen New India Investment Trust, makes the case for investing in India now, citing well-governed, high-quality companies positioned to benefit from long-term structural growth. Aberdeen notes the trust trades at a double-digit discount to NAV, discusses the measures in place to narrow it, and describes a conservative gearing approach in volatile markets. The piece is a third-party podcast promotion rather than an original analytical note, so its explicit view is the bullish India thesis expressed by Thom and endorsed by Aberdeen's framing.

pieces.title: Options income: Time to turn off autopilot
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that a historically wide gap between individual-stock and index-level volatility creates richer option premiums on single stocks, making stock-level call writing more attractive than index-based strategies. The firm contends that active managers should exploit this environment by selectively writing calls on fewer positions to preserve upside and adjusting dividend yield flexibly alongside options income, rather than applying uniform, systematic overlays regardless of market conditions.

pieces.title: Lifetime income strategies get green light as QDIAs
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's ERISA strategist Tina Anstett argues that the Department of Labor's latest advisory opinion (AO) confirms that target date funds with guaranteed lifetime withdrawal benefits can qualify as qualified default investment alternatives (QDIAs), provided they meet all regulatory requirements. The firm presents this as a significant, "much-needed" step that gives plan sponsors and advisors clarity to offer more secure retirement income to participants, and it urges them to review their default options and consider whether a lifetime income strategy suits their participants and fiduciary obligations.

The piece's explicit view is that, for investors, success will depend on adapting to a world in which real assets behave less like static holdings and more like intelligent, interconnected platforms, with AI, automation, cybersecurity, tokenisation and climate readiness rewriting performance rules. It also flags related PGIM pieces on affordable housing financing, power access for European real estate and a €125M refinancing for U Store It.

Dancing Through the Lightning Strikes? The Ongoing Case for Gold
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that gold's sharp rally in early 2026 is a puzzle, since market inflation pricing has been flat over the past year while gold, silver and platinum surged, and that the recent pullback is tactical, driven by easing geopolitical premia, a possibly more hawkish Fed chair and momentum-driven selling, rather than a change in the strategic case. Its explicit view is that gold should be held as a strategic, non-fiat complement to equities, with near-zero long-run correlation to stocks, though it offers no price target and warns that investors should expect considerably higher volatility, with institutional allocations (pension funds are usually at zero) having room to rise. The firm also says the dollar has likely peaked as a safe haven, adds silver on industrial demand, and treats crypto as part of the same non-fiat theme with greater uncertainty.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment's piece, titled "Scraping the barrel": Wen trifft es – und wann?, argues that geopolitical tension in the Middle East is exposing weaknesses in global energy supply chains, with the Strait of Hormuz, carrying roughly 20% of world oil and LNG flows, as the focal point. It reports that the market is not short of oil overall, but that disrupted shipping, damaged infrastructure and rapidly falling inventories are raising the risk of shortages and price volatility, with risks most acute in import-dependent markets such as India, parts of Asia and Latin America, while the US acts as an "exporter of last resort", China and Japan look relatively robust, and Europe faces targeted shortages, particularly in jet fuel. The firm's explicit conclusion is that these risks are regional and product-specific, so investors need to examine them closely when assessing the implications for growth, inflation and asset pr

pieces.title: The Evolving Role of Private Markets in a Portfolio
Opportunistic Credit: Resilience Across Cycles
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that opportunistic credit, an unconstrained strategy spanning performing, stressed and distressed credit and bespoke financing, can offer low-beta, idiosyncratic returns and downside protection, and that today's environment of elevated dispersion, rising distress and aggressive liability management transactions, despite near-record tight spreads, creates a particularly rich opportunity set, driven by high base rates and post-pandemic private equity misallocation, notably the 2021–22 leveraged buyout vintages. PGIM explicitly positions the strategy as complementary to both traditional credit and PE exposure, and stresses that manager selection is critical, citing lending relationships, specialist industry research and macro-to-company synthesis as the sources of edge; it also presents illustrative target IRRs of roughly 15–25% across sub-strategies, while noting these are not guaranteed.

pieces.title: Rear Window
From efficiency to empathy: Using AI to deepen relationships with female investors
The Advantages of Investing in Infrastructure and Other Real Assets
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that surging infrastructure needs, driven by underinvestment, demographics and the megatrends of digitalisation, deglobalisation and decarbonisation, are opening a multi-trillion-dollar funding gap as traditional lenders pull back, and that private capital should step in. The firm's explicit view is that infrastructure offers steady, inflation- and recession-resistant cash flows across the risk-return spectrum, and that the middle market ($50 million to $500 million) offers better relative value than the large-cap segment because it has fewer bidders, attractive valuations and stronger covenant protections. It also contends that clean energy investment continues despite the 2025 federal rollback of IRA incentives, since solar, wind and battery storage remain cost-competitive, though it notes that effective execution requires entrenched sponsor and bank relationships and dedicated underwriting expertise.

Did the December CPI report change the outlook for Fed policy?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's research note finds that the December CPI report, showing headline inflation of 0.3% m/m and 2.7% y/y and core inflation of 0.2% m/m and 2.6% y/y, was broadly in line with expectations and does little to alter the monetary policy outlook. The firm expects the Federal Reserve to remain on hold through early 2026, citing uncertainty over data quality after the government shutdown and the risk that fiscal stimulus and delayed tariff pass-through could reaccelerate inflation in the first half of 2026. It therefore argues that upcoming inflation and jobs reports will matter more for policy, and notes that markets now price a full 25bp cut in July rather than June.

pieces.title: What is Ares’ Role as a Secondary Investor?
pieces.summary: Ares Management presents its secondaries platform as a natural fit for its view that continuation funds, which it has long backed across its primary strategies, are attractive, arguing that general partners hold more information and better aligned incentives than any other party when buying a business. Ares says its role as a secondary investor is to sift a rapidly growing market to identify the best companies, industries, managers and opportunities. The piece is largely a qualitative statement of positioning, with its disclaimer noting that "downside protection" and "risk-adjusted returns" are not guarantees.

pieces.title: From prompt to practice: How advisors can get more value from AI
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that advisors can get more value from AI platforms such as ChatGPT and Copilot by writing precise prompts and treating the exchange as an iterative conversation, with the starting question being "What is the problem I need to solve?" The piece offers sample prompts across client experience, operational efficiency, business strategy and leadership, and urges advisors to add context to them. It presents AI as a tool for both efficiency and stronger client connection, and promotes its Amplifying Human Intelligence programme and hub as ongoing resources.

“Backed” to the Future
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that collateral alone does not make an asset-based finance (ABF) investment worthwhile; outcomes depend more on transaction structure, covenants, governance, lender control and active monitoring, with underwriting done before closing largely determining resilience under stress. The piece presents ABF as a source of spread, income and diversification within private credit, but says the expanding and increasingly uneven opportunity set raises the bar for underwriting and requires investors to distinguish genuinely asset-backed, bilateral deals from asset-light structures that repackage corporate risk. PGIM's explicit view is that experienced managers can add meaningful value, and that the structure and governance around the assets, rather than the assets themselves, ultimately determine how much value investors retain.

Portfolio Design as Gesamtkunstwerk: The Total Portfolio Approach
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that the Total Portfolio Approach (TPA), which organises capital around underlying return streams and risk exposures rather than asset-class silos, is becoming more important because lower expected returns, thinner diversification and the growth of private assets are forcing investors to allocate risk more efficiently. It acknowledges real barriers to adoption, including governance changes, siloed organisational structures and career risk, and says institutions tend to move gradually along a continuum. AllianceBernstein states its view plainly: TPA is better suited to today's environment, and it expects more institutions to move in this direction.

Continental European Half Year Activity & Outlook
pieces.summary: PGIM's Europe private credit team reports that activity in the first half of 2025 was varied across strategies and regions, with notable deals in corporate financing, direct lending and infrastructure, while borrowers and sponsors proceed cautiously amid tariffs, inflation and geopolitical tension. PGIM's explicit view is that resilience is the priority, pointing to local-for-local production, diversified funding sources and long-term partnerships with non-bank lenders as key themes. It also identifies infrastructure (ageing assets, the green energy transition and digital infrastructure) as an opportunity to provide essential financing.

pieces.title: UK small caps: our festive stocking fillers
pieces.summary: Aberdeen's festive piece argues that UK small caps look attractively priced after the November Budget eased worries about UK markets, with bond yields barely moving, and that domestically oriented firms may see sentiment improve. It names Cranswick, Dunelm, Balfour Beatty, Galliford Try, Jet2, On the Beach, Applied Nutrition and CVS as illustrative examples, with the view that Jet2, On the Beach and CVS in particular appear well placed to keep delivering, and that CVS's CMA review being behind it means "now could be the time to fetch some shares." The firm includes a disclaimer that the stocks are illustrative only and not a recommendation.

pieces.summary: PGIM's real estate research argues that medical outpatient buildings are a compelling investment, citing structural demand from population ageing and the shift of care delivery towards outpatient settings, alongside predictable, economically resilient income growth. It also says liquidity and pricing are improving, and that health systems' influence over on-campus properties can enhance performance. The piece explicitly presents the sector as a growing opportunity, positioning it within PGIM's core plus strategies, which target both income and growth.

pieces.title: Why Should Investors Consider ASEAN Today?
pieces.summary: Barings argues that ASEAN is emerging as one of the world's most dynamic growth engines, driven by rising consumption, rapid digitalisation and shifting global trade flows. It highlights under-researched opportunities in the region's small and mid-cap markets, and concludes that the region offers compelling potential for investors.

pieces.title: How much of the AI boom is adding to U.S. growth?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the AI capex boom, with hyperscalers on track to spend nearly $800bn this year, has so far added only modestly to U.S. GDP: an AI-related investment proxy contributed 0.47 percentage points of the 2.1% growth over the past year, after netting out imports. It attributes the gap largely to measurement issues, including overseas data centre spending, the netting-out of imported hardware, the under-recording of U.S. chip design value as IP exports (which Epoch AI estimates understates annualised growth by about 0.3 points), and price rather than volume effects in computer investment. The firm's explicit view is that mismeasurement is directionally clear but its magnitude is not, and that the economic payoff, via a growing capital stock and eventual productivity gains, will unfold gradually, so policymakers may need to lean on alternative data, equity signals and judgement.

pieces.title: Video: The yields in this asset class haven’t been this high for 15 years
pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management's head, Teiki Benveniste, tells Livewire (interview recorded 29 May 2023) that fixed-income yields are "definitely higher" than in years, with selective global credit offering income of 7-8% plus potential capital gains. He argues that default rates will likely revert to historical averages of 3.5-4.5% rather than a catastrophic "zombie apocalypse", since companies refinanced during COVID and debt servicing remains robust, and that the Ares Global Credit Income Fund favours global over Australian credit because of the deeper, more liquid US and European markets.

What role does public and private fixed income have in portfolios?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that public and private fixed income should be seen as complementary rather than competing choices, since each plays a distinct role in a bond portfolio. Public core bonds provide daily liquidity, attractive current yields and historically effective equity hedging, though they carry interest rate risk, and the piece says active management is preferable to passive benchmarks. It presents private credit (mainly floating-rate middle-market loans) as offering higher yields and lower duration risk at the cost of credit and manager-selection risk, and cites an illustrative 80/20 public/private mix that it says has returned about 130bps more than a public-only portfolio with less risk.

pieces.title: Asia Pacific rates diverge as local dynamics lead
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's International Liquidity Fund Management team argues that Asia Pacific rates are diverging as local conditions, rather than global trends, drive policy: Australia has tightened and Japan faces pressure to hike, while China, Singapore and Hong Kong have drifted lower at the short end. The team also highlights a gradual move away from dollar dependence and a regulatory convergence towards global money market fund standards, including proposed limits in Hong Kong and Singapore, which it sees as positive for cash investors. Its explicit call is that, amid high geopolitical uncertainty, investors should prioritise liquidity and capital preservation, favour quality, and diversify across sectors and regions, while noting that elevated front-end yields and upward-sloping curves offer attractive income.

pieces.title: Global View on Debt, Inflation, and Rates
pieces.summary: PGIM's weekly note argues that the U.S. interest-rate dynamics it covered the previous week are now playing out globally, with debt sustainability concerns resurfacing in Europe. It attributes this to a mix of economic resilience (notably in France and Germany, previously seen as sluggish) and elevated energy prices, which are pushing expectations for central bank policy rates higher. The piece is brief and does not state an explicit investment call; the rest of the page is site navigation and cookie notices.

Hybrid in Action: Delivering Bespoke Capital Solutions in a New Market Paradigm
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that hybrid capital, sitting between private debt and equity, is increasingly in demand as companies face higher borrowing costs, limited traditional debt access and volatile markets. It illustrates this with three cases: a preferred equity investment that let a fast-growing company scale without more debt or loss of control, a senior investment in a continuation vehicle giving a sponsor liquidity, and a hybrid solution offering a liquidity-constrained public company equity-like capital with limited dilution. Apollo's explicit view is that hybrid capital can deliver equity-like returns with credit-like downside protection, and that its structured features help issuers and investors navigate uncertain markets.

Will nuclear power AI data centers?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that nuclear power is unlikely to be a quick fix for AI data centres' surging electricity demand, citing long build times (about nine years on average), high construction costs, and reliance on imported uranium, while noting that natural gas will remain the largest near-term source of supply. The piece takes a cautious view of nuclear hype, saying small modular reactors and fusion are decades from grid-scale relevance and that nuclear will be only one part of a diversified solution. It suggests investors seeking exposure to energy supply for AI should consider private infrastructure funds that invest directly in generation assets, rather than speculative long-dated technologies.

pieces.title: DACH & The Nordics
pieces.summary: PGIM's Frankfurt-based private credit team reviews a strong 2025 in the DACH region and Nordics, led by real assets (renewables, digital infrastructure, district heating) and sustained demand for long-dated, local-currency institutional debt, with private placements, shelves and sponsor-backed direct lending all active. The team takes a "cautiously optimistic" view for 2026, expecting higher M&A and 2026–27 debt maturities to create direct lending opportunities, continued corporate demand for non-bank, fixed-rate and shelf financing amid political and economic uncertainty, and expanding European infrastructure investment, which it says governments will drive and institutional lenders can help leverage.

The piece argues that disciplined growth matters and that Barings' ownership by an insurer sets it apart as the asset management industry continues to consolidate. pieces.summary: PGIM reports that global listed real estate fell about 6% in the third quarter of 2026 (per the FTSE EPRA NAREIT Developed Index), as a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields and concerns over asset values outweighed sound operating fundamentals such as limited new supply, stable occupancy and positive rental growth. The piece presents the sell-off as a sentiment-driven de-rating rather than a deterioration in property markets, though it does not set out an explicit investment call or recommendation.

It also highlights a late-quarter shift towards inflation-linked bond ETFs as oil prices rose, and notes that gold ETPs saw net outflows, unlike in previous Middle East oil shocks. The piece offers no explicit investment call, presenting these flows as observations from its ETF Research head.

The piece points to 68 "ISA millionaire" trusts and to Aberdeen's own Asia Focus, Equity Income and Murray International trusts as evidence, and concludes that investment trusts' structure, income advantages, gearing and independent boards make them worth considering. Note that the article is promotional, and its figures are historical and illustrative rather than a guide to future returns.

The firm's explicit view for SGD cash investors is that the S$NEER will likely stay in the upper half of its policy band, MAS will keep a tightening bias, and short-term rates, already down substantially, will keep trending lower at a slower pace, favouring tactical duration extensions within a diversified, disciplined approach.

It makes explicit calls for selectivity: favouring locations and sectors with strong structural fundamentals, grocery-anchored retail, and logistics where positive rental growth and a wider yield spread could drive yield compression, while noting that office selection is increasingly important given limited development and bifurcated tenant demand. It also contends that residential rent controls can, in practice, improve tenant retention, income certainty and performance stability despite investor concern about regulation.

In a Talking Heads podcast, Bloomberg Intelligence analyst George Ferguson tells Andrew Craig that defence shares have lagged in recent months but the opportunity is long-term, with European defence spending likely to remain at around 3.5% of budgets and valuations now broadly in line with US peers. BNP Paribas Asset Management's explicit view is that the sector offers a long-term opportunity, and the piece promotes a passive strategy tracking the Bloomberg Europe Defence Select Index.

pieces.title: Private Credit Secondaries
pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors argues that private credit secondaries have matured into an essential allocation, citing record 2025 fundraising of USD 16.7 billion (more than the previous three years combined) and a Campbell Lutyens finding that 38% of global investors are now active in the segment. It contends that recent private credit volatility, including wealth-channel redemption pressure and software exposure concerns, reflects product design, investor behaviour and liquidity timing rather than deteriorating fundamentals, so secondary buyers able to analyse assets in depth can buy at attractive discounts. The firm therefore presents a global credit secondaries mandate, with the US and Europe as key sources of opportunity, as a timely way to access seasoned portfolios and margin of safety.

pieces.title: Helping clients build retirement wellness in a longer-life era
The Road Less Glided: Rethinking the Retirement Target
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that target date fund glidepaths have grown increasingly alike over the past decade, with many providers moving to higher equity allocations throughout the participant journey, a shift it links to greater concern with longevity risk and funding longer retirements. Its explicit call is that fiduciaries should test whether this prevailing trend suits their own participant populations rather than adopting it by default.

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: September 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's September 2026 Chart of the Month argues that the US dollar could weaken, citing resilient US equities alongside stronger earnings momentum elsewhere, notably in Europe, where second-quarter EPS for the STOXX Europe 600 rose by over 20% year on year, and in Asia. Historically, rising earnings revision ratios outside the US have coincided with broad dollar weakness as capital rotates towards cheaper non-US markets. The firm's fixed income team sees potential for a broad-based decline against G10 currencies, particularly the euro, Australian dollar, New Zealand dollar and Swedish krona, though it flags a renewed dollar rally as a risk if energy prices rise on Strait of Hormuz concerns.

pieces.title: Sixth Street's Origins
pieces.summary: Sixth Street's co-founders Alan Waxman and David Stiepleman recount the firm's origins, tracing its roots to "Project Austin," a business plan begun in 2006 that drew on the perceived mistakes of other general partners, such as hierarchical structures and siloed teams. The firm presents its aim as becoming the first scaled multi-strategy private capital firm operating as a single team, with maximum flexibility and no single-asset-class identity, and says it now plans to "go vertical" by leveraging technology and AI to improve efficiency in both its Core and investment functions. The piece is a promotional, founder-led video rather than a report with data, so its claims about culture and positioning are the firm's own characterisation.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset Midyear Outlook: Expanding the Toolkit
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein's midyear multi-asset outlook, presented by Karen Watkin and Daniel Loewy, argues that 2026 has brought the volatility it anticipated, driven by AI disruption concerns, Middle East conflict and higher energy prices, and that markets may be growing complacent about these lingering risks. The firm says it continues to favour equities, particularly US equities for their earnings growth, profitability and AI exposure, with emerging-market equities as a further route to AI-linked growth. It also recommends building resilience through lower-volatility equities, gold and inflation-sensitive equities, and a flexible multi-asset approach that can shift across equities, fixed income and commodity-related assets.

pieces.title: Built for compute: Inside a data center
pieces.summary: Blue Owl's short marketing piece, a 3D animated tour of data centre construction, argues that data centres are now mission-critical infrastructure for the global economy, driven by cloud, streaming and AI demand, and that delivering them depends on securing land, navigating power and regulatory realities, and executing with precision. The firm presents itself as a builder of this infrastructure, covering site selection, power provisioning, cooling and connectivity, and it explicitly frames physical infrastructure as the foundation of the digital economy. It makes no specific investment call or return claim, though the related-insights links point to its financing activity in AI infrastructure.

Why We Invested in Candid Health: Powering Modern Infrastructure for a More Efficient Healthcare System

Sixth Street argues that Candid's approach of engineering claims correctly at submission, built on a knowledge graph of more than a thousand payor rulesets, addresses the root cause of denials, unlike incumbents that remediate denials after the fact, and it cites growth of 190% in contracted run-rate revenue in 2025 as evidence. The firm's explicit view is that Candid is "building the foundational infrastructure layer for the future of healthcare payments."

Its explicit view is that investors should not panic but should favour the right sectors and seek the highest achievable current yield with minimal volatility, being cautious about the price volatility that higher-duration assets may add to portfolios. The piece also outlines how the fund's positioning has evolved and how Ares's rate-cycle outlook is shaping it.

Ares states that it dynamically allocates across these classes to seek relative value and enhanced yield, and that Teiki Benveniste outlines the current opportunity set, highlighting the areas he finds most attractive. The piece is a promotional overview rather than a data-backed report, and its explicit view is Ares's favourable stance on these segments of credit.

pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that, with rate volatility rising and credit spreads near historic tights, fixed income returns will rely more on income and carry than on price gains, making selectivity and active management essential. It recommends short-duration active strategies to capture elevated front-end yields with lower volatility, core-plus strategies blending investment-grade asset-backed and mortgage-related sectors, and active credit with floating-rate exposure across high yield, bank loans and CLOs. The piece also notes that US Treasury yields offer a more durable income advantage than hedged Japanese bonds, whose yield pickup is mainly FX carry, and that the limited scope for spread compression makes the downside asymmetric.

pieces.title: Infrastructure debt: why is Asia different?
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers argues that infrastructure debt in Asia is distinctive because the region sits at the centre of the global infrastructure build-out, driven by decarbonisation, digitalisation, regionalisation and demographics, notably a middle class forecast to grow from about 2 billion to 3.5 billion people by 2030. The firm's explicit view is that Asia offers the best relative value in infrastructure debt, as other markets are highly competitive, and that it is where emissions reduction and impact opportunities are greatest, with the firm presenting itself as one of the leading asset managers on the ground there.

pieces.title: Guide to Alternatives
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Guide to Alternatives argues that AI is driving investment across public and private markets, that higher interest rates are forcing managers to create value without relying on cheap debt, and that real estate and infrastructure face new trends and risks, including data centres needing private capital. It states that alternatives offer innovation, income and growth but require careful manager selection, because performance varies widely between top and bottom private managers and attractive themes such as AI do not guarantee strong outcomes. The piece is largely descriptive and educational rather than a explicit recommendation to buy or sell any asset class.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: Active small cap allocations offer asymmetric returns
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that small-cap stocks offer asymmetric return potential compared with large caps: lower analyst coverage and liquidity make them less efficient, producing wider return dispersion that skilled active managers can exploit through bottom-up stock selection. It contrasts this with a passive large-cap approach, which it says is heavily concentrated in a few mega-cap names such as the Magnificent 7, limiting upside and making consistent outperformance harder after fees. The firm's explicit view, voiced by portfolio manager Nick Sheridan, is that smaller companies with superior earnings growth give an edge over larger stocks, and that rigorous stock selection rather than macro or thematic bets is central to outperformance.

pieces.title: ETF Watch – June 2026 - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Suffering from home bias? Try Asia and its smaller companies
pieces.summary: Aberdeen, via Gabriel Sacks, Lead Manager of Aberdeen Asia Focus, argues that home bias is a major obstacle to successful investing and that diversification, including across company size, matters more than ever. The piece makes an explicit case that Asian smaller companies, which are under-covered by sell-side analysts, merit a place in portfolios as a sensible means of diversifying away from concentrated home-market and mega-cap exposure, while cautioning against over-diversifying. Aberdeen's own disclosures note that emerging markets tend to be more volatile.

pieces.title: The Market Edit: From French debt to AI, what are markets taking for granted? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's November "Market Edit" argues that elevated yields, resilient earnings and strong appetite for risk do not make every opportunity equally attractive, and it flags three areas to watch: long-run inflation assumptions (with inflation expected to stay somewhat above 2%), French fiscal risk (seen as a eurozone issue rather than a systemic one, with Spain now grouped with the stronger issuers), and AI-linked equities (where it sees no bubble, given established revenue streams and supply constraints). Its explicit preferences are for high yield corporate credit over government bonds, and for some IT and communication services companies whose valuations look reasonable relative to growth, while it judges that the stock-bond correlation has turned negative but that it is too early to assume the old diversification relationship has returned.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Green Shoots and Legacy Risks in Direct Lending
pieces.summary: PIMCO reports that direct lending markets are bifurcating, with newly originated loans showing improved terms (wider spreads, lower leverage, stronger debt servicing) whilst legacy portfolios from peak deployment years continue bearing losses from borrower-friendly underwriting. The firm argues that redemption pressure on non-listed business development companies, though easing from peaks, is tightening financing conditions and creating this divide between new vintage economics and deteriorating existing portfolios. PIMCO contends that persistent valuation disparities across managers and public BDC discounts to book value reflect justified investor scepticism about whether markdowns and credit losses in older portfolios have fully run their course.

The asset manager contends that while mega-cap firms with established platforms are best placed to benefit from AI monetisation, valuations have become more attractive following March's market downturn, presenting an entry point for investors seeking diversified exposure through technology-focused ETFs.

pieces.title: Bridging the technology gap: How Europe is building its digital infrastructure
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is investing in AI, semiconductors and cloud computing to reduce its reliance on external powers and strengthen its digital infrastructure, competitiveness and resilience, with policies such as the European Technological Sovereignty Package, the Chips Act 2.0 and the Critical Raw Materials Act providing a stable, long-term framework. The firm's explicit view is that this structural shift creates significant long-term investment opportunities across technology, energy, defence and raw materials supply chains, though it acknowledges that Europe still lags the US and China in its technology ecosystem.

pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that higher sovereign bond yields have failed to adequately compensate investors for duration risk, citing persistent real yield increases, the possibility that rates remain below pre-2008 norms, and flatter-than-historical yield curves. The asset manager maintains a neutral stance on duration and yield-curve positioning while remaining underweight credit, preferring instead targeted exposures to housing, mortgage credit, asset-backed securities and hard-asset-backed opportunities where specific risks are better compensated.

pieces.title: Market moves & themes that mattered: April 2026
Higher-for-Longer creates opportunity
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S. economy remains resilient, supported by AI-driven business investment and firm payroll growth, but that energy-led inflation is eroding real incomes and could curb consumption if elevated prices persist. Following a June FOMC under Chair Warsh that held rates at 3.50%–3.75% with a hawkish tone and no forward guidance, the firm expects a higher-for-longer regime, with its Global Liquidity team's base case being that the Fed stays on hold through 2026. Its explicit call for global liquidity investors is to anchor portfolios in money market funds and selectively extend into ultra-short duration strategies to lock in higher yields while retaining flexibility.

The firm advocates for portfolio positioning favourable to inflation, including shorter-duration bonds and equities with higher cash returns, whilst recommending active global diversification beyond traditional US market leadership. Janus Henderson expects central banks to maintain elevated short-term rates for an extended period, distinguishing the current environment from previous decades of secular disinflation.

The piece explicitly recommends that charities holding significant cash reallocate a portion into securitised assets, while stressing that active management, with deep analysis of collateral, structures and cashflows, is critical to identifying relative value and achieving consistent excess returns over cash.

pieces.title: Private credit beyond the headlines: the case for investment-grade exposure
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that the current private credit scrutiny, centred on sub-investment-grade middle-market direct lending and software exposure, does not apply to the investment-grade corporate finance and asset-backed finance segments used in its PRIV, PRSD and PRAB ETFs. It cites Apollo estimates that about 95% of the roughly $40 trillion US private credit market is investment grade, and that the sub-IG segment is proportionally smaller within private credit than within public credit. The piece makes an explicit case for IG private credit exposure as a differentiated opportunity, though it stops short of a formal recommendation and notes that allocations are actively managed and may change.

pieces.title: Diversified alternatives: How resilient is your portfolio, really?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the negative correlation between equities and bonds, which has underpinned portfolio diversification since the turn of the century, is not fixed. It cites the mid-1960s to late-1990s period, when the two were positively correlated, and suggests the recent move towards persistently positive correlation may signal a structural change. The firm's explicit view is that, in such a regime, investors should consider "effective"

pieces.title: The role of asset-backed securities in pension scheme LDI portfolios
pieces.summary: Columbia Threadneedle Investments argues that US securitised credit, which it says has historically delivered strong risk-adjusted returns and low correlation with traditional fixed income, can enhance UK and European pension scheme LDI portfolios. It cites a yield premium over similarly rated corporate bonds, shorter average lives and floating-rate coupons (notably in CLOs) that reduce rate and credit sensitivity, and a deep, diversified market of over $14 trillion that should remain liquid in a collateral squeeze. On that basis, the firm states that the asset class merits consideration as a core component of LDI collateral waterfalls.

pieces.title: Opportunities for insurers
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that European insurers should reassess traditional cash management, since bank deposits can carry concentrated counterparty risk and attract relatively high Solvency II capital charges. It presents money market funds and enhanced money market funds as a more diversified, liquid and capital-efficient alternative, with evolving securitisation rules and high-quality asset-backed securities further strengthening the case within insurers' treasury and capital frameworks. The piece is framed as a view on opportunity rather than a specific recommendation, though its stance is clearly favourable towards reallocating cash into these fund structures.

pieces.summary: PGIM's video piece, featuring Dianna Carr-Coletta of its Alternatives Direct Lending Group, responds to investor concern about private credit, particularly direct lending, that emerged in late 2025 and persisted into 2026, arguing that the asset class remains fundamentally sound and that the industry must correct overstated media coverage. PGIM contends that private credit is a long-term, buy-and-hold, income-producing holding with inflation-hedging properties, that its senior secured positions have historically produced very low credit losses (about 1% over the asset class's history), and that investors should understand the difference between illiquid private underwriting and liquid public markets. It explicitly calls on investors to maintain their private credit allocations, citing PGIM's deep, roughly one-to-two-month diligence process and its 40–60 page investment committee memos as the basis for that confidence.

pieces.title: Ein neues Umfeld
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that the global economy is in transition as traditional growth drivers weaken and structural headwinds—including deglobalisaton, high debt, and slower growth—take hold. The firm warns that despite current market resilience, underlying risks are mounting, including concentrated equity gains and diminishing policy effectiveness, while monetary and fiscal tools reach their limits. Insight Investment suggests investors should broaden their outlook across multiple scenarios and reassess risks, noting that artificial intelligence innovation offers potential for productivity gains in this uncertain environment.

pieces.title: China: Waiting for resumed fiscal support
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that China's economy shows a K-shaped divergence in Q3, with strong export growth (particularly in semiconductors and green energy) offsetting weak domestic investment and consumption dampened by weather and slow fiscal deployment. The asset manager expects accelerated fiscal spending in Q4 to restore growth to the 4.5–5 per cent target range, supported by ~2 per cent of GDP in remaining fiscal space and a new "Six Networks" infrastructure framework that integrates traditional infrastructure with AI-related investment. J.P. Morgan forecasts mild domestic recovery, loose liquidity conditions, range-bound Chinese government bonds with a bias to longer-dated yields, and gradual yuan appreciation against the dollar.

pieces.title: Why Necessity Retail Continues ​to Defy Disruption​
pieces.summary: PGIM's webcast, hosted with IPE Real Assets and featuring Mathew Crowther, Rory Morrison and Stefan Zimmermann, argues that European necessity retail (neighbourhood hubs anchored by everyday consumer needs) has proven resilient across economic cycles, shifting shopping habits and technological disruption, and so merits investor conviction as a source of income and cash-flow visibility. The panel is set to cover where opportunities and risks are emerging and how debt and equity strategies differ in their views, and PGIM's related piece, "Beyond Necessity Retail: The Underwriting Test", indicates that lease length, tenant strength and rent affordability are the key tests of whether the sector delivers durable income.

pieces.title: How is AI being monetized?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that AI monetisation is already under way but remains concentrated in the infrastructure layer, with end-user monetisation still early, uneven and opaque, even as hyperscalers spend around $533 billion on capex this year. It notes that a 10% return on current AI investment could require roughly $650 billion in annual revenue, a high bar that assumes sustained, broad adoption. Its expl

pieces.title: Getting to the heart of India’s “revolution”
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that India's "Make in India" initiative has successfully transformed the country into a leading manufacturer of capital goods, with supply chain shifts from China and technological leapfrogging creating broad investment opportunities. The firm expresses a preference for India over China in its Asia-focused fund, citing the value of on-the-ground research to identify smaller companies benefiting from India's economic transformation, while cautioning that macro-level growth does not uniformly benefit all businesses.

pieces.title: Multi-asset portfolios - Striking the balance between active and passive funds - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that traditional mean-variance optimisation is inadequate for today's multi-asset portfolios, which mix active and passive funds, and presents a robust optimisation framework to address this. Its central idea is that investors' confidence in active funds' expected net alphas can be weighed against the uncertainty in their tactical or thematic views to determine the optimal tilt between active and passive funds. The firm reports that, absent views, passive funds are favoured for tracking the strategic asset allocation, while active funds are included for positive net alpha or for reducing tracking error, and that directional and thematic views are implemented mainly through passive and specialised active funds respectively.

pieces.title: View from the markets: Bonds, panic…and crisis? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Tech, Software, and BDCs: Navigating Volatility and AI Disruption in Investment Grade Credit
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that early-2026 volatility in tech, software and BDC credit reflects fears that AI disruption threatens software business models, with spreads widening by up to 35bps in a day and 50bps week-to-date, but with no widespread credit deterioration yet. It views the repricing between likely AI winners and losers as healthy rather than speculative, considers existential threats overstated while acknowledging real risks to growth and balance sheets from slowing revenue and increased M&A or recapitalisation, and advocates a disciplined, selective approach favouring high-quality, mission-critical software and well-structured BDC portfolios.

pieces.title: Absolute return: Playing a vital role in the new world disorder
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, in a piece by portfolio manager Luke Newman, argues that absolute return strategies, and equity long/short funds in particular, may offer resilience in a market marked by higher stock-level dispersion, a return of the cost of capital since 2022, and an unreliable stock-bond correlation that weakens the traditional 60/40 portfolio. The firm's explicit view is that these strategies can broaden sources of return and limit drawdowns, while stressing they are not a substitute for diversification and should rely on liquid, transparent positions rather than leverage or illiquid assets. The piece is cut off before its discussion of liquidity, so its full case on that point is not covered here.

pieces.title: European small caps offer income and growth - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: In a podcast episode, BNP Paribas Asset Management's Damien Kohler argues that European small caps have outperformed large caps this year, helped by exposure to industrial reshoring, infrastructure spending and M&A at depressed valuations, while large caps have been weighed down by earnings downgrades on luxury names and stretched expectations in defence. The firm's explicit view

pieces.title: U.S. Senior Loans in 2026: High Coupons Expected to Anchor Returns
pieces.summary: Voya Investment Management, in a 2026 outlook for U.S. senior loans by Mohamed Basma, reports that loans lagged other credit sectors in 2025 but still posted strong absolute returns for a third consecutive year, supported by high coupons and record CLO issuance despite periodic selloffs and wide dispersion across issuers and industries. Voya expects high starting yields to anchor returns again in 2026, citing solid macro conditions, stable corporate fundamentals, modest defaults and muted repricing, while flagging that M&A could moderate technical support and that credit selection will matter given a bifurcated market. Its base case is total returns of 5-6% in 2026, in line with the asset class's long-term average, and it says conditions would need to deteriorate meaningfully to produce negative returns.

pieces.title: The Winter Sports Boom Is Just Getting Started
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that winter sports, long treated as a seasonal niche, is becoming a mainstream, year-round and global business, with star athletes, growing audiences, expanding infrastructure and rising participation all drawing capital. The piece cites evidence including NHL franchise values doubling since 2022, the Professional Women's Hockey League passing a million fans, private equity deplo

A Season of Moderation in the Year of Boom and Doom
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management expects U.S. economic growth to moderate significantly, with third-quarter growth of 3.8% slowing to 2.4% in the fourth quarter and below 2.0% in 2027, driven by fading fiscal stimulus, weak job creation and subdued consumer spending despite a four-year equity bull market. The firm attributes the sluggish labour market to structural factors—including weak demand in labour-intensive sectors and immigration reversal—rather than cyclical weakness, and notes that wage growth remains below inflation despite nominally tight hiring conditions.

pieces.title: A decade of delivery:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that global short-dated high yield bonds remain an attractive investment after a decade of market turbulence, pointing to higher yields, improved credit quality and lower interest-rate sensitivity compared with longer-dated bonds. The firm contends that this backdrop—combined with disciplined credit analysis and active management to identify mispriced securities—can support income-focused returns with lower volatility than broader high yield or equity markets.

pieces.title: What’s next for managed accounts
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that its managed accounts business has reached US$300 billion in assets under management globally, serving over 60,000 advisers across 35 countries, and identifies four critical success factors for providers: governance, client support, customisation and innovation. The firm argues that risk management is becoming the primary differentiator in the Australian market as regulators scrutinise the sector, and sees significant growth opportunities in tailoring managed accounts at scale and engaging clients with improved transparency about their holdings.

pieces.title: Capital market assumptions
pieces.summary: BlackRock's August 2026 capital market assumptions, anchored by artificial intelligence as a structural driver of returns, favour developed and emerging market equities whilst downgrading high yield debt to underweight. The firm argues that the concept of a static neutral portfolio is obsolete given structural economic shifts, and advocates instead for dynamic, scenario-based portfolio construction tailored to individual investor risk targets and constraints.

pieces.title: Macro Signposts | If Inflation Is the Problem, Why Aren't Wages?
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the Fed's hawkish turn after Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, which lifted the market-implied odds of a September hike to roughly 60%, rests on a judgement about inflation expectations rather than a clear deterioration in the outlook, since its own and consensus PCE forecasts have barely moved since June.

pieces.title: Multi-asset investment views: Staying Alive - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's multi-asset team, led by CIO Laurent Clavel, argues that the macroeconomic backdrop remains robust but risks are balanced, with energy the main threat through near-term inflation and monetary policy expectations. Its explicit positioning is a moderate overweight in global equities (favouring the US and emerging markets for technology and AI exposure, and bank stocks in Japan and Europe) and in commodities, alongside an underweight in government bonds and investment-grade credit and an overweight in high yield and hard-currency emerging market debt. The firm also remains constructive on the US dollar, unhedged, and sees relative-value and active strategies as favoured by low cross-market correlation and wide stock-level dispersion.

pieces.title: Portable alpha strategies
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that portable alpha strategies—which replicate market index exposure through market-linked instruments whilst allocating capital to alternative strategies—can generate superior returns compared to traditional active management, citing 10-year data showing such approaches outperforming top-quartile managers in both equities and fixed income. The firm positions portable alpha as complementary to private asset allocations, offering higher returns within core holdings whilst preserving liquidity and transparency advantages over less-fungible alternative investments.

Many still trade at discounts to global peers because investors view the region through a macro lens, even though these companies earn most of their revenues abroad and have decoupled from European GDP. pieces.title: Running on and DB surplus release
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that trustees should build a clear, shared understanding of "running on" (keeping a defined benefit scheme open to funding rather than buying out or winding up) and of surplus release, now that the Pension Schemes Act 2026 has received Royal Assent. The firm's explicit view is that running on can create real value for members and the sponsor, but only with a clear rationale, a practical plan, and good governance, since it "is not set-and-forget" and "will not be right for every scheme." The piece frames the decisions trustees need to make around time frame, how surplus is shared, governance rules, funding risk management, additional protections, and an investment strategy aligned to the endgame target.

pieces.title: Värde Provides €275 Million Refinancing of Logistics Facility in Germany
pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that an affiliate has provided a €275 million refinancing for a modern, purpose-built logistics facility in Germany, leased long-term to a global e-commerce operator. The firm presents the deal as evidence of its conviction in European real estate credit and the fundamentals of logistics, citing the tenant's quality and the site's position in Germany's distribution network. It also stresses its flexible capital and "execution certainty" for borrowers.

pieces.summary: PGIM argues that the U.S. midterm results should not derail growth, and it keeps a "slower-for-longer" AI capex cycle as its base case, with a 50% probability, in which AI's contribution to U.S. GDP moderates slightly in 2027.

pieces.title: Unlocking AI’s Advantages in Investing
The Debt Maturity Wall: An Opportunity, Not an Obstacle
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that the commercial real estate "maturity wall", over $4 trillion of loans falling due between 2025 and 2029, is an opportunity for private credit rather than an obstacle, because banks are scaling back their CRE lending and many maturing loans cannot be refinanced at current property values and borrowing costs. It sees a refinancing gap that private lenders such as Fortress can fill, lending against properties at attractive advance rates, and says the opportunity set is in the trillions of dollars and should last for many years.

pieces.title: Thoughts on the software reset for private credit
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments' direct lending team argues that the sharp decline in software equities could ultimately lead to a healthier private lending environment, in contrast to periods when overvalued software assets were financed with aggressive leverage. Fidelity says software has made up less than 10% of its direct lending activity in recent years because it judged lending had focused too heavily on loan-to-values rather than business fundamentals. It expects mission-critical areas such as cybersecurity, compliance infrastructure, enterprise controls and secure data environments, including health care, to prove more resilient.

Pricing the known unknowns from Japan’s election landslide
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the LDP's landslide gives Prime Minister Takaichi a strong mandate for growth-oriented, "responsible proactive" fiscal policy, but that political clarity does not translate into market clarity. Five open questions remain: the scale of fiscal investment, the durability of permanent spending such as food consumption tax cuts and defence beyond 2% of GDP, debt management and JGB issuance, the pace of BOJ normalisation given inflation near target, and foreign policy towards China. PIMCO's explicit view is that the key test is whether execution can anchor inflation expectations, preserve fiscal credibility and limit unnecessary term-premium increases, noting that rising JGB yields already price policy risk while equities appear to assume a smoother outcome.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: CLOs continue to lead the way in fixed income returns
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that CLO outperformance is not a one-off "interest rate lottery" win from the post-2022 rate rise, and that higher rates are likely to persist, so investors should consider leaning into CLOs rather than dismissing their returns. It cites BBB CLOs as the best-performing fixed income sector year to date in 2026 and across the 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year periods, and says high-quality floating-rate debt is essential in a post-ZIRP world. The firm's explicit view is that the only reason to have no allocation to high-quality floating-rate debt is a belief that rates will fall to zero and stay there, which it considers very unlikely, and that CLOs are the best route to floating-rate exposure.

pieces.title: Beware Sharpe Ratios for Private Markets
pieces.summary: Dimensional Fund Advisors argues that Sharpe ratios can mislead when applied to private market assets, because their returns are based on periodically updated, potentially stale net asset values rather than continuously traded prices. To illustrate, it notes that over the past five years, publicly traded business development companies showed an annualised quarterly return standard deviation of 13.4% against 2.7% for nontraded BDCs, despite often holding similar underlying investments, and it concludes that investors should be cautious when interpreting Sharpe ratios for private market strategies.

pieces.title: Differentiated value creation: a fireside chat with Brynwood Partners
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Private Equity Group argues that differentiated manager selection, rather than market exposure alone, drives private equity outcomes, using Brynwood Partners as its example: a firm that targets overlooked consumer carve-outs and creates value through operational execution rather than financial engineering. It illustrates this with Great Kitchens, where Brynwood fixed an underused in-plant warehouse problem, returned the business to profitability within a year and sold it to a strategic buyer. The piece makes no explicit recommendation, but it positions PEG's relationships with specialised managers, and its diversified primary, co-investment and secondary platform focused on the small and mid-market, as the means of accessing such opportunities.

pieces.title: It’s not easy being in charge - BNP Paribas Asset Management
China: from scale to returns
pieces.summary: BlackRock's Investment Institute argues that China's economy is two-speed, with weak household spending and housing contrasting with strong exports and strategic industries, so a broad China call is too blunt. Its evidence is sharp sectoral divergence in industrial profits (electronics up 110% in the first seven months of 2026, autos down 20.4%) and in equity performance, with selected AI hardware suppliers expanding margins as revenue doubled while Chinese solar makers' margins collapsed. The explicit view is a tactical neutral on China equities, with selective opportunities in companies where scale translates into pricing power, sustained margins, overseas margin premiums and shareholder returns.

pieces.title: Equity Quarterly: Not so different - BNP Paribas Asset Management
The New Dynamics Driving Opportunity in the Secondary Market
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that rising interest rates have slowed private equity M&A, cutting cash distributions to investors from roughly 20% of net asset value a year in the 2010s to around 10% today, and pushing some limited partners to sell stakes in the secondary market to cover cash shortfalls. Its explicit view, voiced by Nate Walton, Head of Ares Private Equity Secondaries, is that this is a compelling moment to buy such interests at attractive valuations, though the piece's disclaimer stresses that projections and "downside protection" language are not guarantees.

pieces.title: Tokenisation: Why blockchain rails could redefine the future of finance
Small wonders: the hidden gems among smaller companies
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that UK smaller companies are overlooked and trade at a discount: by its estimates, small and mid-cap stocks sit about 20% below their long-term average valuation, despite solid earnings and dividend growth. It makes the case that the small cap premium is structural and that selective, quality-focused active management (favouring low leverage and stable earnings while avoiding "fallen angels") is needed to capture it. The piece, promoting its UK Smaller Companies Growth Trust, presents this as an opportunity to gain diversified exposure beyond AI-led themes.

pieces.title: Webinar Replay: Solving for 2027
Global Reach with a Regional Presence
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that its network of 15 regional offices, staffed by people who know their local markets, lets it act as a true partner to borrowers rather than just a capital provider, and it presents this regional presence as central to its private credit approach. The piece is promotional and makes no specific performance claims or market forecasts, although it notes that its office data is as of 30 September 2025.

pieces.title: Celebrating 20 years of Aberdeen Asian Income Fund
pieces.summary: Aberdeen marks the 20th anniversary of Aberdeen Asian Income Fund, launched in 2005, by closing the London Stock Exchange market on 2 March 2026. It argues that Asia has become an increasingly important source of income, yet remains under-represented in UK investors' income portfolios, and says the Trust, which introduced an enhanced dividend policy in 2025 and yielded 5.8% at end-January 2026, is positioned to help close that gap. Aberdeen also contends that investment trusts which adapt to private investors' needs are well placed to endure, a view voiced by the Chair, Ian Cadby.

pieces.title: My Personal History
Värde Views: Real Estate Credit vs. Corporate Direct Lending
A Comprehensive Guide to Private Credit
pieces.summary: Ares Management presents direct lending private credit as an established, not new, asset class that may offer risk-adjusted returns, yield and diversification, and that is now more accessible to individual investors through new fund structures. The firm argues that the asset class will play a vital role in funding growing companies and economies, with middle-market and non-sponsor lending potentially offering better economics and lender protections, and it presents its own large European direct lending team as a competitive advantage.

pieces.title: When AI gets a body: Robotics and physical AI, seen from Japan
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that physical AI—artificial intelligence embedded in machines that can perform tasks autonomously—is transitioning from research to commercial reality and represents a consequential sustainability technology addressing labour shortages across developed economies. The asset manager reports from its Japan robotics tour that whilst incumbent robot makers retain genuine competitive advantages in precision and reliability, Chinese competitors have rapidly gained market share, requiring disciplined ongoing underwriting rather than retreat from the sector. Janus Henderson frames its investment approach through primary research to assess which competitive moats are widening or eroding before the market fully recognizes the shift, using this forward-looking analysis to inform stock selection across automation value chains.

pieces.title: Longevity hedging update
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that longevity risk, the chance that pension scheme members live longer than assumed, is a significant concern for defined benefit schemes, given falling mortality and rising life expectancy, with medical advances potentially sustaining these trends. The piece, presented by Longevity Pricing Director Howard Kearns, states that the cost of longevity swaps has fallen materially in recent years and that a derivative-based swap can be simpler, more efficient and less expensive than a traditional longevity swap, which it describes as effective but operationally complex and time-consuming.

pieces.title: Global Perspectives: Investment outlook 2026 (EMEA)
Asset-backed securities: How structural mechanisms shape investor outcomes
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that post-GFC reforms have made asset-backed securities more transparent, better aligned with investors and more resilient, pointing to zero investment-grade ABS defaults since 2010 and 2025 rating upgrades on auto loan deals as evidence. Its stated view is that ABS have historically weathered crises with lower default rates and shallower drawdowns than corporate bonds, making them a potentially attractive relative value opportunity, with multiple layers of credit enhancement protecting senior tranches. The piece caveats that protection levels vary with the underlying collateral and that credit risk is assessed before structuring.
