pieces.summary: Wellington Management expects a modest, near-trend US expansion, with growth increasingly concentrated in AI-related investment, infrastructure and resilient profits, and inflation risk elevated by energy, tariffs and supply-chain pressures. Its explicit call for insurers is a moderately constructive but selective risk posture that favours income, downside resilience and liquidity over adding broad credit beta at tight spreads. Within fixed income, it favours senior CLOs, selective front-end and intermediate investment-grade corporates, agency MBS and high-quality taxable municipals, while being neutral on US equities, favouring emerging markets over Europe, holding a small overweight in oil and moving to neutral on gold.

pieces.title: Midcaps: Finding diversified growth in an AI-dominated market
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the AI infrastructure buildout has made US equity markets, including midcaps, highly concentrated and bifurcated, with heightened dispersion, volatility and index concentration risk, and that this makes diversification more valuable. The firm says it selectively participates in the AI theme, favouring companies with durable advantages and earnings that can support extreme valuations (some midcap AI names trade at 60 to 70 times earnings), while seeing midcap growth, particularly healthcare innovation and industrials and transports, as a better source of diversified growth beyond AI.

pieces.title: Murray International Trust in 60 seconds
Why bonds love growth scares but dislike inflation scares
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the stock-bond diversification benefit is regime-dependent: government bonds have tended to cushion equity losses when growth worries dominate, as falling rates lift prices, but they have tended to fall alongside equities during inflation scares, as in the 1970s and 2022-23. The piece's explicit conclusion is that the role of bonds in a portfolio depends on the economic regime, so the right level of interest-rate sensitivity and government bond exposure depends on whether markets are reacting to growth or inflation concerns. It adds that the picture has been more mixed since 2024, and that if inflation keeps moderating, bonds may regain their diversifying role.

Why India is well placed for recovery after a bruising 2025
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that India is well placed for recovery after a weak 2025, when the MSCI India Index returned 3% in US dollar terms against 30.6% for the broader emerging market region, driven by slowing earnings, rising costs, tariff risks and an AI-driven rotation out of the market. It contends that the earnings downgrade cycle has bottomed, that easing trade uncertainty, a likely end to RBI rate cuts and reset valuations make the outlook increasingly constructive, though it expects recovery to be led by public capex and the domestic cycle rather than a sharp rise in private investment. Aberdeen's explicit view is that the current environment is increasingly supportive for investors looking at India, while stating that the timing of a sustained recovery is hard to call.

Morgan Asset Management's 2027 Investment Outlook, titled "Still up, but a bumpier path," argues that corporate and government spending on resilience and new technology will underpin economic growth in 2027, a stark contrast to the austerity-led decade before the pandemic. Despite geopolitical shocks, including 2025's tariffs and 2026's Middle East war and energy price rises, the firm says it remains constructive on the global growth outlook, citing Germany's fiscal push as a key driver in Europe as the EU Recovery Fund winds down. The piece does not set out a specific asset allocation call in the extract provided, and its supporting chart draws on OECD data showing government investment growth easing somewhat but remaining well above prior austerity levels.

pieces.title: In CRE Debt, Timing Could be Everything
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that commercial real estate debt is at a tipping point, with rapid rate rises since 2021 having reset property valuations and regional banks, which historically provided about 45% of CRE lending, now largely stepping back, leaving a gap that private credit lenders can fill at better entry points. Fortress's explicit view, voiced by Spencer Garfield, is that a four- to five-year window exists in which more than $4 trillion of maturing debt, depressed values and sidelined competition create lending opportunities, which the firm says it pursues through disciplined underwriting and asset management to limit downside risk while seeking attractive yields.

The firm judges the tech sector "cheap" despite its rally, while acknowledging this reflects a large upgrade to long-run earnings expectations whose sustainability it questions, and it argues that the current capex wave has a plausible path to justify it. It flags the central challenge as gaining clarity on that path within a horizon shorter than the depreciation cycle of chips, and concludes that investors are complacent about volatility.

Given the Federal Reserve's signal that rates will stay in an elevated range, PGIM's explicit call is that now may be a good time to increase fixed income allocations.

pieces.title: Three ways to reset credit portfolios for a more volatile world
pieces.summary: Wellington Management argues that recent credit market volatility, driven by Middle East conflict, AI-disruption fears and higher oil prices, is largely technical and sentiment-led rather than a sign of weaker corporate fundamentals, and that this is creating selective opportunities in credit. It singles out global high-yield bonds (particularly European high yield, which it sees as more attractive and defensive than US), leveraged loans, which have been hit hard by exposure to technology and software, and select segments of the CLO market. Its explicit view is that multi-asset credit portfolios should take a global, flexible, research-driven approach, while noting that mezzanine CLO tranches have not yet priced in a possible economic slowdown and that spreads may need to widen further before the sector offers more compelling entry points.

pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that the U.S. economy, although relatively stable, is exposed to a prolonged Middle East conflict and the energy supply shock that has pushed oil above $100 per barrel. Its base case is a contained, short-lived conflict with oil falling to around $80 by year end, a modest hit to 2026 growth (expected near 2 percent, cushioned by tax cuts and AI capex), and a temporary headline inflation spike, while it sees a prolonged conflict as unlikely but as materially raising recession risk. Guggenheim also expects core PCE inflation to stay sticky before easing in the second half, the Fed to hold for now, and its most likely scenario to be two rate cuts beginning in the second half of 2026.

pieces.summary: Columbia Threadneedle Investments argues that AI has become a multi-year investment, productivity and financing cycle, with the market shifting from rewarding scarcity in compute, chips and cloud towards demanding monetisation and return on capital. It cites hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending above $750 billion by end-2026 (up about 70% year-on-year), data-centre demand adding roughly 3.4% a year to US power requirements through 2030, and new fixed income segments such as data-centre construction loans and asset-backed securities. Its explicit view is that the opportunity is widening but disruption is uneven, so active selection is essential, since the winners will be those capturing the most value from spending rather than those spending the most.

pieces.title: The case for development in private real estate portfolios
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that developing properties can be a better choice than buying existing ones when stabilised assets trade 25% to 50% above the cost of construction, and that development offers investors an alternative route into real estate, provided they have the execution skills. Citing its proprietary open-ended fund database, JPMAM contends that development has delivered an equity multiple more than twice that of stabilised properties, with no greater downside volatility, including through the 2008 financial crisis. It attributes this to yield cushions, falling construction costs in downturns and the resilience of new, high-quality assets, while cautioning that performance depends heavily on execution, experience and risk mitigation.

pieces.title: The Fixed Income Universe: Investigating the opportunity set for multi-sector portfolios
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (PMs John Lloyd and John P Kerschner) argues that the fixed income universe is far broader than benchmarks such as the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index suggest, since that index is concentrated in Treasuries, agency MBS and investment-grade corporates and largely excludes sectors like CLOs, high yield, emerging markets debt, ABS and CMBS. The firm's explicit view is that actively blending government, securitised, corporate and international sectors within a strategic asset allocation framework can make portfolios more diversified, efficient and better aligned with investor objectives. The paper supports this with a side-by-side comparison of key sectors across metrics such as rate sensitivity, credit risk, yield, volatility and equity correlation.

pieces.title: Combining perspectives to navigate volatility
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that structural shifts such as geopolitical fragmentation, demographics, AI-driven innovation and climate change are reshaping markets and creating volatility alongside new opportunities, so investors will need to focus on megatrends as much as economic data. Its base case is a resilient global economy with inflation normalising, though growth is diverging across regions, with the US supported by fiscal spending and AI investment, Europe regaining momentum, and China slowing. The firm explicitly favours flexibility, selectivity and "combining a diversity of perspectives" to navigate dispersion, and it says the Middle East conflict had not, as of 2 March 2026, warranted changes to its base case.

pieces.title: CLOs unlocked: How fixed income rules are being rewritten for European insurers
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that CLO exposures may move into the mainstream of European insurers' fixed income portfolios as regulatory reforms take effect in early 2027, and its paper sets out the rule changes it expects to drive that uptake and their implications for market participants. The text is a teaser and does not spell out the specific regulatory provisions or quantify the expected shift, so the firm's explicit view is that the change is likely, not a firm call on CLO performance or allocation.

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that a new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, signals a less interventionist Fed that will offer less forward guidance and stop smoothing markets, which should raise volatility and dispersion and favour active managers. It contends that bond maths is already working in investors' favour: with the 10-year Treasury yielding about 4.55% and disinflation reasserting itself, high-quality bonds offer positive returns across most growth and inflation scenarios, with convexity delivering a double-digit total return in a recession-driven rate cut. PIMCO's explicit view is that fixed income deserves a renewed place in portfolios, not because equities are expected to fall, but because bonds offer income, diversification and a truncated downside, and its baseline is that the Fed holds rates steady through the rest of 2026.

pieces.title: 2026 inflation outlook: Navigating uncertainty - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management expects 2026 to bring a more balanced but still uncertain inflation backdrop, with the US running hotter (close to 3%, with tariff effects yet to feed through) and Europe and the UK disinflating more quickly, Europe settling near 2%. Its explicit view is that, given divergent regional policy paths, investors should favour carry and specific inflation-risk exposure over large directional bets on rates or inflation, and that inflation-linked bonds remain attractive because inflation risk is modestly priced and term premia look appealing.

pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private credit has deep historical roots, tracing the modern version to the BDC Act, which created Business Development Companies to fund small and midsized firms after banks retreated in the 1970s recession. The piece presents BDCs as a sound structure, citing their published schedules of every loan, long-term committed capital that avoids duration mismatches, and a bank-to-BDC lending relationship that lets banks share in private loan returns with less risk. Its explicit view, attributed to CFO Jarrod Phillips, is that BDCs' matched-duration funding makes them more resilient than banks, which can face forced asset sales when deposits leave.

BlackRock has developed indicators that measure the degree to which specific geopolitical risks are priced into markets by analysing sentiment in analyst reports and media sources.

pieces.title: Inflation-linked bonds: protection in a more volatile inflation world - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that inflation is becoming structurally more volatile, driven by geopolitics, energy security, supply chains, fiscal policy, climate and infrastructure/AI spending, with the recent Strait of Hormuz disruption cited as an example. Its explicit view is that the question of whether it is "late" to buy inflation-linked bonds is the wrong framing: the firm says they should be considered as a way to build inflation protection into fixed income or multi-asset portfolios, and it highlights that current real yields are much more attractive than for most of the past decade, allowing investors to earn a positive real yield while retaining that protection.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' primer explains that collateralised loan obligations (CLOs) pool bank loans, typically to smaller companies, and securitise them into tranches of varying credit ratings. It notes that the US CLO market, present since the late 1980s and now around $1.2 trillion, is approaching the size of the $1.5 trillion high-yield market and has become more accessible to retail investors. pieces.title: Capitalising on volatility in sustainable equities
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson's Global Sustainable Team, led by Portfolio Manager Aaron Scully, argues that volatility in 2026 can be turned into opportunity through bottom-up stock selection combined with macro insight, focusing on three themes: AI, fiscal and monetary support, and private credit risk. The firm explicitly states that AI is not a bubble, citing supply constraints on data centre build-out and strong demand, while expecting a market downturn within five years; it anticipates stimulus-driven economic support under the Trump administration despite a historically volatile mid-term election year. On private credit, it takes a cautious stance, advising investors to avoid excessive balance sheet leverage and to favour companies with mission-critical products and services that are more resilient in downturns.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's push for strategic autonomy, meaning reduced dependence on other countries in areas such as technology, energy, defence, food and health, is a long-term structural theme that creates attractive investment opportunities. It cites roughly €1.5 trillion of investment expected across Europe by 2035, including the Readiness 2030 defence plan, clean energy and the European Chips Act. The firm acknowledges coordination problems among the EU's 27 member states but concludes that Europe is "still moving in the right direction", although the pace may need to accelerate.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the usual link between energy and metals prices is breaking down, a pattern it calls the "crocodile cycle": metals are rising on constrained supply and steady or growing demand (from the energy transition, AI-related data centres and central bank gold buying), while oil faces downward pressure as supply outpaces demand. The piece cautions that this divergence depends on how these structural forces evolve, and that commodities are volatile, produce no income, and are taxed less favourably than equities in the case of gold and silver. Its explicit call is that a modest commodities allocation can serve as a hedge, and that investors facing uncertainty might "diversify the diversifiers", for instance with private infrastructure or real estate.

pieces.summary: Aberdeen's immediate reaction to the 27 November 2025 UK Budget argues that, despite fears of a large fiscal gap, the official forecasts show the public finances are less dire than expected, yet the Chancellor still chose higher taxes on middle and high earners and a longer freeze on personal tax thresholds. It says the Budget more than doubles fiscal headroom, which should reassure markets and give the government room ahead of the next election, while welfare spending rises and most new taxes are delayed until 2028, raising doubts about whether they will be implemented and whether the sums add up. Aberdeen's explicit judgement is that markets welcomed the extra headroom, but with the government very unpopular, the sustainability of the current Labour leadership is a medium-term question.

pieces.title: China: Late to the AI sprint, strong in the marathon - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that China is not truly late to AI as a structural shift, though its path will differ from the US model: its edge may lie in "full-stack" competition across the AI value chain, from domestic models and alternative accelerators to power, connectivity and large-scale deployment, rather than in leading-edge chips. The firm's explicit view is that markets are too cautious on China AI equities, which often trade at a discount to global peers despite exposure to domestic substitution and AI infrastructure demand; it considers that discount not proof of mispricing, but a source of asymmetry if China's full-stack strategy gains credibility.

It supports this with its Tax Smart SMA data, showing that 92% of index-tracking accounts target U.S. indexes, and with research suggesting international stocks offer similar active tax management opportunities to U.S. stocks, with 64% of MSCI ACWI ex-U.S. ADR constituents having experienced a 5% drawdown in 2026 compared with roughly 70% of S&P 500 constituents.

Its explicit view is that institutional capital should shift from broad sector exposure towards targeted market selection, balancing developed-market liquidity against emerging-market growth, and favour power-secured corridors and high-density, AI-optimised assets.

pieces.title: Active management matters more in today's credit markets
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that active management matters more in today's credit market, where spreads are tight and rate volatility is elevated, and wide dispersion between CCC and BB spreads, near 15-year extremes, rewards issuer selection and relative-value positioning over broad market exposure. The piece makes an explicit case for its own products, the State Street Blackstone Senior Loan ETF (SRLN) and the State Street Blackstone High Income ETF (HYBL), presenting senior loans for floating-rate income and HYBL's flexible multi-sector approach as suited to this environment. It is a promotional piece, and its performance claims, such as HYBL's yield per unit of volatility, rest on figures it presents rather than independently verified data.

pieces.title: The Fortress Risk Management Approach: Defensive and Proactive Strategies
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that its private credit risk management rests on three pillars: infrastructure sized for worst-case conditions, independent re-underwriting of the portfolio supported by early warning data, and proactive borrower engagement. It cites a 0.02% annualised loss ratio in its direct lending business since 2016, against an industry average of 0.9%, and credits this to a systematic approach built over 25 years and tested through the global financial crisis, COVID and recent volatility. Its explicit view is that experience across market cycles is fundamental to how private credit strategies perform when conditions change, not merely a desirable attribute in a manager.

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that U.S. productivity gains, which ran at roughly 2% year on year in Q3 2025, are no longer reaching workers, as labour's share of income has fallen to a record low in a series dating back nearly eight decades. It attributes this to a structural shift rather than a cyclical one, citing weakened bargaining power, globalisation, intangible-heavy superstar firms, technological substitution, and accounting changes, and it expects further decline as AI and tax and trade policy favour capital-intensive firms. PIMCO also warns that a lower labour share could make the economy more sensitive to asset price swings, since capital gains currently support consumption and wealth shocks transmit more quickly into real activity.

The firm points to markets pricing roughly a 20% chance of a January cut and around 60 basis points of easing in 2026, and suggests the December jobs and CPI reports will offer a clearer basis for judging the path of monetary policy.

Its explicit view is that active allocations spanning both can offer yield and manager alpha, and that investors may find it useful to hold three permanent credit components: ultra-high quality for duration and risk, broad credit for income and limited volatility, and speculative credit for potentially higher returns.

The firm views this buying as a strategic shift away from dollar reserves rather than a cyclical trend, and concludes that the early-2026 sell-off was a pause at a higher level, not a reversion. Real yields still drive gold's short-term direction, but they no longer set its floor.

Fortress's explicit view is that investors evaluating BDC managers should ask this question and probe origination capabilities, deal flow and direct sourcing, and it presents its own significant investment in origination as the basis for that advantage.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that value stocks may stage a comeback in 2026, after years of underperformance against a tech-led, growth-heavy market, with cyclical, secular and structural tailwinds (rate cuts, AI infrastructure capex, pro-business tax and policy changes, and a revival in capital markets activity) turning the tide. It notes that value has outperformed growth year-to-date (6.4% versus -4.4%) and has historically protected during volatility, while cautioning that the environment remains risky and uncertain and calls for selective, disciplined stock picking.

Could annuities help clients live longer?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues, citing a working paper on nearly 600,000 Chilean retirees over 18 years, that annuitisation may reduce mortality by about 2.6% over five years and 3.6% over ten, with the authors attributing this partly to relief from the financial stress that market-linked portfolios can create. The firm's explicit view is that annuities may support longevity as well as insure against longevity risk, and that this is "another reason" for advisers to consider guaranteed income within a well-designed retirement income plan, while cautioning that no single study should drive a recommendation.

pieces.title: International equities: Giving credit where credit is due
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that 2026 was a strong year for international equities, with the MSCI ACWI ex-U.S. up 11.3% (to 10 November) and earnings growth driving nearly all of the gain: upward earnings revisions added 34 points, while multiples contracted 23% and currencies cost 2.0%. Its explicit view is that 2027 should bring another year of above-average global earnings growth, with returns shifting toward multiple expansion, particularly in Europe and Japan, while AI-related hardware markets such as Korea and Taiwan may moderate. It also favours value-style, non-AI exposures in Europe and Japan as a diversifier against an expected AI-related correction in 2027.

pieces.title: Making it easier to transition portfolios
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that model portfolios, now representing approximately $315 billion in assets, are increasingly popular among advisors but that tax implications often deter clients from transitioning existing portfolios. BlackRock argues that technology can help advisors present clients with graduated transition options that balance tax costs against portfolio deviation, rather than presenting an all-or-nothing choice, and promotes its Aladdin Wealth platform as a tool to calculate and manage these tradeoffs.

pieces.title: Alternative Lenders Aren’t So Alternative in Commercial Real Estate. Here’s Why.
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that alternative lenders have become permanent, mainstream participants in commercial real estate financing rather than temporary substitutes for banks, with non-bank lenders now accounting for roughly half of all new U.S. construction lending compared to less than 25 per cent in 2019. The firm attributes this shift to banks' tighter regulatory constraints and capital requirements, which have left funding gaps in construction, development and transitional assets that alternative lenders—including debt funds and separate accounts—are systematically filling, often providing mezzanine capital between senior bank loans and sponsor equity.

pieces.title: Beneath the surface. Private markets: An essential layer of economic infrastructure.
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that private credit has become a core layer of economic infrastructure, moving from a niche alternative asset class to a primary source of real-economy financing as banks retreat under post-GFC regulation, with Europe's non-bank lending growing faster than the US's (29x versus 10x since 2007, though bank provision there still stands at 85% of corporate debt). The firm's explicit view is that this shift gives investors a larger responsibility, since through their chosen managers they effectively decide which borrowers get credit and on what terms, and so must deploy capital with discipline. The piece also frames the European market as potentially the more compelling long-term opportunity, though the excerpt is truncated before its full conclusions.

pieces.title: Narrowing the gap: U.S. exceptionalism and developed markets
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Strategic Investment Advisory Group argues that U.S. market dominance, which has drawn disproportionate global capital on the back of GDP growth, high corporate profits and a strong currency, may be at an inflection point, with other developed markets such as Europe and Japan improving, though it is not yet clear whether those gains are structural or cyclical. It contends that the U.S. is unlikely to be displaced, but that even modest convergence could prompt global asset allocation rebalancing and leave passive strategies overexposed to the U.S. The firm therefore favours greater diversification and active management across global benchmarks to allocate more dynamically across currencies, sectors, countries and firms.

PGIM states that it is well placed to meet these needs through currency diversification, tailored maturities and amortisation adjustments, while acknowledging ongoing geopolitical, policy and interest-rate risks.

pieces.summary: Barings argues that private credit attention has been driven by headlines about isolated credit events and capital flows, which do not reflect how traditional middle market direct lending performs across cycles. It contends that the strategy's defining features of seniority, contractual income and downside protection explain its continued role in long-term portfolio construction. The piece is an introductory overview, and the full text is not included in the extract, so any more specific recommendation cannot be confirmed.

pieces.title: Beyond the Game: The Investment Opportunity within Sports, Media and Entertainment
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that sports, media and entertainment is a larger and more investable market than many allocators assume, spanning professional teams and leagues, sports-related products and services, and media and entertainment, which it sizes at over US$3 trillion. It presents private capital as a source of growth funding, infrastructure, digitisation and M&A for a sector whose revenues are becoming more recurring and predictable, citing the shift in sports income towards media rights and the move in music towards streaming subscriptions. Ares explicitly contends that the asset class offers diversification, since demand is less sensitive to interest rates, GDP and public market volatility, and that durable outcomes depend on rigorous underwriting, valuation discipline and strong governance rather than hype.

The firm explicitly favours high-quality credit and duration over lower-quality, economically sensitive credit, which it considers expensive with spreads near historically tight levels, and says it prefers to hold interest rate exposure roughly in line with the broad U.S. bond index, having been underweight duration ahead of 2022. It also sees global diversification, across select developed and emerging markets, as a way to broaden opportunity, and judges richly valued equities a weaker prospect than bonds for returns over the medium term.

Diversified alternatives: Investors should adapt to a new market reality
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that macro-driven volatility, higher interest rates and unstable correlations have changed how risk and diversification behave, so flexible, diversified alternatives (relative value, market neutral, event-driven, credit and commodity strategies) merit a place alongside equities and bonds. Citing the shift to positive five-year equity-bond correlations for the first time since near the start of the century, the firm contends this is a regime change rather than a dramatic turning point, and that such strategies should be treated as complements to traditional assets rather than substitutes. pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that four structural megatrends (demographics, innovation, environment and geopolitics), broken into seven investable categories, will drive long-term equity returns, and that investors who identify these forces could ride out short-term volatility. It states a firm view that quality companies, those earning above their cost of capital with improving momentum and attractive valuations, tend to outperform over the long term, and it presents its unconstrained, behaviourally informed global megatrends strategy as a way to capture that opportunity.

pieces.title: 7 Uses for a Minority Recapitalization
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that a minority recapitalisation, in which senior debt, mezzanine financing or preferred equity is raised against an existing cash-generative business, lets companies fund growth while active shareholders keep majority control, unlike a majority recapitalisation or outright sale. The piece presents this as "the best of both worlds" and says the company's future cash flow repays the debt over time.

pieces.title: View from the markets: What’s the meaning of the emerging market tech stock sell-off? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management (chief market strategist Daniel Morris) argues that the sharp sell-off in emerging market technology hardware and semiconductor stocks, after gains of roughly 85% year to date, is more technical than fundamental and does not signal an AI bubble bursting. It points to steady earnings expectations, continued capex growth among hyperscalers, and below-average or only modestly above-average valuations, and it notes that foreign selling of Korean equities, rather than leveraged ETFs, was the main driver. The firm's explicit view is that 2027 earnings estimates are likely to rise, while the 2026 impact may be limited by production constraints.

pieces.title: Can AI Conquer Demographics and Other Mega Forces?
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that AI-driven productivity gains are unlikely to fully offset downward growth pressures such as a shrinking working-age population and climate change, and that larger gains would likely displace more jobs, particularly white-collar roles in services and financial services. The firm states that it still supports the case for US exceptionalism and an overweight to US equities, while judging that the US's deteriorating fiscal position and debt burden will erode the dollar's global role, with inflation or financial repression the more likely routes out.

The firm notes that pending litigation, including the Elcan v. Commissioner case involving over $736 million in claimed deficiencies, and proposed legislation such as the Getting Rid of Abusive Trusts Act reflect heightened enforcement risk. Janus Henderson argues that advisors and high-net-worth families must now prioritise meticulous execution, including independent appraisals and detailed documentation, to navigate this more challenging regulatory environment.

pieces.title: U.S. Real Estate: Building on Resilience
pieces.summary: Barings argues that U.S. real estate fundamentals remain resilient, with constrained supply improving rental prospects and opportunities emerging across office, retail, logistics and housing, though it adds that rate pressure is unlikely to lift cap rates materially, leaving near-term appreciation more reliant on rental growth. Its explicit calls are to favour modern logistics (especially in migration-led markets), value retail and discounters and grocery-anchored retail in Sunbelt markets, and Class A office and second-tier cities as demand broadens beyond trophy and gateway assets. The piece is supported by a macro outlook citing 2.2% annualised Q2 2026 GDP growth and an Oxford Economics forecast of 2.5% for 2027, while flagging that slowing wage growth and tighter immigration could limit job creation.

pieces.title: Conflict drives structural reset for Gulf economies
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Middle East conflict has triggered a structural shift in Gulf economies, with implications including wider economic dispersion across GCC states, a reallocation of $50–100 billion in sovereign wealth inward from global markets, and a pivot toward domestic resilience, security and industrial capacity rather than consumer-facing growth. The firm contends that this inward capital turn will tighten global funding conditions and reduce GCC purchasing of assets such as US Treasuries, whilst stronger economies like Saudi Arabia and the UAE are better positioned to sustain spending through the disruption than weaker fiscal peers.

pieces.title: The Impact of Spanish Wildfires on Securitisations
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that Spanish wildfires pose limited direct credit risk to securitisations, because fire exposure is concentrated in rural areas outside dense urban mortgage pools, and because insurance, public relief and effective servicing should keep physical damage from becoming credit losses. Based on data through July 2026 (Auto ABS) and February 2026 (RMBS), it reports no clear evidence of widespread arrears deterioration in Spanish RMBS or Auto ABS, and it identifies the quality of fire insurance cover as the key driver of wildfire credit outcomes. PGIM's explicit view is that uninsured losses remain the real credit risk and that its servicer due diligence and ongoing engagement with servicers are how it monitors that exposure.

pieces.title: Monthly Active ETF Monitor
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that U.S. ETF assets reached $16.3 trillion in September with $154 billion in monthly flows, while active ETF strategies captured 36 per cent of year-to-date flows despite representing a smaller share of total ETF assets. The firm notes that active ETF launches are accelerating sharply, with over 1,000 new ETFs launched in the first nine months of 2026—already approaching the previous annual record—and observes that derivatives-based ETFs targeting specific outcomes now represent nearly half of new launches.

PGIM's explicit claim is that its exposure to thousands of real-world situations across businesses of all sizes and sectors lets it help borrowers navigate challenges, identify opportunities and build for the long term; the page contains no quantitative data, performance figures or market views, and its only call to action is an invitation to learn more about its financing options.

PGIM's explicit view is that these conditions make the current market an attractive entry point for value-add strategies, which target higher returns than core or core-plus through development and repositioning.

The firm contends that this income is not confined to telecoms and utilities, that yield is compatible with dividend growth, and that dividends make a meaningful contribution to total returns, so EM is an "underappreciated" opportunity for active, total-return-focused investors in 2026.

pieces.title: John Zito on Software, AI Disruption, and Putting Capital to Work
pieces.summary: Apollo co-president John Zito, in a CNBC interview, argues that AI is accelerating disruption in software, though software will be used more than ever, and that the key question is what the market will pay for it. Apollo, he says, has been underweight the sector for roughly 18 months, expects wide dispersion in outcomes favouring firms with proprietary data, durable moats and adaptable management, and continues to prioritise senior, investment-grade lending backed by hard collateral and downside protection.

The firm views this as potentially capital-efficient and a way to reduce earnings volatility, citing low-to-mid-teens levered yields, a US$2 trillion-plus maturity wall, and structural and cyclical drivers, while cautioning that reporting and capital treatment depend on the vehicle and regulatory regime (US insurers generally classify private CRE debt as real estate).

pieces.title: Charities: the case for asset-backed securities
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that UK charities face a widening funding gap, with income under pressure and costs rising, which may force them either to adopt more conservative spending rules or to draw more heavily on their investment portfolios. In its view, asset-backed securities (ABS) can help by offering a complementary source of diversified income that combines contractual cashflows, a potential yield premium, liquidity and flexibility for responsible investment, and can give trustees greater confidence to spend while staying aligned with their mission and regulatory frameworks.

pieces.title: High Income Bond Fund
Low-carbon transition
pieces.summary: BlackRock identifies the transition to a low-carbon economy as one of five major forces driving substantial capital reallocation, particularly as energy systems are restructured. The firm highlights rising global power demand—notably from data centres and artificial intelligence—as a key dynamic shaping the transition landscape, and reports that institutional investors prioritise affordable low-carbon technology and supportive policy frameworks when allocating capital to the transition.

pieces.title: Small cap and value: Monitoring the shift in market leadership
Leveraged loans: looking beyond TIPS for inflation protection
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that leveraged loans offer strong inflation protection, citing floating-rate coupons, very low duration, and historically low recent default rates, and claims they have been the most consistent inflation-beating asset since 1992 by their share of 12-month rolling periods beating CPI. It also says they have posted positive calendar-year returns in 27 of the past 29 years, while acknowledging default risk. The explicit view is that leveraged loans may provide more complete inflation protection than other asset classes, including TIPS, as the title suggests, and the piece closes with promotional links to Fidelity's high-yield and asset allocation research offerings.

pieces.title: Can AI Earn It Back? The $2 Trillion Test and Other Forces Reshaping Markets and Portfolios
pieces.summary: Apollo's thematic investing team argues that AI infrastructure spending of roughly $5 trillion by 2030 will only be justified if businesses and individuals generate $2 trillion in annual AI services revenue, making whether AI can earn back its investment costs a defining question for this cycle with material implications across debt and equity markets. The firm identifies three key reshaping forces: AI adoption and enterprise ROI pressure, US reindustrialization (which it believes private capital is better positioned to finance than public markets), and structural changes in finance itself. Apollo emphasises that technological innovation in AI has consistently driven demand cycles and increased capability, creating what it describes as a "virtuous cycle" of adoption.

pieces.title: My Personal History Chapter 22
Chart of the Month: The Public/Private Gap
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private buyout valuations, long criticised as stale relative to public markets, have now fallen below public equivalents, with its U.S. buyout public/private gap chart (as of 12 May 2026) showing public multiples recovering faster and moving above private marks for the first time in three years. Ares presents this as a meaningful shift that challenges the narrative of overly optimistic private marks and, if valuation expectations continue to converge, may improve conditions for exits, IPOs and M&A. It stops short of a firm call, saying only that the trend is worth tracking over the next few periods.

pieces.title: What Bond Markets Want From Andy Burnham
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that, whoever succeeds Rishi Sunak... wait, the piece names Andy Burnham as the leading contender, so the summary should follow the text: PIMCO argues that a new UK government will not change the fiscal reality, that bond markets are fragile and focus on near-term borrowing and issuance rather than long-term plans or redefined debt measures, and that the most credible path is to cut the deficit over the next two years to around 3% of GDP. PIMCO views short-dated gilts as attractive, since it expects the Bank of England to deliver less tightening than markets price, while longer-dated gilts carry only modest risk premium, so it prefers to wait and judge the new government on its actions rather than its promises.

Looking beyond Fed moves why floating rate funds remain compelling
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that floating-rate bank loans (leveraged loans) remain attractive despite shifting rate expectations, with current yields of roughly 8% at the start of Q4 that compare favourably with most other income alternatives. Its portfolio manager, Eric Mollenhauer, cautions that credit spreads are not especially wide, so investors should focus on resilient borrowers able to withstand a possibly slower growth environment, and he highlights AI-related data centre financing as a theme the fund is optimistic about, while monitoring AI's effect on software borrowers.

pieces.title: 2026 Real Estate Outlooks
pieces.summary: PGIM's 2026 real estate outlook presents region-specific opportunities rather than a unified global thesis: US retail owners can raise rents given below-market leases and high occupancy; European transaction volumes are expected to pick up across sectors; Asian office markets should see CBD properties outperform non-CBD; Mexican industrial remains tight; and US multifamily credit faces strong demand and upcoming loan maturities. The firm implies that investors should adopt differentiated strategies by country, sector and submarket rather than pursuing broad-based exposure.

pieces.title: The critical role of covenants in private credit
pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that covenants are essential risk management tools in private credit, functioning as early warning systems that allow lenders to intervene before breaches occur and to tailor monitoring to specific borrowers and sectors. The firm attributes significantly lower recovery rates in high yield and leveraged loan markets to the prevalence of covenant-lite deals (over 90 per cent), contending that customised covenants tailored to individual borrowers' circumstances are critical for protecting lenders' interests as market conditions evolve.

pieces.title: 2025 Real Estate Global Outlook
pieces.summary: PGIM's 2025 Real Estate Global Outlook argues that whilst heightened uncertainty is affecting near-term prospects, it has not disrupted the underlying recovery and growth narrative in real estate markets. The firm presents five regional research reports covering the United States, Europe, Asia Pacific, Mexico and private real estate credit markets globally, positioning uncertainty as a source of investment opportunity rather than fundamental concern.

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: The Real Estate Recovery is Running
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the real estate recovery is underway, that Q3 2024 marked the cycle trough, and that it still has considerable room to run, with returns in past recoveries averaging roughly 400 basis points above long-term norms. The firm cites five supporting factors: a favourable supply/demand balance, improving liquidity, rising transaction volumes, REITs trading at a roughly 14% median discount to NAV, and recovering fundraising. Its explicit view is that the discount in public REIT valuations presents an opportunity to acquire high-quality assets below intrinsic value.

pieces.title: ENSO – Understanding how El Niño and La Niña drive multi-year market impacts
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that El Niño and La Niña should be analysed as part of a multi-year ENSO cycle rather than isolated weather events, since their effects can overlap and create compounding economic shocks across regions and sectors. The firm contends that portfolio impacts will be uneven and that investors should prioritise resilience and adaptability in companies with diversified supply chains and pricing power, rather than short-term event positioning, particularly given climate change may intensify ENSO variability.

Global Credit: Wie der KI-Boom die Anleiheemissionen vorantreibt
pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that artificial intelligence financing could reach $400 billion by 2026, driving significantly higher bond issuance volumes across global credit markets. The firm notes that while markets have absorbed the additional supply well so far, it warns of a risk that future issuance may outpace demand, and accordingly adopts a cautious stance focused on selective security selection as an active manager.

pieces.title: Hedge Fund Outlook
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that hedge funds are well-positioned to benefit from current market conditions, which feature competing supply shocks—from AI-driven productivity gains and Iran-related energy price pressures—creating divergent performance across assets, companies and regions. The firm reports that nearly one-third of investors plan to increase hedge fund allocation over the next 12 months, with hedge funds potentially serving as portfolio ballast and capitalising on widening market dispersion. BlackRock implicitly recommends greater hedge fund exposure as a response to supply-driven uncertainty and rising asset differentiation.

pieces.title: Attract High Net Worth Clients
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that wealth managers can attract and retain high-net-worth clients by offering tailored portfolio solutions across multiple asset classes and structures, including separately managed accounts, private credit and infrastructure investments. The firm calls on advisers to evolve their offerings, expand their product range beyond traditional mutual funds and ETFs into private markets, and enhance their practice operations through improved client services, team alignment and client acquisition strategies.

Why wealth managers are shifting toward portfolio advice
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that wealth managers in Asia are shifting from product-focused sales to portfolio-level advice, driven by clients' demand for a holistic understanding of risk, goals and liquidity across their holdings. The firm identifies private markets expansion and generative AI as key enablers of this transition, with AI helping teams convert large datasets into personalised client insights and data transparency becoming essential as private markets allocations grow.

pieces.title: US inflation risk may tilt lower, eventually - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that US tariffs should lift inflation only temporarily, as a one-off rise in the prices of imported goods that will eventually drop out of annual figures. It expects inflation to ease further as a softening labour market slows wage growth, particularly in "super-core" services excluding shelter, and it sees the Federal Reserve's weakening job market as a bigger risk than inflation, so it considers further Fed rate cuts still likely.

Morgan Asset Management's Q1 2026 emerging market debt outlook argues that the positive backdrop from 2025 can extend into 2026, supported by resilient EM growth (forecast at 4.0%, with a 2.4% growth premium over developed markets), Fed rate cuts, and improving sovereign fundamentals. Its explicit views are to stay long EM local-currency rates, favouring countries with the most scope to cut and being more tactical where fiscal or political risks loom; to see EMFX as supported by carry, lower volatility and still-cheap valuations; and to expect corporate and sovereign credit spreads to be supported by limited defaults and negative net supply, though it flags US inflation and fiscal policy, recession, AI and geopolitics as key risks.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management says it agrees inflation risks have eased but places more weight on weaker demand threatening the medium-term target, so it keeps a longer duration bias in GBP strategies and expects volatile market pricing of rate cuts, which it sees as a chance to add duration on sell-offs. For GBP cash investors, it expects lower yields and suggests modestly extending duration while remaining cautious.

Private credit vs. public high yield: Understanding the tradeoffs
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton argues that the private credit versus public high yield debate should centre on how each market lets investors measure, manage and reprice risk, not just on yield or default expectations. It contends that public high yield's transparent pricing, broad issuer access and active secondary market are especially valuable late in the cycle, and that its episodic dislocations reward well-resourced fundamental investors. The firm's explicit view is that private credit retains a role, but that public high yield offers better tools for credit selection, relative value and downside mitigation as dispersion rises; the text is cut off before the final portfolio recommendation.

pieces.title: What is a PGIM Private Shelf?
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece explains its Private Shelf, a multi-year, uncommitted private placement facility in which credit committee approval and documentation are completed upfront, so borrowers can draw notes at short notice, with pricing typically set within days and funds delivered within about two weeks (or with delayed funding of up to 12 months). PGIM presents the product's selling points as speed, flexibility over payment terms and currency, and a low-cost structure with no facility usage, unused commitment or agent fees and a structuring fee charged only at set-up, which can be waived if there is an initial issuance. It also notes that PGIM has provided over 1,300 Shelf facilities globally since 1989, and it encourages borrowers to establish a shelf before any financing need arises so they can act on opportunistic funding windows or favourable rate moves.

pieces.summary: PGIM's weekly view says that recent developments in the Middle East, AI and interest rates could shift the global economic outlook over the coming months. Its base case for the US over the next 12 months is "overheating," now assigned a 50% probability, up from 40% at mid-year, supported by strong domestic demand, resilient consumers, AI-related capital spending, supportive fiscal policy and easy financial conditions. PGIM expects three 25bp Fed rate hikes by year-end (one imminent), followed by an extended pause, but sees the risks skewed towards further hikes rather than fewer.

Europe’s unloved opportunity: Finding quality amid the pessimism
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that European equities are unloved because of pessimism over growth, politics, energy costs, bureaucracy, labour costs, innovation and AI exposure, and that this sentiment has depressed valuations below what company fundamentals may justify. Portfolio Manager Nick Sheridan contends that many of these weaknesses could become opportunities through productivity gains, energy transition, policy reform and better commercialisation of innovation, and that the region offers "a compelling combination of reasonably attractive operational returns and relatively low valuation multiples" that favours active stock pickers. The firm's explicit view is that Europe's challenge lies more in market perception than in the quality of its businesses, though it acknowledges that the outcome depends on whether that perception improves over an investor's holding period.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris reports that oil prices have fallen back towards pre-war levels following the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding, though Strait of Hormuz traffic and Middle East infrastructure remain affected and European natural gas prices stay elevated. He notes that US business activity is still robust, with AI-related investment strong, while US consumer demand has weakened sharply, with Q1 PCE growth revised down to 0.4%, against a long-run non-recessionary average of 2%. BNP Paribas Asset Management concludes that the consumer is the key vulnerability for US equity markets, and flags Europe's weak services PMI as a concern.

pieces.title: Private Fixed Income: A Platform Built on Experience
Multi-asset outlook Q4 2026
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers' Q4 2026 multi-asset outlook argues that growth is improving and still supportive of cyclical assets, but the expansion is becoming more expensive as commodity prices and interest rates rise, with the commodity volatility shock so far largely contained. It contends that the current "improving growth" regime is distinct from slowing-growth and inflation regimes, and that such regimes can persist longer than expected, though it notes that declining growth becomes the most frequent outcome about 12 months after an expanding-growth signal. The firm's explicit view is that its All Roads strategy is adapting to this environment through a more responsive risk model, broader diversification and explicit hedging, with the paper treating the cost of capital and bond-return volatility as distinct risks that the model must recognise separately.

pieces.title: Rethinking fixed income asset allocation
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that traditional fixed income allocation frameworks are poorly suited to the post-pandemic environment, where stocks and bonds now correlate positively rather than negatively, and proposes a "tilt and timing" approach that dynamically adjusts between risk-on/risk-off and risk-parity positioning to navigate both positive and negative correlation regimes. The firm presents backtested evidence from 2006–2026 suggesting that tactical timing overlaid on strategic tilts can generate more consistent returns across different market cycles than buy-and-hold approaches.

The firm expresses high conviction in needs-based property sectors—specifically residential, data centres and necessity retail—linked to essential non-discretionary demand, whilst also identifying tactical opportunities arising from recent real estate repricing.

The piece, featuring Stephanie Wiggins, Head of Agency and FHA Production, presents a cautiously optimistic outlook on the sector without making explicit policy recommendations or investment calls.

It distinguishes between configured agents, such as Copilot Studio builds trained on a team's own documents and standards, which suit consistency and compliance-safe outputs, and adaptive AI, such as Copilot for M365 or ChatGPT, which suits drafting, brainstorming and explo

pieces.title: US-China summit: What a more managed and predictable relationship means for markets
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the recent US-China summit signalled a shift from binary outcomes to "managed competition", with selective cooperation (on trade dialogue, agriculture, energy and aerospace procurement, and people-to-people exchanges) reducing near-term escalation risk while leaving export controls, tariffs and strategic rivalry unchanged. Its explicit view, set out by Head of Greater China Equities Victoria Mio, is that this should improve visibility for investors and support a selective, sector-driven approach to Chinese equities, with semiconductors, internet platforms, healthcare, batteries and selected industrial exporters named as potential beneficiaries.

pieces.title: What is the outlook for hedge funds in 2026?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that 2026 could mark the end of the "alpha winter" (2011–2019), as rate normalisation, elevated single-stock volatility and high equity dispersion create a more favourable backdrop for hedge funds, which it sees as a way to earn returns above cash while reducing correlation to equities and rates. It highlights long/short equity, event-driven (notably Japanese M&A and governance reform) and global macro strategies as areas of opportunity, while cautioning that leverage, crowding and rapid deleveraging are significant risks. Its explicit recommendation is a diversified approach across hedge fund strategies rather than concentration in any single one.

pieces.title: Five Scenarios for the Federal Debt
The case for global short-dated high yield
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that its Global Short-Dated High Yield strategy manages default risk by targeting bonds it expects to be repaid within two years, favouring visible cashflows, excluding CCC-rated issuers and generally avoiding cyclical or early-stage businesses. The piece also highlights the use of call structures to capture call premiums, with 35–50% of the portfolio redeeming each year, and says short-dated high yield offers a potentially compelling risk-adjusted opportunity given elevated yields and flat spread curves. Insight's explicit view is that investors are under-compensated for duration risk and are better paid for credit risk at the short end, with the strategy designed to deliver income across cycles while prioritising capital preservation.

pieces.title: The Case for Industrial Real Estate Mexico
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that Mexico's industrial real estate market has matured into an attractive investment opportunity, driven by the country's role as a preferred manufacturing hub for North America, low labour costs relative to China, new tax incentives in the border region, and strong domestic e-commerce growth potential. The firm contends that the asset class offers risk-adjusted returns above those available in U.S. industrial real estate.

pieces.title: Smaller companies: the secret of South Korea’s success
pieces.summary: Aberdeen (via Asia Focus Manager Gabriel Sacks) argues that while South Korea's KOSPI hit a record 6,900 in May 2026, helped by the settlement of the Samsung family's record inheritance tax bill, the market's long-term success depends on more than the chaebol conglomerates. It contends that smaller, picks-and-shovels companies such as Hyundai Marine Solution and Hansol Chemical, which supply global themes like AI and the energy transition, are key drivers of performance and explains that Aberdeen's South Korean holdings sit towards the lower end of the market-capitalisation range. The firm explicitly says more investors should adopt this approach, and that on-the-ground research and management engagement are essential to finding these "hidden gems".

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: April 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that, after the Strait of Hormuz shutdown pushed oil above USD 100 a barrel, markets are fixated on inflation when they should be focusing on growth: one-year-ahead GDP forecasts typically fall by roughly 0.5% to 1.5% after sharp oil spikes. It contends that central banks are unlikely to respond as aggressively as in 2022, given cooler core inflation, softening wages and labour markets, and policy rates already near or in restrictive territory, so rates may stay on hold or see only moderate hikes rather than the tightening currently priced for some markets. Its explicit call is that, because downside growth risks are not yet reflected in prices, intermediate-maturity (belly-of-the-curve) duration looks increasingly attractive as a source of long-term value.

pieces.title: April 2020
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that whilst the coronavirus shock will produce a near-term GDP contraction more than twice as severe as the 2008 financial crisis over three quarters, the overall cumulative economic damage will be far less extreme because the shock stems from direct activity shutdowns rather than financial system propagation and debt deleveraging. The firm distinguishes between the shock itself (estimated at about 5% of GDP through Q3 2020) and its propagation, asserting that with appropriate policy response the impact will be contained and recovery faster than the financial crisis.

Active ETFs offer more precise exposures, and models let advisers hand off investment decisions to free up time for holistic planning. The piece explicitly favours selectivity, highlighting international equities and securitised credit given equity concentration and rate volatility, and urges advisers to move beyond a traditional 60/40 approach by deliberately diversifying equity exposure and scrutinising the risks taken within fixed income.

Reexamining “To vs. Through”
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues for "to" glidepaths in target date funds, which de-risk only until retirement rather than continuing to reduce risk thereafter. The firm contends this approach is justified because human capital—the ability to earn income—is depleted at retirement, and retirement risk peaks on the day retirement begins. BlackRock's position draws on academic research and a unified framework for lifecycle investing analysis.

pieces.summary: Apollo partner John Cortese, in a Yahoo Finance interview, argues that private credit is a roughly $40 trillion market that is largely investment grade, with Apollo putting about $38 trillion of it in the private IG segment, and that the sub-investment-grade lending people associate with the asset class is only part of it. He says recent credit stress, such as the Tri-Color episode, has not spread to equities because defaults remain moderate: banks expect around 2% in high yield and 3% at the upper end for leveraged loans next year, and public spreads are pricing weaker issuers already. Apollo's explicit view is that secured, low-LTV, first-lien lending in diversified formats remains genuinely investment grade and is set to grow, citing the Apollo and Athene default history as near zero.

From Evolution to Revolution: The Power of Active Fixed Income ETFs
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that active management suits fixed income, and that combining it with the ETF wrapper creates compelling investment approaches. It cites the vast, fragmented bond market, the liquidity and tax advantages of ETFs, and the fact that 80% of core and core plus managers beat the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index over five years. The firm explicitly anticipates the global fixed income ETF market reaching $7 trillion by 2030, with active strategies capturing a significant share, and it promotes its own active fixed income ETFs as a way to pursue yield in areas such as securitised credit and high yield.

The piece positions PGIM as favouring a disciplined strategy across specific geographies and sectors rather than broad-based exposure.

DC retirement: creating confidence to spend
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that today's DC retirees face a poor choice between an annuity, which provides lifetime income but is rigid, and drawdown, which is flexible but carries significant risk. Its stated view is that a well-designed "flex-then-fix" solution, combining equity investment with built-in downside protection and a hedged price for an annuity to be bought later in life, could offer a more appealing third option that delivers sustainable, flexible income with growth potential.

It attributes the rise to wider credit spreads (+70bp) and higher Treasury yields (+40bp) since early September, and states an explicit view that "now could be a good time to consider allocating to the market." It also favours a systematic, full-universe approach to exploit divergence across sectors, ratings and issuers, noting that technology and communications have diverged most.

pieces.title: There’s more to growth than AI
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that tightening liquidity and recalibrating expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts are ending the speculative period that concentrated gains in AI and technology stocks, allowing fundamentals to reassert themselves. The firm observes that profit growth is now broadening across regions and sectors, particularly internationally where earnings cycles are accelerating, creating opportunities beyond the "Magnificent 7" as market leadership expands to reward improving fundamentals rather than momentum-driven performance.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that record investment-grade bond issuance, driven by hyperscalers financing AI infrastructure (with Bloomberg projecting record 2026 volumes and hyperscaler capex near US$1.5 trillion by 2028), brings new risks, including wider spreads on AI-related debt, longer-dated supply that is steepening yield curves, and substantial off-balance-sheet commitments. It therefore recommends that investors consider a global, unconstrained short duration strategy, which it presents as an attractive, lower-volatility source of income and a natural hedge against AI-related debt risk because hyperscalers have issued predominantly at the long end.

pieces.summary: Sixth Street argues that its Investment Committees turn each investment into a curve of possible outcomes and probabilities, then reshape that curve through deal structuring (for example, senior positioning, protective terms, or preferred equity with upside via warrants). The committees then assess relative value across themes, sectors, geographies and asset classes, size positions according to each deal's risk-return profile, and check hidden correlations at portfolio level. In the firm's words, this repeatable process is designed to build balanced portfolios that can weather economic cycles.

pieces.title: Transition Summit 2026
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers (LOIM), reporting on its sixth annual Transition Investment Summit in London, argues that sustainability has moved from a policy- or values-driven agenda to an economic strategy, driven by cost competitiveness, energy security and capital allocation, with the Iran conflict reinforcing the case. The firm's explicit view is that sustainable investing offers a framework for identifying long-term outperformance across sectors, calling for a cross-sector rather than siloed thematic approach and a renewed focus on social dimensions such as healthcare and financial inclusion. Speakers including John Kerry, Jennifer Devine and Greg Jackson reinforced the message that the transition must be justified by clear financial returns and deliver tangible consumer benefits quickly enough to sustain public and political support.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that the FOMC cut the Fed funds rate by 25bp to 3.50%-3.75%, its third cut of the year, while its dot plot still shows only one further cut in 2026, slightly less than markets expected. It highlights that three members dissented, the most since 1988, and that the labour market's "stall speed" is the Fed's main near-term concern. Insight's view is that the labour market will continue to lead Fed policy: it expects the Fed to be cautious about cutting if employment proves resilient, but to look through above-target inflation and cut to prevent job losses if the "low hiring, low firing" regime tips into "high firing".

pieces.title: Unlocking Value in Private Credit: Inside Loomis Sayles’ Integrated Approach
pieces.summary: Loomis Sayles argues that continued growth in private credit will create attractive opportunities for fixed income investors, and says its integrated Private Credit Team, which works with public markets portfolio managers and research analysts across corporate credit, asset-based finance and real assets, is built to source and evaluate them. The firm's explicit view is that private credit can offer higher yields through liquidity and complexity premiums, together with structural protections such as covenants, potentially delivering stronger risk-adjusted returns than public fixed income, though the piece is promotional and the text is cut off before its concluding argument.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that longevity risk could significantly affect UK defined benefit schemes, whether they are running on or planning to buy out within five to 10 years. Using a case study, it shows that rising life expectancy could force a scheme to take materially more investment risk to stay on track for its endgame target. The firm's explicit view is that a longevity hedge can smooth a scheme's path to that endgame, even after allowing for the cost of the hedge over time.

A Changing Fixed Income Playbook
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that fixed income has shifted from the low-rate, low-volatility regime before 2020 to one of higher inflation, more volatile rates and a less reliable bond-equity relationship, so older portfolio assumptions may no longer hold. Its PGIM Multi-Sector Credit Fund now weighs a range of economic scenarios and adjusts exposure across rates, corporate credit, emerging markets and securitised assets. With credit spreads tight across many sectors, PGIM contends that bottom-up security selection, rather than broad market exposure or sector rotation, will matter more for generating differentiation.

Interest rates at 15-year high | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that, with the RBA's cash rate at 4.60% after its fourth hike this year and 10-year government bond yields near 5.40%, higher starting yields give fixed income investors a larger income buffer against price falls than they had in 2021. Its explicit view is that rather than building a portfolio around one rate forecast, investors should use three iShares ETFs for different roles: ISEC for liquid short-term income, ICME for diversified Australian credit income, and ILB for inflation-linked protection.

pieces.title: Investment Stewardship
pieces.summary: BlackRock states that investment stewardship—engaging with companies and voting at shareholder meetings—is central to its fiduciary role, with over 90 per cent of its public equity assets managed through index strategies. The firm operates two independent stewardship teams (BIS for index strategies and BAIS for active holdings) and offers clients additional choice through pass-through voting and climate-focused stewardship programmes. BlackRock argues it is committed to providing clients with stewardship options tailored to their individual investment objectives and preferences.

pieces.title: The Value of Mezzanine Financing
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that mezzanine financing benefits companies mainly through three features: it is less dilutive, since it lets owners maximise leverage without giving up much equity and typically keeps existing shareholders in control of the board and management; it provides capital beyond what banks would usually underwrite; and it is patient, being subordinated to senior debt, requiring no amortisation before a typical 7-8-year bullet maturity. The firm's explicit view is that mezzanine lets business owners retain control and fund growth beyond their senior debt capacity while serving as a patient piece of capital in the background.

Why choose euro fixed income?
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that euro fixed income is worth considering in 2026, citing diversified performance drivers (sovereign, quasi-sovereign and investment-grade credit), a 10-year Bund yield near 3% that is high by historical and volatility-adjusted measures, solid eurozone fundamentals, and the segment's low correlation to equities as a drawdown mitigator. The firm's explicit view is that active management of duration, country and sector allocation can exploit the market's volatility, and that investors are not being well paid for moving down the credit quality spectrum given historically tight spreads.

The firm's explicit view is that the opportunity "has never been better" for managers with deep local relationships, citing infrastructure needs of over $25 trillion through 2030, bank regulatory constraints, and its own shift to over 80 percent bilateral deals, which it says reflects 18 years on the ground. It presents geopolitics and AI-driven disruption in US software lending as tailwinds, while stressing its focus on hard-asset lending in India, Indonesia, Australia and Singapore, and distancing itself from US underwriting concerns.

pieces.title: The Capex Decade: Britain Is Building Again and Investors Should Take Note
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's UK equity PM, Nigel Yates, argues that the market has entered a "capex decade" in which investment in physical infrastructure is rewarded over the asset-light, buyback-driven model of the 2010s, with AI, housing, defence and water as the main drivers. His explicit stance is to favour "enablers" that sell into several capex themes at once, UK mid-caps with domestic infrastructure and defence exposure, and selected regulated utilities with manageable gearing, while taking only a tactical view on housebuilders until the Budget detail and evidence of supply response emerge. He qualifies this with risks including sticky inflation, skills shortages, a possible sharp AI spending correction, and Britain's record of announcing infrastructure faster than it delivers it.

pieces.title: Portfolio manager outlooks 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' 2026 portfolio manager outlooks, published under its Market GPS hub, cover equities, fixed income, alternatives and featured insights on ETFs and ESG. The firm's explicit views are that AI is becoming a broad corporate efficiency story beyond technology, that structural reform in Europe and Japanese earnings growth and policy credibility offer selective opportunities, and that the fixed income credit cycle has further to run, so investors should build in resilience. Its other calls favour emerging markets hard currency debt, selectivity in high yield given rich valuations, and diversified alternatives and absolute return strategies as a "Plan B" against geopolitical and economic change.

pieces.title: Personalizing whole portfolios at scale
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that wealth management firms must pivot towards personalizing whole portfolios at scale using technology to meet rising client demand, enabling advisors to view clients' total assets and build stronger relationships. The firm contends that technology adoption remains incomplete across the industry despite availability, and that aggregating portfolio data in unified systems is essential for operational efficiency and generating actionable insights. BlackRock promotes its Aladdin Wealth platform as the solution to enable this personalised, scalable approach.

pieces.title: Global Insurance Report 2025 – Institutional
pieces.summary: BlackRock's survey of 463 global insurers managing $23 trillion in assets finds that whilst macro risks like inflation persist and risk appetite remains depressed, insurers are increasingly flexible in their operating models and shifting capital into private assets despite higher public market returns. The firm reports that insurers are prioritising technology investment, particularly AI-driven tools for security selection and risk management, and remain committed to net-zero objectives despite broader debate around sustainable investing. BlackRock frames this environment as one where sophisticated investors can capitalise on market dislocations through strategic partnerships and structural shifts in asset allocation.

pieces.summary: Apollo argues that the structural decline in interest rates that characterised the past four decades has ended, causing duration—previously a reliable hedge in balanced portfolios—to become a significant liability as bonds and equities now move in tandem. The firm attributes rising yields to multiple structural factors including deglobalisation, higher labour costs, fiscal deficits requiring heavy Treasury issuance, and AI infrastructure investment, rather than a temporary cyclical tightening. Apollo contends that the conventional response of rotating from long-duration bonds into public credit risks simply trading one vulnerability for another, given that investment-grade and high-yield spreads are near historical tights.

The piece presents these developments as modernising the regulatory framework to reflect insurers' expanding investment opportunities, implicitly positioning KKR's expertise as relevant to navigating this evolving landscape.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that geopolitical tensions can significantly disrupt corporate liquidity, financing costs and working capital, and presents a scenario-based framework for treasury teams to build resilience into their liquidity planning. The firm examines three potential developments: sudden shocks affecting inflation expectations and short-term rates, sustained supply chain and energy disruptions weighing on financing costs, and scenarios shifting from inflationary to growth shocks with implications for central bank rates and counterparty risk. Insight positions short-term euro money market funds as a tool within comprehensive liquidity management strategies to navigate these risks.
