pieces.title: Finding Opportunity in Misperceived Risk
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that market perceptions of risk often diverge from the underlying risk of a business, and that sector labels such as "consumer discretionary" can mask this gap. Using fitness as its example, the piece contends that consumers are more reluctant to cut health and wellness spending than other discretionary outlays, so cyclical risk may be overpriced in some segments. Fortress's explicit view is that investors can be paid for risk that does not exist by analysing actual cash flow drivers, and it advises private credit investors to ask managers whether they avoid complex sectors or look deeper to structure better returns.

pieces.title: Investor Survey: Near-term caution, long-term optimism for AI investment theme
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' 2026 Investor Survey finds that most investors see AI as a durable, long-term structural force, though near-term caution is driven by hype and valuation concerns: 67% fear an AI bubble or market correction within 12 months, and only about half expect AI-focused companies to deliver superior long-term returns. The firm argues that advisers should make investors' implicit AI exposure explicit, given that many underestimate it, and frame AI holdings as part of risk-managed, long-term growth strategies rather than speculative satellite positions, stressing patience and discipline.

The firm is overweight U.S. and emerging market equities, prefers short- and medium-term bonds over long-duration bonds given interest rate sensitivity, and favours real assets and infrastructure exposed to AI demand and energy security amid persistent inflation risks.

pieces.title: How are active ETFs reshaping the European investment market?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that Europe's active ETF market has more than doubled to US$70 billion since early 2024 and is projected to reach US$1 trillion by 2030, with professional investors increasingly viewing "active core" ETFs as replacements for passive index exposures and "high-conviction active" ETFs as alternatives to traditional mutual funds. The firm argues that unlocking this growth potential requires asset managers to develop product suites that align closely with investor needs, combining both core and high-conviction active exposures within the efficient ETF structure.

pieces.title: Seeking diverse exposure to emerging market equities? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that emerging markets offer long-term growth potential, supported by demographics and economic weight (61% of global GDP in 2026, per the IMF), and that ETFs add liquidity and flexibility. It flags the growing concentration of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index in Chinese stocks (25.5%) and the volatility that comes with it, and suggests investors with conviction in opportunities outside China may prefer an ex-China index or a strategy with greater exposure to the rest of the EM universe.

pieces.title: Global Weekly Commentary - Insights
pieces.summary: BlackRock has upgraded US short-term Treasury bonds to overweight, citing attractive yields that now offer a sufficient income buffer against further rate rises, while downgrading US equities to neutral as a risk management move in the new market regime. The firm maintains conviction in AI and technology fundamentals but emphasises a more dynamic approach to portfolio positioning, partly funding the Treasury upgrade through the equity downgrade and trimming its Japanese government bond underweight after yields have risen substantially.

Macroeconomic Update: Resilient Growth, Stubborn Inflation
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that U.S. growth remains resilient, with real GDP expected to expand slightly above 2% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by AI-related investment, tax provisions and strong corporate profits, while consumer spending faces headwinds from fading tax support, cooling wage growth and high gasoline prices. It sees core PCE inflation, currently around 3%, staying near that level through year-end before easing to about 2.5% in 2027, and expects the Federal Reserve to deliver one more h

pieces.title: Asia credit shows healthy fundamental and tighter valuation
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that Asia credit fundamentals remain healthy and that spreads have tightened over the past year, reflecting strong investor risk appetite, though geopolitical risk, heavy supply from large US tech issuers and new bank capital issuance under Basel IV and Enhanced Solvency rules are flagged as watch points. It highlights the shift of Chinese internet companies towards CNH (offshore renminbi) bonds, which it sees as offering attractive spreads and diversification, and concludes that a cautious but optimistic approach is warranted for Asia credit in 2026.

pieces.title: Market growth despite US-Iran tensions
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that markets are looking past fears of an adverse macro impact from the Iran conflict, pointing to inflation pressures confined to energy, resilient corporate earnings, and AI-related capex that together support a stronger growth outlook. It maintains a risk-on stance across its investment teams, favouring bonds for their higher real yields and equities for their constructive earnings outlook, though it cautions that equity gains are concentrated in AI and that returns could broaden or disperse as the cycle matures.

esg-focus-private-markets-investing-winning-combination
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that ESG integration creates more value in private markets than in public ones, because private investors can take concentrated stakes, gain direct access to management, and hold for longer horizons, which together enable hands-on engagement on material ESG issues. The piece sets out a lifecycle framework (from sourcing and diligence through onboarding, the hold period and exit) and explicitly states the firm's belief that private markets offer "a compelling channel" for achieving ESG goals. It also contrasts this with public markets, where dispersed shareholders, rating-agency influence and short-termism make such engagement harder.

pieces.title: Charting an earnings surge, powered by AI capex
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that S&P 500 earnings growth in Q2 was the fastest since 2021 (29% excluding one-offs), driven largely by AI capital spending, with hyperscalers' accelerating cloud revenues easing concerns about returns on that capex. It argues it is too early to call a peak in AI capex, that earnings estimates are more likely to be revised up than down, and that the positive earnings distribution justifies staying overweight equities and the AI theme, with the U.S. the most favoured market and risks managed through diversification.

pieces.title: Mega forces: An investment opportunity
pieces.summary: BlackRock identifies five structural "mega forces" — demographic divergence, AI and digital disruption, geopolitical fragmentation, financial system evolution and energy transition — that it argues will drive macroeconomic volatility and reshape long-term growth, inflation and corporate profitability across sectors and regions. The asset manager frames these forces as creating significant investment opportunities and risks, though it does not articulate a specific strategic call beyond announcing its intention to publish detailed research on each over time.

pieces.title: Unpacking fallen angels
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that fallen angels, corporate bonds downgraded from investment grade to high yield, are often mispriced because forced selling by IG-only investors such as pensions and insurers pushes spreads wider than the issuer's fundamentals justify. It says returns are driven by price recovery and carry, and that these bonds have historically outperformed IG and other high-yield peers. The firm's explicit view is that active management is essential to avoid "falling knives" whose credit quality keeps deteriorating, and it promotes its LOIM Fallen Angels Recovery strategy as the means to do so.

pieces.title: The Investment Implications of the Tariff Decision
Quick View: An argument for the long view during AI volatility
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the Democratic gains in US state-level elections, driven partly by concern over the environmental and social costs of data centres, justified the market's higher pricing of regulatory risk for the AI ecosystem, but that the AI infrastructure buildout will continue, with its location and pace now more uncertain. The firm's explicit view is that stricter regulation would favour incumbents such as hyperscalers over neoclouds, startups and single-product or pricing-driven businesses, and that companies may relocate projects to friendlier jurisdictions, so investors should take a long-term view across multiple election cycles.

pieces.title: Bond Voyage: Beyond capital relief: securitisation reforms and insurer portfolios
Stability in Uncertainty: How Private Placements Support Long-Term Growth
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that private placements offer stable, patient, long-term capital that can help companies pursue growth and manage refinancing amid selective bank lending and volatile public markets. It lists five advantages: fixed-rate, long-dated funding that limits refinancing risk; a broader capital base; independence from public debt markets, which can remain open when those are closed; tailored structures such as delayed draws; and relationship-driven investors who engage early. PGIM explicitly positions private placements as a complement to, or alternative to, bank debt and invites companies to explore them as they reassess capital needs for the second half of the year.

pieces.title: 3+1 Active Investor Series
pieces.summary: BlackRock's portfolio managers argue that US fiscal deficits and capital demand from AI investment are driving higher real interest rates, which equity markets can withstand given productivity expectations. They assess European equities as oversold despite different fiscal trajectories across eurozone countries, and identify geopolitical risks in the Middle East and Ukraine as likely to sustain energy market pressures through 2026. On US equities, BlackRock highlights that whilst S&P 500 earnings growth is expected to reach 30% this year, the concentration of that growth in the top ten stocks creates a case for active management to capture opportunities in broadening earnings across the wider index.

Avoiding pitfalls when seeking income in a higher rate environment
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that higher interest rates have restored attractive income opportunities in fixed income, particularly in short-duration bonds which offer yield without excessive interest-rate sensitivity. The firm cautions against common pitfalls in the current environment—extending duration, sacrificing liquidity, or chasing yield through lower-quality credit—and contends that active management can identify value through global diversification across floating-rate, securitised and other less benchmark-constrained sectors while emphasising security selection and downside protection.

Blackrock voting choice
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that its Voting Choice programme, launched in 2022, allows eligible clients to participate in proxy voting through four options: implementing their own voting policy, directing votes, selecting from third-party proxy adviser policies, or delegating to BlackRock Investment Stewardship. BlackRock argues that greater choice in proxy voting should be available to all investors and has expanded the programme to retail clients, bringing eligible assets to $3.96 trillion as of June 2026.

pieces.title: What most ELN investors aren't pricing in
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the income from equity-linked notes (ELNs) reflects interacting market forces, including implied volatility, counterparty pricing and structural supply and demand for risk, and that these interactions create opportunities for active managers. Its explicit view is that the gap between single-stock and index implied volatility is near historic extremes, so index-based ELNs currently offer less income per unit of risk and the signal favours single-name structures. The piece also contends that genuine ELN diversification spans structure type, maturity, observation dates and counterparties, and that the flexibility to switch between single-name and index-based exposures is a key advantage of active management.

pieces.title: A Record Supply Year Is Taking Shape on Solid Ground
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that 2026 is shaping up as a record year for corporate credit issuance, driven by a U.S. re-leveraging cycle fuelled by M&A and AI investment, and that this supply will likely cause modest spread widening and a steeper credit curve. It remains constructive on the backdrop, citing broadening earnings, stable leverage (median net leverage of 1.8x for investment-grade and 3.2x for high yield) and solid growth near 2 percent, but with spreads historically tight it advises that active sector and issuer selection, quality and diversification will be essential to generate excess returns. Guggenheim also expects rising performance dispersion as AI disrupts industries unevenly, and flags policy risk in healthcare and pharmaceuticals.

pieces.title: Ares Credit Monitor - First Quarter 2024
Resilient markets
Private Credit, Decoded: Why Covenant Discipline Matters
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that in private credit, default rates alone understate lender outcomes, which depend heavily on structural protections such as maintenance covenants, leverage limits and lender control, and it cautions that these protections have weakened in parts of the market. In PGIM's view, maintenance covenants give early warning of borrower stress, allowing lenders to engage before options narrow, so investors should check what safeguards a manager's underwriting actually provides should conditions deteriorate. The piece is promotional in tone, presenting disciplined underwriting and loss avoidance as the basis for resilient long-term outcomes in PGIM's Global Private Credit Fund.

The piece reports that technology-heavy Asian equity markets have significantly outperformed broader benchmarks in 2026, driven by semiconductor demand and AI infrastructure spending, and that investor flows into emerging market technology ETFs have surged accordingly. BlackRock implicitly favours investor exposure to Asian technology through its iShares ETF products.

pieces.title: Integrating Private Assets In DC: Bridging Innovation and Outcomes
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that defined contribution pension plans have reached a point where the integration of private assets is feasible and desirable, moving beyond theoretical discussion to practical implementation. The firm contends that daily-valued private-market strategies can enhance diversification and risk-adjusted returns when structured with robust daily pricing, liquidity management, valuation rigour and fiduciary safeguards. PGIM calls for disciplined evaluation of liquidity mechanics, valuation processes and costs as essential prerequisites for responsible integration at scale.

pieces.title: Enhancing credit income without taking undue risk
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that a multi-sector credit fund, which blends investment grade credit with high yield debt, can offer income between the two asset classes without the volatility of high yield. Citing average yields of 4.3% for global investment grade and 6.6% for global high yield, the firm contends such a fund can target yield levels closer to high yield while keeping risk closer to investment grade. The piece is a marketing-style introduction to its approach and carries no explicit tactical call or market forecast.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the rapid repricing of rates after the Iran War, which took markets from pricing cuts to pricing hikes in six weeks, may overshoot. It contends that a softer labour market and well-beha

pieces.title: Rethinking Securitized Credit’s Role in Your Portfolio
pieces.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management argues that securitized credit, with its depth, breadth and liquidity, can complement other fixed-income sectors by providing income and diversification, and that 2026 market conditions look favourable. It cites resilient CLO returns, a CLO spread premium of nearly 45 basis points over US investment-grade corporates, and possible EU Solvency II changes as supporting factors. The firm's explicit view is that securitized credit should serve as a liquid, low-duration income allocation rather than a replacement for a core benchmarked bond portfolio, with selective, specialist exposure standing out as the opportunity.

pieces.title: Mega IPOs and other shakeups: what effects on private markets?
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers forecasts that mega IPOs in 2026, particularly SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, could generate over $100 billion in proceeds and significantly redirect capital away from the broader private markets, with their performance potentially determining valuations and fundraising across venture and private equity. The firm expresses caution on US private debt amid redemption pressures and deteriorating credit quality, whilst favouring European private debt and experienced credit specialists, whilst emphasising that evergreen private asset funds must communicate clearly to investors about their inherent illiquidity. Across asset classes, Natixis sees private equity gradually recovering with differentiated valuations, venture capital concentrating on AI and energy transition, and infrastructure continuing to benefit from structural trends, though it warns that geopolitical uncertainty and elevated risk aversion persist.

European Bonds Have Room to Run in 2026
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein's European bond discussion argues that the consensus view of a finished rally is too pessimistic, citing soft euro-area inflation, decelerating wage growth, Chinese export pressure and a possible euro appreciation. It expects the ECB to deliver one or two further cuts beyond the current pricing, the Bank of England to cut about four times in 2026, and growth to stay near trend. On credit, it sees continued yield-driven demand for investment-grade bonds at yields above 3.1%

pieces.title: Active ETFs bring a new wrinkle to high yield bonds
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that active management is gaining ground in high yield ETFs: active strategies now make up about 46% of the roughly 84 high yield ETFs available, up from 25% at end-2020, and 78% of the 27 launches over the past three years are active, often from established mutual fund managers. The firm contends that active managers can avoid defaults that passive index products must hold, can capture post-restructuring equity upside, and can add value in downturns, noting that the average active manager outperformed the index by 170 basis points in the four negative-return years of the past 20. It expects investor awareness, and therefore flows into active high yield ETFs, to grow as these products build track records.

Insight contends that a disciplined, research-driven, active approach can capture value in a higher-yield environment across global fixed income markets, and the piece offers its views on the macro outlook and how central banks are likely to respond.

pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that AI is entering two paradigm shifts: the rise of agentic AI, which it expects to mark the onset of autonomous agents able to perform entire roles currently held by human employees, and the growing importance of sovereign AI, as governments treat control over the technology as central to national sovereignty and competitiveness. The firm's explicit view is that the next upside will come from companies that move from small-scale adoption to full integration with their core businesses, and that the likeliest winners will be those turning models into sticky products with defensible economics, since LLMs alone are no longer a durable moat.

Meta Future of GCC Capital Markets
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that deeper GCC capital markets can link national transformation, household financial security and long-term competitiveness by channelling savings into productive investment. It contends that workplace and retail savings pathways will only broaden participation if they have credible public and private investable opportunities able to absorb capital at scale, and that market infrastructure (liquidity, settlement, disclosure, market making, securitisation, derivatives and investor protection) determines whether this capital can grow. BlackRock calls for domestic savings pools and international investors to reinforce sovereign wealth funds, and for reforms to savings channels, investable supply, infrastructure and cross-border access to advance together as a priority.

The piece describes "From Purpose to Placement," a VIP board matchmaking event run by the Apollo Opportunity Foundation alongside UNGA, where more than 15 Partners and Managing Directors met leaders from 10 nonprofits. Apollo's stated position, via Lauren Coape-Arnold, is that board service is "a real investment in leadership, in community, and in the kind of impact that compounds over time," not a compliance exercise.

pieces.title: 3 distinct opportunities available to the yield-seeking investor
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the yield-seeking investor should move beyond the defensive fixed income positioning of the pre-2022 era, when ultra-low rates made risk-taking the sensible default. It contends that higher rates, a more frequent geopolitical shock risk, and the now comparable attractiveness of private markets such as direct lending versus public markets such as corporate bonds make income opportunities as compelling as growth ones. Its explicit call, voiced by Teiki Benveniste, Head of Australia at Ares Asia Wealth Management Solutions, is that holding both private and public markets is complementary, valuable and sensible.

The piece's explicit call is for investors to consider the role credit opportunities can play in portfolios today, though it is promotional in tone and offers no supporting data, performance evidence or specific market views.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, says that Brent crude, at about $86 a barrel after a 20% weekly rise, is the key price to watch during the Middle East conflict, with markets implying a short war and easing intensity. He notes that oil, the dollar and Treasuries have moved in ways that differ from past Middle East crises, while equities have diverged sharply by sector and some crowded trades have unwound. The firm states that the turmoil has not changed its fundamentally constructive outlook for risk assets this year, though a sustained, much higher oil price would challenge that view, and it points to encouraging services PMIs and weak US payrolls as supporting possible Federal Reserve cuts.

pieces.title: CEO Sessions: Private credit’s expanding role
European upper middle market lending
pieces.summary: Invesco argues that European upper middle market borrowers (companies with €50 million or more in EBITDA) can be financed through both direct lending and broadly syndicated loans, so a strategy that combines the two can follow borrowers as their financing preferences shift and deploy capital across market conditions. It cites a potential direct lending spread premium of 100–300 basis points over syndicated loans, while stressing that liquidity, returns and diversification benefits are not guaranteed and that size and senior security do not eliminate credit risk. Invesco's explicit view is that investors already allocating to private credit should consider broadening exposure within existing portfolios through this borrower-led, senior secured floating-rate approach, supported by its roughly 20-year European lending record and more than €24 billion deployed since 2018.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's push for strategic autonomy, backed by more than €1.5 trillion of planned investment by 2035 across defence, infrastructure, energy, technology and food security, will generate new bond issuance and potentially strengthen issuers' credit profiles in those sectors. The firm's explicit view is that fixed income investors can potentially benefit from diversification across sectors, regions and issuers, but should take a selective, bottom-up approach, with infrastructure resilience described as the most important pillar.

pieces.title: Resilience reshapes the GCC’s investment cycle
pieces.summary: BlackRock estimates the Gulf Cooperation Council will invest $2.1 trillion through 2030, with regional conflicts reshaping priorities towards resilience infrastructure and strategic redundancy rather than scale, particularly alternative export routes and ports to reduce dependence on vulnerable maritime chokepoints. The asset manager identifies opportunities concentrated among enablers of this cycle—project-finance banks, utilities, ports and logistics firms—with the UAE offering clearer exposure to the theme and Saudi Arabia providing access to a deeper project pipeline, though execution risks and valuation timing remain important considerations.

pieces.title: Brazil election: Lula's surprise win rattles markets
pieces.summary: Schroders reports that Lula narrowly beat Flavio Bolsonaro in Brazil's October run-off (51.8% to 48.2%), a result markets had not priced in, and that the ensuing sell-off (the Brazilian market fell 20% in US dollar terms on the Monday) reflects fiscal concerns rather than politics, with long-term yields rising to around 14.8%. Schroders argues that a centre-right Congress and an independent central bank should constrain the government, expects the central bank to pause the easing cycle, and says it would expect the government to appoint a credible cabinet and take visible steps to contain spending, while noting that Brazilian valuations (MSCI Brazil at about 7.8x forward P/E) are likely to stay under pressure until the cabinet and fiscal strategy become clearer.

pieces.title: What's next for UK markets?
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that UK equities had a strong 2025, with the FTSE All-Share's best performance in over a decade, though returns were concentrated in banking and defence (HSBC alone contributed 14% of market returns), and 2026 has lagged the US tech rebound but offered stability. The firm's explicit view is that the market offers more opportunity than headline valuations suggest: it is adding to FTSE 250 and small-cap holdings (such as Kainos, XPS Pensions, Taylor Wimpey and Genuit), which trade at a higher yield than the FTSE 100 (3.7% versus 3.1%), and it judges that sell-offs in "AI loser" companies such as RELX, Experian and LSEG are indiscriminate, since their earnings have not yet been hit and their proprietary data and recurring revenues remain defensible.

pieces.title: Increasing resilience with global short-dated high yield
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that global short-dated high yield bonds can make portfolios more resilient amid persistent inflation, heavy government issuance, shifting central bank policy and geopolitical shocks, capturing most of the high yield risk premium while materially reducing interest rate sensitivity. The firm explicitly positions the asset class as a core holding or an outsourced credit sleeve within a broader income allocation, citing structurally more robust market conditions, high absolute yields, low default rates and a growing institutional investor base as supporting factors.

Benefits Of Credit Tenant Lease Financing And Outlook For 2024
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece explains credit tenant lease (CTL) financing, a fixed-rate, real estate lending structure underwritten mainly on the creditworthiness of a single tenant under a long-term lease rather than on property value, with leverage of up to 100% loan-to-value and maturities matching the lease term. It highlights uses such as sale-and-leasebacks, build-to-suit construction-to-permanent financing, and office or specialised assets, and argues that European tenants and owners have an opportunity to adopt the product, which is far more established in the US. PGIM expects the CTL market to stay active in 2024 despite broader real estate financing pullbacks, though the piece is largely promotional and offers no market data of its own.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that climate and nature risks can affect financial outcomes through multiple channels—physical hazards, policy changes, technology shifts, and ecosystem degradation—but that identifying risk differs from measuring its financial significance. The firm contends that models and scenario analysis are useful tools for exploring uncertainty rather than predicting single outcomes, and that investment judgement based on company-level research remains essential alongside quantitative tools, particularly for nature-related risks which require location-specific analysis.

pieces.title: Global Fixed Income’s Top 5 Investment Ideas for 2025: Bonds Take Center Stage
pieces.summary: New York Life Investments, via its MacKay Shields global fixed income team, argues that bonds are well placed for strong performance in 2025, citing a resilient U.S. economy, moderating inflation and a shift toward a higher steady-state interest rate environment. Its explicit calls are to fade "animal spirits" in favour of diversification and valuations, to favour high yield over investment-grade corporates, to see securitised assets as a compelling value proposition, to back resilient emerging markets selectively, and to exploit rate volatility along the yield curve. The piece is a short, three-minute promotional summary that points readers to a fuller outlook document rather than setting out the underlying analysis.

It expects refund disputes to be protracted and trade uncertainty to persist, though it sees only marginal, not significant, implications for inflation and growth. The firm says it will be monitoring legal challenges and policy developments closely.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: Maximising income per unit of risk amid higher-for-longer rates
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson argues that, with the Fed on hold amid energy-driven inflation, investors should prioritise selective risk-taking and security selection over macro calls, and should maximise income per unit of risk, notably by balancing duration and credit spread exposure. It sees the roughly $6 trillion US securitised market (about $15 trillion including agency MBS) as a useful toolbox for this, and specifically favours staying up in credit quality near the front end of the yield curve, which it believes offers attractive income with limited rate sensitivity. The firm also contends that optimising income per unit of duration may enhance return consistency and reduce portfolio volatility, with securitised credit sectors combining low duration, attractive spread income and strong credit quality.

Geopolitics and the economy: How war-triggered oil price shock was largely avoided - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Talking Heads podcast, with Ghent University energy politics professor Thijs Van de Graaf, argues that dire predictions of a catastrophic oil price shock from the Iran conflict largely failed to materialise, citing low pre-war oil prices ($60 a barrel) and oversupply, Gulf pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, 400 million barrels of Western strategic stock releases, temporary sanctions relief, and China's cut of almost three million barrels a day in imports. The piece says the IEA expects physical oil balance by the fourth quarter, though full recovery will take months given sea mines, slow Gulf output restoration and damaged infrastructure, and it flags possible longer-term effects of an oil glut and a shift towards electrification, renewables and nuclear. The firm's stated position is that the shock was cushioned more than expected, but the

pieces.title: Sharesify Podcast with Iain Pyle
The income edge: Planning for your financial future
Instant Insights:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's March 2026 Instant Insights note reports that the FOMC signalled an extended pause while still projecting one rate cut in 2026, matching market pricing, and raised its year-end PCE inflation forecasts to 2.7% from 2.4% (headline) and 2.5% (core), which it attributes to the oil price shock linked to the war in Iran. Insight's explicit view is that the Fed will retain its easing bias and "look through" the energy-driven spike, provided the supply shock is not protracted, though it warns that a longer shock would raise the risk of second-round effects and unanchored long-term inflation expectations, and says it will monitor Middle East developments closely.

pieces.title: The Value of Private Assets in DC Schemes Post-Retirement
Senior Loan Talking Points
pieces.summary: Voya Investment Management reports that U.S. senior loans declined slightly in early October as rising Treasury yields and wider credit spreads outweighed coupon income, though the asset class outperformed duration-sensitive fixed income in September. The firm notes that primary market issuance has moderated whilst investor demand remains supported by continued CLO issuance and retail inflows, with performance bifurcated between higher-quality loans and weaker CCC-rated credits.

pieces.title: Public insights on private credit: Déjà Vu: History doesn’t repeat, but it sure rhymes
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton, through its Benefit Street Partners unit, argues that the 2026 sell-off in direct lending is driven by sentiment rather than credit fundamentals, with evergreen fund redemptions now exceeding 2022 highs, and that the pattern mirrors the 2022 dislocation. The firm's explicit view is that this volatility creates an attractive window to deploy capital into direct lending at wider spreads and on stronger terms, citing BDC price-to-book ratios sliding back toward 2022 lows and single-B yields widening from multi-year lows. It urges disciplined, fundamentals-driven credit selection and frames the current environment as "a compelling opportunity" for investors willing to underwrite rigorously.

pieces.title: A Quantum of AI Debt Tests Credit Market Capacity
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments' Q3 2026 Corporate Credit Quarterly argues that AI-driven financing has become a major source of corporate credit supply, with issuance spreading from hyperscalers to data centre operators, utilities, infrastructure platforms and equipment suppliers, and that this is testing investor appetite for issuer and sector concentration. Guggenheim expects AI-related funding needs to keep expanding and sees hyperscalers' continued borrowing as likely to push AI-related spreads wider, though it does not expect that pressure to spread meaningfully into other sectors. Its explicit stance is that the widening in AI-related high yield spreads, particularly for neocloud and single-tenant data centres, reinforces the case for disciplined security selection.

pieces.title: Navigating supply surges: How AI is reshaping global investment grade credit
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that AI-driven capital expenditure by hyperscalers is driving record investment grade issuance and a sharp rise in tech's index weighting, a concentration that echoes past sector booms but with far stronger corporate fundamentals. The firm's view is that the market can most likely absorb this supply, with only temporary pressure on spreads, and that heavy issuance offers opportunities to build positions in

pieces.title: China’s Green Surprise Powers a New Investing Story
What a Decade of Market Shocks Taught Us About Credit
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that the post-2008 playbook of broad duration and credit exposure has become less reliable, as higher and more volatile inflation and interest rates have undermined bonds' diversification role and tight spreads and flat yield curves offer limited extra compensation. Marking the tenth anniversary of its Multi-Sector Credit Fund, PGIM contends that a shorter-duration starting point and a global multi-sector mandate, combined with active sector allocation, bottom-up security selection and disciplined risk management, may help investors seek income, diversification and resilience. The piece is promotional in tone, and its view is explicitly framed as a "may" rather than a firm forecast.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: An Oil Shock (Mostly) Like No Other
pieces.summary: PIMCO reports that oil prices have risen 25 per cent since February following a geopolitical shock similar to past supply shocks, yet credit spreads and broader risk assets have remained resilient—a divergence from historical patterns that PIMCO attributes to the U.S. economy's structurally lower oil intensity and robust AI capital expenditure cycle. The firm notes that Treasury yields have risen instead of falling as in past energy shocks, reflecting expectations of further central bank rate increases, and observes tentative signs of supply normalisation, though it warns that the geopolitical situation remains fluid and renewed disruptions could confront policymakers with stagflationary pressures.

pieces.title: European Real Estate: Is the Cycle Stuck in Neutral
pieces.summary: Barings argues that European real estate is stuck between recovery and expansion, with inflation and rate uncertainty curtailing transactions, though occupier markets remain healthy thanks to prime stock shortages and a slowing development pipeline. Its explicit view is that renewed inflation pressure is temporary and should ease in 2027, that prime rents will keep rising, and that rental growth of around 3% (higher for prime assets) and income returns near 5% should offset modest yield-driven capital value declines. Barings also stresses that returns will increasingly depend on income growth, active management and identifying mispriced opportunities, and that rate movements are currently the main driver of real estate debt returns.

pieces.title: Ares Global Credit Monitor
Quick View: Warsh delivers clarity, not guidance, in Jackson Hole
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through Head of Global Short Duration and Liquidity Daniel Siluk, reads Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote as providing the clarity markets wanted: a firm commitment to the 2.0% inflation target, with short-term rates as the main tool, and no forward guidance or mechanical policy reaction. The firm argues that with growth resilient and policy not clearly restrictive, the burden of proof now sits with incoming inflation and labour data, and that the market's move towards pricing possible rate hikes, read as hawkish, reflects this shift. Its explicit view is that the speech did not signal an imminent rate rise, as Warsh stressed a "discipline, not a decision".

pieces.title: Sham Telang and Jeremiah Stone on SnapLogic's Partnership with Sixth Street
pieces.summary: Sixth Street's Senior Operating Advisor, Sham Telang, and SnapLogic's CTO, Jeremiah Stone, describe a partnership built on collaboration and a peer CTO community that Sixth Street convened, with support on go-to-market, financial operations and technology

pieces.title: Commodity investing needs an upgrade
IS YOUR FIXED INCOME STRATEGY BUILT FOR TODAY’S MARKET?
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that traditional, index-inspired bond allocations have become less reliable for income, diversification and ballast, and that investors can improve outcomes by moving to actively managed fixed income ETFs suited to today's rate uncertainty and credit opportunities. It makes an explicit case for active flexibility, presenting its own ETFs across three approaches: upgrading cash-like holdings with ultra-short, municipal and AAA CLO strategies; managing rate risk through short-duration and securitised funds; and diversifying or extending duration via core plus and AAA CLO aggregate duration products.

pieces.title: Private credit 101 | Succession
pieces.summary: 7IM's "Private credit 101" explains that private credit is a long-standing lending arrangement that grew into a $2 trillion-plus market after post-2008 bank regulation pushed lending outside the banks, and that recent headlines stem from evergreen funds offering limited quarterly withdrawals, which can strain when investors seek to exit at once. The piece argues that the comparison with 2008 is misplaced because banks are now better capitalised, and that a closer parallel is the 2014 US shale downturn, with expected pockets of strain (such as small software companies) and some investor losses. 7IM's explicit view is that such defaults are a normal part of risk-taking in lending rather than a systemic threat.

pieces.title: From Cycles to Structure: Europe’s Investment Story
Building resilience with flexible fixed income opportunities - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that global bonds should be supported in 2026 by continued central bank easing and relatively high yields, with investment-grade and high-yield corporate bonds still attractive against cash. The firm says its broad outlook for global fixed income is positive but expects volatility, so it favours flexible strategies, such as absolute return and income funds, alongside diversifiers like TIPS, ABS and floating-rate securities, over traditional, less flexible bond portfolios.

pieces.title: Aviva Investors brings flagship Global Equity Income strategy to institutional and wealth management firms in Canada
The value of multi-sector investing in fixed income
pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that volatile fixed income markets, driven by uncertain inflation, Fed tightening, and heavy AI-related debt issuance that is crowding out credit, favour a more flexible multi-sector bond approach over traditional sector-constrained mandates. The piece explicitly favours longer-dated US Treasuries (10- and 30-year), which it sees as under disproportionate pressure from inflation fears and as likely to benefit if energy-driven inflation eases or geopolitical tensions settle. In credit, it highlights attractive spreads in AI hyperscaler debt below the Magnificent Seven, and maintains a core position in asset-backed securities for relative value and diversification.

pieces.title: My Personal History Chapter 21

Insurance Midyear Outlook: Finding Value in Tight Markets
An introduction to asset-backed securities
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that asset-backed securities (ABS) are inherently complex but can still be a compelling opportunity, citing potentially higher yields than corporate bonds of comparable credit risk. The piece is an introductory explainer that sets out how ABS are created and how they work, and how investors might use them to target a particular risk/reward profile, whether to meet specific return goals or to diversify an existing portfolio. Its explicit view is positive but qualified: the asset class is complex, yet Insight believes it merits consideration.

pieces.title: Commodities, Real Assets and the Return of the Physical Economy
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that the Iran war and resulting energy shock have pushed commodities up investors' priorities, and that the shift in geopolitical order, including US retreat from its post-war role in underpinning globalised trade, makes supply disruption more likely beyond oil. It frames commodities, particularly industrial metals, as a strategic tilt to real assets and a thematic trade linked to AI, deglobalisation and resource nationalism, while expressing a distinct, positive view on gold, which it treats as closer to money than a commodity. The firm also sees unravelling supply chains pushing up both the level and volatility of inflation, and it suggests implementation via commodities directly, mining equities or Latin America, though the full article is only available as a PDF.

pieces.title: ares-new-private-markets-climate-solutions-q-and-a
pieces.summary: Ares Management's Andrew Pike and Meaghan Conway describe how the firm's climate infrastructure strategy has shifted from thermal power towards renewables and resource efficiency, and from decarbonising the power sector to decarbonising the wider economy, with a flexible capital approach spanning debt and equity. They argue that data analysis and sustainability-linked loan ratchets, which adjust interest margins against measurable targets, are central to identifying opportunities and improving portfolio companies, and that environmental and financial performance reinforce each other. Ares's explicit view is that energy-efficiency and sustainability gains both lower costs and raise business value, and it cites fibre-to-the-home as an example of an asset that delivers both social and environmental benefits.

pieces.title: Responsibility Insights
Blended Finance: Bridging the Sustainability Funding Gap
Cash investment policy statement
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that organisations should adopt a cash investment policy statement (cash IPS) to set out short-term investment objectives, risk tolerance, return requirements, permissible investments and constraints such as tax and ESG guidelines, giving the investment team and board a common, disciplined framework. It presents capital preservation and sufficient liquidity as likely primary objectives, with yield, tax-advantaged returns and above-benchmark returns as possible additional goals, and stresses that higher-return strategic cash carries trade-offs that should be documented. The piece also urges regular review of the IPS in response to changing regulatory, political and market conditions, and notes that credit analysis should be assessed in-house or outsourced.

pieces.title: Why governance matters in European small caps
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that governance is a major, often underappreciated driver of long-term value in European small caps, where concentrated ownership and limited scrutiny can magnify both upside and downside. It highlights dual-class share structures (common in Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands), weak delisting protections and boards that hesitate to challenge entrenched management as key risks. The firm's explicit position is that it engages actively and constructively with companies, advocates for minority shareholder protection and holds boards accountable, treating robust governance as central to its commitment that "clients come first – always".

The Next Era of Climate Investing
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that climate investing has moved from a policy-driven, scalable "Climate 2.0" phase (roughly 2015 to 2023) into a more disciplined "Climate 3.0", with fundraising now constrained (climate fund closes fell to 112 in 2025 and 32 by early May 2026) and rising rates, geopolitics and less predictable government support reshaping the cost of capital. It identifies four shifts in that new phase: AI-driven demand for expanded generation capacity, with a broader low-carbon mix including nuclear and geothermal; underinvestment in grid, storage and transmission as bottlenecks; dual-use and defence-adjacent technologies, which require tighter impact guardrails; and a wider role for adaptation. PGIM explicitly rejects the view that this is the end of climate investing, and says it will underwrite assets on their measurable carbon trajectory and system role rather than their

Beyond the AI boom: A framework for evaluating data center bonds
pieces.summary: T. Rowe Price argues that the AI and data center build-out differs from other large infrastructure because data centres are built in one to two years while supporting power and water systems take three to 10, and because their costs fall on local communities while their benefits are spread globally, creating permitting, ratepayer and local-opposition risks that can delay cash flows. It presents a proprietary framework to complement traditional credit analysis of data center bonds, aimed at judging whether such deals can credibly qualify for impact-oriented mandates as labelled and unlabelled issuance grows. The piece does not make a specific investment call, but its explicit position is that these risks must be assessed beyond conventional credit metrics.

pieces.title: Sharesify Podcast with Samantha Fitzpatrick
CMBS: A tale of two (office) markets?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that rising office delinquencies in CMBS (from 1.6% in 2022 to over 12% in 2026) reflect genuine pressures from higher rates, refinancing risk and hybrid working, but that performance is sharply bifurcated: trophy assets in top markets such as New York City are leasing strongly, with Manhattan prime vacancy near 6.3% and rents about 10% above pre-pandemic levels. The firm's explicit view is that CMBS remain a valuable allocation for diversification, income and risk management, that conduit pools dilute exposure to the better office assets, and that active, asset-level selection is essential, with AAA single-asset single-borrower office deals offering spreads roughly 20 to 25bps wider than conduit equivalents.

pieces.title: Are data centers to blame for higher electricity bills?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that data centres are a real but not the main cause of rising US electricity bills, with much of the increase predating the data-centre boom and rooted in supply-side pressures such as ageing transmission and distribution infrastructure, weather-related outages, and the costs of grid modernisation. The piece notes that data centres could rise from about 6% to 14% of US electricity consumption by 2030 and flags cost allocation between businesses and households as a key determinant of household bills. It explicitly suggests that investing in private infrastructure funds that supply electricity to consumers and businesses could allow investors to benefit from higher electricity prices and demand.

pieces.title: What's the Risk? 7 Numbers that Reveal Hidden Exposures in Today's Portfolios
Data Integrated Frameworks for Asset Owners
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that asset owners should adopt unified data and AI platforms to drive strategic value and resilience amid market volatility and regulatory change. The company contends that such integrated frameworks—combining centralised infrastructure with decentralised team ownership of datasets and workflows—enable organisations to break down operational silos, improve governance, and accelerate innovation. BlackRock positions API-driven integrations and unified platforms as essential for asset owners to maintain competitiveness in an increasingly complex operating environment.

pieces.title: Investors are turning to Europe
pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors reports that European private credit is experiencing unprecedented investor demand, with Europe-focused funds capturing 46% of global private credit fundraising in the first three quarters of 2025 compared with 23% in 2024. The asset manager attributes this shift to diversification needs away from an overweight US market, where margin compression and rising default rates have compressed risk-adjusted returns, and to Europe's more resilient, unlevered funds with lower technology sector concentration. Allianz identifies the core mid-market segment as particularly attractive, driven by regulatory changes reducing bank lending appetite and growing demand from mid-sized borrowers seeking long-term financing partners for digital transformation and energy transition projects.

pieces.title: Core plus quarterly outlook Q4 2025
Seeking Clarity in Private Debt
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that Direct Lending, a private debt asset class that has grown as banks retreat from middle-market lending, is often wrongly grouped with broadly syndicated Bank Loans, and that the two differ in liquidity, origination and risk. It holds that the distinction matters most between Control and Participation Direct Lending, and that investors should check how much of a portfolio is self-originated and how much control the manager has, since these determine downside protection and economics. Ares explicitly contends that origination fees of 2% to 5% should be passed on to the funds or accounts that hold the loan to avoid conflicts of interest, and it classes Bank Loans as liquid credit akin to bonds rather than private debt.

pieces.title: Systemic risk, where art thou?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that implied correlations among U.S. equities, at about 0.15 against a 5-year average of 0.30, are near historic lows, meaning the S&P 500 is behaving more like a "market of stocks" than a single stock market, with idiosyncratic risk dominating and systemic risk underpriced. The firm warns that any mean reversion in systemic risk could lift the equity risk premium that investors demand, compressing valuations, which it considers a particular vulnerability given that much of the index's 17.9% gain in 2025 came from multiple expansion. It advises investors to acknowledge this possibility, monitor implied equity correlations as an early signal, and, should those correlations rise towards their historical average, consider prioritising capital preservation over capital growth.

pieces.title: How European and US credit indices differ
pieces.summary: Insight Investment compares the US and European corporate bond markets, noting that both are large and liquid, with financials dominating the European investment grade market while the US is weighted more towards industrials, technology and energy. The piece cites a quotation that US credit has delivered stronger annual USD returns since 2000, but that these higher returns have come with higher volatility. Its explicit view is that investment grade bonds in both regions have historically provided reliable income with very low default risk, making them suitable core holdings for investors seeking stability and diversification.

pieces.title: The week in markets: Investors are asking harder questions
United States Overview: 2025 Review & 2026 Outlook
pieces.summary: PGIM's US Private Credit platform reports steady deal flow through 2025 despite economic and geopolitical uncertainty, with middle-market companies prioritising balance sheets, supply chains and liquidity. PGIM expects financing demand to remain resilient in 2026, pointing to tariff-driven adjustments, data centre construction spillovers into related industrial sectors, and a likely pick-up in M&A as conditions stabilise. It explicitly sees heightened opportunity in sponsorless and founder-owned companies, where its strategic direct lending and mezzanine solutions are positioned to capture meaningful activity.

pieces.title: Finally Coming Into View? ‘Old-Economy’ Stocks Show Their Colors
Healthcare making a comeback? | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that healthcare is positioned for a strong 2026 after underperformance throughout 2025, citing resolution of US drug pricing policy uncertainty following the Trump administration's Most Favored Nation framework and a return of investor focus to the sector's innovation pipeline, including GLP-1 drugs and AI applications. The asset manager highlights that healthcare valuations were at 30-year lows before rallying strongly in the final quarter of 2025 and notes the sector offers diversification benefits for equity portfolios.

pieces.title: Neuberger Next Generation Space Economy Fund
Gilt market risks
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that gilt pricing is shaped by long-end spreads, funding frictions, differences across maturities, coupons and convexity, and shifts in the investor base, all of which feed into UK issuance strategy and the cost of government borrowing. The piece identifies political risk as the most significant domestic factor, though the page summary gives no specific forecast or market call.

Macro Markets Podcast Episode 80: Fixed-Income Outlook: Sunny with a Chance of Tail Risks
Yield, resilience and diversification: the ABS opportunity
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that investment grade asset-backed securities, particularly European ABS, could complement a traditional fixed income portfolio, citing attractive all-in yields, strong credit resilience, superior ratings stability and diversification from corporate bonds. It attributes the yield premium over equivalently rated corporate bonds to technical and regulatory factors (capital charges, due diligence burdens and complexity) rather than higher credit risk, and contends that European securitisation has consistently shown lower default rates than the US, supported by risk retention, full recourse mortgages and stronger social safety nets. The firm's explicit view is that ABS represents an opportunity for investors, with the piece noting a supportive primary and secondary market backdrop, though the text is cut off before its concluding recommendation.

pieces.title: AAA CLOs: Compelling Income in a Volatile World
pieces.summary: PGIM (authors Edwin Wilches, Gabriel Rivera and Connor Byrnes) argues that AAA-rated collateralised loan obligations offer compelling income, citing attractive yields, floating-rate protection and a default-free track record, against a backdrop of elevated rates, shifting issuance trends and growing global demand. The piece's explicit view is that active management can help investors enhance risk-adjusted return potential through AAA CLOs, though it notes that no strategy can guarantee returns or eliminate risk.

The great municipal repricing: why now may be the best opportunity in years
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the municipal bond market selloff in September has created a compelling entry point, with yields at two-decade highs offering historically attractive tax-equivalent income and favourable value relative to other fixed income assets. The firm notes that strong credit fundamentals and elevated starting yields can compensate for near-term volatility, meaning investors need not time the peak to benefit from current opportunities. J.P. Morgan recommends considering gradual capital deployment to capture today's yields whilst maintaining flexibility for further rate moves, and suggests an up-in-quality approach to credit selection given tight spreads.

pieces.title: The New Economy
pieces.summary: Ares Management presents the "New Economy" as a shift in which technological change, including AI, cloud adoption and automation, is driving sharply higher demand for real assets such as data centres, power, real estate and infrastructure. It argues that supply of these assets is lagging demand, and it positions the period as a major investment opportunity, with real estate offering one of its best entry points since the global financial crisis. The piece is an advisor-facing series, and Ares explicitly states it is focused on these real assets and ready to guide investors through what it expects to be a highly transformational period for commercial property.

pieces.title: Credit Currents Quarterly 2Q 2026: Uneven Resilience
Making portfolio optimisation understandable for humans - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that portfolio optimisers remain underused because they are seen as black boxes, and presents a framework from its paper "From Black Box to Explainable Portfolio Optimization" that decomposes tactical asset allocation weights into their sources: strategic benchmark replication, tactical views, net-of-cost fund alpha, and binding constraints such as sustainability floors. The firm's explicit view is that once every tilt is traceable, institutional investors, portfolio managers and robo-advisers should be able to adopt these methods at scale, and that such transparency could enable automated, client-customised construction and LLM-based advisory tools.

pieces.title: August 2019
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that conventional and unconventional monetary policy will be exhausted in the next economic downturn because global interest rates are near zero and cannot fall further to stimulate growth. The firm proposes a framework for "monetary-financed fiscal facilities"—a coordinated mechanism where central banks activate temporary emergency spending programmes, funded and calibrated to achieve explicit inflation targets, then close once conditions normalise. BlackRock contends this approach would enable effective policy coordination whilst preserving central bank independence and credibility, avoiding the risks of uncontrolled fiscal spending.

The firm highlights AI-driven capital expenditure as a "picks and shovels" theme benefiting smaller companies in data-centre supply chains. It contends that misconceptions about small-cap risk, interest-rate sens

pieces.title: Software-as-a-Service selloff and the implications for private markets
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton argues that the recent SaaS equity sell-off, which it links to fears that agentic AI (triggered by Anthropic's Claude release) could displace software workflows, reflects a broader valuation reset driven by slowing growth and a greater focus on profitability rather than the extinction of software itself. It cautions private market investors against generalising across the sector, pointing instead to differences in where companies sit in the software stack, whether they are AI infrastructure or easier-to-disintermediate applications, and how each asset is priced and structured. Franklin Templeton sees potential mispricing opportunities, and notes that private credit managers can use tighter covenants, enhanced reporting and collateral terms to manage software-sector risk, while highlighting that software accounts for roughly 26% of BDC portfolios, with heavy near-term loan maturities.

pieces.title: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt: The Road to Superintelligence
Re Rating Korea: A Structural Case
pieces.summary: Barings argues that Korean equities have re-rated since 2025, driven by AI and advanced technology demand that has lifted earnings expectations, especially for semiconductor leaders, with improving governance and shareholder-friendly reforms adding to the case. The piece points to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix's dominance in memory chips (roughly 70% of global DRAM and 50% of NAND revenue last year) and argues that memory demand is becoming structural rather than cyclical, improving earnings visibility. Barings presents this as a constructive, structural case for Korea, though the text as provided is truncated and the full article is not visible.

pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments expects U.S. real GDP growth of about 2 percent in 2026, with core PCE inflation finishing the year above 3 percent before moderating in the second half. It sees

pieces.title: Incorporating structured credit into customized LDI portfolios
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that liability-driven investment (LDI) portfolios face ongoing funded status drag, so they need consistent returns above the liability discount rate just to stand still. It contends that public and private structured credit can supply contractually defined cashflows and incremental spread that complement a liability-hedging portfolio, with less reliance on the uncertain, drawdown-prone returns of equities. Insight's explicit view is that structured credit can improve portfolio yield while preserving diversification, cashflow and funded status stability, albeit without equities' upside potential.

pieces.title: What you need to know about a weak U.S. dollar in a multi-asset portfolio
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S. dollar entered a cyclical bear market in 2025 that is likely to last several years, driven by narrowing growth and interest rate differentials, fiscal convergence across major economies, and policy uncertainty that has pushed foreign investors to hedge dollar exposure even while holding U.S. assets. The firm distinguishes this cycl

pieces.title: European loans: Built for what comes next
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that European leveraged loans are well placed to withstand the weaker macro outlook of 2026, citing a floating-rate coupon of about 7.1% that rises if the ECB hikes, a non-cyclical sector mix (about 57% of the loan market versus 20% of European high yield), and spreads near their 10-year median while high yield trades at decade-tight levels. The firm's explicit call is that loans offer three structural advantages, "rate insurance", defensive positioning and adequate compensation, that let investors avoid taking a directional view on rates and deliver a more predictable return profile across multiple scenarios.

pieces.title: Absolute return: Building resilience in volatile markets
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Luke Newman, argues that absolute return strategies will play a pivotal role in 2026 by offering diversification and resilience amid elevated volatility, stock dispersion and geopolitical risk, which it considers underappreciated, particularly where equity and fixed income correlations turn positive. The firm's explicit view is that such strategies are increasingly used for diversification rather than as a lower-risk equity proxy, and that conditions favour equity long/short approaches built on fundamental stock selection, with regional opportunities noted in US sectors beyond mega-cap technology, European defence and financials, and UK companies with substantial US dollar revenues.

pieces.title: UK equities are back — but opportunity lies beyond the market leaders
UK equities: while stocks last
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that UK equities are undervalued and attracting heavy takeover interest from overseas buyers, private equity and company management, with 27 approaches worth over $70bn by end-July 2026 and an average premium of 39%, while domestic investors have been slow to act. It warns that reliance on this external demand is unsustainable and calls for deeper domestic participation, including scrapping stamp duty and increasing pension fund involvement in UK shares. Aberdeen's explicit view is that the market's "sale" may not last and that UK-listed global franchises are trading at unjustifiably low valuations.

pieces.title: AI’s big questions
pieces.summary: BlackRock outlines a three-phase framework for tracking AI's economic impact: infrastructure buildout, adoption across sectors, and widespread transformation. The firm estimates annual investment in data centres and AI chips could exceed $700 billion by 2030, equivalent to over 2 per cent of US GDP, and sees significant near-term investment opportunities in foundational technology layers, utilities, energy and real estate, whilst cautioning that value creation may not accrue to the sectors adopting AI most heavily.

Does the AI boom still have room to run?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the recent sell-off in AI stocks, which has seen some major semiconductor names fall 20-40% this month, does not signal the end of the AI boom, pointing instead to demand that remains strong (token consumption at Alphabet is up roughly 600% year on year) and an infrastructure buildout that is still early. It expects hyperscaler capex to top $1 trillion in 2027 and the AI ecosystem to stay capacity-constrained for several years, with opportunities in optical networking, CPUs, behind-the-meter power and high-bandwidth memory. The firm's explicit call is that turning defensive too early carries its own risk, and it recommends an active approach spanning several layers of the AI value chain, while acknowledging that the economic returns to the biggest spenders remain unproven and could keep markets volatile.

pieces.title: 10 Things to Consider When Thinking Long Term About Capital
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece, a 10-point infographic-style guide dated 6 September 2025, argues that companies should weigh factors such as debt funding need, lender relationship, risk profile, disclosure, covenants, currency, rate type, maturity profile, speed of execution and capital structure diversification before adding long-term financing, which it presents as typically suited to businesses that have already shown scale and stability. Its explicit view is that private placements offer advantages over public bonds in several respects, including greater privacy, maturity and amortisation flexibility, covenant structures familiar from bank lending, and pricing off treasuries that adds diversification, while it concludes by offering PGIM's guidance on structuring financing to support long-term business success.

It highlights a sector difference: European investment grade is dominated by financials, while the US skews towards industrials, notably technology and energy. The firm's explicit view is that, despite differences in size, sector mix and yield, investment grade bonds in both regions have historically delivered reliable income with very low default risk, making them suitable core holdings for investors seeking stability and diversification.

pieces.title: What New Defined Contribution Guidance Could Mean for the Future of Retirement
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that recent US Department of Labor guidance on alternative investments in defined contribution plans clarifies that ERISA is a process-based law, giving fiduciaries flexibility to use private markets and guaranteed income solutions without fear of second-guessing by the courts if they follow a rigorous, documented process. The firm contends that private assets and insurance-based income products, often embedded in target date funds, can enhance diversification and help retirees manage longevity and market risk, and it calls on plan sponsors to apply a disciplined process to broaden the toolkit available to DC savers.

pieces.title: Sixth Street: Flexible Capital Since Day One
pieces.summary: Sixth Street presents itself as a global, multi-strategy private capital firm, founded in 2009, that rejects the idea of focusing on one sector, strategy or geography. pieces.title: How to Complete a Private Placement
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece explains the steps of a private placement, a private sale of corporate debt or equity to a small group of institutional investors such as insurers, and argues that the process closely resembles obtaining bank financing. It says a first transaction typically takes six to eight weeks, moving through deal launch, negotiations, due diligence, a credit risk analysis, pricing (a spread over the U.S. Treasury rate), rate lock and closing, and that the issuer-lender relationship typically lasts three to 25-plus years. The piece makes no explicit recommendation; its main view is that the process is less familiar than public markets but ultimately comparable to bank debt.

pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton argues that AI disruption in software is a core underwriting issue for private credit lenders, not just a question of how much software exposure a manager holds, and that markets wrongly treat the sector as a binary of AI winners and losers. It contends that narrow, single-purpose software tools face the greatest pressure, while system-of-record platforms with switching costs, proprietary data and regulatory protection are better placed, and that because private credit loans run for four or five years, lenders must judge whether a borrower's business model will stay durable for the full life of the loan.

The piece highlights five themes it sees as offering potential for outperformance: resource demand, AI enablers, information-led products, market leaders consolidating their positions, and long-term defence contracts. The firm contends this framework can generate modest excess returns and a yield advantage over the index while keeping tracking error low, chiefly by tilting towards shorter-maturity corporates and high-quality securitised credit and holding neutral duration and yield curve exposures.

The firm's explicit view is that direct lending should be held as a long-term, buy-and-hold allocation, with investors rewarded for patience through predictable income and an inflation hedge, and that the difference between illiquid private underwriting (a 40 to 60 page memo and a month or two of diligence per deal) and liquid public markets should be explained to clients.

Rowe Price argues that fixed income keeps the same core roles despite recent volatility, rising rates and recession risk, and it names dependable income and portfolio stability as the two main ones. It supports the first with data showing income, rather than price movement, has been the main driver of total returns across major fixed income categories from 2007 to 2025, and it supports the second by pointing to core bonds' buffering of equity downturns and to bank loans and short-duration bonds mitigating inflation and interest rate risk. The firm's explicit view is that investors who understand how to use fixed income can benefit from these roles, with core strategies tracking the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate or flexible multi-sector strategies offered as the means to limit equity volatility.

pieces.title: Macroeconomic Update: Inflation Remains a Persistent Challenge
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments expects US real GDP growth of about 2.0% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by AI capital expenditure (around 1 percentage point of growth in 2026) while warning that narrow growth drivers and persistent inflation pose substantial risks. Core PCE inflation, at 3.4% in the 12 months to May, is expected to stay above 3% through the rest of the year even as monthly prints cool, with AI-related technology goods inflation and supply disruptions from the Iran conflict cited as upside risks. Guggenheim's baseline call is that the Fed holds rates on hold into 2027, though it flags elevated hike risks if inflation proves persistent.

pieces.title: Apollo’s 13th Employee on the Firm’s Evolution and Principal Investor Mindset
pieces.summary: Apollo's Co-President Scott Kleinman reflects on the firm's evolution from its 1996 founding as a small, creative value investor into a nearly $1 trillion asset manager, arguing that its core philosophy of seeking excess returns per unit of risk through flexible, contrarian capital deployment has remained constant throughout. Apollo identifies three strategic priorities shaping its future: scaling origination capabilities, expanding wealth management delivery and accessing the 401(k) market. The firm positions itself as a trusted steward of capital positioned to navigate varied market environments.

The firm's explicit view is that regenerative agriculture and related nature-based opportunities may offer economic value, particularly in private markets, while public markets have a role in identifying and repricing nature-related risks.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: Insatiable demand for compute power rationalises massive capex
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that demand for AI compute is growing exponentially, driven by more complex agentic use cases even as cost per task falls, citing Google's monthly token processing rising from 9.7 trillion in May 2024 to 1,300 trillion by October 2025 as evidence of a Jevons' Paradox dynamic that justifies sharply higher hyperscaler capex (Alphabet up to US$185 billion for 2026, Amazon US$200 billion, Meta up to US$135 billion). The firm's explicit view is that the magnitude and duration of AI spending are still underappreciated, that monetising tokens at scale is central to returns, and that tech valuations at a relative five-year low (a forward P/E of about 22% versus a 36% five-year average, per Bernstein) give active stock pickers scope to find under-recognised earnings power.
