Morgan Asset Management argues that three long-term themes (economic nationalism, tech adoption and capital rewiring) will lift its 2027 long-term return assumptions, with a balanced portfolio's projected return rising 60 basis points to 7.00%, but that the path will be more volatile, with higher forecast volatility for inflation, rates and equities and a more positive, unstable stock-bond correlation. Its explicit view is that resilient portfolios should diversify both asset classes and themes, holding inflation hedges, real assets and gold against supply shocks and duration against demand shocks, and that the tilt toward tech adoption in an optimised portfolio is a net positive, though investors seeking less exposure can reduce U.S. and emerging market equities and financial alternatives in favour of developed ex-U.S. equities, core real estate and gold.

pieces.title: Pick your poison: Geopolitics or AI - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that AI is now a bigger source of market volatility than geopolitics, with tech stocks showing roughly twice the volatility of the rest of the market since last summer and earnings surprises that are only in line with expectations. The firm recommends caution in the short term while remaining strategically optimistic on tech, citing earnings growth of 31% expected for tech this year versus 10% for non-tech, and it advises diversifying tech exposure across industries and regions. It flags valuation risk as greater in some value indices (MSCI Japan and Russell 1000 Value, both with P/E z-scores of 1.8) than in the Nasdaq 100 (0.2), and identifies a tail risk in US rates: strong growth and a firmer ISM reading may make the two expected Fed cuts difficult, which could pressure tech and small caps before markets recover.

pieces.title: Fixed Income Perspectives: Don’t Reach for Yield as Risks Intensify
pieces.summary: Voya Investment Management's fixed income team argues that, despite geopolitical risks from the Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz disruption, high-quality fixed income still offers attractive yields and portfolio resilience, so investors need not reach for risk. The piece says the shock raises downside risks to growth without changing its base outlook, and that private credit stress is not systemic. It expects the Federal Reserve to delay rate cuts until uncertainty subsides, leaving rates higher for longer. Voya favours securitised credit and higher-quality segments, is neutral on agency MBS, and is more cautious on energy-importing emerging markets.

pieces.title: Artificial Intelligence
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that artificial intelligence is transitioning from single-turn question-answering to autonomous "agentic" workflows that complete multi-hour tasks, driving a dramatic increase in compute demand and infrastructure investment. The firm argues that while AI capability is advancing rapidly—task completion ability has doubled roughly every three months since 2024—the pace of productivity gains will be determined primarily by organisational adoption and integration rather than further technological breakthroughs, with most firms currently early in implementing these systems at scale.

pieces.title: The Fed’s reaction function
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the global economy is in an expansion regime rather than stagflation despite the Iran-war oil shock, and that in such a regime higher real yields are consistent with stronger growth and capital demand, so the cost of capital is likely to persist. The firm's explicit view is that real yields should not be expected to fall back, with the US sitting about 30 basis points above its expansion benchmark, possibly reflecting AI-related capex, and a European capex wave could push global real yields higher. It flags the main market risk as the volatility of real yields, driven by uncertainty over how the Federal Reserve's reaction function will evolve, and identifies a genuine stagflation regime as the key upside risk to yields.

pieces.summary: Gemcorp Capital argues that, despite the recent strain on private credit (direct loans to private equity, with heavy software exposure) from investor redemptions and AI-driven capital demands, asset-based finance (ABF) is a growing and attractive corner of private markets, with the private ABF market projected to reach US$9 trillion by 2029 from US$6 trillion today. It makes an explicit case for ABF's diversification, low correlation, self-liquidating structures and hard-asset security, while cautioning that its subcategories require specialist underwriting, that diversification and close proximity to collateral matter, and that risks are real. The piece offers its SHIELD framework (short-duration credit, hard-asset collateral, differentiated income, enduring demand, adequate loan-to-value and secured debt) as a lens for assessing any ABF strategy.

pieces.title: Goldilocks and carry
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that a "Goldilocks" economy, with solid growth and subdued inflation, supports positive fundamental outlooks across equities, bonds and select commodities, while AI is driving volatility in some sectors and opportunities in others. It views carry as a key return driver in 2026, favouring credit as spreads widen and value over growth equities, given the roughly 3% earnings-yield premium. The firm states that its long-only teams remain risk-on, with a neutral fixed income stance, overweight Europe and Asia versus the US in equities, and a view that market declines offer buying opportunities, while warning that policy or corporate missteps could trigger sharp repricing.

pieces.title: Empowering Retirees
pieces.summary: Apollo presents a video featuring its and Athene's leaders arguing that Apollo's asset management and Athene's retirement income products, combined, can support retirees'

pieces.title: Compounding Opportunity
pieces.summary: PIMCO's 2026 cyclical outlook argues that global growth has proved more resilient than expected despite tariff pressures, with AI-related capital spending and productivity gains supporting activity, but that the gains are unevenly distributed in a "K-shaped" pattern across firms, households and countries. PIMCO's explicit calls are that active fixed income offers compelling and durable opportunities given attractive starting yields, that investors should diversify into local-currency emerging market bonds, where real yield premiums look largely idiosyncratic and diversifiable, and that in a late-cycle credit environment they favour securitised credit and asset-based finance while reducing generic and private corporate credit exposure.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: CLOs continue to lead the way in fixed income returns
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that CLO outperformance is not a one-off "lottery win" from the post-2022 rise in rates, because it expects higher rates to persist, and it says CLOs have also benefited from tighter credit spreads. It cites BBB CLOs as the top-performing fixed income sector year to date and over the 1-, 3-, 5- and 10-year periods, and AAA CLOs as outperforming most indices over longer horizons. The firm's explicit view is that investors should consider leaning into CLOs, particularly higher-quality tranches, as the best route to floating-rate exposure in a post-ZIRP environment, and that a zero allocation to such debt only makes sense if rates are expected to fall to zero and stay there.

Investing Outside the Credit Box: Hedging and Diversifying via Securitized Assets

pieces.title: Rethinking glide path design - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that target date fund glide paths are often set by rules of thumb because academic models do not scale to real multi-asset portfolios, and it presents a practitioner-focused, two-step framework from a recent paper. The framework builds a robust efficient frontier and then works backwards from retirement to choose a portfolio for each year, balancing expected terminal wealth against Value-at-Risk. The firm contends that this approach is transparent, scalable to many asset classes, and adaptable (for example, to a more defensive profile or to annuities as the retirement asset), though the piece is largely a descriptive overview of its own research rather than a set of explicit recommendations.

pieces.title: Instant Insights:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's note reports that US headline CPI rose 0.9% in March, lifting year-on-year inflation from 2.4% to 3.3%, the highest since May 2024, driven by a record 21.2% jump in gasoline prices and a 10.9% rise in energy overall. Core CPI was milder, up 0.2% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year, though tariff-sensitive goods and airline fares showed some pass-through. Insight's explicit view is that, provided long-term inflation expectations remain anchored, the Fed will "look through" the energy-driven spike and keep rates on hold over the coming months, with the April 7 US-Iran ceasefire having eased near-term expectations somewhat.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Narrowing the Visibility Gap in Defaults
What Makes Infrastructure an Appealing Investment?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that infrastructure is an appealing asset class because its physical assets hold value, its long-term contracts with creditworthy counterparties offer some downside protection and a return profile largely uncorrelated with public equities, and it can hedge against inflation and market swings. Quoting Keith Derman, Partner and Head of Infrastructure Equity, the firm also presents the current wave of investment in new infrastructure as an important opportunity for investors to participate in. The piece's explicit view is that infrastructure merits a place in portfolios, though its disclaimer cautions that "downside protection" and "risk-adjusted returns" do not guarantee against loss.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that U.S. population ageing and below-replacement fertility, partly offset by immigration that may slow under current federal policy, are creating credit pressures in the municipal market. It says school districts face shrinking enrolment and rising competition, so it favours districts with strong reserves, conservative budgeting,

pieces.title: S13:EP127 Eva Pilgrim
Capturing safety and stability through CLOs amid uncertainty
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that European CLOs, particularly AAA tranches, offer resilience and relative value in 2026: their spreads (around 120bps, broadly stable despite record issuance of over €51 billion year-to-date) look attractive against historically tight IG credit, and their 12-month total return volatility of 0.7% compares with 2.2% for euro IG. The firm presents short-duration, high-quality CLOs as a defensive anchor amid a shifting rate environment and points to supportive regulatory developments, including EU securitisation reform and Solvency II recalibration, as tailwinds. Its explicit call is that investors should build CLO allocations at the top of the capital structure to balance yield and stability, combining that exposure with rigorous credit underwriting and active manager selection.

pieces.title: How Is Liquidity Evolving in Private Investment-Grade Credit?
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that private investment-grade credit has moved from a niche, illiquid asset class towards a more liquid, standardised segment of the market, driven by evergreen fund structures, growing syndication, third-party pricing, and the emergence of secondary trading. It contends that the asset class is becoming an integral

DealStreetAsia: Asian Markets Provide Scale That Private Credit Needs
ares-global-real-estate-debt-white-paper-vf
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that directly originated commercial real estate debt in the U.S., U.K. and Europe is currently attractive, citing four drivers: higher-for-longer base rates, rising equity subordination as lenders' loan-to-value detachment points fall, wider credit spreads as banks retrench, and a funding gap created by structural changes in the banking sector. It states that floating-rate, senior-secured loans with healthy equity cushions can offer lower volatility, steady returns driven mainly by high current income, and diversification as a complement or substitute to investment-grade fixed income and core real estate equity. The firm's explicit view is that these conditions have created attractive near-term, risk-adjusted return opportunities, which it expects to persist over the next 24 to 36 months.

It also flags a divided FOMC and a leadership transition at the ECB, and notes that US inflation data may be distorted by the government shutdown. The piece makes no explic

pieces.title: My Personal History Chapter 24
Enhancing Corporate Pension Allocations Through Private Investment Grade
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that UK defined benefit schemes, now better funded than in a generation, should use privately originated investment grade credit within their cashflow-driven investing (CDI) portfolios, because tight Sterling IG spreads leave public credit income dominated by the gilt rate and limit how efficiently assets can match liabilities. Apollo's "Fixed Income Replacement" framework adds private IG corporates, IG asset-backed finance, IG warehouses and high-conviction IG credit to public bonds, targeting 150–200bps of excess spread over public IG through origination, structure and security selection rather than added credit risk. Its explicit view is that schemes should broaden the allocation to private IG credit rather than retreat from credit, allowing them to match the same liabilities with less capital or to match further into the future with the same capital.

pieces.title: Community Collaboration Strengthens Biodiversity Management at Isagen and Neoen
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management reports on biodiversity initiatives at two of its operating businesses, Isagen and Neoen, arguing that partnerships with Indigenous peoples and local communities strengthen conservation outcomes. The piece describes specific projects: Isagen's restoration of native Guáimaro trees in Colombia with rural communities, and Neoen's conversion of land in Australia into a national park protecting endangered species on Ngadjuri Nation territory. Brookfield presents these collaborations as models demonstrating how developers, Indigenous representatives and local stakeholders can jointly achieve long-term conservation goals.

pieces.title: Opportunities & Challenges for Asset Managers & Asset Owners
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that asset managers and owners must modernise their technology infrastructure to navigate current market pressures including rising rates, inflation and geopolitical instability, whilst consolidating risk management across enterprise-wide systems rather than siloed teams. The firm contends that vendors should be chosen based on their capacity to anticipate industry trends, prove trustworthiness, and demonstrate long-term commitment through the accelerating shift towards artificial intelligence and machine learning applications. BlackRock implicitly positions its Aladdin platform as exemplifying the responsive, integrated technology partner that institutions require.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: Biopharma dealmaking gains momentum
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that biopharma dealmaking has gained momentum, with both the value and breadth of biotech M&A rising in the first half of 2026 despite higher interest rates, and that biotech IPO activity has rebounded, including two of the largest biotech IPOs on record in the second quarter. The firm argues that demand for differentiated biotech assets should remain strong, as large pharmaceutical companies must replace hundreds of billions of dollars in drug revenue facing patent expiry, and it says it continues to find attractive opportunities among small- and mid-cap biotechs with promising clinical programmes.

pieces.title: The new credit continuum
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers argues that the traditional premium of private credit over public credit has largely eroded, so the key question for investors is no longer "public or private?" but "what am I being paid for?". The piece, drawing on a Loomis Sayles discussion, points to convergence driven by post-crisis bank retrenchment and higher rates, and highlights sourcing, liquidity and flexibility (including interval funds, with their periodic rather than daily liquidity) as the increasingly important differentiators. Its explicit view is that investors should judge opportunities on fundamentals, risk compensation and relative value rather than asset-class labels, and that a marginal dollar may be better directed elsewhere if the pay is not consistent across an asset class.

pieces.title: The Alternative Outlook for 2026
The ‘inverted pyramid’: winners from new US food guidelines - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the US government's revised dietary guidelines for 2025-2030, which place "real food" such as high-quality protein, full-fat dairy and healthy fats at the centre and invert the 1992 Food Guide Pyramid, will shift both consumer behaviour and public food spending, including school meals and SNAP ("food stamps") purchases. The firm's explicit view is that companies with established capabilities in real-food supply chains and reformulation technologies stand to benefit disproportionately, and it highlights five areas of opportunity: high-quality protein (including farmed salmon and dairy), fresh produce, herbs and spices, fermented foods and gut health, and reformulation.

pieces.title: Private credit is not a monolith
pieces.summary: Wellington Management argues that private credit is "not a monolith" and that treating it as one obscures meaningful differences in risk. The firm proposes a three-dimensional framework (underlying assets, vehicle structure, and leverage form and amount) to map those differences, and it contends that asset-level underwriting is the primary driver of outcomes, with vehicle design and leverage format mattering as much as leverage quantity. It also cautions that recent headlines are painting the asset class with too broad a brush.

It contends that numbers and third-party analysis alone can miss weaknesses or strategic gaps, and that the firm's commitment to in-person engagement is a genuine differentiator rather than a means of inflating active share.

pieces.title: Why Manager Selection Defines Private Credit Outcomes
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that, as private credit matures and manager performance diverges, broad exposure is no longer enough and manager selection largely determines outcomes. It cites a figure that first-quartile private credit managers outpaced third-quartile managers by more than five percentage points a year on average over the decade to end-2024. PGIM's explicit call is for deeper diligence on sourcing, underwriting, portfolio construction and alignment of interests, alongside stress indicators such as entry leverage, covenants, PIK usage and workout performance, in order to identify managers with the breadth to handle complexity without compromising underwriting standards.

pieces.title: Is the market underestimating China’s AI potential? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Chinese equities, which have lagged other emerging markets this year, are underpinned by an innovation ecosystem (led by the STAR 50 index, up around 30%) that the market is underestimating, particularly in AI infrastructure, the application layer and domestic substitution. Its explicit view, as expressed by David Choa, is that China's stock market offers a useful diversification and hedge against US tech dominance for global asset allocators, although China is at least one to two years behind the US in AI capital expenditure and its hyperscalers' cumulative AI investment is under a third of the US level.

pieces.title: Private Market Perspectives 2025: Full Picture
pieces.summary: Wellington Management presents its "Full Picture" approach, which combines public and private market insights to inform private investing, and summarises discussions from its Annual Meeting on private markets, including growth in private credit. The page is a hub listing related pieces, mainly on the convergence of public and private markets, private credit maturity, and AI's effect on credit and private companies. It makes no explicit investment call; its main position is that investors benefit from view

Capturing yield, safety and diversification through BBB CLOs
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that BBB-rated CLOs offer high-yield-comparable income from an investment-grade, floating-rate structure at a time when tight credit spreads make income the main driver of fixed income returns. It contends that structural protections such as subordination, performance triggers and collateral diversification shield BBB tranches from single-name default losses that can permanently erode high yield and leveraged loan portfolios, and it calls for a disciplined, active approach focused on CLO manager quality, structural protections and collateral fundamentals, with a global lens on relative value.

pieces.title: A Dynamic Commodities Allocation: The Forgotten Diversifier
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that commodities deserve a strategic, dynamic place in multi-asset portfolios rather than being treated as a tactical add-on, citing a macro regime of more frequent shocks, supply constraints that slow the response to price rises, and the diversification value of assets driven by physical supply and demand rather than discount rates or earnings. It notes that commodities have historically performed well during high-inflation periods, when equities and Treasuries delivered returns close to zero in real terms, while lagging during low-inflation periods, so allocation size should reflect the intended role, risk budget and cyclicality. PGIM stresses that commodity strategies vary widely in benchmark design, net exposure, signal breadth and risk controls, and that allocators should judge them on economic rationale, signal robustness across regimes, risk distribution and implementation quality.

Citi and HPS Announce €15 Billion Private Capital Program to Expand Direct Lending in EMEA
pieces.summary: HPS Investment Partners (BlackRock) reports a €15 billion Private Capital Program with Citi, intended to finance sub-investment grade debt for corporate and sponsor-owned borrowers in Continental Europe and the UK, with the Middle East to follow, over an initial five-year term. Citi will source the opportunities through its origination network, and HPS presents the collaboration as a way to expand its direct lending in EMEA and deliver tailored financing across a broad range of borrowers. The piece makes no explicit market call or forecast; its stated view is simply that private credit demand is rising and that the partnership is a response to it.

pieces.title: In Conversation with Jim Zelter & Eric Needleman
pieces.summary: Apollo's Jim Zelter and Eric Needleman argue that private credit is far larger and more investment-grade than the commonly cited direct lending segment (around $1.8–2 trillion), with an addressable market of roughly $40 trillion. Apollo contends that growth will be driven by bespoke financing solutions tied to the industrial renaissance, energy transition and data infrastructure, and that transparency, secondary trading and bank partnerships are making private credit more tradable and accessible. The firm states that origination is the primary source of alpha in the asset class.

pieces.title: Harry Seekings: Europe Requires ‘Rewiring’ to Meet Energy Demand
pieces.summary: Apollo partner Harry Seekings argues that Europe needs a fundamental "rewiring" of its infrastructure to support rising energy demand, the energy transition and digitisation, and says the Global Industrial Renaissance seen in North America applies there too, with investment needs arguably greater. He attributes the need for creative capital raising and deployment to structurally higher interest rates and stickier inflation, which make financing more expensive, and states that Apollo is "best placed" to bridge the gap between equity owners' perceived value and current-rate reality.

It explicitly contends that active management is essential in this space, citing manager selection, risk management, execution in illiquid markets and the capture of relative value, and it presents actively managed AAA CLO ETFs, which hold over US$44 billion in assets, as the preferred route.

pieces.title: Diversifying private risks
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that recent weakness in private debt, whilst notable with 14-15 per cent underperformance versus 5 per cent gains in public bonds, does not signal systemic financial risk, citing stable credit default swap spreads for financial sector bonds and easy overall financial conditions. The piece warns that private investors overlooked illiquidity risks inherent to the asset class and advocates for balanced portfolio exposure to avoid being caught without liquidity access during inflationary periods or capital constraints.

The text provided is only a teaser and the disclaimer, so it states no specific market view or positioning call. Any substantive conclusions would need to be taken from the video itself.

Real Estate
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that real assets offer inflation protection, income generation and diversification in a constrained environment. The firm identifies Asia Pacific data centers as a selective opportunity despite structural growth drivers, emphasising that investability increasingly depends on market depth, power availability, regulation and execution capability. PGIM also presents a blended approach to public and private real estate across regional markets as a way to capture global investment themes.

pieces.title: How do markets perform post-midterms?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that the S&P 500 has delivered positive returns in the 12 months following every midterm election since 1950, averaging 15% gains, and argues that current market conditions—featuring strong earnings growth, economic resilience, robust capital expenditure and a less hawkish Federal Reserve than expected—support a constructive outlook for risk assets post-election. The firm contends that while elections create short-term uncertainty, markets subsequently refocus on fundamentals, and advises investors to remain invested rather than attempting to trade around the election.

Active ETFs: broadening the sources of portfolio returns - Australia Institutional

It presents liquid alternatives, such as managed futures and equity long-short strategies, and option-based income or out

pieces.title: European Equities: Finding Durable Growth Beyond the AI Trade
The Rise of Private Markets
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the rapid growth of non-bank corporate lending is not a short-term cyclical phenomenon that threatens financial stability, as some commentators suggest, but a long-term structural shift. In its view, banks and public markets have gradually moved their focus from small and medium-sized companies to larger ones over several decades, leaving private capital to serve growing middle-market firms, a role it considers critical. The firm, a leading US private credit manager, supports this view with proprietary insights drawn from roughly two decades of operating experience.

pieces.title: Why Private Markets Have a Role in Portfolios
Understand asset risk by decomposing into factors.
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that advisors should decompose portfolio risk into underlying factors—such as equity beta, sector, interest rates and foreign exchange—rather than relying solely on overall volatility metrics, as assets with identical aggregate risk can have markedly different exposures and react differently to market movements. The firm contends this factor-based analysis enables advisors to construct portfolios better aligned with clients' risk and return objectives and to communicate portfolio risks more clearly. BlackRock implicitly promotes its Aladdin Wealth platform as a tool for performing such risk decomposition analysis.

Why infrastructure is having a moment
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that listed infrastructure has transitioned from a defensive, income-focused allocation to a structural growth story, driven by AI-induced electricity demand, the low-carbon energy transition, and geopolitical fragmentation. The firm contends that infrastructure's resilient performance, defensive characteristics, strong income profile and exposure to essential, long-lived assets make it an essential diversifier in modern portfolios, particularly as global data centre capacity is projected to nearly double by 2030.

pieces.title: European ABS: a generational allocation shift?
Myron Scholes on Time: The total portfolio approach and dynamic risk management
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the total portfolio approach, which still relies on a static reference portfolio that lets fund risk drift with markets, should evolve to start from a drawdown budget and manage total risk to it daily. It contends that dynamic risk budget utilisation (taking more risk when opportunities are rich, less when they are not, and knowing when to re-risk after losses) and planning for shocks so that long-horizon funds can supply liquidity rather than be forced sellers should lift compound returns, which it describes as a fund's "North Star". The firm's explicit view is that this requires quantitative talent, a crisis playbook and a CIO who builds trust with the board.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset 2026 Outlook: Navigating Key Controversies
Iran conflict: What investors need to know - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chris Iggo reports that the US and Israel have launched coordinated military action against Iran, apparently aimed at regime change and curbing its nuclear capability, with the market impact so far showing higher oil, a firmer dollar, weaker equities and wider credit spreads. The firm argues that the scale of any sustained market move depends on how long the conflict lasts and how far it escalates, and it sees a prolonged energy shock as a growth negative, with inflation break-evens rising in the interim and sectors such as airlines, hospitality, and Middle East and regional bank and sovereign credits most exposed. It takes no explicit tactical call, but describes markets as "in risk-off mode" given the uncertainty.

pieces.title: AI bubble?
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that, despite AI-driven valuation concerns, its long-only teams remain risk-on for now. It contends that AI stocks, unlike during the dotcom bubble, are backed by strong earnings and largely self-financed investment, while retail-led bullishness is offset by more defensive institutional positioning. The firm's explicit calls include overweighting emerging market equities and bonds, European and Asian equities, and technology, while viewing US equities as offering limited risk-reward, and it advises treating market declines as opportunities to add exposure.

pieces.title: Bettina Ducat on active investment
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers' Co-Head, Bettina Ducat, argues in a finews.com interview that active management's value extends beyond beating an index after fees, and that alpha is most available where markets lack consensus, particularly in areas shaped by structural shifts such as the transition economy. The firm contends that passive products suit well-understood, benchmark-type exposures, whereas active investing should identify the economy emerging tomorrow, and that specialisation and a systems-level research approach to sustainability can outperform the cost-driven standardisation of scale. The piece is an interview with a firm executive, so its claims are the firm's own view rather than independently verified evidence.

pieces.title: Geopolitics: Europe’s Place on the Global Stage
7 asset allocation myths it’s time to leave behind
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that seven conventional asset allocation principles—including the 60/40 portfolio, stock-bond diversification, and efficient markets theory—fail to account for changing macroeconomic regimes and market inefficiencies. The firm contends that successful portfolio construction requires dynamic, regime-aware strategies that exploit persistent opportunities in return dispersion, market mispricings, and diverging central bank policies rather than relying on static allocations.

pieces.summary: BlackRock's insights hub showcases research and analysis across asset classes and regions, with particular focus on pension plan management as funded levels exceed full funding, Canadian retirement readiness, fixed income allocation frameworks, and machine learning applications in macro investing. The firm emphasises its role as a fiduciary committed to offering clients simpler solutions, lower fees and broader choice across public and private investments.

pieces.title: Preparing for Dislocation in Credit Markets
pieces.summary: Apollo partner Chris Lahoud argues that credit markets are complacent, with widening spreads so far concentrated in lower-quality credits and software, and that a default cycle driven by AI's effect on software could follow, possibly with geopolitical risk as an added trigger. Apollo's explicit call is to stay patient for now: it sees leaning into weaker businesses or software as premature, expects conditions may worsen before they improve, and says it is preparing through scenario analysis, heat maps and scoring of AI-exposed holdings so it can deploy quickly if higher-quality credits reprice attractively.

pieces.title: Investment themes for emerging market debt
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Q4 2026 emerging market debt outlook argues that EM fundamentals are outperforming developed markets, with EM growth forecast at 4.1% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027, EM corporate EBITDA growth expected to accelerate to 8.3% in 2026, and EM high-yield bonds leading fixed income returns year to date. Its explicit view is that EM central banks will calibrate policy rather than launch full hiking cycles, with divergence across regions: duration can be added where easing room exists, while a more tactical stance is warranted where fiscal, political or inflation risks are elevated. The piece positions carry, emerging market FX and selective credit as central to returns, describing EMD as a core allocation.

pieces.title: Quick View: What to glean from Big Tech's Q1 earnings
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson's Research Team argues that Q1 earnings from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta show AI driving growth rather than merely absorbing capital: core businesses accelerated, cloud revenues rose sharply (AWS 28%, Azure about 39%, Google Cloud 63%), and agentic AI emerged as a shared theme. Aggregate capital expenditure of roughly $750 billion is projected for 2026, which the firm sees as a major injection into semiconductors, power and data centre supply chains. Janus Henderson's explicit view is that these results "help reinforce the durability of the AI investment cycle" and counter the bear case that AI spending crowds out core profitability.

It contends that a disciplined, multi-factor, security-selection approach can generate modest but consistent excess returns while keeping interest-rate, credit and issuer risk close to benchmark, rather than relying on large directional bets. The firm explicitly rejects calls on the direction of rates or credit markets as the source of return, and also argues that conventional debt-weighted indices are not necessarily optimal for risk-adjusted returns.

pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that the war in Iran will affect the global economy mainly through oil prices, with a rule of thumb that each 10% rise in US oil prices adds about 0.2 percentage points to headline inflation, and that energy shocks are stagflationary because they also slow growth by acting as a tax on households and businesses. Because the Federal Reserve's dual mandate leaves it pulled between inflation and growth, AllianceBernstein expects policy stasis in the near term, with the Fed waiting to see which effect dominates. Its explicit call is that markets have overpriced the chance of a Fed rate hike, that recent rises in yields and falls in equities are overdone, and that its forecasts still have the Fed cutting rates over the next 18 months or so.

It says private markets can add diversification, particularly via the lower middle market, but that rising return dispersion makes manager selection and underwriting discipline more important, and that liquidity, transparency and complexity trade-offs may not suit every client. For 2026, PGIM expects shelves to stay popular, sees refinancing and M&A rising if interest rates stabilise, and presents its ability to serve clients in both uncertain and stable markets as a competitive strength.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that its systematic US high yield alpha strategy delivered 94 basis points gross alpha in its first full year, outperforming its 100 basis point target despite a low-dispersion environment. The firm argues that systematic approaches offer advantages over traditional active management by deploying diversified positions across all ~900 high yield issuers rather than concentrating on analyst-covered names, and claims its three proprietary models—quality, value, and structural themes—can generate alpha across different market conditions.

pieces.title: The evolution of UK QT

pieces.title: Quick View: Venezuela marks latest chapter in global realignment
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the U.S. removal of Maduro from Venezuela is part of a broader geopolitical realignment, with limited near-term market impact but potentially significant longer-term effects on oil supply, Venezuelan sovereign bonds and the emergence of regional spheres of influence. The firm expects that easing sanctions and foreign investment could revive Venezuela's output, which has fallen from around 3 million barrels per day in the early 2000s to under a third of that, possibly doubling to 2 million barrels per day within two years. It advises continued attention rather than immediate repositioning, noting that selective opportunities may emerge once companies see whether a pro-Western regime takes hold.

pieces.title: Take Two: ECB raises rates and cuts growth forecast - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's weekly "Take Two" briefing reports that the European Central Bank raised its deposit-linked benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 2.25%, its first hike since 2023, and cut its growth forecasts while raising inflation projections because of the Middle East conflict. The note also covers firmer US and Chinese inflation, a softer-than-first-estimated Japanese Q1 GDP reading, and the wider profit-margin gap between US and European companies. Its explicit view is that the US-Europe valuation gap reflects a 1990s-style productivity boom amid rapid technological change, and that once profit margins are adjusted for, the S&P 500's price-to-earnings ratio looks much closer to that of the Stoxx Europe 600.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset Team: Capital Market Assumptions
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson's Multi-Asset Team (Nicholas Harper and Adam Hetts) publishes its 2026 long-term, model-based capital market assumptions, setting out expected ten-year returns for 20 major asset classes across equities, fixed income, currencies and commodities. The firm's explicit view is that long-term expected returns still look attractive, with fixed income yields remaining high and non-US equities trading at more attractive valuations than US equities, although that valuation gap has narrowed compared with previous years. It also argues that the changing environment has implications for asset class diversification across portfolios.

pieces.title: The Misconceptions Behind Asset Diversification
Brazil Election 2026: What It Means for EM Debt
Back to the Future: Investing in the Forces Reshaping Tomorrow
EU-China Trade: Do Not Expect Another “Liberation Day”
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that a broad EU–China trade rupture ("Liberation Day") is unlikely, citing a €360.6 billion Chinese trade surplus with the EU in 2025 that widened by a further 9% in the first half of 2026, and rising pressure on European sectors such as machinery, metals, chemicals and motor vehicles. It expects Brussels to rely on safeguards, anti-dumping investigations and sector-targeted instruments, with a managed competition outcome as the base case and a targeted dispute as the main downside. PGIM's explicit call for investors is to look beyond headline tariffs and assess company and sector exposure to Chinese inputs, pricing power, inventory buffers and alternative suppliers.

pieces.title: The Value of Staying Invested: Lessons Learned from Timing the Private Markets
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that investors in evergreen private market funds should stay invested rather than time entries or exits, drawing on more than two decades of hypothetical data. It finds that entry timing made little difference across private markets, whereas poor exit timing cost roughly twice as much as perfect exit timing gained, and that moving to cash from private credit reduced long-term wealth because the income was hard to replace. Ares explicitly concludes that evergreen funds are best used for long-term strategic allocations, not for market timing or avoiding short-term volatility.

Wirtschaftsordnungen im Wandel
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that capitalism is cyclically shifting away from neoliberalism towards "Neofiscalism", characterised by greater state intervention through fiscal and industrial policy alongside central bank constraints. The firm identifies rising inflation, country divergence, and deglobalisation as structural consequences, and contends that active management will play a larger role in navigating this new economic order.

pieces.title: Harnessing private credit to strengthen DC outcomes
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that private credit, now a $2.0 trillion asset class, can improve defined contribution pension outcomes by offering higher yields, structural protections and diversified income streams across the accumulation and decumulation phases. The firm contends that Long-Term Asset Funds provide DC schemes with a practical, regulated access route to private credit strategies that were previously difficult to reach, and that a diversified approach to private credit—spanning corporate lending and asset-based financing—can deliver better value and resilience for DC savers than public fixed income alone.

pieces.title: The upside of US midterm gridlock for markets
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the Democratic wins in the 2026 US midterms, which leave the White House and Congress divided, could be neutral to positive for markets. It expects gridlock and heavier use of presidential vetoes to limit fiscal expansion and raise pressure to end the Iran war, easing bond yields and energy prices, while state-level restrictions on data-centre development pose a risk to AI capex that the firm sees as more likely to slow and broaden growth than end it. The firm explicitly rejects the view that the result marks the end of US expansion or of AI as an investment theme.

pieces.title: Emerging Asia: The Growth Story Investors Can't Ignore
Roth catch-up contributions in 2026: What’s changing and what you need to know
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson wealth strategist Ben Rizzuto explains that, from 1 January 2026, SECURE 2.0 requires participants aged 50 or over who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 Social Security wages to make any catch-up contributions as Roth contributions, with the standard limit set at $8,000 and a $11,250 "super catch-up" for those aged 60 to 63. He argues that participants should check whether their plan offers a Roth option (without one, catch-up contributions are not possible), learn how to make Roth contributions, and treat the change as a prompt to review their wider retirement strategy. The piece presents this as an opportunity rather than a hassle, though it stresses the content is educational and not tax or financial advice.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset Views: Potential opportunities through diversification - BNP Paribas Asset Management
CLOs: from niche to portfolio role
pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that collateralised loan obligations (CLOs) are being reassessed by institutional investors as a portfolio building block rather than a niche allocation, driven by attractive floating-rate income, regulatory reform (particularly Solvency II changes that reduce capital charges on senior tranches) and structural protections that have historically limited losses. The firm contends that CLOs have been misunderstood primarily due to regulatory treatment rather than underlying credit quality, and that active management and structural analysis are critical to determining whether the complexity of CLOs is adequately compensated by returns.

pieces.title: India: short-term noise versus long-term opportunities
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that India's recent weakness, driven by energy-price exposure from the Strait of Hormuz closure and investor preference for AI-linked markets such as Taiwan and Korea, is cyclical noise rather than a change in the country's structural growth path. It cites reform, demographics, infrastructure and domestic consumption, and says the Reserve Bank of India's downgrade to 6.7% growth is modest and the risks remain theoretical for now. Aberdeen's explicit view is that the current dislocation makes quality Indian companies cheaper to buy, and it highlights themes it sees as well established, including financialisation, digital infrastructure, power grid and electrification, and consumption, as expressed through holdings in its New India Investment Trust.

pieces.title: Aviva Investors launches Emerging Market Debt Opportunities Fund
Building America: investing in infrastructure and the workforce
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that the US infrastructure buildout will require approximately $10 trillion by 2033 and will generate substantial demand for skilled trades workers, creating a significant investment opportunity alongside workforce development needs. The asset manager contends that apprenticeships and training programmes offer accessible career pathways with strong economics and job security, and calls for scaled collaboration among governments, unions, employers and educational institutions to close the labour supply gap.

pieces.title: Accessing unique private equity opportunities in the small and middle market
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that secondaries, co-investments and stapled deals, and the overlooked small and mid-market, offer private equity investors and GPs ways to unlock liquidity and value amid subdued exit and fundraising conditions. It cites record 2025 secondary volume of $226 billion (up 41% on 2024) and a ten-year low in distributions to NAV in 2024 as drivers of LP demand for liquidity. The piece presents the small and mid-market (under $5 billion fund size and under $3 billion enterprise value) as a relatively attractive, less competitive segment, positioning its own Private Equity Group as the differentiated route into it.

pieces.title: Ares Australia Management Launches Ares Diversified Credit Fund
pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management, the joint venture between Ares Management Corporation and Fidante Partners, has launched the Ares Diversified Credit Fund, an unlisted open-ended vehicle targeting high single-digit annual net returns and monthly income, with daily inbound and quarterly outbound liquidity at net asset value. Ares argues that the fund's structure, which passes through all income including origination fees on directly originated loans, distinguishes it from other Australian offerings and offers "compelling performance with meaningful downside protection" relative to traditional fixed income. The initial seed offer opens on 16 November 2020, with seed investors receiving loyalty units equal to 1% of their initial investment if they hold for one year, and the release describes this as the second of several products planned over the next two years.

Don’t be derailed by the US midterm elections
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the 3 November 2026 US midterms matter for markets mainly because they will determine control of Congress, and that a divided government, the outcome current polling points to, would likely prolong political uncertainty. It judges that Republicans face an uphill battle to hold the House given weak presidential approval and cost-of-living pressures, while the Senate is a closer contest that could go either way. Its base case is policy gridlock and greater congressional oversight of the administration, with the President likely to focus on foreign policy and trade, where he has more discretionary authority.

Resilience Meets Crosscurrents: What’s Shaping Credit in 2026
pieces.summary: Ares Management's outlook, "Resilience Meets Crosscurrents: What's Shaping Credit in 2026," describes a strong 2025 for global credit, with issuance up, spreads near historical lows, and refinancing and repricing making up 55–60% of volume, while credit quality remains robust (leverage at 4.8x, the lowest since 2010, and interest cover at 3.0x). The firm expects 2026 to bring a shift towards M&A-driven issuance, a couple more Fed cuts, and a more bifurcated market, and it advises investors to balance opportunities in private and public credit with closer scrutiny of valuations and credit quality. Its stated view is that credit remains an active but discerning market, with the main risks being sector dispersion, inflation, a fragile jobs market, and AI-linked and sovereign debt pressures.

pieces.title: View from the markets: Is high-yield credit flashing a warning sign? - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris argues that the recent sharp widening in US high-yield spreads (from 267bp to a 318bp peak in early October) reflects mainly rising fixed-income volatility, Fed rate-hike worries, French fiscal concerns and heavy supply, rather than a deteriorating US economy, which he says the data does not support. He points to resilient year-on-year employment growth and improving goods-sector hiring as evidence, and notes that the widening is concentrated in CCC names. The firm's fixed-income team remains overweight US high yield, sees opportunities in BBB-rated names, and views the index's current yield as attractive if rate volatility eases, while cautioning that higher official rates could pressure some sectors.

pieces.title: What is asset-backed lending?
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that asset-backed lending (ABL) is a distinct area of private credit from direct lending: it offers short-duration, first-lien senior-secured loans underwritten on the quality, cash generation and liquidation value of collateral such as receivables, inventory, equipment and real estate, rather than on a borrower's future earnings. The firm contends that this structure brings lower risk, higher recoveries, lower exposure to economic cycles, less reliance on leverage and more frequent capital return than most direct lending funds, and it explicitly views ABL as offering superior risk-adjusted return potential, while still seeing a place for both strategies in diversified private credit portfolios. The piece is the first of a three-part series, with later instalments promised on why ABL is well positioned in 2026 and on LOIM's own Asset Backed Loan strategy.

pieces.title: Federated Hermes | Financing the AI build-out: the role of securitized credit
pieces.summary: Federated Hermes argues that securitised products (ABS and CMBS) currently finance only a small share of US data centre development, which is mainly funded by corporate balance sheets and the corporate bond market, though data centre ABS issuance reached about $13.2bn year to date (roughly 10% of Esoteric ABS) and SASB CMBS about $6.5bn. The firm contrasts the two structures: ABS uses master trusts that allow follow-on issuance and faster principal recovery on default, whereas CMBS is backed by a fixed mortgage pool that can face lengthy foreclosure, while both carry bullet-repayment refinancing risk and tenant concentration risk, particularly for hyperscaler tenants. Federated Hermes concludes that the sector remains niche but is maturing, and that success depends on bottom-up analysis of tenants, facilities, and deal-level legal and cash flow mechanics,

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is regaining investor interest on the back of improving growth and policy, a wide valuation discount to US equities (MSCI Europe at about 14 times forward earnings versus 20 times for the US, as of March 2026), and structural spending on defence and infrastructure. It also cites diversification benefits, noting that US assets make up over 70% of the MSCI World index. pieces.title: 2027 Sustainability outlook: Navigating transition, opportunity, and risk - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's 2027 sustainability outlook argues that sustainable investing is shifting from purely green assets towards financing the transition of high-emission businesses, with credibility judged by governance and technical and financial capacity rather than by stated targets. It also contends that climate adaptation and nature-related dependencies deserve equal weight with mitigation, and that AI's efficiency gains must be weighed against rising absolute environmental pressures and social effects. The firm says investors should use stewardship and forward-looking frameworks, such as the Nature Transition

Unlocking opportunity in the leveraged loan market
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that the leveraged loan market has matured enough, through a $1.5 trillion US market, record H1 2025 secondary trading of $517 billion, narrower bid-ask spreads, better pricing and data, and growing electronic trading, to support indexed exposure, which it is now delivering in an ETF. The piece presents loans as attractive for their yield and near-zero duration, and promotes the firm's scale, index-sampling skill and risk management as its edge. Its explicit call is that investors should consider loan beta via an ETF, with readers directed to their sales representative for more information.

pieces.title: 2027 Private Markets Outlook: The New Architecture of Capital
pieces.summary: HPS Investment Partners (BlackRock) argues that private capital will play a larger financing role as demand for long-term funding in areas such as AI and power grows. It expects greater dispersion across private markets, so underwriting, valuation, structuring and execution will matter more as capital converges on the same themes. It also contends that investors are moving from simply gaining access to private assets towards weighing liquidity, diversification and the role each asset is meant to

pieces.title: Macro Signposts | Fed Policymaker Comments Raise the Stakes for Inflation Data
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that Fed Governor Christopher Waller's hawkish remarks, which signal possible rate hikes if core inflation runs hot again, raise the stakes for incoming inflation data even though June CPI cooled. The firm's baseline remains a Fed on hold through 2026, with inflation pressures easing gradually, though it has revised its year-end inflation forecast higher and tempered its easing expectations, and it sees the core PCE reacceleration (3.4% in May) as a mix of supply shocks, AI-related demand and tariff effects, with labour costs not a source of pressure. PIMCO does not forecast rate hikes, but it notes that Waller may favour tightening to anchor expectations even if inflation proves supply-driven.

pieces.title: Systematic Insights: Is high yield an AI sweet spot?
pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that high yield markets have modest AI exposure of approximately 6% by market capitalisation, despite a spike in AI-related issuance in April 2026, and argues this creates a "sweet spot" for selective stock-picking opportunities. The asset manager contends that AI-focused high yield sectors offer significantly higher spreads than non-AI sectors whilst the market's low overall AI exposure provides diversification protection against broader AI market pullbacks. Insight Investment's systematic models identify potential value in higher-quality AI issuers in neocloud and legacy data centre businesses, whilst flagging certain hardware suppliers and power generation companies as potentially underpriced for their risk.

pieces.title: Investment maze
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the upheaval in the global order during 2025 is a lasting shift rather than a temporary shock, so relying on broad passive market exposure is insufficient and portfolios need a range of purpose-built strategies. Its prescribed approach combines efficient core allocations (for example, decarbonised equity and fixed income, and synthetic high-yield exposure via CDS index options to avoid cash-bond liquidity and cost penalties), differentiated active solutions such as private-markets secondaries for uncorrelated alpha, embedded convexity, and conviction about how the economy is being reshaped. The firm presents these as its own products and capabilities, so its performance and cost claims should be read as self-reported.

pieces.title: The case for asset-backed securities
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that investors willing to understand asset-backed securities (ABS) may earn higher returns than from corporate bonds of the same rating without taking on more credit risk. It cites five supporting characteristics: robust credit quality backed by diversified, secured loans; a persistent yield premium over comparable corporate bonds since the global financial crisis, attributed to regulation, complexity and negative sentiment; limited spread and duration risk, particularly outside the US; diversification across granular underlying obligors; and potential illiquidity premium from less liquid asset-based finance. The firm's explicit view is that ABS are a strategically valuable complement to corporate bond portfolios.

pieces.title: Euro IG Credit: Qualität trifft auf attraktive Erträge
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that euro investment grade credit, meaning bonds from financially sound issuers rated at least BBB-, remains one of the most attractive fixed income asset classes, sitting between government bonds and high yield in terms of risk. The firm's explicit view is that the asset class remains compelling for investors seeking income and diversification, citing attractive yields, robust corporate balance sheets and diversification benefits. However, it cautions that tight credit spreads and a growing new-issue supply make an active and selective approach more important than ever.

pieces.title: The Rise and Rise of Private Debt for Insurance Investors
The Market Edit: Three Signals to Watch - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's first "Market Edit" argues that markets have defied expectations: inflation has proved sticky, long-term rates remain high, yet the economy and equities have held up. It flags three signals to watch, namely whether the oil shock spreads into wages and inflation expectations, whether AI-driven productivity can support growth despite higher rates, and whether high valuations are becoming a bubble. Its explicit view, attributed to strategist Alessandro Tentori, is that AI-linked equities are expensive but not yet in a bubble, and that higher-for-longer interest rates may reflect a new equilibrium rather than a temporary deviation.

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: Maximizing income per unit of risk amid higher-for-longer rates
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson argues that, with the Fed on hold amid inflation driven by higher energy prices, investors should maximise income per unit of risk by favouring selective security selection over macro calls or broad beta exposure. Its explicit view is that staying up in credit quality near the front of the yield curve may offer attractive income with limited rate sensitivity, and that securitised credit sectors, with their low duration, spread income and strong credit quality, can help balance duration and spread exposure to steady returns and reduce volatility.

How CRE Debt Can Boost Pension Fund Portfolios

pieces.title: Back Leverage for U.S. Real Estate Debt Funds
LDI focus: Diversification benefits of US securitised credit
pieces.summary: Columbia Threadneedle Investments argues that US securitised credit offers diversification, higher-quality assets with attractive yields, and lower market sensitivity than similarly rated corporate bonds, making it a useful addition to LDI portfolios. It attributes the sector's quality improvements to post-crisis reforms such as Dodd-Frank risk retention and enhanced loan-level disclosure, and says that securitised assets have historically outperformed comparable corporate credit on both absolute and risk-adjusted bases. The piece makes an explicit recommendation that blending securitised assets into LDI portfolios can enhance collateral waterfall resilience and improve risk/return dynamics.

pieces.title: Vision, Ambition, and Humanity in the Age of AI: Insights from Blackstone’s CEO Conference
pieces.summary: Blackstone's Rodney Zemmel reports on the firm's annual CEO Conference, attended by more than 200 CEOs from its portfolio companies, where discussion centred on AI's potential to produce measurable results and on leadership in a fast-changing environment. The piece presents a series of quotes from external and internal speakers, including Netflix, Anthropic, Alphabet, ServiceNow and Stryker, with the common thread that AI's value extends beyond cost-cutting to transforming outputs and that investment and action should happen now. Blackstone's own explicit call is that leaders who move now will define AI's impact, and it recommends three priorities for portfolio companies: equipping teams to use AI daily, focusing transformation on one business area that will materially move results, and using AI-assisted software development as a proving ground.

pieces.title: Equities: AI rivalry — shared ambition, different paths
What’s next for the UK markets?
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that UK equities, after a strong 2025 driven by a narrow group of large-cap banks and defence stocks, offer overlooked value in mid- and small-caps and domestic names, with the FTSE 250 yielding more than the FTSE 100 (3.6% versus 3.0%), a rare occurrence. It contends that the sell-off in data and information businesses such as RELX, Experian and LSEG, hit by AI disruption fears, is indiscriminate, since their earnings have not yet been affected, and that firms with proprietary data and recurring revenues are well placed. Aberdeen says it is adding to mid-cap and UK domestic holdings (including Kainos, XPS Pensions, Baltic Classifieds, Taylor Wimpey and Genuit) on the view that these are not priced for a recovery it expects in the year ahead.

pieces.title: From Data to Decisions: The Role of Factors in Systematic Fixed Income
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that factors, which it defines as quantifiable characteristics or sources of risk or return, are central to systematic fixed income because they help explain bond performance and identify securities with the greatest return potential. It contends that factor selection is a key driver of success, that investors must keep looking for new factors and monitor how well existing ones perform as markets change, and that advanced systematic approaches should use a dynamic, multi-factor, quantitatively driven method for security selection that differs from traditional discretionary strategies.

pieces.title: Higher yields and investing

Chart to Watch: Japan’s rate reset creates opportunities in financials
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Japan's shift from ultra-low rates, which began when the Bank of Japan ended negative rates in March 2024, is structurally improving profitability for banks and insurers, with higher net interest margins and stronger investment income. It cites strong April-June earnings from banks and broadening profit growth beyond AI-related sectors and expor

pieces.title: A look at the proposed evolution of the SFDR - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Chart to Watch: ROE, reform and re‑rating
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that equity valuations broadly track profitability, measured by return on equity (ROE), and that international markets trade at a discount to the US because their ROE is lower. It notes that many international markets sit slightly below the level their profitability alone would imply, and attributes this to governance and capital-return reforms (exchange-led initiatives in Japan and Korea, and activist pressure elsewhere). The firm's explicit view is that valuations have room to move higher and that the valuation gap could narrow over time, provided these reforms produce sustained ROE improvement.

pieces.title: Eye on the Market Outlook 2026: Smothering Heights
Significantly Misunderstood: Why SRT is Not Capital Relief
pieces.summary: Man Group argues that significant risk transfers (SRTs) do not provide capital relief to banks, contrary to common market misconception, because the loss-bearing tranches of funded SRTs function as regulatory capital that increases rather than reduces total capital available to absorb losses. The firm contends that bank capital should be defined as loss-bearing resources rather than equity alone, and that securitisation regulations ensure banks hold more total capital after an SRT issuance than before it, owing to capital non-neutrality rules.

pieces.title: Exploring Private Infrastructure as a Next Generational Investment Opportunity
pieces.summary: Ares Management, through its Australia and New Zealand wealth solutions head Teiki Benveniste, argues that private infrastructure is a "generational" investment opportunity, driven by rising power demand, digitalisation, AI and automation, and focused on de-risked core assets with contracted cash flows in the operational and contracted revenue phase. The piece promotes Ares' yield-focused strategy, proprietary deal origination and disciplined approach as delivering consistent yield, diversification and relative downside protection, though it is primarily a webinar promotion and includes a caveat that diversification does not assure profit and downside protection is not a guarantee against loss.

Investment themes for emerging market debt Q3
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Q3 2026 emerging market debt outlook argues that the asset class has a supportive backdrop: EM growth is steady at 4.1% for 2026, the inflation shock from the energy crisis is far milder than in 2022 (about 30% of its size), and central banks are calibrating rather than launching full hiking cycles, with real-rate buffers of over 100bps. It also points to solid sovereign fundamentals, with no defaults in 2025, more rating upgrades than downgrades, and low, idiosyncratic default risk. The explicit positioning call is to favour credit for core carry and local-currency debt to outperform, while using the dispersion in central bank policy to be long duration where easing is feasible and more tactical where fiscal or political risks are elevated.

The firm attributes its position to nearly two decades of local expertise and reputation in the region, which it says give it differentiated access and let it devise innovative solutions for complex situations. The piece itself makes no forward-looking call, and its disclaimer stresses that the award reflects activity from November 2024 to November 2025 and is not indicative of future performance.

What Does the Growth in Power Demand Mean for Investors?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that surging power demand, the fastest growth since the 1950s to 1970s, is pushing the energy sector to replace ageing infrastructure and build new capacity, and that this requires a mix of technologies (renewables, gas, coal and nuclear) balanced against security, affordability, environmental and decarbonisation goals. Its explicit view, voiced by Steve Porto of Ares Infrastructure Equity, is that access to affordable, predictable energy creates a "big investment opportunity" for the firm.

pieces.title: Why Now for GP-Led Secondaries
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that GP-led secondaries, where a fund manager moves existing assets into a continuation vehicle, have become a lasting feature of private markets, with CVs rising to 16% of private equity exit value in 2025 from 5% in 2020 and the segment now around 50% of secondary volume. The firm contends the asset class offers high-quality, already-performing assets with 18–20%+ gross underwriting targets, lower loss ratios than primary buyout, and a built-in return boost from value created between signing and closing, while positioning GP-led deals as the "alpha" complement to LP-led "beta" exposure. Its explicit call is that GP-led secondaries are a structural, long-term allocation for investors focused on capital appreciation with downside protection, though the figures cited are largely Ares-sourced or drawn from third-party sponsors and are unaudited.

pieces.title: 2026 investment outlook
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers expects macroeconomic volatility to ease in 2026, with a base case of 1.5% developed-market growth, 2% inflation and 3.5% emerging-market growth, and forecasts returns across asset classes converging at around 5%, driven by carry and price appreciation. The firm's explicit calls are for convertible bonds, Asian listed markets and genuinely decarbonising high-carbon companies in equities, and for GP-led secondaries, energy-transition infrastructure and hedge funds within alternatives, while stressing diversification given risks such as a less accommodative Federal Reserve or a derating of US tech stocks.

View from the markets: Asia may not follow US rate hikes - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chi Lo argues that, although the US Federal Reserve remains in tightening mode amid persistent energy-driven and AI-related inflation, Asian central banks may not follow it with widespread rate hikes. Asia's policy decisions are shaped by wider targets, notably the exchange rate, growth and bond yields, and by the region's large current account surpluses, which cushion currencies, along with subsidies that have so far contained oil-induced inflation. The firm's explicit view is that Asia is far from a broad-based rate-hike cycle, and that a hawkish Fed would likely produce only a tightening bias unless rate differentials cause large, persistent regional currency depreciation, with a sustained oil shock being the main route to wider hikes.

pieces.title: Positioning government bond portfolios for a higher yield environment
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that government bond yields have risen to multi-decade highs primarily due to higher real yields rather than inflation expectations, driven by elevated government borrowing, reduced central bank demand, and increased private sector participation in bond markets. The firm takes a constructive view on duration, particularly at the long end of US, Japanese and Australian government bond curves, where it sees the best opportunities due to a combination of attractive valuations and technical support from restricted supply and potential institutional demand.

pieces.title: CLOs: Opportunity Amid Growing Dispersion
pieces.summary: Barings argues that CLO market dispersion has widened since January's spread compression, driven by the Iran war, AI-related disruption, private credit scrutiny and persistent inflation. Senior tranches have held up, while BB and BBB mezzanine tranches have been more volatile, so outcomes now hinge on collateral quality, issuer-level credit analysis and manager selection. Barings sees a "constructive, but selective" outlook: it favours AAA and AA tranches for durable floating-rate income, views wider mezzanine spreads as attractive for higher-quality deals with limited tail risk, and regards CLO equity as opportunistic, mainly in discounted secondary positions.

The firm's explicit calls include a long duration bias in markets such as the UK and Brazil, expectations of multiple US Federal Reserve cuts that should steepen yield curves, a long yen position versus the US dollar on the view that the Bank of Japan will tighten further, and a short position in corporate credit at the start of the year, with a readiness to add exposure if spreads widen.

pieces.title: Gemcast Ep 11: Developed market private credit under strain

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that global growth will remain resilient over the next six to twelve months despite widening risks, supported by three buffers: continued AI investment spending, consumers and China's ability to absorb higher energy costs, and central banks' measured policy approach. The asset manager contends that elevated bond yields now offer attractive income potential and downside protection, and recommends selective positioning in credit and AI-related investments with focus on adequate risk compensation. PIMCO cautions that these buffers are interconnected and vulnerable to shocks from fading AI investment, worsening energy prices, or deteriorating financial conditions, which current asset valuations may not fully reflect.

It contends that, with valuations reset and fundamentals stabilising, the segment offers insurers differentiated risk-return profiles, regulatory advantages and structural protections, and it urges insurers to reassess its role in portfolios and match exposures to their liability structures and regulatory requirements.

Citing a 2022 Cerulli Associates study, the piece says direct indexing assets are projected to grow at a 12.3% compound annual rate, and it explicitly urges advisers to adopt systematic tax-loss harvesting and tax-managed transitions, warning that those not doing so may be leaving tax benefits "on the table."

The firm contends that these funds suit professional investors such as treasurers and insurers who prioritise capital stability over yield, and that they can complement bank deposits by diversifying counterparty risk. The text ends mid-sentence, before the promised section on what to look for in a manager, so its full set of criteria is not captured.

pieces.title: Power of Stress Testing with Aladdin Wealth
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that stress testing is a valuable risk management tool for wealth managers, enabling advisors to communicate portfolio risks to clients through historical and hypothetical market scenarios while also allowing firms to monitor risk across their entire business. The company promotes its Aladdin Wealth platform as capable of conducting stress tests at multiple organisational levels, incorporating current portfolio exposures rather than historical returns to provide more accurate assessments of how current holdings would perform under past or simulated future market events. BlackRock positions stress testing as essential for building client trust, aligning portfolios with stated goals, and enabling firms to respond quickly to market disruptions.

Systematic investing
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that systematic investing—combining alternative data, machine learning and human expertise—can improve investment outcomes across equities, fixed income and alternatives. The firm advocates for technology-driven portfolio construction using data-driven insights and scientific testing, and presents research supporting factor-based strategies, portable alpha approaches, and systematic methods applied to private markets and hedge funds. BlackRock's output suggests it views systematic, quantitative approaches as increasingly essential for managing concentration risk, capturing alpha, and constructing resilient multi-asset portfolios.

It points to long-term contracts (typically 10 to 20 years, with minimum-bill protections) underpinning durable earnings growth for utilities such as Entergy, and to behind-the-meter gas-turbine power providers such as Solaris and Williams as a growing contracted market. Its explicit call is that recent share price weakness in utilities, despite strong earnings outlooks, creates an attractive entry point for an undervalued sector, which investors can access selectively through active strategies.

pieces.title: Strong Earnings and a Resilient Economy Power S&P 500 to a New High
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments' weekly viewpoint reports that the S&P 500 rose 2.3% in the week to 8 May 2026, its sixth straight weekly gain, on a ceasefire in the US-Iran conflict, strong Q1 earnings (aggregate growth of 25.3% year on year, with 81% of reporting companies beating expectations) and a resilient labour market. Guggenheim says the outlook through year-end remains favourable and, while acknowledging the index is overbought and due a period of consolidation, it would view any setback as a good buying opportunity, citing a supportive macro backdrop and its expectation that the Fed will still cut rates at least once this year. The note also flags Fed officials' hawkish caution on inflation and the Iran-related risks to rates, although markets price little chance of a cut before year-end.

pieces.title: Today’s private credit opportunity
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that private credit represents a major growth opportunity as private firms stay private longer and bank lending evolves, with the asset class expected to double from $2.1T to over $4T by 2030. The firm contends that innovation—including lower entry points, better liquidity and greater transparency—is democratising access to private credit for retail and retirement investors, positioning it as a core portfolio allocation alongside public securities rather than an alternative investment. BlackRock's implicit call is that investors should consider private credit as a standard component of diversified portfolios, supported by its recent acquisitions in the sector to expand client access.
