pieces.title: View from the markets: Is this the new (old) normal for government bond yields? - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's chief market strategist, Daniel Morris, argues that government bond sell-offs will persist, with the driver shifting from oil prices to strong US growth (Q2 GDP revised up to 2.2%) and risks of overheating and further Fed hikes. He suggests yields could partially normalise towards 1980s–1990s levels, where 10-year Treasury yields exceeded nominal GDP growth, so US yields above 5% may be more likely than below, though he judges this less damaging than the 2022 rise given the lower debt-service burden relative to budgets. He also notes that oil around $100 per barrel reflects a split between normalising Strait of Hormuz flows (pointing towards $70) and a risk of sharply higher prices if Iran's control of the strait breaks down.

pieces.title: Small business owners: Big opportunities to save for retirement
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that small businesses are underserved on retirement saving, with only 55% of firms under 50 employees offering a workplace plan, and that the barriers of cost and administration have largely fallen thanks to SECURE 2.0 tax credits and bundled, off-the-shelf plan products. It calls on small business owners to treat a workplace plan as feasible and worthwhile, both for their own retirement and their staff's, and to start by checking state mandates, employer contribution policy, cost and administrative duties, available credits, and whether a ready-made or customisable solution suits them best.

pieces.title: Systematic Insights:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that high yield bonds may now be structurally less risky than in the past, citing five factors: improving credit quality (a rising share of BB-rated issuers), a shift of highly leveraged LBO financing to private credit, record-low duration, stronger issuer fundamentals with default losses averaging below 1% a year over five years, and a lower beta to equities. The firm's explicit view is that high yield may deserve a permanent, core role in diversified portfolios, positioned as the "missing link" between investment grade corporates and higher-risk markets such as private credit, particularly for investors seeking income and diversification.

pieces.title: Quick View: Another one bites the dust at the top of UK politics

The company contends that firms using the right multi-faceted technology provider—rather than assembling disparate components themselves—can recapture fees, reduce costs and provide better client value whilst managing the operational complexity of personalised portfolio construction at scale.

pieces.title: Navigating AI concentration risks in liability-aware portfolios
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that AI-related issuance is raising concentration risk in fixed income, particularly for liability-aware investors such as DB pension plans. Hyperscalers' share of the US investment grade market has risen from about 3% to 5% over five years, and roughly 35% of AA long corporates, a common basis for pension discount curves, though Insight's modelling suggests a full downgrade of AA hyperscalers would lower longer-dated yields by only up to 6bp, or 20–40bp on pension obligations. Insight's explicit recommendation is that plan sponsors should monitor these effects and review how their discount curves are constructed, since yield-maximising filters could make curves more sensitive to hyperscaler pricing and sudden downgrades.

Where to invest in stocks amidst the AI selloff?

Morgan Asset Management argues that the recent AI-related selloffs, in July and from October to mid-November 2026, reflect a rotation in investor focus rather than a broken AI thesis, with the market shifting from rewarding AI capex builders to rewarding AI adoption and monetisation. It expects hyperscaler capex to reach about $1.2 trillion in 2027 but to slow meaningfully thereafter as financing costs rise, and it favours quality over momentum, selective hyperscalers and software companies with competitive positions, and non-tech sectors such as financials, health care and industrials as AI adoption winners. The firm also advises investors to review portfolio diversification given the likely continued volatility.

pieces.title: Pensions & Investments Ring the Bell: 2025 Influential Women in Institutional Investing

PGIM presents this recognition as reflecting Marcus's leadership, industry impact and commitment to advancing women in finance, with her background in business, architecture and the built environment contributing to the firm's performance.

pieces.title: The case for a smarter approach to global equities
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that rising market concentration has rendered traditional global equity allocations less effective and advocates a hybrid approach that deploys passive management in efficient, well-researched markets such as US large-caps whilst deploying active management in less efficient areas such as US small and mid-caps and ex-US stocks where stock selection can add value. The firm contends this pragmatic allocation strategy is more likely to generate outperformance than purely passive or active approaches.

pieces.title: 2026 Direct Lending Outlook
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management's 2026 Direct Lending Outlook says that U.S. middle market direct lending deal flow slowed sharply after the April 2025 tariff announcement, then recovered after Labor Day as policy uncertainty eased, and it now sees the market as back at its favourable early-2025 level. Principal's explicit view is that improving economic clarity, Fed easing and the roughly $2 trillion of private equity dry powder should drive higher transaction volumes in 2026, creating "an environment ripe with attractive investment opportunities," with lower and core middle market direct lending offering compelling risk-adjusted returns and protection from broadly syndicated loan (BSL) and public market volatility. The piece also cautions that the path will likely "take a few twists and turns."

pieces.title: Chart to Watch: When bond markets move together
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that the third quarter of 2026 saw an unusually large and tightly synchronised rise in 10-year government bond yields across the US, UK and Europe: US Treasuries rose 82bps, German Bunds 72.5bps and UK gilts 66.7bps, the narrowest spread among major synchronised selloffs since 2000. The firm argues this points to common forces increasingly driving sovereign bond markets, which may erode the diversification benefits of geographic spread, so investors should focus on the sources and concentration of their duration exposure rather than assume geographic diversification alone will mitigate risk. It cautions, however, that a single quarter does not establish a new regime.

The firm, through Mark Affolter, Co-Head of SME, calls women's sports "under-monetized" and says Ares sees Asia and venue-led real estate as areas where it expects to invest more capital, concluding that institutional capital and infrastructure have not yet caught up with audience demand.

pieces.title: Global uncertainty gives way to opportunity in bond and equity markets - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that global equity and bond markets are resilient despite Middle East and Iran-related tensions, which have pushed up energy prices and inflation expectations. In fixed income, it sees opportunities in short-duration bonds, high-yield credit (around 7% in the US and 6% in Europe) and selected emerging market bonds, while expecting the Fed and Bank of England to hold rates through 2026. In equities, it takes a "cautious optimism" view, pointing to upward earnings revisions for 2026, tech valuations near long-term averages, and opportunities in emerging market tech, European defence and industrials, Japan and, if the Fed cuts, US small caps.

pieces.title: Systematic Insights:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that global high yield deserves a place alongside global equities and global aggregate bonds, citing a $2.8trn market that is diversified across regions, historically offered better risk-adjusted returns than US high yield (currency-hedged) and similar returns to pan-European high yield with lower volatility, and can deliver competitive yield once hedging costs are considered (euro high yield at roughly 7.4% hedged versus 6.8% for US high yield). The firm's explicit view is that global high yield may add robustness and a potentially compelling source of higher yield to risk allocations, supported by the improved credit quality of the US market (over 50% BB-rated, around 20% secured) and mild defaults since the pandemic.

pieces.title: Absolute return: why discipline matters in today's market

The piece makes explicit calls on both sides of the book: it sees long opportunities in select financials, European aerospace and defence, and rate-sensitive assets such as utilities, real estate and quality housebuilders, and short opportunities in companies facing cost-price mismatches (such as hotels and leisure), US consumer names facing rising competition, and policy-sensitive businesses. Grant calls for breakthroughs in batteries, grids and demand response to counter the inflexibility of supply, and for carbon reduction or capture, including gas with carbon capture, to be pursued at lowest cost. He also argues that carbon transparency and regulation along the value chain are needed so that end-consumers' preference for lower-carbon products can reward producers upstream.

pieces.title: February 2021
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that current low interest rates and asset valuations depend on an increasingly fragile assumption that this regime will persist, despite unprecedented peacetime sovereign debt accumulation following Covid-19 fiscal support that far exceeds the economic shock. The firm identifies a critical risk: if long-term yields rise above growth rates, the intellectual consensus justifying large deficits would collapse, as governments could no longer stabilise debt-to-GDP ratios, yet investors have recently foregone traditional risk compensation on government bonds despite their increased riskiness. BlackRock does not make an explicit tactical call but implies that this debt tolerance warrants close monitoring as a key determinant of future asset allocation outcomes.

Its real estate analysis says rent growth since 2023 has not kept pace with rising discount rates, creating a "double hit" of slower NOI growth and higher required returns, while infrastructure's inflation linkage runs through contracts and regulation and transportation assets reprice through renewal and capacity cycles. The firm's explicit view is that future returns will rely more on current income and growth than on multiple expansion, so investors should separate risk-free rate moves from changes in the equity risk premium in scenario analysis.

pieces.summary: Evelyn Partners argues that US private credit stress, though real after the First Brands and Tricolor collapses and the early-2026 sell-off in software loans, is unlikely on its own to trigger a systemic credit crunch comparable to 2008. It supports this with four points: the sector is small (about 4% of private non-financial credit), funds are heavily equity-financed (65–80% of assets versus around 10% for banks), portfolios are diversified across sectors, and fund lifetimes align with loan maturities. The firm's explicit view is that the market's structural features provide resilience, though it acknowledges that the sector faces its first sustained period of stress in years.

The discussion covers the 2026 macro and rate outlook, the diversification and risk-management benefits of absolute-return bonds, and the strategic role of emerging-market debt. pieces.title: Direct lending selective exposure
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that a more selective direct lending market makes disciplined underwriting and careful manager evaluation more important, as performance dispersion across borrowers and managers widens and outcomes increasingly reflect each manager's process rather than broad market conditions. It highlights the traditional middle market as an area of opportunity for risk-adjusted returns, citing pricing and structural features, and urges investors to select managers whose approach stays consistent across market environments rather than simply allocating to direct lending. The piece also stresses looking beyond financial metrics to where risk lies, and ongoing monitoring after closing, while closing with promotional links to Fidelity's private credit and alternative investment strategies.

Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S. economy remains resilient, with growth near 2% in 2026, a softening labour market (non-farm payrolls averaging just 17,000 to 22,000 a month over three and six months), and inflation drifting towards the Fed's 2% target, though still above it. It expects the Fed to keep an easing bias, with the fed funds lower bound moving towards 3.00%–3.25% and cuts slowing, and it concludes that money market funds and ultra-short duration portfolios are well positioned to offer attractive returns and stability for cash investors. It also flags risks including a possible government shutdown, a K-shaped economy, and concentrated AI-equity and private-credit concerns.

It describes private placements, typically senior, fixed-rate and longer-term debt from institutional investors, as one funding route alongside bank and public markets. PGIM's explicit position is that getting the refinancing process right can help companies unlock new opportunities and achieve their strategic goals, and it illustrates this with its work for Centerspace.

pieces.title: Alpha models for data-abundance
pieces.summary: BlackRock describes its Augmented Investment Management (AIM) system, a machine learning platform launched in 2014 that combines vast investment signals with human expertise to design systematic alpha models. The firm argues that machine learning enables portfolio managers to optimise signal combination more efficiently than traditional discretionary methods, whilst customising models to perform better during negative market regimes by overweighting adverse historical conditions in training data. BlackRock identifies signal decay and regime-specific overfitting as ongoing challenges, and indicates it is researching adaptive algorithms and macroeconomic indicators to improve model resilience over time.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that decumulation, the post-retirement phase of converting pensions into income, is fundamentally different from accumulation and needs a new approach, since no single product can meet the shifting trade-offs between income, liquidity, growth, protection and longevity. Its explicit view is that the future lies in personalised, system-based solutions, combining AI, governance, advice and modular investment components to deliver individualised retirement outcomes at scale.

pieces.title: Keep saving
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece urges investors in their 30s and 40s to keep contributing to workplace 401(k) plans despite competing financial priorities, arguing that this helps keep retirement goals on track and captures the long-term benefits of tax-deferred growth. Illustrating the point with a hypothetical comparison of $5,000 annual contributions from age 25 at a 6% return, PGIM contends that time combined with tax deferral can significantly enlarge retirement savings relative to a taxable account. The remainder of the page is site navigation and cookie and terms boilerplate, so the substance is limited to this single message.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris describes Q2 2026 earnings as a "blowout", with S&P 500 earnings up 26% year on year and emerging market technology profits more than doubling, yet equities have fallen since late June, driven by higher oil prices, a hawkish-leaning bond market and a sharp correction in Korean and Taiwanese tech. The firm argues the tech sell-off reflects stretched positioning and a recalibration of earnings outlooks rather than a fundamental reassessment of profits, and says that with valuations now more attractive there is potential for a sustained recovery at some point. It also expects non-tech markets, supported by AI-spending spillovers and resilient US consumer demand, to hold up in the near term.

The firm states that foreign inflows of almost JPY 10 trillion have shifted towards long-only cash equities, that valuations remain reasonable at around 17x earnings, and that the earnings benefit from AI capex "is only just beginning" and may not yet be reflected in share prices. pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris argues that equity markets and credit spreads signal the Iran war is effectively over, though oil at $99 a barrel and still-elevated government bond yields suggest otherwise. The firm's multi-asset team is overweight risk, reasoning that investors still in risk-off positions may be able to exit at better prices, since the Middle East situation is unlikely to resolve smoothly and a resumption of hostilities cannot be ruled out. It also flags the upcoming Q2 earnings season as the next driver, with high expectations for emerging market hardware and Nasdaq 100 companies.

pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that its early, long-standing focus on sports, media and entertainment (SME) gives it a durable edge: it began investing in 2007, and it says the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift from high-net-worth ownership towards institutional private capital. The firm credits its flexible full-capital-structure mandate, geographically and sector-diversified portfolio, and active board-level engagement with building one of the most resilient institutional track records in the category. Its explicit view is that the sector's opportunity set, including adjacent businesses across ticketing, data, hospitality, music and venues, remains large (it cites a nearly $3 trillion market) and will keep expanding.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Software Stuck in a Trough
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that credit risk in software is likely understated: weaker growth and less reliable sponsor support could lift defaults over time, even though near-term refinancing pressure is low, and losses in a sector-led default cycle could exceed expectations because recoveries tend to fall when distressed supply concentrates. It also warns that BDC valuations look stable only because opaque, stale marks compress price dispersion, so private credit values could reset sharply under stress, and it therefore advocates selectivity, downside mitigation, and caution toward strategies reliant on smooth reported valuations.

pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the roughly 50% rise in announced AI-related capex by major US technology firms, to around USD 700bn in 2026 (about 2.3% of GDP), gives the US economy short-term cyclical protection through direct and multiplier effects. The firm's main caveat is that this buffer depends on equity markets: it contends that a sustained stock market correction could weaken consumption through a negative wealth effect, which US spending has relied on in recent years, and so offset some of the capex stimulus. The piece frames the key question as quantitative, namely how large and how persistent a market decline would need to be to cancel out the AI investment boost.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that sustainability is central to helping investors navigate a world reshaped by environmental pressures, technology, demographic shifts and geopolitics, and that integrating ESG considerations with financial analysis helps identify material risks and opportunities. The piece, based on an interview with Chief Sustainability Officer Jane Ambachtsheer, presents the firm's updated Global Sustainability Strategy to 2030 as a way to connect sustainable investment practice with long-term returns, which it describes as its underlying ambition. Its explicit view is that traditional financial analysis alone is insufficient to capture today's risks and opportunities.

pieces.title: European equities: Strategic reforms set the stage for growth
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Robert Schramm-Fuchs, argues that European equities are well positioned for further progress in 2026, supported by strategic reforms (notably in Germany and at EU level, including bank capital and securitisation changes), easing trade tensions, and early signs of a global macroeconomic rebound, though geopolitical risks remain. The firm's explicit view is that banks, defence, electrification and grid investment, semiconductor equipment, civil aerospace, luxury goods and globally exposed companies with strong US revenues all offer upside, with European equities presenting attractive entry points.

pieces.title: ESG outlook: How are responsible investing trends converging with broader economic realities?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that responsible investing is moving from aspirational ESG ideals to a financially material, results-driven approach, shaped by geopolitical realignment, demographic and lifestyle shifts, and a higher cost of capital. It explicitly rejects blanket exclusions in defence and energy, favouring company-by-company fundamental research and engagement, and says that ESG risks should be weighed as financial inputs. The firm also contends that consumer and healthcare companies most exposed to the "conscious consumer" trend have significantly underperformed, citing its own analysis.

pieces.title: Absolute return bonds for an uncertain world - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that its global absolute return bond strategy suits an uncertain 2026, when inflation and central bank policy are hard to forecast, because it aims for returns of about 2.5% a year above cash (gross of fees) with rolling 12-month drawdowns limited to -2.5%, and its duration can range from -4 to +4 years. The firm's explicit views are that the Bank of Japan will raise rates, so it is overweight the yen against the dollar; that the Fed will cut several times later in 2026 to steepen the yield curve; that UK and Brazilian rate cuts are underpriced, supporting an overweight to interest rate risk in the first half; and that New Zealand rate hikes are priced in prematurely. It also favours US agency mortgage-backed securities and remains underweight corporate credit.

Morgan Asset Management argues that the historical relationship between Treasury yields and equity prices has weakened since mid-2021, with the critical yield threshold at which stocks begin to suffer higher yields having shifted downward over time from 4.5% (1965-2008) to 3.5% (2009-2021). The firm attributes this looser correlation to inflation shocks dominating market concerns and, more significantly, to the outsized influence of the "Magnificent Seven" technology companies, which now comprise 40% of the S&P 500 and are driven primarily by artificial intelligence investment cycles rather than broader economic conditions. J.P. Morgan Asset Management suggests that the AI capital expenditure boom and the hyperscalers' ability to monetise that investment may allow equities and bond yields to move independently regardless of current yield levels.

pieces.title: Where to invest as US equities rise | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that US equities remain positioned for further growth, driven by resilient corporate earnings, AI investment spending and supportive monetary policy, with the firm highlighting that US equity ETFs have attracted substantial inflows as investors return to the market. The asset manager presents a range of iShares ETFs—from broad-based S&P 500 exposure to technology-focused funds—as investment options to capture this trend, emphasising that technology sector expansion and AI-related capital investment are the primary engines of US economic growth.

pieces.title: Swiss policy prudence
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the Swiss National Bank's decision to hold its policy rate at 0% was a prudent, wait-and-see response to Middle East-driven uncertainty, with the real interest lying in its medium-term growth and inflation outlook and its stance on the franc. The firm views the energy price spike as a timely offset to Swiss disinflation, though it could weigh on growth, and sees the recent franc appreciation (about 2.5% on a trade-weighted basis) as within tolerance. It expects the SNB to intervene in FX markets only to dampen volatility, not to push the currency lower, and does not anticipate further monetary policy changes this year, supported by Switzerland's wide interest rate differential with other countries.

The asset manager advocates building diversified global equity portfolios through conviction-led stock selection combined with risk management, positioned around secular themes including "Net Zero 2.0"—a market-driven transition underpinned by cost competitiveness, AI infrastructure demand and energy security concerns in an increasingly multipolar world.

Fortress explicitly positions itself as one of the earliest private credit providers, dating to the early 2000s, and states that "not all private credit platforms are created equal." The piece is a promotional video rather than a data-driven report, so its claims about Fortress's differentiation are unverified.

The firm presents a checklist for trustees and providers to test whether a given approach delivers confidence to spend, responsible income management and later-life security.

The firm argues that with constrained domestic policy options, President Trump would likely pivot towards areas of greater discretionary control such as trade and foreign policy, whilst political brinkmanship over the debt ceiling could create budget standoffs and shutdown threats.

pieces.title: Europe investment opportunity
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Europe's decade of underperformance versus the U.S. stems from structural weaknesses—lower productivity, regulatory burdens and a shrinking workforce—but that recent geopolitical shocks have prompted meaningful reform efforts in defence spending and energy policy. The firm takes a selective approach to European investing, identifying near-term opportunities in defence technology, financials as infrastructure conduits, and private equity in advanced manufacturing and infrastructure.

pieces.title: Better together: Unlocking stronger results across the housing sector
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management argues that U.S. housing is a segmented ecosystem with a structural shortage of roughly three million homes, driven by underbuilding, zoning, and build costs, and that this imbalance is not temporary. Its subsectors (multifamily, affordable, build-to-rent, senior, student and manufactured housing) respond differently to interest rates and GDP growth, so Brookfield contends that a diversified allocation across them can enhance returns, reduce volatility and provide downside protection for institutional capital. The piece is effectively a case for cross-subsector exposure, with manufactured housing presented as relatively defensive and multifamily as more cyclical.

pieces.title: How inflationary is the oil price spike?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S.-Iran conflict and the resulting energy shock will push U.S. headline CPI, which was 3.3% year-over-year in March, up to a base-case peak of about 4.0% by May, before it drifts lower to around 3.0% by December and below 2.0% by April 2027. It frames three scenarios: re-escalation with inflation above 5% and crude well above $120/barrel; a 2022-style spike peaking near 4% but falling quickly, though with a lower starting point than 2022; and rapid resolution with inflation near peak and declining gradually but still above 3.0% through February 2027. Across all three, the firm concludes that inflation stays above the Fed's 2% target into 2027, so rate cuts remain off the table for now.

pieces.title: Public insights on private credit: The evolving landscape of upper middle-market direct lending
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton's Benefit Street Partners arm argues that upper middle-market direct lending is shifting towards borrower-friendly terms, citing S&P and Morgan Stanley data that show maintenance covenants falling from 97% of deals under $350 million to 38% above $1 billion, and PIK toggles rising from 3% to 44% over the same range. The firm contends this convergence with the syndicated loan market is a structural rather than cyclical change, and it suggests that opportunity and resilience may lie instead in the core and lower middle markets, where covenant strength and relationship-driven origination remain prevalent.

pieces.title: Partner Story: Port of Tyne
pieces.summary: PGIM's partner story profiles Port of Tyne, a trust port in South Shields servicing container, RoRo, automotive, biomass, cruise and bulk customers, and presents PGIM's £45 million 10-year Senior Secured Notes (2023) as long-term patient capital that lets the port plan decades ahead and supports regional jobs in Northeast England. PGIM frames the relationship as a trusted, long-term partnership built on personal knowledge of the company and regional conditions, and its infrastructure finance team positions long-term debt for infrastructure assets as its offering.

pieces.title: Balanced forces, remaining uncertainty

What’s behind the divergence between international and U.S. tech?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that international technology stocks decoupled from U.S. tech in late 2025 and early 2026, with the MSCI ACWI ex USA Information Technology Index moving sharply higher while U.S. tech traded sideways to lower. The firm attributes the rally mainly to upward earnings revisions linked to AI infrastructure spending, not multiple expansion, since non-U.S. forward P/E ratios have compressed. It explicitly maintains that the discount to U.S. tech remains historically wide, that non-U.S. markets offer good opportunities in firms benefiting from AI investment rather than being disrupted by it, and that recent sell-offs triggered by Middle East tensions do not alter its view of the underlying fundamentals.

pieces.title: Why insurers are reassessing senior securitisations
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that changes to Solvency UK and Solvency II are prompting insurers to reassess senior securitised credit, which they largely avoided after the financial crisis partly because of capital and operational barriers. It contends that UK and European insurers are notably underweight securitisation compared with US peers, and that high-quality senior CLOs, alongside selected RMBS, ABS and CMBS, could offer resilient income and diversification if capital treatment becomes more risk-appropriate. M&G stresses that realising this opportunity still depends on careful collateral and structural analysis, ongoing monitoring and robust manager oversight, and that its relevance will differ between internal model and standard formula insurers.

pieces.title: Market moves & themes that mattered: September 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that global equities declined in September 2026 as rising bond yields, higher oil prices and geopolitical tensions weighed on markets, with AI-related technology stocks outperforming while most other sectors lagged. The asset manager notes that government bond yields reached multi-decade highs, credit spreads widened and market breadth deteriorated significantly, although strong economic data and continued AI investment demand provided some support to equity markets.

pieces.title: MBS just had its best year since 2002
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that agency mortgage-backed securities had their best calendar year since 2002 in 2025, with the Bloomberg U.S. MBS Index returning 8.58% and 171 basis points of excess return over Treasuries. pieces.title: Making the right moves in the AI age
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that AI is the dominant investment theme of the era, and that investors who ignore it risk missing good returns, but that exposure should not be limited to US mega-cap tech. Morgan Asset Management argues that direct real estate offers diversification and stable income: it has historically shown low or negative correlation to the S&P 500, tends to be less volatile, and generates durable rental income that can hedge inflation and complement fixed income. The piece says real estate correlations spike in recessions but typically revert quickly, and that current price resets may present opportunities. Its explicit view is that sector selection matters, favouring industrial (data centres, warehouses, logistics) and apartments, which show strong demand, while cautioning that offices face challenges from hybrid working and excess supply.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that derivatives can help Asia-Pacific insurers manage asset-liability risk and capital under risk-based capital regimes, letting them adjust duration, currency and equity exposures without continually trading physical holdings. It cites Europe's Solvency II experience and offers examples, including decomposed cross-currency hedges and option-based equity programmes that it says could cut capital requirements by up to 40% while preserving up to 80% of equity returns. The firm stresses, however, that such strategies need strong governance, counterparty, collateral and liquidity controls, and clear evidence that positions serve a hedging purpose rather than speculation.

pieces.title: Beyond winners and losers: How to position a sustainable portfolio for the AI era
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Global Sustainable Equities team argues that AI should not be read as a simple winners-and-losers trade, and that the market's binary framing creates mispricing a long-horizon, sustainability-led process can exploit. It sorts companies across the AI value chain into four lenses (AI Enablers, Physical Bottlenecks, AI Beneficiaries and AI Resilient businesses), while keeping its two existing tests of whether a company makes the world better and can create long-term wealth. The firm explicitly states that AI has made disciplined, sustainability-led stock selection more valuable, and that its portfolio deliberately balances exposure across all four lenses, with AI Beneficiaries (where many current holdings sit) and AI Resilient businesses acting as ballast against the AI narrative.

pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that its 25 years of operating through the global financial crisis, COVID-19 and the recent regional bank failures have taught it how credit markets behave under stress and where risks lie, with those lessons now built into its underwriting and processes. Co-CEO Jack Neumark states that the firm's experience, reflected in its people, culture and borrower relationships as well as its models, was an advantage when banks retreated from lending, allowing Fortress to deploy established strategies. The piece's explicit message is that experience matters most when markets test assumptions, though it offers no specific forecasts or investment recommendations.

Global Living: Tapping into Structural Growth
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that structural shortages in housing across major cities, driven by high mortgage rates, urbanisation, planning constraints and build costs, make living-sector real estate a compelling, needs-based opportunity with predictable cashflows and relatively low risk. It contends that demographic shifts (ageing populations, student and graduate demand, rising family rental demand) support elevated occupancy and rental growth, while noting that opportunities vary by region, with US suburban and senior housing, and European development routes, looking most attractive. PGIM also states that the sector is becoming more operational, as scaled management platforms and non-traditional segments such as student, senior and micro-living drive returns, with unlevered total returns expected to remain elevated in the US.

Its explicit view is that these segments face supply bottlenecks and favourable industry structures, including rationalised memory pricing and foundry capacity allocated to GPUs, which should sustain pricing power over the near to mid term

View from the markets: Is emerging market equity outperformance sustainable? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, argues that emerging market equities' recent outperformance, roughly double the MSCI World's US dollar return since the start of 2025, follows a long period of underperformance from 2010, and that its durability depends on whether gains in Chinese internet retail and interactive media rebound or tech hardware and semiconductor stocks keep rising. The firm views the hardware and semiconductor outlook as the stronger of the two, citing robust earnings growth and upward forecast revisions, and judges that hyperscaler capital spending is likely to continue in the near term regardless of doubts about its long-term profitability. It also notes that Chinese software stocks trade at roughly half US multiples, but cautions that low valuations do not guarantee superior returns.

pieces.title: Could 8 be a lucky number in US high yield bonds?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that US high yield bonds yielding above 8% may present an attractive entry point, citing historical data showing that 12-month returns have been positive in most instances when yields were at current levels, supported by strong corporate fundamentals and low default rates. The asset manager notes that current yields of 8.2% sit at the 54th percentile of historical data since 1994, suggesting yields have spent roughly equal time above and below this level, and argues that the starting yield is one of the best indicators of future fixed income returns.

What Is Driving Demand for Digital Infrastructure?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that demand for digital infrastructure, led by AI workloads and cloud expansion from the largest hyperscalers, is very strong, citing an estimated $7 trillion data centre buildout over five years (per a April 2025 McKinsey report) and $600–700 billion of data centre investment from the five largest hyperscalers this year alone. Its explicit view is that structural supply constraints (limited energy, tight supply chains, construction labour shortages, complex permitting and restricted access to suitable land) mean oversupply is unlikely and that the sector offers a compelling opportunity, with Ares Digital Infrastructure focusing on top-tier markets, hyperscale tenants, strong contracts and robust product design to achieve durable outperformance.

The paper stresses that implementation (strategy duration, funding source and accounting treatment) must be assessed against volatility, Solvency Capital Requirement and IFRS constraints, and it presents the euro high-yield universe as compatible with insurers' climate commitments. Its explicit stance is that high yield merits consideration as a complement to investment-grade holdings, with the caveat that its higher credit risk and volatility require careful integration.

Aberdeen's stated view is that Sacks remains constructive on emerging markets, that active management is beneficial in Asia, and that the portfolio is overweight China relative to the index, with attractive valuation opportunities identified.

pieces.title: Demystifying and simplifying investing
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that low financial literacy and misconceptions about investing are barriers to European retail investment, citing surveys showing only 18% of EU citizens have high financial literacy and 81% of French respondents fear losing their savings. The company calls for improved financial education and simplified, affordable investment products—such as exchange-traded funds—alongside supportive policy, positioning retail investment as essential for Europe's economic resilience and capital market development.

The firm argues that sustainability must be integrated into portfolio construction because it drives material investment risks and opportunities, and that investors should review their strategic asset allocation to ensure resilience to post-pandemic trends.

The firm argues that active management across rates, credit and securitised assets—rather than benchmark-constrained investing—better enables portfolio managers to adapt to changing market conditions and capture opportunities as leadership shifts between different bond market segments.

pieces.summary: PGIM argues that private markets are becoming a more strategic allocation and that a single multi-asset framework, combining private equity for growth, private credit for income and private real assets for income, inflation sensitivity and diversification, can be more effective than static allocations to each class. It also contends that flexibility to shift exposures as relative opportunities change, and a direct investment structure with fewer fee layers and more control than fund-of-funds, matter as much as the allocation itself. The supporting evidence is a set of annual private asset class returns from 2016 to 2025 and a hypothetical historical analysis of model allocations, which PGIM presents as illustrating diversification benefits rather than as a forecast.

pieces.title: Ares Management on Finding Value in Today’s Credit Markets
pieces.summary: In a podcast episode hosted by Lonsec, Ares Management partner and portfolio manager Samantha Milner describes the firm's global credit approach, which draws on its scale, cross-platform collaboration and direct lending data to inform credit selection. Ares states that its fund targets consistent income with a focus on capital preservation, moving up in quality during uncertainty and rotating into higher-yielding credit when risk-off conditions create dislocations.

pieces.title: European CRE: Uncertainty Extends the Opportunity
pieces.summary: Barings argues that European commercial real estate's recovery has been postponed by Middle East tensions, which have revived inflation concerns and raised the prospect of two ECB rate rises, though it expects these to be more modest than before. Despite this, Barings sees the market as resilient, citing chronic shortages of modern space, a falling development pipeline and rising rents, and it does not expect significant value shifts. It concludes that renewed uncertainty will slow the transaction recovery but extend the opportunity to buy at attractive prices, and it advises investing structurally in enduring trends such as demographics, technology and ESG, particularly for inflation protection.

pieces.title: Torsten Slok’s Mid-Year Outlook: Three Forces Driving Markets
pieces.summary: Apollo's Chief Economist, Torsten Slok, outlines his mid-year 2026 view of three forces shaping markets: the AI boom, which he argues extends well beyond technology, an industrial renaissance reshaping manufacturing and investment, and government policy supporting growth. The piece also covers implications for inflation, interest rates, asset allocation and credit markets, but the excerpt gives no expl

pieces.summary: PGIM's interview with Morgan Laughlin, its Global Head of Digital Infrastructure, argues that AI is splitting the data centre market into large-scale AI training campuses and low-latency infrastructure serving cloud, enterprise and retail users, and that the more durable value may lie in the latter. PGIM's stated view is that structural supply constraints in key metropolitan markets make low-latency, cloud-capable assets more attractive than headline AI demand growth, with Laughlin saying the firm is "more comfortable investing in a low-supply story than an overwhelming demand thesis." The piece also points to growing institutional allocations to digital infrastructure and an asset-level, real estate-led approach as PGIM's differentiated lens on the sector.

pieces.title: Higher yields, more room for error | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock's iShares division argues that Australian government bond yields have risen sufficiently to provide a meaningful buffer against further increases, with the starting income now able to absorb approximately 92 basis points of additional yield rises before one-year returns turn negative—a substantially better risk-reward proposition than the 28 basis point buffer available at the start of 2022. The piece attributes recent yield increases to a combination of domestic factors, including a July CPI surprise that has raised the probability of further RBA rate hikes to around 70 per cent by September, alongside global pressures from oil prices, hawkish Fed communications and Japan's bond sell-off. BlackRock implicitly endorses taking on interest rate risk at current yields whilst offering its Enhanced Cash and Credit Income Active ETFs as alternatives for investors with lower risk tolerance.

pieces.title: Research in focus: Quarterly sector update
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' quarterly sector update reports that global equities extended their gains in Q4 2025, helped by resilient U.S. growth, solid earnings, easing trade concerns and two further Federal Reserve rate cuts, with healthcare, materials and financials leading and real estate and consumer sectors lagging. The firm argues that AI demand is a powerful cross-sector theme and, given valuation concerns and policy uncertainty, says investors should focus on companies aligned with durable secular trends such as AI adoption, electrification, digitisation and healthcare innovation. It also takes a constructive view on utilities, which it expects to benefit from AI-driven electricity demand, while remaining defensive on energy because it sees more downside than upside risk for oil prices.

pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that combining a quantitative model with independent fundamental research gives investors broader return opportunities in a core equity portfolio at relatively low tracking error, and it reports that its 10-year tests of the model found higher average returns for stocks scored attractive than for those scored unattractive, across slow-, moderate- and fast-growth companies. It also reports that fundamental analysts, across more than 80 AB active strategies, identified stocks with positive return potential even where the quantitative model scored them unattractive, particularly among moderate- and faster-growth companies, which the firm presents as evidence that fundamental research adds insight rather than merely confirming the model. The piece's explicit position is that the two research streams should operate independently and that this independence helps mitigate unintended portfolio biases, though the performance data are historical and the article itself notes that past performance does not guarantee future results.

Does war in Iran change the 2026 outlook?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that geopolitical shocks usually fade for US investors, but a conflict in Iran is a notable exception because it threatens energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. It judges that energy shocks can be both recessionary and inflationary, yet cushioned by 2026's relatively strong energy market, spare OPEC+ capacity, record US shale output and the US economy's reduced oil intensity, so sustained conflict is more likely to produce inflation than recession. Its explicit recommendation is that investors stay diversified across asset classes and regions and avoid trying to time the market.

Its explicit view is that a 50% allocation to private markets (private equity, private credit, private real estate and private infrastructure) is the optimal outcome of this approach, illustrated by a hypothetical model portfolio based on historical index returns over 20 years. pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein's piece is a short interview in which analyst Sydney Kyne describes an AI agent she built to automate collecting European insurance fund-flow data, which previously took up much of a morning because regulators publish newsletters in German, Italian and French. The agent ingests the newsletters, translates them, extracts the relevant figures and populates the firm's proprietary database in minutes, after some training on regulatory and insurance terminology. AllianceBernstein's implicit view is that freeing analysts from data collection lets them focus on judgement-led interpretation of what the flows imply, which is where, in Kyne's words, the value lies.

pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers argues that the Federal Reserve's September rate hike mattered less than its unanimous decision and clear forward guidance, which strengthened its inflation-fighting credibility and signalled a contained hiking cycle of only one or two further increases. The firm expects disinflation to take hold as tariff and energy pressures fade, seeing core PCE reaching 2.5 per cent within a year, and identifies opportunities in longer-duration bonds and mortgage-backed securities as reduced inflation risk premiums and subdued volatility support fixed income markets.

pieces.title: Supporting Greek shipowners with flexible financing solutions
pieces.summary: Macquarie Asset Management reports that it has deployed over $US2 billion in shipping finance across Greece since 2017, completing more than 75 transactions with shipowners ranging from established companies to new market entrants across various vessel types. The company argues that Greek shipowners value financing partners offering flexible structures and certainty of execution, and positions itself as capable of meeting diverse financing needs across different ownership models and strategic objectives.

The firm's explicit position is that long-term sustainable investing can deliver diversified exposure while keeping long-term financial returns central, and that climate and nature are interlinked, so nature must be part of the solution to the climate crisis.

It explicitly stays overweight global equities, reduces its Eurozone overweight in favour of emerging markets and Japan, re-engages with the Nasdaq and adds back mega-cap tech, while keeping duration neutral and flagging rising Japanese yields as the key risk to global bond markets.

Morgan Asset Management argues that, despite a volatile start to 2026 for the AI trade, the broader AI boom remains intact, supported by earnings, valuations, adoption and strong balance sheets (the "EVAL" framework). It says Magnificent 7 earnings have been revised up 6.9% for 2026 while the S&P 493 have been revised down 0.4%, that the Mag 7 trade at 28.6x earnings (not extreme, and well below the internet-era peak of nearly 70x for info tech), and that hyperscaler net leverage of 0.9x compares favourably with 2.6x for the average investment-grade issuer. Its explicit stance is that AI is not a bubble, though it could still form one, so it favours broadening exposure beyond the Mag 7 to other AI innovators and enablers and employing selective stock picking and diversification rather than chasing the herd.

The firm contends that this favours company-specific analysis, and it favours equity long/short absolute return strategies that combine

pieces.title: Investing in Asia small caps: Looking beyond the obvious
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that successful investing in Asia's smaller companies requires looking beyond headline themes such as AI and the technology supply chain, pointing to the Aberdeen Asia Focus Trust's outperformance over five years, which came partly from overlooked areas like plantations, financial services, logistics and Indonesia (notably OCBC Bank NISP). Aberdeen also stresses reasonable valuations, patience with illiquid, under-researched companies, and a diversified four-region portfolio (India, China, ASEAN, Korea/Taiwan). Its explicit calls are to keep selectively adding to Korean semiconductor equipment, industrial technology, communications infrastructure, power and data-centre-linked businesses, and port and logistics infrastructure, to view Vietnam as an area of considerable interest, and to be more selective in India given elevated valuations.

pieces.title: PREPARING FOR THE RETIREMENT YOU ENVISION
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that the years immediately before retirement, roughly the 50s and 60s, can be among the most important for saving, and that increasing contributions, using catch-up provisions, and staying invested can strengthen financial readiness. Its explicit call is to act now: PGIM notes that savers aged 50 or over can make catch-up contributions above the standard 401(k) limit to build savings before leaving the workforce. The rest of the page is navigation and cookie and terms text, so the substance is limited to this brief, generic message.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management reports that the Federal Reserve, Bank of England and Bank of Japan all held rates last week, but inflation concerns split policymakers, with three Fed members and three of nine Bank of England members voting for a 25bp hike. The firm argues that geopolitical disruption, trade and supply-chain pressures, and heavy AI infrastructure spending could keep inflation, and ther

pieces.title: Delving into the Data Center Lifecycle
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that its vertically integrated digital infrastructure model, spanning data centre development and operations, lets it avoid the froth and risks that concern investors and reach attractive opportunities directly. Michael Steele, Head of Ares Digital Infrastructure, says the firm is disciplined on location, customer quality and lease terms, and designs facilities to be fungible across use cases so that obsolescence does not erode investor returns. The piece is promotional and carries standard disclaimers that "downside protection" and "risk-adjusted returns" are not guarantees.

pieces.title: A brighter productivity outlook for the AI era
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that artificial intelligence will durably lift U.S. productivity growth by approximately 40 basis points annually over the next 10–15 years, with adoption remaining gradual and concentrated in the 2030s and beyond. The firm has rebuilt its long-term capital market assumptions to incorporate both efficiency gains from AI scaling and the capital investment required to deploy it, and expects this productivity boost to drive U.S. GDP growth back above 2 per cent. J.P. Morgan Asset Management recommends balancing portfolio exposure across the AI value chain and funding cycle, spanning public and private markets, to capture this opportunity.

pieces.title: Ramp Co-Founder and Co-CEO Eric Glyman on AI Adoption, Jobs, and Token Spend
UK equities: Income today, growth tomorrow?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that UK equities remain overlooked despite offering a rare mix of income and growth, with valuations at a significant discount to global peers, particularly the US, and many UK-listed companies earning substantial revenues overseas. The firm's explicit view is that this valuation gap, a contrarian opportunity for patient, long-term investors, should narrow as fundamentals improve, with dividend yields paying investors to wait for that recovery.

pieces.title: Europe's Climate Resilience
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Europe faces mounting climate risks requiring a new integrated framework to define acceptable risk levels, clarify public and private sector roles, and mobilise investment in adaptation. The firm calls for improved climate data, aligned risk assessment standards, and deeper European capital markets to scale climate resilience solutions, positioning this as both a fiscal imperative and a growth opportunity for European companies and investors.

pieces.title: 2026 Global Real Estate Views​
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that global real estate markets are entering a new cycle offering attractive cash flow and growth potential despite near-term uncertainty. The asset manager identifies 2026 as the strongest investment vintage in the current cycle, advocating selective capital deployment across regions, sectors and capital types to capitalise on rising values and manage widening performance gaps between winners and losers.

pieces.title: Thematic Equity Investing in a World of Disruption and Realignment
The Real Estate Reset: Early Cycle Opportunities
pieces.summary: PGIM Real Estate (authors Caitlin O'Connor and Brandon Short) argues that private real estate is entering an early-cycle recovery after a period of price resets, with rising transaction activity, constrained new supply and high occupancy supporting rental growth, particularly in high-quality assets. PGIM states that valuations look more attractive than equities and fixed income, and that the sector offers income-driven returns and diversification, though it calls for selective, disciplined allocation across needs-based and cyclically dislocated sectors.

pieces.title: The Business of Pickleball
Finding value in core bonds
pieces.summary: Fidelity argues that its Investment Grade Bond strategy, with credit spreads near the tight end of historical ranges, is deliberately underweight corporate credit, and it still aims for a modest yield advantage over its benchmark by investing in less efficient non-agency securitised markets such as CMBS, CLOs and ABS. Within ABS, Fidelity says it currently favours aircraft leasing bonds, which it views as offering structural protections and att

pieces.title: Fixed Income Perspective: From trading alpha to origination alpha
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues, through Head of Fixed Income Alex Veroude, that alpha is shifting from trading mispriced securities, which faces rising competition and tighter spreads, towards originating assets, enabled by tokenization and AI that open up a far larger investable universe (estimated at $35 trillion in the US alone). The firm contends that origination can lock in wider spreads or lower valuations, tilting portfolios towards durable income and more reliable outcomes, and that this requires integrated portfolio construction, stronger governance and technology-enabled sourcing. It presents this as a structural, long-term change and the first in a series on fixed income.

pieces.title: Agriculture Timber Market Update
pieces.summary: PGIM reports that despite 2026 opening with geopolitical volatility and ongoing headwinds including trade uncertainty, immigration pressures and weak commodity prices, the U.S. agricultural sector has demonstrated financial resilience and remains globally competitive. The firm highlights regional variations in agricultural performance across eastern, central and western regions alongside timber markets, and emphasises growing investment opportunities in farmland backed by its agriculture expertise and financing capabilities.

pieces.title: matt-c-pei-sponsored-interview
The Case for Investing in U.S. Senior Housing
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that U.S. senior housing is an attractive investment despite near-term market uncertainty, citing fully recovered occupancies since the 2020 shock, demographic tailwinds over the next two decades, high affordability and resilient demand through cycles, and easing expense pressures that should support net operating income recovery. The firm's explicit view is that current pricing does not reflect this growth outlook, so it sees an opportunity to invest in the asset class during a period of low liquidity.

pieces.title: Filling the Gap: The Expanding Role of Direct Lenders in Europe

LDI health check
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that defined benefit pension schemes should conduct regular reviews of their liability-driven investment (LDI) strategies to assess whether their hedges remain robust, efficient and aligned with scheme objectives in a low-spread, volatile environment. The firm presents a framework of key questions for schemes to evaluate their hedges' adaptability and addresses longevity risk as an emerging concern for schemes in run-on, offering guidance on mitigation.

pieces.title: Megatrends – A multi-decade investment story - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Fortress's 'One Team' Approach to Corporate Credit
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that the breadth of a corporate credit team's remit matters: a single team working across liquid and illiquid credit, senior and junior capital, and even equity widens the comparison set for a new loan, enables relative value analysis across companies and instruments, and supports long-term borrower relationships as companies' needs change. Andy Frank, Global Head of Origination, presents this one-team model as a true differentiator and asserts that Fortress can serve as a capital partner for borrowers through all market cycles.

pieces.title: Partner Story: SOL SpA
pieces.summary: PGIM's partner story (April 2023) describes its private credit relationship with SOL Group, the Italian technical and medical gases producer founded in 1927, which began in 2012 when PGIM stepped in as banks retreated during the European sovereign debt crisis. The firm reports five transactions totalling more than €250 million over more than a decade, and credits its Italian office and "boots-on-the-ground" local knowledge with building trust. The piece's explicit message is that PGIM's regional presence and personal engagement are central to its lending approach, and it presents the relationship as a model of long-term partnership.

pieces.title: Investing in Private Debt
Inflation Quarterly Update – July 2026 - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Global Macro Outlook
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that whilst inflation will fall sharply this year as energy and goods prices decline, it will not reach central banks' 2% targets due to persistent wage pressures from tight labour markets, and that central banks will not cut rates in 2023 despite market expectations. The firm expects mild recessions in developed markets this year and remains underweight on developed market equities in the near term, though it is constructive on risk assets over a multi-year horizon, anticipating a more favourable environment later in 2023 as markets adjust to the reality that lower inflation will require higher rates and economic contraction.

Income Strategy Update: Where Income Meets Resilience
pieces.summary: PIMCO's Income Strategy Update argues that, given geopolitical conflict, stress in private credit and AI-driven market change, the Income Strategy should lean defensively toward quality, liquidity and global diversification rather than take on incremental risk. It contends that yields across high-quality fixed income, near 20-year highs, are a meaningful return driver, and favours

pieces.title: Currently, the US job market is in ‘low-hire, low-fire’ mode - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the US labour market has entered a "low-hire, low-fire" equilibrium, with job creation slowing through 2025, though the headline jobs data may overstate the weakness. It suggests that a shrinking labour supply, driven by reported immigrant departures and possibly a decline in population, means even modest job growth, such as that from 2026 fiscal stimulus under the One Big Beautiful Bill, could lift wages and add to inflationary pressure. The firm's explicit view is that the supply of labour has fallen, though it notes the effectiveness of the administration's immigration measures remains to be seen.

pieces.title: A Case for Absolute Return
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that absolute return strategies, which aim to deliver positive returns regardless of market direction, can help investors navigate uncertainty and diversify portfolios, since they are uncorrelated with traditional equities and bonds and may smooth returns, particularly as asset correlations weaken. The firm's explicit view is that, given record equity highs and persistent concern about volatility, a well-managed absolute return strategy gives investors a useful additional tool for managing risk, and the paper goes on to make the case for an allocation to an equities absolute return strategy.

pieces.title: PERE Credit: Alt-Agency Lenders on the Rise
Quick View: Nvidia results
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Richard Clode argues that Nvidia's first results after Jensen Huang's departure show AI demand remains robust, with the company raising its 2027 revenue growth guidance from 70% to 75% and saying demand still outstrips supply, while the investment debate is shifting to whether AI capital expenditure holds up in 2028. The piece views the results as an "outsized" beat and raise that the shares' already depressed valuation does not fully reflect, though it flags leadership transition, regulation, financing risks and supply commitments (now US$390bn) as considerations investors must weigh.

pieces.title: react-news-real-estate-debt-qanda

AI scarcity in Asia: beyond broad benchmarks
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Asia's critical role in AI supply chains—particularly in semiconductors and manufacturing—does not justify broad regional equity exposure, citing concentration risk and volatility in markets like South Korea where two companies now represent over half the index. The asset manager has moved to neutral on emerging market equities and favours selective investments in specific bottleneck solutions across automation, power infrastructure and datacenters, rather than betting on entire country benchmarks to benefit from AI scarcity.

pieces.title: High Net Worth Investor Survey: Investors Still Embrace Alternatives
pieces.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management reports that high-net-worth investors remain committed to alternatives despite recent private credit concerns, with 93% of alternatives owners satisfied with their investments and 38% planning to increase allocations. The firm argues that investor familiarity with alternatives is critical: only 50% of investors understand alternatives, but those who do are five times more likely to invest in them, suggesting advisors should prioritise education to close this knowledge gap. Goldman Sachs implicitly calls for greater integration of alternatives into workplace retirement plans, highlighting that 91% of millennials would participate if given the option.

pieces.title: What’s Pushing Long-Term Bond Yields Higher?
pieces.summary: PIMCO attributes the recent rise in long-term bond yields (the 30-year U.S. Treasury near 5.3%, with similar moves in Europe, the U.K. and Japan) to rising sovereign debt, AI-related corporate issuance and lingering energy-linked inflation anxiety, and notes that the move has been driven mainly by real yields rather than inflation expectations. It expects episodic fiscal-credibility volatility to persist and a higher term premium to endure absent an economic downturn, while arguing that current yields look historically normal to attractive. PIMCO says it continues to view bonds as attractive and would add exposure if yields rise further.

pieces.title: Form ADV Part 2A Canada ULC
Mexico Regional Insights
pieces.summary: PGIM Real Estate has published research examining whether Mexico is capturing a greater share of advanced manufacturing investment and whether industrial tenants are proceeding despite current uncertainty. The piece positions Mexico as a significant industrial real estate opportunity, building on PGIM's two decades of investment in the sector there. No explicit investment recommendation is stated in the available text.

pieces.title: Bloomberg TV: Scott Kleinman
JH Explorer: Takeaways from the 2026 J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference
Unravelling myths: The hidden truths of Emerging Markets Debt
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that hard currency emerging market sovereign debt (EMD HC) is now a mature, diversified asset class spanning over 70 countries, more than half rated investment grade, and that investors remain under-allocated to it despite its diversification and return potential. The firm's explicit view is that EMD HC deserves closer attention from investors seeking resilient portfolios, offering the emerging market risk premium alongside the defensive qualities of hard currency bonds, with active management needed to exploit the asset class's complexity and inefficiencies that passive strategies overlook.

pieces.title: Private Credit: Beyond the Noise
Currency alpha
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that currency markets offer persistent, economically intuitive return sources that have been largely uncorrelated with equity and bond markets, positioning its currency alpha strategy as a liquid diversifier that seeks consistent performance across varied environments. The firm's approach blends five quantitative factors (carry, momentum, value, volatility and quality) with one macro fundamental driver, and it credits diversification to the spread of currencies and drivers as well as its portfolio construction method. The piece is promotional rather than analytical: it makes a qualitative case and offers no performance data, quantified correlations or specific market call.

The firm says 30-year mortgage rates, down from close to 7% a year earlier to 6.1% in early February 2026, are lower but not low enough to trigger a large wave of prepayments, and it states that it remains "very constructive on credit," expecting positive second-round effects across securitised assets and contained fixed income spreads.

pere-interview-with-bill-benjamin-and-julie-solomon
pieces.summary: Ares Management has named Julie Solomon co-head of its real estate business alongside Bill Benjamin, citing the platform's growth to about $49 billion of assets under management and the need for succession planning, with Benjamin saying that "to get the business to the next step, I want a partner." The firm describes the split as complementary, with Benjamin historically focused on investments and Solomon on operations and capital raising, and says it will remain "nimble" by involving both co-heads in all aspects of the business rather than a siloed approach. The piece, a PERE interview published in April 2024, also frames the Black Creek acquisition as a model to extend vertically integrated operating capabilities into other high-conviction sectors such as multifamily.

pieces.title: UK growth capital: funding the journey to scale
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the UK excels at creating innovative companies but struggles to fund them through to global scale, with a particular shortfall in later-stage growth capital, evidenced by weak IPO and follow-on activity on the London Stock Exchange and a low share of pension default assets in UK quoted equities (3%, against 62% overseas). The firm's explicit call is for institutional investors, notably UK pension funds, to treat later-stage funding as a priority, backing quoted growth companies on AIM and the Aquis Growth Market alongside venture capital rather than choosing between them, so that more of the value created by British innovation stays in the UK.

pieces.title: Commercial Real Estate Is More Than Just Office: Here's What's Driving Growth
US high-yield: Embracing credit divergence, unlocking opportunities - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the US high-yield market has moved up in quality over 15 years (57% BB-rated versus 37% before the financial crisis, and 12% CCC versus 16%), so spreads should be judged on a quality-adjusted basis and are structurally justified at tighter levels, though they may trade in a slightly wider range in 2026 with greater dispersion across sectors and ratings. The firm's explicit view is that carry should again drive returns, that short-duration high-yield offers a buffer against long-end volatility, and that it sees opportunities in "extension trades" on bonds it expects to be called later than priced.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Macro Multi-Asset Quarterly for Q4 2026 argues that earnings are set to accelerate into 2027, while near-term inflation, which it attributes partly to deglobalisation, may force central banks to keep rates higher for longer than markets expect. It sees capital flowing back to sectors and regions starved by the AI boom, and notes that 75% of forecast super-growth stocks (above 25% expected growth) now sit outside the US. The firm's top-down framework rests on corporate profits, liquidity and investor sentiment/valuation.

pieces.title: Taking an absolute return approach to convertible bond investing - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that absolute return convertible bond strategies, chiefly convertible bond arbitrage and low-delta carry, have delivered steady, low-volatility returns that are largely decorrelated from equity markets, and that this remains true through recent shocks including COVID, the Ukraine war and the Iran conflict. It cites a Bank of America survey in which 42% of respondents rated CB arbitrage the most attractive strategy, and the firm states that it believes arbitrage offers a way to capture convexity and issuance premiums while hedging equity risk, particularly as stretched AI-linked valuations favour relative-value over outright exposure. The piece also acknowledges that arbitrage is not risk-free, citing liquidity, funding and credit risks.

2026 Insurance Midyear Investment Outlook - AP Institutional
pieces.summary: Invesco's midyear 2026 insurance outlook argues that risk assets have held up despite the Iran war and private credit worries over AI-driven software exposure, with yield curves and credit spreads signalling no near-term recession, but that very tight spread compensation and inflation risk warrant caution. Invesco explicitly advises insurers to be wary of spread duration, since spread risk is skewed to the upside, and to diversify away from crowded public markets. It recommends selective allocations to private credit and real asset debt as a source of more resilient income, differentiated return drivers and better capital efficiency.

Morgan Asset Management's International Liquidity team reports that the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25bps to 4.35% in May, its third consecutive hike, citing capacity pressures and higher fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict, and warns inflation could stay elevated for longer. The team expects the RBA's hawkish stance to persist until inflation clearly returns to target, and sees opportunities for AUD cash investors in higher yields and tactically extending duration, while advising they remain disciplined and diversified given heightened geopolitical uncertainty.

Morgan Asset Management argues that, despite a US-Iran stand-off that has pushed Brent to $111/bbl (up 83% year-to-date), the feared Hormuz shock has not caused a global demand collapse or recession. Rerouting via bypass pipelines, emergency stock releases and demand reduction have absorbed the disruption, though these buffers are thinning. The firm expects a geop

After 60/40: The Hidden Cost of Uninvested Capital Through the J-Curve
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that the J-curve of closed-end drawdown funds is a total-portfolio problem, not just a fund-level one: uncalled capital sits in low-yielding cash or exposes the portfolio to timing risk, and a 10% private markets target in a 60/40 portfolio can take several vintage commitments to reach. Using 2000 to 2020 buyout vintages, it notes funds typically took about four years to reach their trough (roughly 50% net called)

New world disorder: Finding investment opportunity amid persistent volatility
pieces.summary: In a discussion published by Janus Henderson Investors, portfolio managers Luke Newman and Robert Schramm-Fuchs argue that persistent geopolitical volatility, sticky inflation and rising equity-bond correlations call for liquid diversifiers and absolute return strategies to rebuild portfolio resilience.

pieces.title: Given the uncertainty over inflation, protection matters - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Why we still invest in what people actually need
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that asset markets have become overly concentrated in AI-linked stocks (the Magnificent Seven make up roughly a third of the S&P 500, and TSMC about 45% of the Taiex), and that investors have lost sight of more basic needs such as food, property and healthcare. Its explicit view is that Asian smaller companies in these sectors, including Century Pacific Food, Hang Lung Properties, Vijaya Diagnostic Centre and WuXi XDC, can offer diversification against an AI-dominated market, while noting that holdings are illustrative rather than recommendations. The piece also states that its fund keeps around 20% of holdings in tech, and carries standard warnings on smaller-company risk, gearing and currency exposure.
