pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private credit is simply credit, namely capital lent to sound borrowers for repayment

pieces.title: Quick View: SaaS isn’t dead
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the selloff in SaaS stocks, driven by fears that AI and "vibe coding" will displace enterprise software, is overly simplistic, since coding is only a fraction of software's value and incumbents with domain expertise, workflow design, compliance and security are hard to replicate. The firm's explicit view is that AI and SaaS are not either/or, that several best-in-class incumbents are "in the catbird seat" to become disruptors rather than the disrupted, and that 2026 will act as a sorting mechanism between vendors that adapt and those that become structurally impaired. It also judges that application software trading at about 20 times 2027 earnings, a discount to its historical average, may represent opportunity if beaten-down companies show credible AI roadmaps, though execution volatility is a bigger risk than valuation.

pieces.title: South Korea’s Rising Governance Tide: How to Ride the Value-Up Wave
El Niño is only half the story: The investment case for understanding ENSO
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that investors should view El Niño and La Niña as part of a dynamic climate system rather than isolated events, as sequential phases can compound operational and economic pressures across multiple years rather than offsetting each other. The firm contends that the same region or sector can face different disruptions under each phase—for example, El Niño flooding followed by La Niña drought—creating sustained challenges rather than recovery periods. Janus Henderson calls for investors to focus on portfolio resilience through companies with strong adaptation capabilities rather than attempting to predict individual climate outcomes.

pieces.title: AI: Achieving Scale
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that AI is a generational shift comparable to the internet, with monetisation now under way across chipmakers, hyperscalers and AI application companies, and that current infrastructure spending is being used rather than wasted, unlike in the 2000 internet cycle. It states a clear view that AI demand is healthy and capex growth is sustainable, since leading model providers can fund it from operating cash flow, while acknowledging risks such as sharply cheaper models, open-source competition and "bubble-like" pricing in parts of the market. The piece, which is cut off mid-sentence, concludes that PGIM's long-standing fundamentals-focused growth approach leaves clients well positioned, and it signals that markets will ultimately separate winners from losers.

pieces.title: The Rise of Continuation Vehicle Transactions in Credit Secondaries
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that continuation vehicles, once a niche private equity tool, have become a mainstream liquidity solution in credit secondaries, accounting for about 60% of the roughly $20 billion in FY 2025 credit secondaries volume. It contends that slow DPI progression in private credit funds, where 2019 vintages average about 0.7x, makes CVs a useful way for LPs to access liquidity while GPs extend exposure to performing assets, and it explicitly expects continued growth in the sector. The firm presents CVs as a structural tool for managing liquidity needs rather than a one-off, and it backs this with its own activity, reviewing around 30 CV transactions averaging $1.4 billion in 2025.

pieces.title: How is the U.S.-China AI race evolving?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S.-China AI race is shifting from a contest of capability alone to one where cost and efficiency matter as much, with Chinese open-weight models (such as Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3) now within roughly one generation of the U.S. frontier and far cheaper to run. The firm judges that the U.S. still leads on capability, that Chinese models have gained traction in agentic workloads, and that the two ecosystems will remain parallel but increasingly interconnected. Its explicit call is for investors to diversify across model developers, enabling infrastructure and companies that can turn cheaper intelligence into lasting productivity gains, while noting that AI leadership cannot be taken for granted.

pieces.title: What should investors expect from the Trump-Xi meeting in China?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's ahead-of-summit piece expects the Trump-Xi meeting to extend the year-long "tariff truce", but not to deliver "tariff peace", as tariff and non-tariff barriers stay structurally elevated and the U.S.-China trade war enters its ninth year. It expects low odds of a major shift in geopol

pieces.title: Global Weekly Commentary - Insights
pieces.summary: BlackRock has upgraded its tactical stance on US Treasuries to neutral, favouring short-duration bonds at yields of 5.25% to lock in income with a buffer against further rate rises, partly by downgrading US equities from overweight to neutral. The asset manager emphasises adopting a more dynamic approach to portfolio management in the current market regime whilst maintaining conviction in fundamental views, particularly around artificial intelligence opportunities and emerging market equities.

pieces.title: Developing countries: How will they weather the energy shock? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the current energy shock, like that of 2022, is a negative-sum game in which net importers of oil and gas suffer far more growth damage than exporters gain, and that emerging-market central banks may tighten policy to defend their currencies. The piece sees several mitigating factors compared with 2022: agricultural commodity prices have not yet been hit, AI is supporting Asian growth, and the US Federal Re

pieces.title: AI Era Spurs Recalibration—Not Retreat—in Software
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that recent software sell-offs driven by AI fears are often disconnected from company fundamentals, and that the right response is recalibrating underwriting rather than retreating from the sector. It says its direct-lending software portfolio, weighted towards foundational infrastructure, mission-critical and regulated-sector businesses, is better placed to absorb AI disruption, that effects will unfold over years, and that dislocation could create opportunities in opportunistic credit, secondaries and digital infrastructure for well-capitalised managers.

pieces.title: The rise of decommissioning bonds in transition finance - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that decommissioning finance, which funds the retirement, dismantling, remediation and repurposing of high-emitting assets, is shifting from traditional balance-sheet provisions and general obligation bonds towards labelled transition bonds with defined use-of-proceeds, reporting and impact objectives. The authors see potential benefits for investors in better vis

pieces.title: Navigating market volatility: A guide for retirement investors
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's piece argues that market volatility is normal, noting that intra-year declines have averaged around 14% even though annual returns were positive in 34 of the past 45 years, and that time in the market matters more than attempts to time it, since missing the 10 best days over two decades would have roughly halved a portfolio. It advises investors to zoom out, check that their asset allocation suits their stage of life, keep diversified across stocks, bonds and regions, and, if still saving, keep funding their retirement plan, with target-date funds presented as a useful tool. The explicit call is to stay invested and avoid reacting impulsively to short-term market moves.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that President Trump's second-year focus on affordability (including targeted mortgage-rate measures) and foreign policy, such as the Venezuela and Greenland initiatives, could shape all areas of markets in 2026, and that an active approach is crucial to navigating the shift. Across its fixed income, housing, healthcare and energy teams, the firm sees support for grow

pieces.title: Strategic reforms set the stage for growth in European equities
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Robert Schramm-Fuchs, argues that European equities are well placed to progress in 2026, supported by a global macroeconomic rebound, easing US-European trade tensions, and strategic reforms, particularly in Germany. The firm names banks, defence, AI-related semiconductor and electrical equipment firms, and electrification and grid investment as themes it expects to matter, and it contends that European reforms are not reflected in current valuations. Its supporting data show the MSCI Europe trading at a forward P/E of 15.2 against 22.5 for the S&P 500 at 31 December 2025, a discount of 32.4%.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that low-risk, benchmark-unconstrained absolute return bond strategies, which aim for positive returns regardless of market direction, can serve three purposes for clients today: reducing broad credit exposure when spreads are tight, improving resilience against tail risks, and providing a strategic allocation for relatively low-risk, cash-plus returns. The piece is a short, general framing rather than a specific forecast, and it does not make a explicit market call beyond endorsing these uses of the strategy.

pieces.title: U.S. Agriculture Market Update: Fall 2025
pieces.summary: PGIM's autumn agriculture report identifies record global crop harvests depressing commodity prices, whilst premium farmland demand remains robust, alongside three consecutive years of U.S. agricultural trade deficits. The firm highlights headwinds including elevated input costs, labour shortages, tariff risks, and emerging demand shifts from GLP-1 drug adoption. PGIM positions itself to serve institutional investors seeking farmland asset diversification amid these market conditions.

pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private credit is, if anything, more transparent than bank lending, citing quarterly SEC filings from business development companies that itemise every loan, oversight by 25 global regulatory bodies plus state regulators, and ARCC's quarterly disclosure covering over 585 portfolio companies. The piece, the first in its "Demystifying Private Credit" series, is written by Ares and makes the explicit call that asset allocators avoiding private credit over transparency concerns may be missing opportunities in a $2 trillion market.

pieces.title: India: a turning point?
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that India's market has become more resilient despite the Middle East conflict, the weaker rupee and the Strait of Hormuz disruption, helped by strong GDP data, steady earnings and valuations that now sit near their long-term average. The team says it is "more optimistic" on the outlook but keeps a balanced, quality-focused approach. It finds financials the most attractive on valuation (almost 30% of the portf

European market resilience in a shifting world
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (author Robert Schramm-Fuchs) argues that European equities are resilient despite weak near-term data: eurozone growth stalled at 0.1% in Q1 2026, inflation has re-emerged on higher energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict, and the ECB has raised rates and kept further tightening open. The firm contends that markets are looking through this cyclical softness to structural drivers, namely tight supply of critical resources, policy support for renewables, steel and chemicals, and innovation in semiconductors and electrification. Its explicit view is that European stocks remain attractive because large listed companies are global businesses whose earnings have far outpaced domestic GDP and should continue to do so, though it stresses selectivity in a world of shifting regimes.

pieces.title: On the ground in Asia
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that Asia is emerging as an independent trading bloc, with intra-regional trade now over half of the region's total, and that this shift is changing the opportunities available to investors. Aberdeen's explicit view is that managing Asian assets requires investment staff physically on the ground, so it has moved Isaac Thong, manager of the Aberdeen Asian Income Fund, from London to Singapore, arguing this gives better access to companies, local languages and consumer trends. The piece presents this as a strategic judgement rather than a forecast, and it cites TSMC, the fund's largest holding, as an example of conviction built through proximity.

pieces.title: Iran and transition commodities
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the Iran conflict and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz affect more than fossil fuels, disrupting energy-transition materials through sulphur and sulphuric acid, which are used in refining copper, nickel and zinc and in fertiliser production. It expects short-term volatility to persist while the crisis is unresolved, with the effects on oil and gas prices limited if the conflict is brief and a wider commodity impact if it is prolonged, and it sees a recession risk if Brent stays around USD 140 for over two months. The firm's explicit view is that transition materials will benefit over the long term, whatever the conflict's duration, as governments expand strategic stockpiles and seek diversified energy supply, and it maintains a constructive long-term outlook for its Transition Materials strategy.

pieces.title: Looking Inside Today’s High Yield Market
pieces.summary: Barings argues that high yield fundamentals remain resilient despite geopolitical shocks, including the war in Iran and its effect on energy prices and inflation, with spreads widening only incrementally and default expectations broadly stable below long-term averages. It identifies pockets of strain in cyclical sectors such as building materials and chemicals, and in some U.S. software issuers, but says these are a modest share of the index. Barings calls for discipline and selectivity rather than complacency, and says BB and select single-B bonds stand out, while CLO-driven pressure has pushed some single-B and CCC loans below f

pieces.title: Dynamic currency hedging for Swiss investors
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that Swiss investors should consider dynamic currency hedging, which adjusts hedge ratios over time, as an alternative to traditional static hedge programmes that maintain a fixed level of protection. The paper contends that fully hedged portfolios face rising hedging costs from interest-rate differentials and risk missing gains if the Swiss franc weakens, and that static hedging can create liquidity pressures from collateral calls during market stress. Insight states that its systematic framework, powered by its Alt-FX strategy and drawing on momentum, volatility, value, carry and quality factors, may improve resilience and returns, though its supporting evidence is based on historical simulations.

Enjoy the party, but watch out for the hangover
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that investors should focus less on predicting when an AI-led tech bubble will peak and more on building portfolios that can withstand the depth and duration of drawdowns, noting that both avoiding a theme and chasing it blindly can hurt returns. Its explicit view is that AI is a genuine transformative technology but that valuations and sector concentration are stretched, so exposure should be gained through diversified, dividend-focused equity income strategies that favour cash flow, financial strength and defensive businesses. The piece supports this with historical evidence: during the 2000–2002 TMT bubble, the highest-yielding stocks returned +11.1% while the MSCI World Index fell 46.3%, and equity income strategies also outperformed growth assets in 2022.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that recent Middle East developments, whilst encouraging, do not represent a fundamental shift in the global economic outlook and cautions against treating geopolitical news as a basis for investment decisions. The firm contends that market moves have been driven by speculation around lower oil prices and increased liquidity rather than by changes to underlying economic conditions, and emphasises that maintaining discipline and diversification remains critical as historical precedent suggests fundamentals ultimately dominate short-term geopolitical events.

pieces.title: Bonds Fixed Income Horizons Survey 2026: U.S. asset owners prioritize diversification and flexibility
pieces.summary: Capital Group reports that U.S. institutional investors are shifting allocations towards fixed income for defensive positioning, with nearly one-third planning to increase bonds funded by reductions in equities and alternatives. Rather than simply raising overall credit risk, investors are prioritising diversification across credit sectors and maintaining portfolio flexibility to exploit future valuation disparities, reflecting selectivity amid tight spreads and macroeconomic uncertainty. The firm also notes that private credit has become mainstream, with 60% of surveyed U.S. institutional investors now holding at least 10% in the asset class, and observes that U.S. Treasuries remain viewed as a reliable portfolio anchor despite evolving macro risks.

pieces.title: Assessing the Macro Landscape: The State of Goldilocks
pieces.summary: Barings argues that markets remain in a "Goldilocks" state of resilient growth without recession, despite tariffs, inflation, labour softness and geopolitical tensions, with major asset classes posting positive year-to-date returns. It expects a soft landing in the U.S., with inflation peaking by mid-2026, and flags risks including stretched valuations, rising fiscal concerns in Japan, Italy, the U.S. and France, and elevated long-end yields. Barings's explicit call is that, in a shifting multipolar world, investors should consider a more diversified approach through regional allocation and security selection, including exposure to both U.S. and Chinese AI markets, and a balanced approach to build a resilient portfolio over the long term.

pieces.title: Beyond the Asset: Rethinking Infrastructure Finance
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that infrastructure is increasingly defined by economic function rather than asset category, so the label alone says little about credit risk; the underlying business (demand resilience, revenue visibility, counterparty strength and competitive position) matters more. It contends that infrastructure financing has evolved into a broader capital ecosystem spanning development, construction, refinancing and hybrid structures, and that a single infrastructure allocation may no longer capture this range. PGIM's explicit view is that investors should take a more precise view of what counts as infrastructure and where risk sits, with manager selection and underwriting discipline becoming key drivers of outcomes, and that "infrastructure debt remains fundamentally a credit business."

pieces.title: 2026 Investment Perspectives
Why are institutional investors turning to forests and farmland?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that institutional investors are increasingly allocating to natural capital—forests, farmland and related assets—seeking diversification from concentrated technology-driven markets and portfolio exposure to assets with low correlation to public markets. The firm notes that private investment in nature has grown roughly fivefold since 2016, driven by economic factors such as US housing shortages and potential tariff benefits for domestic timber, and contends that as the market professionalizes, more of these fragmented assets may become accessible through managed investment vehicles.

pieces.title: AI is changing How Credit Investors Underwrite Entire Sectors

pieces.title: Equities: How emerging markets help investors escape US AI mania
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that emerging markets offer investors a more balanced route to growth and a way to reduce portfolio risk, given that US equities are "priced for perfection" and market concentration is at historic highs. It cites 18% expected 2026 earnings growth for EM equities, lower valuations (the MSCI EM Index trades at a 42% discount to the S&P 500, against a long-term average of around 32%), and diversification across sectors and geographies. Aberdeen's explicit view is that EM is a more resilient way to access technological change, and that valuations remain compelling; it also expects EM to recover quickly should US markets correct.

Beyond the blockchain: The changes needed for tokenised funds to realise their full potential
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson, after a day of meetings in Washington with the Coalition for Tokenized Markets, argues that tokenised funds already work technically, and that scaling them is held back by surrounding infrastructure, especially investor identity and verification, which cannot travel across platforms. It says tokens are confined to whitelisted wallets in "walled gardens", limiting secondary liquidity, collateral mobility and cost savings, and it points to Bank Secrecy Act reliance rules as a key obstacle. The firm's explicit view is that the next step lies not in waiting for the CLARITY Act, which it notes has stalled at a cloture vote, but in existing rules and in the joint development of intermediaries, custody and regulation, with investors advised to watch portability signals rather than individual product launches.

pieces.title: Why is the job market so tough for recent college graduates?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the weak job market for recent college graduates (5.6% unemployment versus 4.2% overall) reflects a skills and preferences mismatch rather than AI displacement, with hiring concentrated in lower-wage care roles and degree-holding jobs failing to keep pace with new graduate supply. It cites remote work as explaining about two-thirds of the rise in young-graduate unemployment, according to NY Fed research, and points to immigration policy as widening the gap. While it does not rule out a future AI labour shock, the firm contends that AI should not yet be blamed for graduates' difficulties and draws historical parallels, such as bank tellers and radiologists, to suggest AI's effects may prove unexpected.

pieces.title: Higher rates, solid growth
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that September's volatility is being driven less by weak growth or earnings, which remain solid, than by rising real yields, fuelled by stronger growth, government borrowing and tighter monetary policy. It says real yields have already passed the level at which they converge with potential growth in the US, UK, eurozone and Japan, raising the risk of slower growth and pressure on technology valuations. The firm's explicit call is that it remains broadly risk-on across asset classes while closely monitoring whether higher rates begin to weigh on earnings and economic activity.

The firm sees the shift as a cost-saving move that would ease gilt supply and could help narrow the UK's g

pieces.summary: Insight Investment examines how geopolitical shocks affect corporate treasury management across three scenarios: an acute disruption impacting inflation and rates, prolonged supply-chain pressure on funding costs, and an extended disruption triggering a growth slowdown with policy and refinancing implications. The paper analyses how liquidity pressures evolve through these stages and considers the role of short-term euro money market funds as part of a treasury liquidity strategy.

Apollo identifies three areas it sees as attractive: private real estate relative to stretched public equity valuations, European real estate credit where fragmented lending markets offer attractive spreads for scaled global platforms, and housing, which it presents as a structural tailwind given a projected US shortfall of around four million homes by 2029. The firm concludes that capturing these opportunities will favour vertically integrated managers with operating platforms, global reach and stable capital bases, and it describes 2026 as a year of opportunity for allocators.

The firm presents the appointment as a means of deepening partnerships and delivering solutions for its institutional and wholesale clients.

pieces.title: Inflation
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that plan fiduciaries should treat inflation as a core liability risk rather than a secondary macroeconomic concern, citing a shift towards "neofiscalism" (greater state involvement, deglobalisation and structural spending pressures) that may make structurally higher inflation more likely. The piece says the exposure is most material for public pension plans with explicit inflation-linked benefits such as cost-of-living adjustments, where unhedged inflation can have significant and persistent funded-status effects, and it suggests that a structural inflation-hedging policy can potentially mitigate these risks.

The firm also flags Middle East conflict as a source of volatility, says cheaper dollar hedging for European investors (currently about 170bp, expected to fall to around 115bp in 12 months) is likely to be temporary as US inflation and Fed cuts remain uncertain, and favours active management given wide dispersion of returns. pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that natural capital—the total economic value of natural resources—is currently underpriced in markets but will see asset repricing as physical risks from resource strain and biodiversity loss increase costs for companies, whilst policy responses and technological advances also reshape valuations. pieces.title: Navigating volatility in 2027 with inflation-linked bonds - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that geopolitical shocks, trade tensions, energy insecurity and AI-driven investment are making inflation more elevated, volatile and unpredictable, so investors should prepare for a wider range of outcomes rather than a return to pre-pandemic price stability. It contends this strengthens the case for inflation-linked bonds as a structural portfolio component rather than a tactical trade, citing higher real yields as a buffer against further tightening and as more attractive entry points. The firm also stresses that a diversified, active approach is essential to manage changing inflation dynamics and interest-rate sensitivity across markets.

pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that the global real estate market has reached a cyclical bottom and investors should capitalise on an expected uptick in activity. The firm identifies geopolitical fragmentation—including trade tensions, pandemic disruption and the Ukraine invasion—as driving companies to restructure supply chains towards reshoring and near-shoring, which BlackRock sees as creating new real estate investment opportunities, particularly in industrial and logistics assets.

pieces.title: Why are AI labs raising red flags around AI safety?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that calls from AI labs for a slower frontier, following Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's essay and similar statements from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and xAI, have several overlapping drivers: genuine safety concerns, IPO-related financial incentives, and political pressure from public opposition and a growing number of state AI bills. It contends that a slower race would shift compute further towards inference, potentially trimming hyperscaler and "picks and shovels" capex growth, but that adoption rather than model training will ultimately determine capex and regulation is unlikely to derail AI adoption. Its explicit portfolio view is that investors should avoid treating AI as a single theme, building resilience through diversification within and beyond it, including government bonds, gold and real assets such as core real estate and infrastructure.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that a diversified, risk-managed approach across geography, sector, asset class and investment style is essential in 2026, given US trade policy, Middle East conflict, shifting monetary policy and concentration risk in AI-linked US technology stocks. Its explicit view is that the firm favours high-quality companies with strong cash generation, robust balance sheets and durable growth, particularly in industrials and information technology, where it sees opportunities in electrification, AI integration and decarbonisation, while staying alert to AI valuations drifting into speculation.

pieces.title: Build vs Buy Framework for Asset Managers insights
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that asset managers should abandon the traditional build-versus-buy binary choice in favour of a hybrid model: buying standardized infrastructure and compliance foundations while building proprietary research and alpha-generating capabilities. The firm contends that the economics of in-house development have shifted due to regulatory complexity, data proliferation, expensive engineering talent, and the operational costs of maintaining legacy systems over decades. BlackRock calls on asset managers to adopt more disciplined ownership criteria, retaining only capabilities that directly drive competitive advantage, and to leverage modern platforms' open APIs and governance structures to innovate on top of shared infrastructure rather than around it.

pieces.title: Ares’ Early Days of European Direct Lending
pieces.summary: Ares Management presents its early European direct lending business as a case of first-mover advantage: it launched in 2007 with a blueprint carried over from its US business, then benefited from the post-2008 retrenchment of banks, which made lending to businesses less attractive for banks and more so for non-bank lenders like Ares. The firm's explicit view, voiced by Partner and Co-President Blair Jacobson, is that "it pays to be first," since its five- to six-year head start and existing relationships on the continent gave it an edge when the market took off in 2012–2013. The piece is the first in a "Demystifying Private Credit" series and carries a disclaimer that its opinions and forward-looking statements should not be relied upon.

The firm cites a 2024 global CLO default rate of 0.05% and record European issuance near €60 billion in 2025 as evidence of a supportive backdrop. Morgan Asset Management argues that headline money market fund metrics, WAM and WAL, can mask very different positioning, and that this matters if the Federal Reserve returns to hiking. Two funds with the same WAM can regain reinvestment flexibility at different speeds depending on how their maturities are spread, while two funds with the same WAL can differ sharply in how much of their portfolio resets higher, depending on floating-rate allocation size. The piece takes no explicit market call on the rate path; its practical recommendation is that cash investors look through the averages to maturity distribution, fixed versus floating exposure, and liquidity posture.

The piece also suggests investment banks, which have lost underwriting share to direct lenders, have an incentive to highlight the sector's problems, and it cites Capital IQ data showing smaller US M&A deals to be more stable through downturns.

pieces.title: Spreads May Be Converging Across Public and Private Markets, But Liquidity Is Not
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that proposals to engineer secondary trading in private credit, though often framed as fixing valuation opacity or "jump risk", are being used to justify an erosion of the illiquidity premium in direct lending, since spreads over public credit have compressed even as public liquidity is at post-crisis strength. It contends that private credit faces structural obstacles to genuine liquidity (permissioned transfers, information asymmetry, confidentiality, and lack of trading infrastructure), that forcing liquidity into idiosyncratic assets would produce thin, noisy pricing, and that the recent large deals reflect the established 144A market rather than improved liquidity in true private credit. Its explicit view is that investors are often not adequately compensated for illiquidity in private corporate credit, and that the absence of mark-to-market pricing reflects a distinct risk profile that should be priced rather than treated as a structural flaw.

pieces.title: Tech Hits Turbulence
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that the recent tech sell-off, linked to the Democratic sweep in the US midterms and heightened scrutiny of AI and data-centre development, is a short-to-medium-term adjustment rather than a fundamental break, with the economic backdrop still resilient and demand for compute still strong. Its explicit view is that investors should become more selective rather than retreat, expecting a slower, more disciplined AI build-out (with AI capex perhaps nearer $1 trillion than the $1.5–2 trillion some forecasts had for 2027) rather than a collapse in demand. PGIM also distinguishes frontier-AI campuses, where political and grid pressures are most acute, from low-latency cloud infrastructure, where demand is more resilient, and notes that projects with existing approvals and power may gain value as new supply slows.

The firm therefore calls for scaling up transition finance, backed by credible transition-plan assessment frameworks, the Climate Transition Bond Guidelines, and rigorous impact reporting such as project-level carbon footprints rather than avoided emissions.

pieces.title: Diamond Lessons

Morgan Asset Management argues that quality stocks, defined by strong balance sheets, stable earnings growth and high return on equity, have outperformed developed markets by about 5 percentage points a year since 2000, despite underperforming in 2025 by 5 points, their worst relative year since 2003. The firm notes that quality has historically held up well in drawdowns, outperforming in 78% of such episodes over 30 years, and that its valuation premium has more than halved since July 2024. It therefore views a quality-centric approach as an attractive way to build resilience, while cautioning that investors should check whether heavy technology or AI exposure in quality strategies undermines their defensive role.

pieces.title: Why do correlations turn positive?
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that equity and bond prices move together when inflation surprises to the upside, supply-side shocks dominate, or central banks tighten into slowing growth, as seen in the oil-driven sell-off of spring 2026. It attributes the erosion of government bonds' hedging role to high debt-to-GDP levels, steeper curves and fiscal pressure on governments, and it expects periods of positive correlation to recur given structurally higher inflation from tariffs and deglobalisation. Its stated response is for investors to broaden manager mandates towards unconstrained, absolute-return bond portfolios that are less reliant on traditional sources of return.

pieces.title: Could the U.S. be the frog in the pot?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the United States debt crisis is already occurring gradually rather than as a sudden shock, with markets slowly penalising U.S. fiscal excess through rising borrowing costs rather than a dramatic collapse. The firm contends that since the U.S. lost its AAA credit rating in 2011, Treasury yields have consistently traded higher than those of other AAA-rated countries, raising financing costs across the economy and eroding American competitiveness. Janus Henderson posits that Treasuries have lost their status as the "risk-free rate" in absolute terms, with eight of nine AAA-rated countries now borrowing at lower yields than the United States.

pieces.title: Euro investment grade credit in today’s world
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that euro investment grade credit (bonds from financially strong issuers rated BBB- or better) remains an attractive fixed income asset class, sitting between government bonds and high yield, for investors seeking income and diversification. The firm views corporate fundamentals as generally supportive and yields as favourable against history, with strong investor demand also helping underpin the market. It cautions, however, that expensive valuations relative to government bonds and rising new issuance are less supportive factors, so active and selective investing is needed to succeed.

pieces.title: Why storytelling is an advisor’s most powerful communication tool
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that financial advisors should use storytelling as a primary communication tool to help clients understand and retain complex financial concepts by creating emotional connections and context. The firm contends that stories are more memorable and effective than data alone at building trust, helping clients process information, and demonstrating that an advisor understands both technical and human dimensions of financial decision-making.

pieces.title: The Financing Gap in Sports: Unlocking a $2.5 Trillion Opportunity
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that sports has become a scalable, investable asset class, with a $2.5 trillion global industry anchored by media rights worth over $60 billion a year in inflation-linked contracts. It sees institutional capital (private equity, sovereign wealth funds and pensions) as still early in entering the sector, and says franchises are under-levered at around 10% loan-to-value, leaving significant whitespace for private credit and hybrid financing. The piece explicitly frames this as an opportunity for private credit to offer "equity-like upside with credit-like risk," and cites roughly 13% annual compounding in sports asset values over six decades.

pieces.title: Benefits of dividend reinvestment planning
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that dividend reinvestment through a platform option or a trust's Dividend Reinvestment Plan is a simple, long-term way to compound investment trust holdings, and it explicitly calls reinvestment "the sensible long-term strategy" for investors who do not need the income for day-to-day spending. It supports this with a hypothetical compounding example and Evelyn Partners' figures showing FTSE 100 total return of 1,926% over forty years with dividends reinvested, against 391% on capital alone. The piece also advises prioritising ISAs and SIPPs for tax efficiency and comparing platform reinvestment fees, since costs can erode the compounding benefit.

pieces.title: A diversifying opportunity: The case for small cap investing
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that small-cap equities can enhance portfolio diversification and offer growth potential, citing their M&A target appeal, lower concentration risk, under-researched status (which may create mispricing opportunities), and agility in adapting to supply chain shifts such as near-shoring. The firm's explicit view is that small caps merit consideration as a diversifying allocation, while acknowledging that they require careful research to manage their associated risks.

pieces.title: Private Credit: Outsized Promise in the Middle Market
pieces.summary: PGIM, in a piece by Dianna Carr-Coletta, argues that middle market private credit offers strong downside protection, citing maintenance covenants, lower leverage and more favourable terms compared with covenant-lite upper market deals, and that access to both sponsored and non-sponsored origination helps investors capture relative value and limit exposure to the LBO cycle. PGIM's explicit view is that private credit's low correlation to public markets and stable performance across cycles make it a defensive allocation in volatile conditions, though it concedes that competition and limited M&A activity mean that only disciplined managers with differentiated sourcing are best placed to deliver.

pieces.title: The Fundamentals of Private Markets: An Introduction
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that private markets (private equity, private real estate and private credit) can offer higher risk-adjusted returns, inflation hedging, diversification and stable income, citing a shrinking number of US listed companies and rising stock-bond correlations that have weakened the traditional 60/40 portfolio. Its explicit view is that private assets "may act as a compelling complement to traditional holdings" and may boost risk-adjusted returns, though its supporting figures are illustrative, based on selected indices and past performance, and it stresses that not all private market investments are equal.

pieces.title: Europe’s Next Phase of Asset Management Integration
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Europe's asset management industry should deepen integration by streamlining cross-border fund distribution through the Commission's Market Integration and Simplification Package proposals, particularly "passporting upon authorisation" to reduce operational costs and accelerate market access. The firm contends that this integration need not require a single centralised supervisor; instead, improved coordination between national regulators through standardised information-sharing forums would enhance efficiency while preserving local accountability. BlackRock calls for digitalisation initiatives and reduced regulatory duplication to strengthen Europe's competitiveness as an asset management centre whilst lowering costs for end investors.

The piece offers no explicit argument or investment call, functioning instead as an informational tool for tracking relative conditions across major emerging economies.

pieces.title: Securitization could help plug Europe’s funding gap
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that securitisation could help close Europe's estimated €1tn-a-year funding gap, but that the EU's proposed securitisation reforms under the Savings and Investments Union are too timid. It contends that the 1985 UCITS 10% single-issuer cap is outdated and is holding back a market that is about 0.3% of GDP in Europe versus 4% in the US, and it calls for removing the cap for securitisations while keeping existing UCITS safeguards on concentration, liquidity and credit quality. PIMCO estimates that removing the cap could unlock around €150bn of pent-up demand, whereas the Parliament's proposed 20% cap would add only about €20bn, roughly 2% of the funding need.

Macro Signposts | Campaign Spending: The Hidden Boost Behind U.S. Consumer Resilience
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that record midterm election spending, which the national accounts record as personal consumption expenditure, and retroactive tax cuts under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which it estimates added about $160 billion to household cash in the 2026 filing season, helped U.S. consumption hold up despite energy prices roughly 40% higher. It estimates the election spending alone added about 0.5 percentage points to real consumption growth through the first three quarters of 2026, offsetting much of the drag from energy. PIMCO expects consumer resilience to weaken in 2027 as both one-off boosts fade, so the outlook will depend increasingly on whether energy prices reverse.

pieces.title: Year of the Fire Horse bodes well for Asian investment
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that Asian markets enter the Year of the Fire Horse on a strong footing, citing a 21.2% gain in the MSCI AC Asia Pacific index in 2025 (in GBP terms) against 16.7% for the MSCI World (Hedged to GBP), driven by a rotation away from US mega caps and a rerating of China as its Covid-era restrictions have been unwound. Its two Asia trusts, Aberdeen Asian Income Fund and Aberdeen Asia Focus, are presented as complementary routes into the region, with both managers expecting continued earnings strength and positive sentiment, while acknowledging geopolitical risks, over-optimism on AI earnings, and weak traditional sectors in China. The piece's explicit view is that Asia's outlook remains constructive, with AAS's portfolio companies still able to deliver 10–15% earnings growth, though both managers

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that U.S. consumer health remains solid overall, though a K-shaped recovery leaves lower-income households under strain, with rising defaults and delinquencies in cards and auto loans.

pieces.title: Middle East conflict: energy risks in focus
pieces.summary: BlackRock views the Middle East military escalation primarily as a volatility shock rather than grounds for wholesale portfolio de-risking, though it flags a material risk of sustained stagflation if the conflict disrupts energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz for an extended period. The firm is maintaining its current investment stance whilst monitoring whether the conflict persists beyond an estimated two-week window, and argues that long-term government bonds are unreliable portfolio protection given potential stagflationary risks from escalation.

Morgan Asset Management argues that infrastructure is a compelling allocation on three fronts: a large structural need for investment (roughly $4 trillion a year to maintain and upgrade traditional transport and utilities, plus net zero-driven renewables spending), a record of steady income and diversification that has held up better than bonds over the past decade, and historically strong inflation protection, particularly from utilities. The piece's explicit view is that infrastructure merits a place in portfolios for stable income, diversification and inflation hedging, while acknowledging that inflation may settle slightly above the Fed's 2% target over the long run.

pieces.title: Global smaller companies: When everyone owns the same names, what next?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (portfolio manager Nick Sheridan) argues that market leadership is gradually broadening away from the mega-cap technology names that have dominated returns, with global smaller companies showing resilience amid geopolitical uncertainty and modest valuations relative to large caps. The firm states that smaller companies are under-owned and under-researched, offering greater scope for bottom-up stock pickers to find mispriced and earlier-stage growth businesses, and that the combination of improving earnings expectations and valuations supports the conditions for a re-rating. It also highlights regional differences, from US innovation and European industrial exposure to Japanese governance-led value, as a source of diversification within the small-cap category.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that deglobalisation and artificial intelligence are driving structural change that creates opportunities for active managers, particularly as investors become more selective. Its small-cap portfolio manager, Jonath

pieces.title: Dialogue over disruption: Trump and Xi reinforce a path of stability
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the latest Trump-Xi meeting produced few concrete breakthroughs but reinforced a more investable path of strategic competition managed through sustained dialogue, with the trade truce extended to 10 January 2027, a formal AI dialogue agreed, and energy and rare-earth supply kept under discussion. The firm's explicit view, voiced by China equities specialist Victoria Mio, is that this gradual stabilisation should reduce the geopolitical risk premium on Chinese equities over time and sharpen stock-picking opportunities in AI, semiconductors, electric vehicles and biotechnology.

pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that CLO ETFs provide institutional investors with transparent, liquid access to a market historically dominated by large investors, leveraging its expertise in both credit investing and ETF management. The firm highlights that senior AAA CLO tranches offer attractive credit characteristics and potential portfolio benefits including income, low interest-rate sensitivity and diversification, whilst noting that Solvency II reforms may improve capital treatment for insurance investors.

pieces.title: PE Secondaries: Private Credit Under Pressure
Consumer delinquencies pose limited risks to financial stability
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that rising consumer credit delinquencies, worsened by the post-Middle East gasoline price spike, pose limited risk to financial stability, as the stress is concentrated in subprime auto and card segments that are small relative to the wider market. It credits stronger structural protections in securitisations (higher subordination, wider spread cushions, cash-flow triggers and tighter underwriting) and better-capitalised banks for containing contagion, and so considers comparisons with 2008 overblown. Its explicit view is that financial stability risks should remain manageable for investors, though pockets of pressure in structured credit are likely.

pieces.title: Castlelake Repays Castlelake Aircraft Structured Trust 2021-1
pieces.summary: Castlelake reports the full repayment of Castlelake Aircraft Securitization Trust 2021-1, a $595 million aircraft ABS, about two years ahead of schedule, which it says is the first full repayment of an operating lease aircraft ABS since COVID-19 and its seventh fully repaid or refinanced aircraft ABS. The firm credits its active asset management, remarketing and servicing platform, and argues that consistently repaying ahead of or on schedule reinforces investor confidence in the ABS sector.

pieces.title: Monthly Market Views: Looking beyond oil and China’s resilience - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's monthly views attribute the recent fall in fixed income returns to rising inflation expectations from the Middle East conflict, and argue that short-maturity inflation-linked bonds and money market or floating rate securities offer some defence against higher rates. The firm says a prolonged conflict would sustain rate volatility, whereas de-escalation could open value in credit and ease central bank tightening, and it holds that investors should watch AI-related industries as closely as oil-linked ones. It also takes a positive view on China's relative resilience, citing low oil exposure and a large oil inventory, and gives inflation-linked bonds a positive rating, with Euro investment grade credit positive only if the conflict ends soon.

The piece is a promotional vehicle for a video interview with Matt Hansford and related viewpoints, and it makes no firm forecast or specific recommendation. Its explicit view is that the breadth of portfolio finance, and the capabilities needed to access it, make it a flexible tool for diversification and capital efficiency.

pieces.summary: Barings argues that, with U.S. equity valuations elevated and fixed income yields attractive, investors may be better served over the next three to five years by replacing part of their broad equity exposure with high-carry credit, particularly on a risk-adjusted basis. The piece frames this as a secular rather than tactical shift, contrasting the once-a-decade need for holistic allocation changes with the three or four tactical opportunities that typically arise each year, and attributes the past 15 years' strong equity returns to low rates, Fed balance sheet expansion, lower corporate taxes and debt-funded buybacks. The explicit call is Barings' view that high-carry credit can outperform generic equity beta over that horizon. The article is truncated behind a paywall, so the supporting analysis beyond the introduction is not visible.

pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that Octus has recognised it as one of the leading private credit lenders in India for 2025, a ranking based on activity from January to December 2025 and detailed in a linked report. The firm points to its APAC presence since 2008 and more than $13 billion invested across the region as a differentiator in sourcing deals and structuring tailored financing for India's large conglomerates, which it frames as addressing a structural capital need. The piece makes no explicit investment call, and its disclaimer stresses that the recognition does not indicate future performance of Värde or its funds.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment's Adam Whiteley, Head of Global Credit, reviews a decade of global investment grade credit management, citing automation in bond trading that has improved execution and liquidity, and a shift towards more quantitative tools alongside the firm's fundamental process. The piece makes the case for active management, arguing that active fixed income managers have more scope than global equity managers to exploit pricing inefficiencies, and that the median active fixed income manager outperforms its benchmark. It also cites three past calls: caution in late 2019, a risk-on stance in April 2020, and an overweight on European credit in 2022.

The piece also flags Brazilian and New Zealand local government bonds as attractive relative to fundamentals, though it is framed as the managers' own view rather than a formal recommendation.

The firm's explicit view is that the equity market is in the early stages of a "broadening out" trade that could drive a re-rating of REITs, and it suggests investors seeking diversification may want to reconsider the sector, given its low correlation with other asset classes and with technology in particular. The piece also highlights more specific opportunities, including Japanese property companies, Hong Kong property shares and European M&A activity, though the text is truncated before the detail on these.

The piece, written by practice management consultant Bryan Powell, says teams often drift after the first quarter, and

pieces.title: Infrastructure Co-Investments
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that infrastructure co-investments help limited partners achieve portfolio objectives by accelerating capital deployment, reducing fees, and improving diversification compared to traditional fund commitments. The firm identifies mitigating the J-curve effect as a key attraction, noting that co-investments enable faster capital returns and earlier visibility on portfolio company performance. BlackRock positions co-investments as a necessary strategy for investors to meet their targets in the current macroeconomic environment.

pieces.title: What are GP-led and LP-led Transactions?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the secondaries market has grown beyond a pure liquidity tool into a source of investment opportunity, with GP-led deals letting managers retain high-performing assets while offering LPs access to otherwise closed opportunities, and LP-led deals typically offering entry at a discount of up to five or ten points that can combine with later NAV growth. Ares, through Nate Walton, contends that the return profiles differ: LP-led returns come from discount capture plus NAV creation, whereas GP-led deals start closer to par because the GP sits on both sides of the transaction, making a deep discount harder to achieve.

pieces.title: The Real Opportunity in Tokenisation
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that tokenisation's main value lies in improving how private-market investments are distributed, administered and transferred, not in changing the investments themselves, and that private markets may be its most significant use case. It explicitly rejects the idea that tokenisation creates liquidity, noting that valuation cycles, redemption terms and underlying constraints remain unchanged, and it flags real estate as the most complex frontier given its non-standardised assets and transfer restrictions. PGIM's stated call is that investment managers should assess which products suit digital ownership structures and whether their operating models are ready to support them, with success dependent on market infrastructure rather than technology alone.

Europe's Quiet Convergence: Investment Outlook For A More Stable Euro Area
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the euro area's growth outlook remains weak, with annual growth likely below 1% over the next five years, but that the bloc has become markedly more stable as economic divergences between northern and southern members have narrowed through convergence in growth, fiscal positions and external balances. It attributes this partly to policy, citing NGEU, EU common issuance and the ECB's sovereign-stabilisation tools, while flagging remaining risks such as labour immobility, fading NGEU effects from 2028 and political risk around 2027 elections. PIMCO's explicit view is that the ECB, after one more hike beyond the one already delivered, will rely on rates rather than fragmentation tools, and that it maintains a constructive stance on peripheral sovereigns, mainly Italy and Spain, and sees EU bonds as an attractive source of carry.

Investing in India: The Outlook is as Bright as Ever
pieces.summary: Aberdeen's fund managers argue that the outlook for Indian equities remains positive over the long term despite current market challenges. In a podcast discussion, they highlight emerging opportunities in Indian stock valuations, emphasise the importance of corporate governance and high-quality companies, and point to India's growing consumer market and financialisation story as drivers of future returns. The managers contend that India's domestic economic strength provides resilience regardless of external shocks.

pieces.title: Staying invested through market volatility
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that investors should maintain their positions through market volatility rather than attempting to time markets or react to short-term movements. The asset manager contends that staying invested through downturns allows investors to capture subsequent recoveries, that new market highs typically precede further gains, and that focusing on business fundamentals rather than market headlines produces better long-term outcomes than trading on sentiment.

pieces.title: Iran War Fallout: The Real Market Risks Aren’t Just Oil
Systematic Credit: A New Frontier
pieces.summary: Man Group argues that credit markets are undergoing a structural shift toward electronic trading, comparable to what equities experienced decades ago, and that this creates a new opportunity for systematic managers. It cites rising automated execution (around 60% of participants), falling trading costs (down to 7.5 bps from 12 bps), a 37% decline in the Amihud illiquidity ratio since 2023, and $1.1 trillion of corporate bonds moving from illiquid to liquid over five years, and it sees more systematic potential in securitised markets such as specified pools, CLOs and ABS. Man Group's explicit view is that this is a "revolution, not evolution" that will reward systematic, broad-universe managers with strong risk management, though its data is from Trace and ICE BoAML as at September 2025, and the piece is promotional in tone.

pieces.title: Low fees, reduced taxation: Understanding the efficiencies available to passive ETFs
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that, for US equity exposure, synthetic UCITS ETFs can be more efficient than physical ones because a swap can deliver the index total return without the 15% or 30% dividend withholding tax that a European-domiciled physical fund suffers on US dividends, which it illustrates as roughly 0.2% a year on a 1.3% yield. The piece's explicit position is that the gap between a synthetic fund and its index should be kept as low as possible, comprising the total expense ratio and the swap spread, and that investors should be shown both components transparently, which Janus Henderson says it does on its website.

pieces.title: U.S. Real Estate: Gradual Recovery Supported by Low New Supply
The Changing Face of Infrastructure Debt
pieces.summary: Barings argues that infrastructure debt is regaining prominence, citing its resilience, diversification benefits, risk-adjusted returns, stable long-term cashflows and historically low default rates amid economic uncertainty, rising digital demand and shifting energy systems. Drawing on a Q&A with Richard Parker, head of EMEA infrastructure, the piece stresses that a disciplined definition of infrastructure underpins successful investment and that selectivity matters more than ever, particularly in fast-growing digital subsectors such as data centres. Barings' explicit view is that the most attractive opportunities lie across global markets, shaped by constrained bank balance sheets and electrification, though the excerpt does not set out a specific allocation or call.

pieces.title: Infrastructure debt in 2024: watch the webinar
pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management promotes infrastructure debt as an attractive investment strategy, arguing that it offers appealing risk-return characteristics compared to equity or corporate bonds and benefits from secular tailwinds including decarbonization, digitalization, deglobalization and demographic change. The piece, presented as a webinar discussion between two UBS infrastructure specialists, emphasizes the importance of subsector diversification and highlights that investor surveys rank infrastructure debt among top strategies, though it provides no specific performance data or forward guidance.

Its explicit call is to "pair them", positioning senior-oriented real estate credit alongside direct lending as a diversified, resilient private credit allocation, supported by its own analysis of historical risk and return.

The firm's explicit view is that the market is undervalued relative to comparable entertainment content and that the mismatch between women's share of household spending and sports marketing's focus on men creates sustained upside. The piece is framed as a case for institutional investment, though the text is truncated before it reaches any specific recommendation.

How bitcoin is redefining portfolios | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that bitcoin has evolved from a niche asset into a mainstream portfolio holding with a $2 trillion market cap, driven by geopolitical instability, distrust of traditional institutions, blockchain technology adoption, and younger investors' demographic preferences. The firm positions bitcoin as a diversifying safe-haven asset with low correlation to equities and compares its characteristics favourably to gold and US Treasuries as a store of value. BlackRock implicitly advocates for bitcoin inclusion in portfolios, promoting its ETFs as a simpler alternative to direct cryptocurrency ownership.

pieces.title: Beyond Credit Benchmarks with Flexible Income
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that a multi-sector credit strategy, which invests across the fixed income universe without benchmark constraints, can offer enhanced income potential while maintaining diversification through a high-conviction, best-ideas approach. The piece explicitly positions multi-sector credit as a compelling candidate to bolster or replace traditional core credit exposure, and it is accompanied by a standard risk disclosure covering bank loans, call, credit, emerging market, securitised product and sovereign debt risks.

pieces.title: Securitised and CLOs: Resilience, diversification and the case for active
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that securitised credit, including CLOs, has held up well despite geopolitical uncertainty, rate volatility and sector-specific stress, with spreads repricing in an orderly way, supported by diversification, short duration, floating-rate structures and structural protections. It judges software exposure in European CLOs manageable rather than systemic, since only about 4% of the investable universe sits in the most-concerned sub-sectors, and it highlights data centres as an attractive, structurally driven opportunity with long lease terms and high-quality tenants. The firm's explicit view is that dispersion across sectors and structures makes bottom-up analysis, active management and disciplined underwriting central to capturing opportunities in the market.

pieces.title: Multi-asset chart of the week
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's multi-asset chart of the week flags two market developments: the yen's rebound after the late-July coordinated US-Japan intervention has faded, with rate differentials, fiscal concerns and geopolitical risk still weighing on it, and an accelerated BOJ tightening cycle could spill over into global markets. It also reports that the July drawdown in the US momentum factor was one of the deepest and fastest since 2009, driven by a sell-off in AI-related semiconductor stocks over crowding and earnings-durability concerns. The firm's explicit view is that sharp currency and rate moves can trigger broader dislocations, as the 2024 carry trade unwind showed, though it notes today's backdrop differs.

pieces.title: Real Estate Secondary Market Volume Hits Record $20 Billion in 2025
pieces.summary: Ares Management reports that real estate secondary market volume reached a record $20.3 billion in 2025, up from $14.6 billion in 2024, with its own secondaries group recording 189 transactions. GP-led deals rose 60% to $14.5 billion, while LP-led volume grew to $5.8 billion as falling fund distributions and improving discount optics encourage more liquidity sales. Ares explicitly anticipates that secondary volume will roughly double over the next several years, given that global direct real estate volumes remain 34% below 2021 levels and more than $2 trillion of NAV sits in closed-end private real estate funds and related vehicles.

pieces.title: Video: The deep divide in credit markets, and how to take advantage
pieces.summary: Ares Management (via its Australian arm, Ares Australia Management) argues that a large part of the credit market offers negative real yields and excessive interest rate duration risk, while credit segments with high cash yields and lower duration risk look more attractive. Its Head of Ares Australia Management, Teiki Benveniste, presents these asset classes as potential yield enhancers and diversifiers for portfolios, with the piece promoting this view through a video that charts the divide. The article is a Livewire-published video piece distributed by Fidante Partners, and it contains no explicit trade recommendation beyond this positioning.

pieces.title: Key Takeaways From PIMCO’s Sustainable Investing Report 2025
pieces.summary: PIMCO's 2025 Sustainable Investing Report argues that sustainable fixed income has matured, with appeal holding up amid geopolitical and trade uncertainty, and that AI-driven data centre growth is adding energy-demand complexity. PIMCO says it embeds sustainability in research, engagement and portfolio construction through proprietary frameworks built by credit and ESG analysts, deliberately relying less on third-party data or backward-looking metrics. It also points to resilience and adaptation finance, and to mobilising private capital through development finance institutions, as the next areas of opportunity.

pieces.title: An advisor’s guide to managing investor emotions during elections
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that election cycles trigger cognitive biases—including attachment bias, herding, and confirmation bias—that cause investors to make emotionally driven decisions contrary to their long-term financial interests. The firm advises wealth advisors to educate clients about these biases and help them recognise when political identity is influencing investment decisions, rather than allowing such emotions to override sound financial planning.

Authorised participants create and redeem ETF shares to keep prices aligned with underlying asset values, while market makers provide liquidity on exchanges; both are incentivised by arbitrage opportunities to prevent material price deviations. BlackRock argues this self-policing mechanism ensures cost-effective trading for ETF investors across all market conditions.

Navigating inflation shocks
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that inflation shocks, though rare, should be built into portfolio construction, since they can hit all asset classes at once and undermine the usual protection bonds provide. Drawing on its "40 40 20" analysis of macro regimes from 1968 to 2026 and the 1990–1991 Gulf War as a precedent, it contends that energy-driven inflation can persist well after the trigger fades, so inflation hedges such as commodities, inflation swaps and rate-volatility strategies should be maintained. The firm says it has already moved to a more defensive stance in response to the current Iran-related oil shock while keeping meaningful market exposure, given the high uncertainty over its duration and economic impact.

pieces.title: What’s behind the surge in global earnings growth?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that global equity returns in 2026 have been driven almost entirely by earnings: international equities are up 13.1% year to date, with upgrades to earnings expectations (up 22 percentage points) doing most of the work, while multiples have contracted. The firm attributes the surge to five themes: the AI-related capex boom (the largest contributor, expected to persist given capacity constraints), higher energy prices (a temporary boost), weaker developed-market currencies (likely to fade), resilient domestic sectors such as banks and industrials, and governance-driven improvements in return on equity, especially in Japan. Its explicit view is that, despite persistent geopolitical tensions and modest growth, earnings can keep delivering outsized growth in 2026 and 2027, supported by largely secular rather than cyclical drivers.

pieces.title: Which bonds should investors buy after the rise in Treasury yields?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S.-Iran conflict and the near-doubling of oil prices have pushed up short-term Treasury yields and removed expected Fed rate cuts, flattening the curve against consensus, while long-term inflation expectations have barely moved. The firm's explicit call is that, should the conflict resolve by summer, oil and near-term inflation will ease, allowing the Fed to cut rates this year and into next, a path markets are not pricing. It therefore favours short- to intermediate-maturity bonds, which it sees as attractive at yields near 4% with meaningful upside, and notes that crowded speculative short positions could unwind sharply and amplify a rally.

He points to benign money market conditions, the weaker safe-haven appeal of government bonds, and positive short-term rates that make these funds more competitive with bank deposits. Insight's explicit view is that money market funds are capital-preservation and flexibility instruments, not return-maximising ones, and that investors should keep liquidity buffers well above regulatory minimums to prepare for unexpected shocks.

The asset manager expresses cautious optimism on the outlook while acknowledging risks including inflation pressures and the Bank of Japan's rate hikes, and notes that Japanese valuations remain relatively attractive compared to US and Australian peers.

It argues that plans are shifting towards fixed income and less liquid assets such as private credit, but that the rising payout ratio, the highest of any market globally by Insight's measure, creates an underappreciated liquidity risk of forced selling. Insight's stated response is to expand the LDI toolkit with overlays and cashflow-driven solutions, and to favour surplus-driven approaches such as self-management over rushing into pension risk transfer.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Moody's and Fitch are recalibrating their CLO rating methodologies to reflect a larger body of historical default and recovery data, which shows CLOs have performed better than earlier assumptions implied, with Fitch estimating 5-15% of its CLO ratings could rise by mostly one to two notches and Moody's around a third of sub-AAA tranches. The firm views these upgrades as a largely technical, evidence-based adjustment rather than a loosening of underwriting standards, one that could tighten spreads, improve liquidity and widen the eligible investor base, while maintaining that ratings are only one reference point and that collateral, manager behaviour and deal structure remain critical to active CLO selection.

pieces.title: Higher bond yields & value
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the recent surge in global bond yields reflects higher real rates, larger term premia, fiscal concerns and heavy issuance rather than a renewed inflation shock, so the 2022-2023 tightening cycle is unlikely to repeat. On that basis, the firm says fixed income now offers attractive income and long-term return potential, and it favours gradually adding diversified duration and selective credit, notably high yield and emerging-market corporate debt. On France, it judges the fiscal problem serious but not comparable to Greece's crisis, and it prefers to stay close to benchmark weight rather than underweight French government bonds or add tactically.

Driven by geopolitics, trade fragmentation, industrial policy, technology and demographics, this shift is seen as reshaping policy choices and risks, including central bank independence, financial repression and the future of money. The piece offers no explicit market call; its emphasis is on the macro forces investors should monitor as the order evolves.

The piece highlights Denmark's multi-pillar pension structure, high participation rates above 90%, and governance framework as factors that have supported capital market development, while cautioning that other Nordic countries have taken different approaches. BlackRock calls for closer collaboration between governments and social partners, material tax incentives, and automatic enrolment schemes to strengthen pension participation and channel savings into financial markets across Europe.

pieces.title: UK Budget: What Investors Should Know
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the UK Budget was more benign than pre-Budget expectations of a £40 billion hole and possible income tax rises implied, since the OBR's productivity downgrade was largely offset by higher inflation and nominal wages, leaving 2029-30 borrowing only £6 billion worse and headroom at £22 billion. It nonetheless criticises the back-loaded tax rises, the reliance on £4 billion of unspecified savings and implied real-terms cuts to unprotected departments, and the persistent around-5%-of-GDP deficits, which together weaken credibility. PIMCO's stated view is that gilts remain attractive, particularly the 5-year sector, as it expects Bank of England easing to deepen, while it stays cautious on long-end gilts because of fiscal credibility risk.

pieces.title: European Private Credit: Views From the Ground - Mid-Year 2026
pieces.summary: PGIM's mid-year 2026 update, drawing on comments from Josh Shipley, Head of European Private Credit, says European businesses are proving resilient despite geopolitical tensions, inflation and supply chain disruption, adapting operating models and passing on costs where they can. PGIM notes that pipeline visibility is less predictable than in previous years, but argues that financing demand remains intact, driven by refinancing, capex and growing use of private markets as alternative capital. It takes a "cautiously optimistic" stance, and flags that high energy prices could feed through to inflation and logistics costs in the coming months.

pieces.title: Navigating private markets for insurers
pieces.summary: Invesco argues that UK and European insurers should keep refining private market allocations around income durability, capital efficiency and liability alignment, citing still-attractive yields, improving capital markets and an evolving regulatory backdrop. Its explicit positioning is constructive on private credit (direct lending) and real estate debt, underweight on private equity (preferring growth and venture over buyouts, with distressed credit as an alternative for higher-return mandates), and overweight on real assets, favouring income-driven core real estate equity and infrastructure. Invesco also flags rising EIOPA scrutiny of valuation, governance and look-through under Solvency II, which in its view favours simpler, income-generating exposures over complex or beta-driven structures.

It forecasts 0.9% GDP growth in 2026, notes that trade has driven much of the region's recent performance, and points to rising saving intentions, weakening real incomes and further ECB rate hikes as risks. AllianceBernstein's explicit view is that investors should watch consumption closely, as household spending could shift from Europe's main growth engine to its biggest vulnerability.
