pieces.title: New Infrastructure Debt Era Takes Shape
pieces.summary: Barings argues that the infrastructure debt market is resilient and maturing into a more mainstream asset class, with demand from existing and new investors rising as investors seek essential assets with stable cashflows despite geopolitical and economic uncertainty. It points to energy security concerns following Middle East tensions and the energy transition, including electrification, power generation, transmission, storage and digital infrastructure, as drivers of a deep and durable pipeline. Barings's explicit view is that the asset class is in good health and poised for strong growth in the coming years.

pieces.title: Income restored
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that higher global bond yields—now averaging 5.6% in their strategic portfolio, up from 2.3% five years earlier—have restored income as a primary source of portfolio returns, with over 80% of the global bond universe yielding above 4%. The asset manager attributes this structural reset to a new macroeconomic regime characterised by AI-driven capital spending, supply constraints, and persistent inflation pressures. BlackRock argues that while income opportunities are abundant, investors must adopt a flexible, selective approach because long-term government bonds' traditional risk-cushioning role has weakened and yields no longer consistently compensate for risk.

pieces.title: Transition Investment Summit
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers (LOIM) reports on its third Transition Investment Summit, arguing that long-term market returns will be shaped by system-level economic change, driven by pain points where existing models become unviable, rather than by near-term shocks such as inflation or geopolitical conflict. It frames this shift as a move toward a "CLIC" economy (circular, lean, inclusive and clean) and contends that these changes are happening faster than in past transitions, so investors should engage with them now. LOIM's explicit view is that sustainable investing must rest on economic logic, and that the clearest opportunities lie in identifying mispriced assets across public and private markets as value chains are reconfigured, with the energy system expected to see the most disruption.

pieces.title: Alternatives: Solving for alpha, income and diversification
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that public markets face headwinds from elevated valuations, low real yields and rising stock-bond correlation, so investors willing to look beyond a traditional 60/40 portfolio may benefit from an alternatives sleeve. The firm contends that each alternative asset class plays a different role (enhancing returns, generating income or providing diversification), so investors should first define their goal and then choose accordingly, with real assets such as real estate and infrastructure highlighted for income, inflation protection and low correlation to a 60/40 mix. It also makes an explicit point that manager selection is critical, given the large performance dispersion between top and bottom managers, particularly in private markets.

The firm's explicit view is that private credit will face periods of stress and defaults may edge higher through 2026, but that it represents "a risk, but not the main event" and is unlikely to derail a constructive outlook for risk assets.

pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that private lending to commercial real estate is expanding rapidly because traditional lenders have scaled back their CRE exposure, and that senior secured, asset-backed loans can offer attractive yields and defensive risk characteristics. The firm states that its own approach centres on downside protection through conservative loan-to-value ratios, active monitoring and diversification across sectors and regions. Its executives go further, presenting CRE lending as a source of current income that sits apart from public equity volatility and a means of taking market share from commercial banks, with Fortress explicitly seeing significant opportunity in real estate lending, net lease and related private lending strategies.

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that a persistent oil shock from the Iran conflict implies higher inflation and weaker growth, yet risk assets have shrugged this off, with equities and investment-grade credit spreads diverging from the more cautious signal in government bonds, which it reads as markets pricing a mild stagflationary outcome. The firm sees the balance of tail risks skewed toward a negative growth shock rather than a 2022-style inflation re-acceleration, given a more balanced labour market, higher starting yields and softer demand. PIMCO's explicit view is that the case for high-quality fixed income is stronger today, since nearly all U.S. and European bonds now yield at least 25 basis points more than cash and the Agg's yield exceeds the S&P 500's earnings yield, and it dismisses comparisons with the 2023–2024 yield highs as misleading because policy rates have since fallen.

pieces.title: Video: Why it’s important to “time” your credit exposure (but not how you might think)
pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management's Teiki Benveniste argues that, over the 12 months to 31 January 2022, fixed-rate credit underperformed floating-rate credit regardless of credit quality, because fixed coupons can only adjust to rising rates through falling prices, whereas floating coupons reset every one to three months. He adds that duration is a further source of differentiation within fixed-rate credit, citing investment-grade bonds' longer interest-rate duration (about eight years versus four for high yield) as the reason they lagged sub-investment-grade. The piece presents this as a way of "timing" credit exposure through duration and rate sensitivity rather than through entry and exit points, though it stops short of an explicit recommendation.

The firm advocates a multi-asset approach to navigate volatility and regional dispersion, emphasising active investment, diversification across countries and sectors, and flexibility to adjust allocations as risks and opportunities evolve.

pieces.title: What’s the earnings outlook for the first quarter of 2026?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that S&P 500 earnings fundamentals are stronger than recent market sentiment suggests: 2026 earnings growth forecasts have risen from 14.9% at end-December to 17.6%, and Q1 2026 profits are expected to grow 12.6%, with tech (semiconductors in particular), materials and financials leading, and energy flat for the quarter before accelerating later in the year. The firm's explicit view is that, despite geopolitical risk that could shave mid-single digits off EPS growth, investors should anchor decisions in these solid fundamentals rather than in short-term sentiment swings.

pieces.title: Alternative Investments Outlook 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Alternative Investments Outlook 2026 argues that a once-in-a-generation capital expenditure cycle, driven by AI and the convergence of public and private markets, is reshaping the global economy. It notes that private markets, now estimated at nearly USD20 trillion, are broadening beyond institutions and the wealthy to retail investors, retirement plans and pension funds, while acknowledging lingering concerns over valuations, transparency and liquidity. The firm's explicit view is that the next phase will reward selectivity, discipline and the ability to connect signals across public and private markets.

Sustainable investing: power, compute and capital
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that AI is a multi-year, capital-intensive infrastructure build-out constrained by power, grid capacity, chips and cooling, so sustainable investors should frame it as industrial expansion rather than software adoption. Because power is the binding constraint, the firm contends that tokens per watt is the key competitive metric, and that investors should favour bottleneck segments such as power and electrical infrastructure, cooling, computing, memory and energy storage. It accepts that the build-out is carbon-intensive and that portfolio carbon intensity may rise near term, but takes a systems-level view that AI-driven efficiency gains can ultimately lower the economy's carbon intensity, with stewardship focused on transition plans and capital discipline.

pieces.title: EU securitisation reform marks progress, but the job is not yet done
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors welcomes the progress in the EU securitisation reform, which could help revive issuance and unlock significant new lending, but argues that the current proposals risk falling short of their aims. Its main concern is the proposed investor sanctions regime: it backs the Council's removal of investor-specific sanctions under Article 32, and it consid

Healthcare equities: Healthier prospects in 2026 - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management, through a Talking Heads interview with Senior Portfolio Manager Jon Stephenson, argues that US healthcare equities look set for a strong recovery in 2026, after underperforming from 2023 to 2025 due to biotech sell-offs, Inflation Reduction Act drug price negotiation, and drug pricing and FDA concerns. The firm's explicit view is that the outlook has improved markedly: drug pricing is clearer after "most favoured nation" deals with the US administration proved less onerous than feared, FDA disruption has been milder than expected, and innovation, M&A (particularly large-cap biopharma buying small and mid-cap firms to address patent cliffs), and resilient procedure volumes make the sector "much more investable", with opportunities across med tech as well.

Why asset-backed loans now?
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers (LOIM) argues that asset-backed lending (ABL), being secured by real collateral with short average maturities (around 18 months, or 1.5 years in the comparison table), is structurally defensive and insulated from the redemption, valuation and sector pressures hitting direct lending and BDCs, particularly those with software concentration, leverage and mismatched liquidity. The firm's explicit view is that ABL is a cycle-agnostic, all-weather source of stability suited to investors seeking capital preservation and uncorrelated returns in 2026, with its own strategy's software exposure below 1%.

pieces.title: Risk-on positioning
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that markets have looked past the Iran-related oil-supply shock, with equities driven higher by AI-related capex and earnings, and that resilient growth is keeping stagflation at bay even as inflation rises. Its explicit call is to maintain risk-on positioning across asset classes, though it flags rising real yields (above 2% in the US and 1% in Europe) as an emerging threat to corporate earnings and valuations. The firm's teams express this through a neutral overall multi-asset market exposure of about 150% tilted toward defensives, a long-duration fixed income stance, and continued overweights in technology and structural growth themes.

pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that deeper, more integrated European capital markets are essential for economic growth and that the EU should learn from Germany's success stories in retail investment (particularly ETF savings plans), blended finance (public-private partnerships for climate and venture capital), and private markets financing for innovative companies. The firm calls for a pragmatic policy approach across the EU that replicates these conditions to foster investment, attract diverse funding sources and improve market efficiency.

Private Equity: Accessing alpha opportunities outside public markets
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that companies are staying private for longer, citing high costs of going public and easier access to private capital, which leaves more mature, faster-growing businesses outside public markets. It contends that private equity offers a broader opportunity set, noting that over 85% of U.S. companies with $100 million or more in revenue are privately held, and that global private equity has outperformed public equity by an annualised 4% over the last 20 years with fewer negative years. The firm explicitly expects this long-term outperformance to continue, while anticipating that the strong recent returns of large-cap public equities, particularly in technology, will normalise over the long run.

The Credit Market Lens: The Other Side of Higher Yields
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that higher bond yields have restored bonds' income and hedging roles in multi-asset portfolios, while the cost of capital is starting to bite unevenly, with pressure concentrated in CCC-rated borrowers, fiscally vulnerable European sovereigns such as France, leveraged AI financing and weak residential housing. Its explicit views are that credit decompression should deepen, that low-quality borrowers will likely underperform the broader market, and that the AI debt wave will accelerate this differentiation as rising supply forces weaker issuers to compete on price with stronger alternatives. PIMCO characterises the housing weakness as a prolonged adjustment rather than a new crisis, and notes that the recent tech-driven sell-off, in which Treasury yields fell as equities declined, is encouraging evidence but not yet proof that the stock-bond hedge has been fully restored.

pieces.title: The next five years: Five ways U.S. CRE will differ from the last five
AI-conscious asset allocation: portfolio construction in a capital investment boom
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the AI investment boom is larger and faster-moving than past tech capex surges, bringing exceptional opportunities alongside elevated valuations, extreme volatility and wide disruption, and that history suggests leadership often changes and outcomes diverge sharply across industries. Its explicit recommendations are to take a targeted, active approach to core AI equities, to spread AI-related returns and risks across the full range of asset classes, and to revisit assumptions about portfolio risk diversification, with fundamental analysis and flexibility offered as a counterweight to market enthusiasm.

pieces.title: Solvency II Reform: Why European insurers should revisit securitised credit
Unconstrained Equity investing. Ignore the noise
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that traditional equity investing is needlessly complex, requiring frequent trading to balance alpha generation with benchmark-relative performance constraints, which increases the risk of buying high and selling low. The company advocates its Global Unconstrained Equity Fund as an alternative: a concentrated portfolio of a small number of companies believed capable of sustaining high returns over a decade or longer, held for extended periods and unconstrained by benchmark considerations. BlackRock positions this as a simple, fundamentally sound approach for investors prioritising long-term capital growth over short-term performance noise.

Adapting Active Fixed Income to a New Risk Regime
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that fixed income excess returns are shifting from systematic rate and credit risk premia towards idiosyncratic selection, citing a flatter yield curve, more persistent two-sided rate volatility, tight spreads and flatter spread curves. It contends that an overweight to rates and credit beta suited the post-GFC period but should now be used selectively and tactically, with most excess return sourced from sector rotation and security selection. In practice, PGIM favours selective systematic exposure, breadth over concentration, disciplined risk budgeting and beta-aware measurement.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's liquidity strategist reports that the Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4.00% in a more hawkish vote than expected, with eight members backing the move and Catherine Mann preferring 50 basis points. The piece argues that energy-driven inflation is the immediate pressure, but that the decisive question is whether second-round effects spread into wages and prices, and that policy is not on a pre-set path. JPMAM's explicit view is that a further increase by February remains likely, that UK money market rates price in too many hikes (around three more) and so offer value, and that its sterling liquidity strategy keeps a longer-duration bias within a defensive stance (weekly liquid assets above 45% and a WAM of 45–50 days).

pieces.title: The investment approach that works in every market cycle
pieces.summary: Published by Livewire in December 2022 and featuring Ares Management partner Greg Margolies, the piece argues that private credit investors should stick to the same portfolio basics in every rate environment: rigorous credit selection, senior secured loans in defensive industries, high-quality management, and companies with a moat around their cashflows.

pieces.title: What if inflation doesn’t go away?
Chart of the Month: February 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that, although European high yield spreads are near decade lows, valuations should be judged against a much stronger credit profile. The market has shifted towards BB-rated issuers, with secured debt rising from about 5% of the market in 2000 to over 40% today, and the firm contends that the leveraged loan market, now predominantly single-B rated, is no longer the "up-in-quality" alternative it once was. Its explicit conclusion is that high yield's valuations reflect its status as the higher-quality leveraged credit market, even for investors uneasy about current spread levels.

pieces.title: Macro Signposts | The AI Investment Boom Goes Beyond America
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that whilst the U.S. AI investment boom supports American demand and equity valuations, much equipment is imported, limiting direct GDP contributions domestically; instead, this spending transmits growth to Asian economies embedded in semiconductor manufacturing. The firm identifies deceleration in AI capex growth—rather than an absolute collapse—as the key risk to global growth, given that economic expansion depends on the rate of spending change rather than its level.

pieces.title: The New Role of Geopolitical Risk in Bond Investing
pieces.summary: Barings argues that geopolitical risk has become a more important driver of bond-market volatility since 2025, and that recent shocks differ in quality because they originated in the U.S. and have been inflationary for it. Unlike traditional shocks, which tended to lower Treasury term premiums and yields, these have pushed both higher, helping explain why long-term yields remain elevated

pieces.title: Two-Faced Trades
Lessons from Tommy Fleetwood
ETFs continue providing liquidity when markets need it most
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that ETFs provide liquidity when markets are most stressed. ETF exchange volume hit a record 43% of total U.S. exchange activity during the Iran war sell-off, and the piece attributes this to ETFs' structural role as a "pressure valve", with authorised participants keeping spreads tight, particularly in fixed income. The firm expects new volume highs to recur whenever volatility spikes, given ETFs' growing role, now around $16 trillion in AUM.

pieces.title: Global smaller companies: Where markets hide their best ideas
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Nick Sheridan, argues that volatility and wide stock dispersion in 2026 make global smaller companies an attractive area for disciplined, value-focused stock picking, citing under-coverage and persistent mispricing, higher long-term earnings growth potential, and structural tailwinds from deglobalisation, AI-driven efficiency and M&A. The firm explicitly contends that passive exposure is a "blunt and inefficient tool" in this segment, and that active, bottom-up selection focused on incremental returns on invested capital is the practical way to exploit that mispricing.

pieces.title: Webinar Replay: A Compelling Vintage: Finding Value Early in the Cycle
pieces.summary: PGIM hosted a webinar featuring its European and Americas real estate investment research heads to discuss investment opportunities in the upcoming real estate cycle. The firm argues that real estate now offers an attractive combination of cash flow from resilient, basic needs-driven demand alongside growth potential, and highlights specific strategies including living and market momentum approaches, portfolio construction and private credit as areas where investors can find value.

pieces.title: Reducing Emissions Through Innovation
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management reports that Clarios, its energy storage business, has launched IdleLess™, a software platform using AI and machine learning to monitor fleet vehicle batteries and reduce idling. The company argues that the technology can cut unnecessary idling by up to 60%, delivering fuel savings of approximately $4,500 per vehicle annually whilst lowering greenhouse gas emissions, and positions this as evidence of how innovation in connected battery technologies supports both operational efficiency and emissions reduction.

pieces.title: European sovereignty: Energy security presents strategic investment advantage - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is redesigning its energy system to make energy security a pillar of geopolitical sovereignty and economic stability, citing the EU's Green Deal, its 2026 digitalisation and AI roadmap, and its Electrification Action Plan as evidence of a structured, well-funded shift. The firm explicitly views this as a "hugely significant long-term investment opportunity" in renewables, grid modernisation, electric vehicles and battery supply chains, with growing EU preference for European companies. It also frames the EU's reduced reliance on Russian oil (from around 26% in 2021 to about 2% now) as an early step in that broader resilience agenda.

pieces.title: Book Review Summer ‘26
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein's summer reading list reviews eight recent books that it describes as explicitly not investment books, covering themes such as the global economy and supply chains, AI, demographics, inequality and societal resilience, all of which it argues shape the strategic backdrop to investing. The firm highlights the return of the physical economy (demand for raw materials and energy) and demographic change as forces that will make the coming decades very different from the post-WWII period, and it recommends the books as work-adjacent reading for the summer break. The full review is only available as a PDF, so the individual titles and detailed arguments are not included in the text provided.

pieces.title: Redrawing the Asian income map
pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that Asian investors' income portfolios are concentrated at home and in a narrow set of sectors, and that drawing income from a wider mix of regions, credit cycles and private markets could improve risk-return trade-offs. Its explicit view is that income should be built as a diversified system across assets and regions rather than a collection of the highest local payouts, with EM hard-currency and global credit highlighted as under-used, and private credit, real-estate debt and infrastructure debt positioned as complements to public income rather than substitutes.

pieces.title: Diversifikation neu denken
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that institutional investors should move beyond traditional 60/40 portfolio allocation because recent inflation and interest rate shocks have undermined the historical diversification benefit of bonds during market stress, with stocks and bonds showing positive correlation at times. The firm advocates a Total Portfolio Approach that allocates capital based on contribution to overall portfolio objectives rather than asset class alone, and highlights five strategies—absolute-return bonds, currency alpha, capital-protected equity strategies, short-duration bonds and commodities—as sources of alternative diversification to reduce reliance on traditional beta exposures.

pieces.title: View from the Markets: Taiwan GDP, need I say more? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chris Iggo argues that markets are being driven by optimism over a possible US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and by the AI capital spending boom, which has pushed equity indices in Taiwan, Korea, Japan and the US to new highs; he points to Taiwan's 13.7% Q1 GDP growth and a 24.3% rise in US intellectual property investment as evidence of the scale involved. His explicit view is that there is little reason to bet against the AI trade, with Asian equities and technology-themed strategies likely to remain the highest-beta way to benefit, while the macro backdrop stays fragile, with higher inflation, softer growth and stagflation risks that he considers less likely than they were a few weeks ago. He also favours short-duration, inflation-linked and higher-yielding credit over long-duration government bonds, which would need a bullish shift

pieces.title: Public Proxy for Private Credit
pieces.summary: Dimensional Fund Advisors' Wes Crill argues that, although private credit's opacity makes its true condition hard to gauge, publicly traded business development companies (BDCs) offer a continuously updated market signal. He reports that a BDC index has fallen more than 13% over the year to March 10, 2026, while US stock and bond markets have risen, suggesting the market now values private credit assets less highly than a year ago. The piece states no explicit investment recommendation.

pieces.title: Riding the AI wave: How can tech investors harness change and volatility?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that AI is a long-term technology wave, now in its later stages, that will keep driving economic transformation and tech share gains through 2026 and beyond, with demand for compute expected to outstrip supply. It says tech valuations sit within their five-year range and well below the internet bubble, so it favours active, selective stock picking, valuation discipline and diversification across the Magnificent 7 and emerging leaders, while expecting volatility along the way.

CRE debt: A strategic complement in private markets
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that commercial real estate (CRE) debt is well placed for 2026, citing the Mortgage Bankers Association's forecast of a 27% rise in CRE originations, conservative loan-to-value ratios, and property values that have already fallen roughly 20% from their peaks. It contends that CRE debt's low volatility and historically steadier returns make it a valuable diversifier alongside private equity and private credit, improving return per unit of risk and reducing drawdowns. The firm's explicit view is that CRE debt offers attractive risk-adjusted returns and merits a place in portfolios as a complement to other private market allocations.

pieces.title: A Conversation on the Credit Markets
AI, geopolitics, and the reshaping of technology investment
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that geopolitics is now reshaping technology investment, as AI, semiconductors, data and critical infrastructure become tied to national security and governments and companies prioritise supply-chain resilience and control over price, creating structural demand for domestic AI, regionalised supply chains, power and networking. The piece, by tech equities specialist Richard Clode, concludes that this fragmentation increases dispersion between companies and so favours active stock selection. It also flags risks in the data centre capex cycle, where higher capital costs could prompt rotations from equities to fixed income if returns disappoint.

What is the outlook for energy stocks?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that geopolitical shocks typically hit equities briefly but move oil and energy stocks more sharply and for longer, with the current Iran-related disruption being no exception so far: the S&P 500 is down just 1.5% twelve days in, while the energy sector is up only 1.7% since the conflict began. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens within weeks, the firm expects energy profits to rise in the first half of the year before fading in the second, with U.S. upstream, refining and petrochemicals the main beneficiaries and oilfield services facing near-term headwinds. Its explicit call is that it is now too late to chase a broad energy rally, and that investors should favour active stock selection focused on quality and strong balance sheets.

pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers reports that its Commodities team has won two LSEG Lipper Fund Awards for risk-adjusted performance over five- and 10-year periods, ranking first in the Commodity Blended category for the fourth successive year on the 10-year measure. The piece also promotes its long-only, futures-based Transition Materials strategy, arguing that metals such as copper, silver, tin and nickel-linked inputs, together with lumber, are essential to electrification and offer a diversifier to oil and gas exposure. It further contends that the Iran war will likely prompt countries and companies to expand strategic stockpiling of these materials, providing structural support for the asset class.

China New Year outlook
pieces.summary: Aberdeen's 2026 China outlook argues that trade strength, a firmer renminbi and policy support are reshaping China's growth mix, with net trade contributing almost a third of 2025 GDP growth and consumption's share rising. Aberdeen says it expects AI to dominate the narrative but favours the less glamorous "plumbing" (data-centre infrastructure, components, automation and software), and it names equipment makers, AI players and hardware suppliers it sees as long-term opportunities. On consumption, Aberdeen favours firms with pricing power, channel control and cash conversion, including yield-oriented pet food names over traditional staples such as beer and condiments.

pieces.title: Emerging market and Asia Pacific equities
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that emerging market and Asia Pacific equities are at an inflection point, having doubled S&P 500 returns over the past year and now matching its three-year performance. The piece contends that this advance resembles the early-2000s investment cycle rather than past stimulus-driven recoveries, driven by a weakening dollar, persistent inflation supporting corporate pricing power, and broadening investment and earnings growth beyond North Asia as China pursues technological self-sufficiency and the broader industrial cycle strengthens across the region.

pieces.title: Tailoring Insurance Investments: Yield Enhancement Strategies to Optimize Capital-Constrained Insurance Portfolios
Family Office Investment Solutions
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that an increasing share of equity value creation is occurring before companies reach public markets, as firms remain private longer due to abundant capital availability and the ability to avoid quarterly reporting requirements. The firm contends that this represents a durable structural shift rather than a cyclical trend, and recommends that family offices adjust their portfolio construction by allocating to late-stage venture and growth equity strategies rather than relying solely on traditional public equity and private equity buyout exposures.

pieces.title: The next frontier for EU retail investors: digital advice made simple
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that EU retail investor participation is constrained by a regulatory gap between full financial advice and execution-only services, and contends that simplified advice—streamlined, goal-focused guidance delivered through user-centred digital platforms—could democratise access to investment guidance. The company calls for regulators to formally recognise simplified advice within the MiFID framework with proportionate requirements, and to reform suitability tests that apply uniform risk assumptions across different financial goals.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that European credit is attractive for 2026, citing its diversification benefits against US exposure, supportive macro conditions (inflation near the ECB's 2% target and fiscal expansion), resilient corporate fundamentals, and yields of around 3% for investment grade and 5%+ for high yield. It acknowledges that policy-driven volatility is likely to persist and explicitly concludes that unconstrained strategies, which actively manage credit and duration exposure, are best placed to profit from that volatility.

Sixth Street Growth Approach
pieces.summary: Sixth Street presents its Growth team as a flexible capital provider to technology companies and other fast-growing businesses, offering capital alongside a "More Than Capital" operating value creation team and a peer operating network, with examples drawn from sectors including fintech, data centres, healthcare and live events. The firm argues that its edge lies in combining capital, sector expertise and its wider platform to help portfolio companies grow, solve customers' problems and navigate uncertainty as genuine partners, a point its executives make in a set of interview-style video clips. Notably, the piece is promotional and offers no performance data, fund metrics or specific outcomes to test these claims against.

pieces.title: Private Equity Secondaries: From Niche to Necessary
High yield and EMD:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that high yield and emerging market debt have so far held up relatively well against the global energy shock from the Iran conflict and the disruption to Strait of Hormuz oil transit, despite WTI crude futures rising around 55% year-to-date. It attributes US high yield's relative resilience to investor confidence in issuers, lower interest rate sensitivity than investment grade, and a higher energy sector weighting (around 11%) that has benefited from tightening spreads. The firm says it is biased towards defensiveness on emerging market rates in its systematic strategies given uncertain conditions, while contending that volatility may create value opportunities, particularly for systematic investors able to act quickly.

pieces.title: Our approach to sustainability
pieces.summary: BlackRock frames its approach to sustainability and the energy transition as grounded in fiduciary duty to clients, emphasising that it offers investment choices across sustainable and transition-focused strategies rather than imposing particular sustainability views. The firm manages $1.3 trillion in sustainable and transition assets as of December 2025 and assesses sustainability factors only when they are financially material to investment risk and return. BlackRock argues that it participates in industry sustainability initiatives to facilitate dialogue on client interests whilst maintaining independent stewardship and proxy voting decisions.

pieces.title: Castlelake Prices $1.1 Billion Commercial Real Estate CLO, CLCRE 2026-FL1
War, supply disruptions – and a modestly pro-risk stance
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that global growth should prove resilient if the Middle East conflict stays contained and short-lived, though the stagflationary effects of an unrelenting run of supply shocks, including the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, leave policymakers with no good options and widen the range of inflation and growth outcomes. On that basis, it reaffirms a modestly pro-risk stance over 12 to 18 months, with trimmed risk in some portfolios: overweight U.S. equities (technology and communication services), a short-duration bias in U.S. rates, neutral on U.S. high yield, long Italian and UK government bonds, overweight the euro and emerging market equities, and value-oriented stock selection given unusually high dispersion in U.S. equities.

pieces.title: Top 10 Benefits of a Minority Recapitalization
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece (3 June 2025, Private Credit section) argues that a minority recapitalisation, funded by mezzanine or subordinated debt and/or preferred equity, lets business owners raise liquidity or fund growth without giving up majority control, and lists ten benefits including lower dilution than issuing common equity and a more patient, buy-and-hold partner. It closes by promoting PGIM itself, which says it offers a streamlined, finance-contingency-free process and describes its approach as "about relationships, not transactions."

The gulf's next chapter: beyond sovereigns, towards capital formation
pieces.summary: New York Life Investments argues that the Gulf Cooperation Council's investment case is shifting from sovereign debt towards corporate credit, infrastructure and private credit, as 2026's geopolitical stress tests have demonstrated that balance sheet strength rather than resilience is now the distinguishing feature. The firm contends that the region's strongest opportunities lie in globally diversified corporates such as DP World and in selective real estate exposure where contractual cash flows and developer backlogs support debt service despite weakening market conditions.

pieces.title: Five reasons to consider US short-duration high yield bonds - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that US short-duration high yield bonds can offer stable, consistent income with lower volatility and a reduced risk of principal loss, making them a potentially useful part of a diversified portfolio. It cites greater liquidity (roughly a third of the approximately $1.5 trillion US high yield market has expected take-outs within three years), more predictable risk horizons amid AI-related disruption, low defaults supported by abundant refinancing capacity, and yields comparable to longer-dated bonds. The firm's explicit view is that a higher-quality, actively managed short-duration approach, backed by bottom-up credit analysis, can deliver more predictable long-term outcomes.

pieces.title: The RealReal CEO Rati Sahi Levesque: Resale, Robots, and the New Luxury Consumer
Sports as an Asset Class: The $2.5 Trillion Opportunity
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that sports represents a $2.5 trillion asset class that remains significantly undercapitalized compared to its size and stability, creating an opportunity for institutional capital deployment through financing rather than ownership alone. The firm has established Apollo Sports Capital to provide comprehensive debt, equity and hybrid capital solutions to sports organisations, exemplified by a recent multi-billion-dollar financing agreement with the New York Yankees. Apollo contends that structural changes in team ownership and media rights, combined with sports' fixed supply and growing demand, are opening the sector to institutional investment at an inflection point.

pieces.title: Multi-Sector Credit Asset Allocation Perspectives: Navigating rate uncertainty
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that rate uncertainty, driven by an on-off US-Iran truce, a less communicative Federal Reserve under Chair Kevin Warsh, and the inflationary effects of AI-related capital spending, should shape fixed income positioning. Its explicit call is to favour short duration and floating-rate assets, notably securitised credit and loans, over more rate-sensitive corporate bonds, with AI-driven investment-grade supply seen as limiting spread upside while agency and commercial mortgage-backed securities offer a more favourable technical backdrop.

pieces.title: Seizing the future: Market opportunities in the low-carbon economy
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that energy-security pressures and surging AI-driven power demand are extending near-term reliance on fossil fuels, but will strengthen the long-term case for domestic, lower-carbon energy, as clean technologies, such as solar and batteries, benefit from manufacturing learning curves. The firm cautions that the fastest-scaling clean technologies are not always the best investments, citing solar's volatile pricing and intense competition despite its cost advantage. Looking under the hood of U.S. auto ABS
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that U.S. auto asset-backed securities offer an attractive yield opportunity, with a spread premium of about 35 basis points over similarly rated short-duration credit, at a time when corporate valuations look stretched and rates are expected to fall. The firm contends that stress in subprime auto loans, where delinquencies have reached recession-like levels, is largely confined to that segment and to idiosyncratic events such as the First Brands and Tricolor bankruptcies, since prime borrowers (roughly 75% of the market) remain on solid footing. Its explicit view is that active, selective management is essential, favouring older subprime vintages (2020–2021) over 2022–2025 deals, which have weaker performance and are an increasing share of the index.

pieces.title: Is the Fed preparing to raise interest rates?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that the FOMC held the Federal Funds target range at 3.50-3.75% in a 9-3 vote, with three officials dissenting in favour of a quarter-point hike, and that Chair Warsh gave no clear signal on the path ahead. The firm's base case is that the Fed will not hike this year, despite markets pricing in one to two increases by year-end. It sees a September hike as a real possibility depending on the data, but judges

The firm reports that infrastructure debt fundraising proved resilient in 2023 despite broader sector challenges, and contends that strong underlying infrastructure fundamentals and stable long-term inflation expectations position debt investors well to capture risk-adjusted returns as transaction volumes recover.

Nonfarm payrolls rose 130k against 65k expected, the unemployment rate fell to 4.3%, and private wage growth held at 3.7% year on year, while 2025 job growth was revised down sharply to an average of 15k a month. pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that its positive market outlook rests on three risks: renewed Middle East escalation, a bond supply shock in which governments and AI-related borrowers keep borrowing heavily, and disappointing returns from AI. Its core scenario is that energy flows gradually normalise without a full resolution, and it says a stagflationary escalation would challenge both stocks and bonds.

US Municipal Bonds: Case Studies
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's whitepaper argues that municipal revenue bonds, often treated as a minor portfolio line item, finance essential infrastructure such as transport networks, water systems and medical facilities, and sets out to make those links tangible through real-world examples. It states that the US municipal market's fragmentation creates considerable opportunities for active managers, but that these require specialist, bond-by-bond credit analysis of the underlying assets. The examples are presented as illustrative only and explicitly not as investment recommendations.

pieces.title: Expansionary SNB policy
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the Swiss National Bank held its policy rate at 0% in June, diverging from the hawkish ECB and Fed, and that stabilising the franc is now its main priority, with its readiness to intervene in FX markets reaffirmed. The firm views Swiss inflation (0.6% in May) as still low and the economy as resilient despite a slight rise in unemployment, and says it sees no need for further policy changes this year. It also reads the latest meeting as a subtle signal of slightly higher rates over the medium term.

pieces.title: Long-Term Capital Partners for Longevity & Stability
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece, dated 21 January 2026 and filed under private credit, presents the firm as a long-term capital provider spanning senior credit, subordinated debt and equity, and says it looks through market cycles and volatility to judge a company's growth prospects and financial profile. Its explicit stance is that this through-cycle approach allows PGIM to invest through periods of heightened risk and leverage and so keep companies supplied with capital over the long run. Beyond this positioning, the text is largely promotional and offers no market data or specific investment call.

pieces.title: Have Rate Hikes Tipped the Scales Toward Value Equities?
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that rising interest rates and persistent inflation could favour value equities over long-duration growth stocks, since value companies derive more of their worth from visible cash flows over the next three to five years, whereas growth valuations depend more on distant profits that are discounted more heavily when rates rise. The firm cites its research showing value stocks outperforming growth three, six and 12 months after rate-hike cycles began, and says the AI-driven market and concentration in growth stocks make value a useful diversifier. Its explicit view is that portfolios heavily tilted toward growth during the low-rate era may benefit from selective exposure to value stocks with visible free cash flow and credible normalised earnings, while growth still has a place in diversified allocations.

pieces.title: Beyond Necessity Retail: The Underwriting Test
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that necessity retail's durable income depends on more than necessity demand, lease length or headline covenant strength, and that investors should underwrite the tenant itself, including store-level profitability, strategic relevance and rent affordability. It contends that contracted rents above market levels can create valuation risk at exit, and that income resilience should be stress-tested against vacancy, reletting costs and rental resets. PGIM also notes that equity investors and senior lenders weigh these factors differently, with lenders prioritising income certainty and downside protection.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset Views – It’s a wild world (but a wide world) - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's February multi-asset report describes a modest, risk-management-driven trim to its equity overweight, mainly in the US, as oil prices rose on US-Iran tensions, while it stays positive on risky assets, with its machine learning indicators still signalling a bull market. It argues that rapid AI-driven sector rotation has caused unusually w

pieces.title: The Power Of Private Markets
A big role for small and middle-market private equity investments
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that small and middle-market buyouts (companies with $10 million to $300 million in revenue) offer structural advantages over large-cap private equity: a much larger opportunity set, lower purchase multiples, less acquisition leverage, and scope for value creation through operational improvements and add-on acquisitions. It contends that current conditions, including extended hold periods and constrained distributions, favour these smaller companies, which can exit through sales to strategic buyers and financial sponsors rather than relying on IPOs. The firm's explicit view is that these dynamics may enhance returns for long-term investors equipped to select managers carefully, given the wider return dispersion at the smaller end of the market.

pieces.title: Why Japanese Government Bonds Deserve a Second Look
Absolute return: Dispersion and opportunity in an era of disorder
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Ben Wallace, argues that equity markets have entered a new regime in which stock dispersion has risen sharply, close to 2009 peaks on Morgan Stanley data for MSCI Europe. The piece attributes this to three factors: the return of a real cost of capital, which makes valuation, business models and management matter again; geopolitical and policy shocks amplified by social media; and AI, which is separating companies that can adapt or differentiate from those that cannot. The firm's explicit view is that this environment is less forgiving for passive or diversified exposure but gives absolute return investors more scope to profit from stock selection through long and short positions, and that traditional equity-bond diversification may offer less protection than before.

pieces.title: Making the Total Portfolio Approach Work: The Role of Systematic GTAA in Enhancing Total-Fund Outcomes
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that systematic Global Tactical Asset Allocation (GTAA) overlays offer asset owners adopting the Total Portfolio Approach a transparent, scalable and capital-efficient way to exploit short-term market dislocations, with active risk deployed in a measurable, repeatable and governance-friendly manner. The paper's explicit case rests on five benefits: return sources with low or negative correlation to reference portfolios, easier risk budgeting, access to a wider opportunity set, liquidity through largely futures-based overlays, and better diagnostics of macro exposures across regimes. The text is an introductory overview and offers no performance data, so the claims are asserted rather than evidenced in the excerpt provided.

pieces.title: Income Options: The Case for Derivative Income Strategies in Today’s Market
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that derivative income strategies, particularly equity funds that pair a portfolio with an options overlay, merit strong consideration as yield sources as traditional income options weaken and dividend yields sit near 20-year lows. It cautions that the category, now around 200 equity strategies, varies widely in quality: it favours active stock selection and a disciplined, rules-based overlay (selling out-of-the-money index calls on a consistent share of the portfolio) over market timing or high-yield, higher-volatility approaches. The firm's explicit view is that such strategies can be a "compelling" part of a diversified, outcome-oriented portfolio, and that investors should scrutinise overlay design, beta exposure and distribution treatment before selecting one.

pieces.title: Exploring the future of fixed income
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that fixed income investors should prioritise spread-adjusted volatility and downside protection over headline yields in an environment of higher rates and tight spreads. The firm contends that active management remains essential in fixed income given differentiated regional opportunities and compressed valuations, whilst traditional bonds can still serve a useful role in multi-asset portfolios provided the mix of exposures is carefully calibrated for higher inflation and interest rates.

pieces.title: Equities: quality investing
LDI health check
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's short piece argues that UK defined benefit pension schemes should run a health check on their liability-driven investment (LDI) strategy to identify weaknesses and build confidence in longer-term decisions, testing whether the hedge is robust, efficient, aligned with scheme objectives and adaptable to change. It highlights collateral management as an area The Pensions Regulator has flagged for improvement, and Insight's stated view is that schemes should pursue greater diversification and dynamism in response. The page itself is a teaser that points readers to a fuller paper, "A new world for UK DB schemes."

pieces.title: Successfully Failing
pieces.summary: PGIM's David Blanchett argues that "probability of success", the retirement industry's most common measure, is misleading because it reduces outcomes to a pass or fail verdict. It ignores the size and timing of any shortfall, the guaranteed income that sets a spending floor, and the flexibility retirees have to adjust. PGIM's view is that the better question is how much of a retirement goal is actually funded, and that on this measure some retirees could spend around 20% more without taking on extra risk.

pieces.title: Regional Q&A: Apollo in Japan
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that Japan is undergoing structural economic change characterised by wage growth, governance reform and corporate capital redeployment, creating demand for longer-duration funding and private capital solutions that banks cannot meet. Apollo contends that its integrated platform across asset management, capital solutions and retirement services is well-positioned to serve Japanese corporates, institutions and investors seeking alignment, flexibility and long-term partnership. Apollo asserts that private capital will play an increasingly important complementary role in Japan's financial ecosystem, particularly in supporting demographic challenges and meeting investor demand for income and diversification beyond public markets.

Värde Provides €45 Million of Asset-Based Financing to Everphone
pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that an affiliate has provided €45 million of mezzanine financing to Everphone, a Berlin-based device-as-a-service provider, to refinance existing mezzanine debt and fund a portfolio of rental contracts under its Asset-Based Finance strategy. The firm presents the deal as evidence of "expanding opportunity" to offer tailored capital solutions to scaling businesses across Europe, with Värde's Global Head of Asset-Based Finance, Missy Dolski, describing it as a sign of the firm's long-standing role as a trusted financing partner. Värde also frames the transaction as one that supports Everphone's growth and its push to lead the circular economy for enterprise technology, though the release itself is promotional and offers no financial terms beyond the headline amount.

It contends that market moves often reflect prevailing narratives rather than fundamentals, so investors must reassess information, challenge initial reactions and adjust positioning. pieces.title: Structure, not risk, driving US and European private credit divergence
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that the sharp repricing of private credit linked to software, triggered by AI-related concerns, exposed structural rather than risk-based differences between the US and European markets. In its view, European private credit, particularly on insurance balance sheets, has proven more resilient because capital is long-term and liability-matched, so mark-to-market moves do not force selling, whereas US business development companies and semi-liquid vehicles (around 40% of US exposure, by its estimate) amplify volatility through leverage, liquidity promises and frequent NAV reporting. The piece explicitly rejects the idea that European insurers are simply more cautious, noting they actively buy unitranche and sponsor-backed loans, and it concludes that the resulting "structure, not risk" gap favours unlevered or leverage-neutral direct lending for long-dated liabilities.

pieces.title: The Rise of ABF: Video Interview with Missy Dolski
pieces.summary: Värde Partners' Global Head of Asset-Based Finance, Missy Dolski, argues that asset-based finance (ABF) has become a standalone asset class within private credit, with growth ahead in areas such as fund finance, where she sees subscription lines (a trillion-dollar market largely held on bank balance sheets) potentially becoming a separate segment. Värde explicitly favours the middle market, where deal sizes below roughly $150 million avoid crowded pricing competition, and it stresses a relationship-led, on-site diligence approach, with LPs increasingly seeking ABF's current income and downside protection as diversification from direct lending.

pieces.title: 2026 Midyear Credit Outlook
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping credit markets in ways that require investors to reconsider traditional approaches. The firm contends that whilst credit fundamentals remain sound, spreads offer diminishing protection, public capital markets face record financing demands for AI infrastructure, and diversification strategies must adapt to new AI-related risk factors. Apollo advocates that private investment-grade credit will be crucial for meeting the substantial funding gap created by the AI buildout.

Beyond the Banks: How Private Credit is Reshaping Football Finance in Europe
pieces.summary: PGIM's article argues that European football's shift into a sophisticated business, with revenues from broadcast deals, sponsorship, merchandise and year-round stadium operations, has created room for private credit lenders that can underwrite complex, asset- or revenue-specific structures. Rather than displacing banks, PGIM sees private credit as complementing them with longer-term, flexible capital, and its Head of Private Credit, Josh Shipley, describes such lenders as well positioned to support both club-level and stadium financings. The piece is a gated marketing piece promoting PGIM's financing capabilities, with case studies on Sporting Clube de Portugal's stadium SPV and Atlético de Madrid.

pieces.title: Buffer ETFs: Strategies for Equity-Market Uncertainty
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that buffer ETFs, also called defined-outcome ETFs, suit risk-averse investors who still need equity exposure for long-term goals, offering downside protection up to a set buffer in exchange for capped upside over a one-year or three-month outcome period. The piece reports that assets in the category reached $84.2 billion since 2018 and expects growth to continue amid geopolitical uncertainty. It presents laddered buffer ETFs, which spread cap-timing risk across staggered outcome periods, as a simpler, model-friendly option compared with standalone funds, and it explicitly positions buffer ETFs as a key solution for risk-minded investors.

pieces.title: Seeking Steady Income in an Unsteady World
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that, amid de-globalisation, sticky inflation, geopolitical risk and an AI-led market narrowed to a few powerful stocks, investors should pursue income through a broader, diversified multi-asset approach rather than chasing high yields, which it says tend to bring lower quality, illiquidity and larger drawdowns. Its explicit recommendations include favouring profitable companies with sustainable dividends, using low-beta equities and Treasuries for defence, accepting that dividend-focused equity exposure may cost growth exposure, and drawing income from sources such as high yield, investment-grade and emerging-market corporates, REITs, convertibles and risk-controlled option strategies, guided by four pillars: efficient income, diversified defence, a growth engine, and expanded yield sources.

The firm contends that its 28 years of CLO experience, combined with active management within an ETF structure, allows it to manage the complexity of these securities whilst providing daily liquidity and operational simplicity that passive or traditional access routes do not afford.

The firm nonetheless warns of heightened tactical risk, since investor demand for gold has run well ahead of jewellery demand and retail interest is extreme, so it expects volatility to rise and advises investors to position for it as a tactical overlay. It concludes that more investors should consider a gold allocation.

pieces.title: Income Strategy Update: Standout Returns, Powered by Active Management
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that global divergence in growth and policy, combined with attractive starting yields and elevated equity valuations, makes 2026 one of the best opportunities for active fixed income in over a decade. Its explicit positioning for the PIMCO Income Strategy is defensive and flexible: a tilt towards high-quality assets, slightly shorter duration than the aggregate benchmark concentrated in the 5–10 year part of the curve, a modest underweight to the U.S. dollar, and selective exposure to the U.K., Australia and several emerging markets. The firm also expects most developed-market central banks to ease, with the Fed moving towards about 3%, and signals that longer maturities may play a larger role later in 2026 as valuations evolve.

pieces.title: Under a Warsh Fed, Expect a Thoughtful Policy Approach
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that Kevin Warsh, nominated by President Trump as Fed chair, will likely be confirmed and serve as an effective, thoughtful chair, with Fed independence still well supported. It expects him to favour at least two 25-basis-point cuts in 2026, possibly a third, bringing the funds rate to roughly 2.75%–3.25%, but to be more cautious thereafter if inflation expectations rise. PIMCO also flags that his likely shift away from extensive forward guidance and towards a smaller, shorter-duration balance sheet could make the transition in communication policy bumpy.

pieces.title: Extreme investing scenarios
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that 2026 begins in a "Goldilocks" environment of aligned growth, inflation and interest rates, but with valuations high, the odds of extreme melt-up and melt-down scenarios have risen, making research essential. Its CIO contends that markets have been driven by sentiment rather than fundamentals, and flags an AI-related downside (over-investment leading to a readjustment) alongside a possible upside from underestimated productivity gains. The firm says its multi-asset strategies, now normalised in risk and exposure, are designed to balance downside protection with participation in concentrated bull markets.

The piece frames rising global bond yields as the latest stage of a long normalisation from the ultra-low rates of the 2010s. pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Improved Optics But Unchanged Economics in Software Loans
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that software loan spreads have partly recovered since the summer sell-off but have widened again since early September, and that the valuation gap versus the broader leveraged loan market, about 8 points of bid price versus roughly 10 in June, remains significant. It says AI disruption risk and elevated refinancing costs will keep that gap material and sustain high dispersion across issuers, with investment-grade software firms and their equities not offering a meaningful read-across for leveraged loan credits. PIMCO's explicit view is that the improvement is more optical than economic for weaker credits, and that choices made in the low-rate era will drive differentiation between winners and losers in the sector.

Barings makes no explicit investment view or call in this piece.

The company contends that technology now enables deeper, more sophisticated risk analysis at scale and calls for advisors to adopt tools like its Aladdin Wealth platform to provide clients with more transparent, factor-based insights into portfolio drivers and potential outcomes.

pieces.summary: PIMCO's piece argues that higher yields pose limited debt-servicing risk for most U.S. corporate issuers, since median interest coverage remains around 6x for USD investment grade and 3x for high yield, and index-level yields-to-worst are only marginally above average coupons. It identifies CCC-rated borrowers as the exception: PIMCO estimates that coupons on their 2027 and 2028 maturities could roughly double if refinanced at current index yields, which it sees as an acute pain point if late-cycle pressures weaken earnings further. PIMCO's explicit view is that refinancing risk is relatively benign across the market but concentrated at the lowest end of the quality spectrum.

Checkpoints: How to know retirement savings are on track
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that most savers lack a clear retirement target, so their saving is largely guesswork, and it proposes age-and-income "checkpoints" as a directional benchmark for how much they should have saved today. Citing its 2026 Defined Contribution Plan Participant Survey, it notes that 53% of workers don't know how much they need to retire securely and 59% think they should be contributing more, and its checkpoints assume saving 5% annually to age 65, retiring at 65, investing in a target date fund, and taking Social Security into account. Its explicit call is that a checkpoint can turn uncertainty into action, while individuals who fall short should consider planning tools or a financial professional.

pieces.title: Research enhanced equity: index-like precision, powered by active insight
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that research-enhanced equity strategies offer a middle ground between passive indexing and active management, maintaining index-like risk profiles while deploying small, diversified stock-level tilts to seek incremental returns. The firm contends that this approach is increasingly relevant given current market concentration, particularly in the S&P 500 where the top ten holdings represent roughly 40% of the index, suggesting that meaningful growth opportunities exist outside the largest companies despite their recent outperformance. J.P. Morgan positions research-enhanced strategies as suitable for investors seeking benchmark alignment without full passive constraints, or as a complement to higher-conviction active allocations.

pieces.summary: Schroders argues that European value equities are an overlooked opportunity: they have outperformed the S&P 500 over one, three and five years, and a heavy US bias now limits prospective returns and diversification. It contends that passive European value indices, such as the MSCI Europe Value and Enhanced Value, hold surprisingly little genuinely cheap stock and are heavily concentrated in financials (38% of MSCI Europe Value), so active managers can offer better valuation discipline, sector control and diversification. Schroders' explicit view is that investors should question their US-heavy allocations and that active European value is a stronger route to diversified returns than passive exposure.

pieces.title: Fixed Income Under the Spotlight: Navigating the Fixed Income Valuation Conundrum
pieces.summary: MFS Investment Management argues that credit risks have risen but remain contained, with stress visible in leveraged loans, private credit, office commercial real estate and some consumer lending, while private credit's lack of transparency and mark-to-market pricing is a growing concern. With spreads tight and returns likely to come from carry rather than spread compression, the firm favours a defensive, top-down and sector-led approach, combining bottom-up selection in areas such as structured credit, defensive corporates, idiosyncratic high yield and emerging market sovereigns, and maintaining portfolio liquidity to exploit future dislocations. Its explicit positioning is a slight overweight in investment-grade credit with a defensive bias and added hedges, a tactical reduction in higher-beta high yield, and a slight overweight in duration, with lower conviction on curve steepeners.

pieces.title: The Odds Are Changing: Investing in 2026
Exploring the Opportunity in Alternative Real Estate
pieces.summary: Barings argues that alternative real estate sectors (such as senior housing, data centres, manufactured housing and health care-linked property) are attracting institutional interest because their demand drivers, including demographics, health care use, digital infrastructure and essential services, evolve more steadily than traditional property types tied to economic cycles. It also contends that fragmented ownership creates operational inefficiencies that experienced investors can exploit, and that constrained new supply in these sectors supports resilient cash flows, so Barings views them as meaningful complements within diversified real estate portfolios rather than niche exposures.

pieces.title: The Virtuous Cycle
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that capital markets are essential for mobilising investment in innovation and growth whilst enabling more people to share in economic prosperity. The asset manager calls on policymakers and the financial industry to collaborate on expanding market access, strengthening market structures, and supporting technological innovation to unlock capital markets' full potential globally.

pieces.title: 2026 Credit Outlook: Growing Divergence Amid AI’s Big Build-Out
Yahoo Finance: Stephanie Drescher
pieces.summary: Apollo's Chief Client and Product Development Officer, Stephanie Drescher, argues in this Yahoo Finance interview that private markets have become a core component of total portfolios, offering advisers additional tools to balance return, income, volatility and liquidity against specific planning goals. She explicitly contends that private market building blocks should be treated as alternatives to public stocks and bonds rather than add-ons, and highlights asset-backed finance (roughly a $20 trillion market within a $40 trillion credit market) as a recommended example, citing the stability of investment-grade exposures such as aircraft leases, fleet finance and music royalties. Apollo's stated view is that its origination platforms, which employ an incremental 4,000 staff, provide genuine alpha for clients.

pieces.title: How BlackRock’s models stayed ahead in 2026
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that its Australian model portfolios returned 6–15% in the year to 30 June 2026, outperforming peers by maintaining overweights to equities, US shares, emerging markets and gold despite geopolitical shocks and inflation. The firm argues that market dispersion rewarded selective positioning focused on resilient earnings trends, and it has now rebalanced to lock in gains and shift from broad equity exposure to more deliberate risk allocation, retaining participation in AI-related structural themes while holding elevated cash.

pieces.title: Aviva Investors & Amro Partners acquire German PBSA development scheme
AI, energy innovation and the UK stock market
Beyond the bubble debate: where disruptive technology is creating value - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that AI's disruptive impact is spreading beyond the technology sector, so the biggest opportunities may lie in companies across the wider economy that capture efficiency and productivity gains, rather than only in tech stocks. It acknowledges parallels with the dotcom bubble, including intense competition, debt-financed infrastructure spending and circular financing arrangements, but concludes that the market is not yet in bubble territory, citing the strong balance sheets of hyperscalers, existing infrastructure, the early stage of adoption and valuations that are below their late-1990s levels. The firm's explicit view is that AI is the most impactful digital transformation theme since the internet, while investors should remain alert to risks such as a possible slowdown in spending.

pieces.title: Värde Recognized by Octus As the Leading India Private Credit Lender in H1 2026
pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that Octus has recognised it as the leading private credit lender in India for H1 2026, citing its local APAC presence since 2008 and more than $13 billion invested across the region. Värde attributes its position to the longevity of its presence in these markets, which it says helps it source opportunities and structure tailored financing for India's large conglomerates and businesses. The piece makes no forward-looking call, and it includes a disclaimer that the recognition does not indicate past or future fund performance.

pieces.title: European Overview: 2025 Review & 2026 Outlook
pieces.summary: PGIM's European private credit team, in its 2025 review and 2026 outlook (published 12 January 2026), reports relatively consistent deal flow across the credit spectrum despite economic and geopolitical uncertainty, and argues that longer-term, flexible institutional financing has helped borrowers manage risk and diversify their capital structures. Looking ahead, PGIM expects demand for institutional finance to remain robust, with infrastructure investment (notably renewables and digital infrastructure), a cautious pick-up in M&A, and greater appetite from sports owners and leagues for alternative capital all rising in 2026. The firm's stated view is that volatility is likely to persist, but that it hopes positive momentum will follow as European growth indicators improve.

pieces.title: Federated Hermes | Why our improved credit outlook explains tight spread levels
pieces.summary: Federated Hermes argues that its confidence in moderate, credit-friendly global growth has improved, leading it to modestly upgrade its overall appetite for credit risk, with the reduced use of "uncertainty" in the Fed's Beige Book cited as supporting evidence. Its main stated concern is valuation: even after adjusting for duration and quality, spreads remain on the rich side of fair. Accordingly, it says it remains fully invested at the higher end of credit quality, avoids weaker US credit at the high-yield margins, and favours strong ABS, selective European sub-financials and CLO positions, with a gradual trim of double-B exposure.

High yield bonds outlook: Increasing selectivity in 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' fixed income portfolio managers Brent Olson and Tom Ross expect modest economic growth and supportive central bank policy to sustain positive high yield bond returns in 2026, with income as the main driver, though they argue for a more selective approach given rich valuations and a later stage in the credit cycle. The firm points to easing refinancing pressure as new-issue coupons fall toward 7.2%, close to the 6.6% average on existing US bonds, and to yields of 6.7% in the US and 5.1% in Europe at end-November 2025. It flags tight average credit spreads, but notes that spreads on CCC-and-lower bonds have widened and that value can be found by looking beyond the averages, with potential opportunities in mergers and acquisitions that could lift weaker issuers to stronger credit ratings.

Are high yield bonds the place to hide in levered credit?
pieces.summary: Columbia Threadneedle Investments argues that high yield bonds are the most defensible part of levered credit because they combine stronger credit quality with limited exposure to AI-driven disruption. It contrasts this with leveraged loans (about 13.5% software and technology exposure) and private credit (at least 20%), which it says carry greater concentrations in software businesses under pressure, whereas US high yield has only 3.5% software exposure and a larger share of BB-rated issuers than 15 years ago. The firm's explicit view is that if credit losses come, high yield is where it expects to see the least damage.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Australian institutional multi-asset note, written by CIO Laurent Clavel, argues that global growth remains resilient but is losing momentum, with inflation sticky and markets pricing more rate hikes than its economists expect. Its explicit stance is to keep a moderate overweight in global equities (favouring the US, Japan, emerging markets, financials and healthcare), a moderate overweight in commodities, and a moderate underweight in sovereign bonds and investment-grade credit, while moderately overweighting high yield and emerging-market debt. It holds the current risk budget steady rather than adding to it, and it judges French political and fiscal risks to warrant vigilance rather than a broad de-risking.

It argues that this softness is distorted by the government shutdown, so inflation will likely pick up, and that the labour market's reliance on healthcare hiring and the oppos

pieces.title: The Evolving Real Estate Environment
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that global real estate markets are recovering after a turbulent period of interest rate changes, price swings and a slow post-COVID recovery, with slowing construction reducing supply and transaction and debt markets reopening. It explicitly views this as an attractive entry point for disciplined investors, citing a significant repricing of high-quality assets from their peaks and an expectation that reduced supply will lead to further rent growth. The piece is largely promotional, and its forward-looking statements carry an explicit disclaimer advising readers not to rely on them.

pieces.title: When Geopolitics Becomes an Economic Input
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that geopolitical risk is no longer a series of one-off shocks but a structural feature of a fragmented, multipolar world, so it should be treated as an essential economic input and reflected in investment decisions. It contends that this environment rewards flexible, multi-sector and active strategies over passive indices, favouring selectivity across countries, sectors and asset classes. Specifically, PIMCO says that higher starting bond yields give fixed income more cushion than in 2022, that shorter-dated inflation-linked bonds and inflation swaps can be more targeted hedges than long-dated TIPS, and that commodity volatility offers relative-value opportunities rather than directional bets.

pieces.title: Research in focus: Quarterly sector update
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Q3 2026 sector update reports that global equities rose on strong earnings and resilient growth, though higher commodity prices and interest rates weighed on valuations, with energy, technology and healthcare outperforming while rate-sensitive utilities, industrials, real estate and consumer sectors lagged. The firm argues that AI remains a powerful theme but that investors are becoming more selective, and it says its bottom-up, fundamentals-led approach and long-term secular themes such as compute demand, electrification and healthcare innovation continue to offer opportunities. The piece's explicit view is that AI will prove more pervasive and value-creating than many investors expect, while also expecting growing divergence between companies that monetise AI investment and those that fail to earn adequate returns on it.
