pieces.title: Covered call options
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that covered call strategies, which generate income by systematically selling call options on portfolio holdings (typically around 20% of the portfolio for high-income versions), lower portfolio beta and volatility at the cost of capped upside, and that standard performance metrics can mislead because the returns are negatively skewed, with frequent small gains and occasional larger losses. The firm's explicit view is that the strategy adds value mainly when markets are calmer than options pricing implies, since the embedded short volatility exposure then benefits the investor, and that investors should therefore judge covered calls by how they behave across different market conditions rather than by income alone.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: A data-driven look at public credit liquidity
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that public corporate bond liquidity is healthier than at any point since the global financial crisis, citing TRACE-based measures of depth (Amihud illiquidity), breadth (turnover, including off-the-run and small-issuer bonds) and transaction costs. It contends that the common case for weaker liquidity rests on a measurement break in the Fed primary dealer series from 2013 and on a misreading of Rule 144A private placements, which it says are liquid and should not be conflated with illiquid true private credit. PIMCO's explicit view is that investors assessing liquidity risk should distinguish clearly between public markets, 144A placements and private credit, and that the trade-offs between public and private credit depend on how market structure actually functions.

pieces.title: Quick view: Brazil election: Bolsonaro has the upper hand
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Jair Bolsonaro's stronger-than-expected first-round performance in Brazil's election, combined with Congressional gains for the right, increases the probability of market-friendly fiscal and structural reform. However, the firm states that electoral optimism alone will not improve Brazil's credit story; fiscal credibility and policy execution—rather than rhetoric—are crucial, and it plans on-the-ground research in November to assess whether political change translates into tangible reform.

pieces.title: View from the markets: Déjà vu: What’s next for markets after the latest spike in oil prices? - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Daniel Morris argues that this is the sixth oil price spike since the Iran war began, each followed by falling prices, and that markets are likely to follow the same pattern. Across past episodes, energy was the only sector with positive average returns, while technology hardware ranked second and remained resilient to rate moves because AI-driven earnings growth now dominates. The firm explicitly remains positive on the long-term build-out of AI infrastructure and suggests that a stable or falling rate environment would support the Russell 2000 small-cap index, with gold also benefiting when oil falls.

pieces.title: The appeal of Insight’s approach to floating rate credit
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that a flexible approach to floating rate credit, combining access to a broad range of floating-rate and credit-related assets with disciplined selection, is well suited to investors seeking income. The piece presents diversification, credit quality, capital preservation and liquidity management as core priorities, and suggests the strategy may appeal to those wanting a more conservative risk profile than traditional high-yield bonds. The text is largely a rationale for the strategy; it offers no specific market call or forward-looking view.

pieces.title: Quick View: Will the broader implications of Japan’s rate hike remain underappreciated?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the Bank of Japan's hike to a 1% policy rate, while widely anticipated, understates the likelihood of further tightening, as inflation is becoming embedded in corporate and household behaviour and may overshoot the 2% target. The firm's Head of Japanese Equities, Junichi Inoue, explicitly says upward pressure on rates is likely to persist and that market positioning underestimates this trajectory, and he sees Japanese banks and insurers benefiting from higher rates and many sectors' earnings holding up on pricing power.

pieces.title: After 60/40: Manager Selection Matters
pieces.summary: Apollo's Christopher Lvoff argues that public markets have largely become a source of beta, with 91% of public equity managers underperforming the S&P 500 over 20 years, whereas private markets still offer alpha but with far wider dispersion between managers. Citing the 60/40 diversification benefits of private markets and the gap between top- and bottom-decile managers (roughly 30% in private equity versus 2% in public equities, and 13% in private debt versus about 1% in public fixed income), Apollo concludes that manager selection is what matters most in private markets. It also notes that entry valuations affect exit timing and distributions, though the piece does not make a specific allocation recommendation.

Midwest
pieces.summary: PGIM's Midwest year-in-review reports solid 2025 activity across its Chicago and Minneapolis offices, with deal flow driven mainly by direct origination, a Q2 slowdown linked to tariff effects, and a Q3 pick-up as companies adjusted to tariff uncertainty. It notes that tariffs weighed heavily on the industrial, import-reliant borrowers common in the region, while broader M&A declined and refinancings and dividend recaps increased. PGIM says it is "cautiously optimistic" for 2026, expecting higher activity as M&A recovers, sponsors recycle capital, and rates stay steady or fall, while acknowledging geopolitical and macro risks.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Victoria Whitehead, in the Q3 2026 Fixed Income Quarterly Outlook, is positive on euro investment grade credit, citing robust corporate fundamentals, a supportive macro backdrop and favourable technicals. With spreads tight after strong compression in the first half, she expects returns to come mainly from carry and security selection rather than further spread tightening. Explicit preferences include European financials (particularly banks and selected subordinated debt), BBB-rated credits and European industrials linked to infrastructure and defence spending, while the firm is cautious on data-centre REITs, private-equity-related issuers and highly rated defensive sectors, and is underweight the long end of technology.

Morgan Asset Management argues that liquidity portfolios should prioritise resilience over precision in a repricing environment, where rates and spreads can move quickly under elevated geopolitical and energy-driven uncertainty. It sees the Fed as likely to stay in a "wait-and-see" posture, with front-end volatility persisting even without frequent moves, and judges that the global cutting cycle is over, with hikes possible if inflation accelerates. Its explicit guidance is to maintain liquidity buffers, pace reinvestment, use duration in China to smooth yield repricing, and stay disciplined on valuation given tight credit spreads.

pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the commercial real estate market may be near a bottom after a steep fall in transaction volumes, citing U.S. Q1 2024 volumes down 16% year-on-year, the smallest decline since Q3 2022, while acknowledging that the path ahead will not be smooth and that office values have further to fall. It favours industrial and, over the longer term, multifamily, and it is cautiously optimistic that thawing debt markets, maturing loans and ample buyer dry powder will narrow bid-ask spreads and lift transaction volumes in 2024.

pieces.title: Project Glasswing: Advancing the evolution of cybersecurity
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Anthropic's Project Glasswing, with its Mythos Preview model, shows AI's growing role in cybersecurity, as AI lowers the barriers for both defenders and attackers to find and exploit software vulnerabilities. The piece outlines five implications (faster exploitation, demand for multi-LLM protection, application security, security-observability convergence, and tighter SEC disclosure rules) and concludes that AI-driven demand for protection and governance should grow, making cybersecurity "a fertile area for active stock selection." It frames AI developers such as Anthropic more as partners than as disruptors of cybersecurity vendors.

pieces.title: ECB kicks off the fight against inflation
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that the ECB raised its three key rates by 25bps in June 2026, its first hike since September 2023 and the first by a G-7 central bank since the Middle East conflict began, with new forecasts revising inflation up and growth down, mainly due to the conflict. The firm's explicit view is that the hike is unlikely to be a one-off, and it expects a follow-up move in September rather than at the July meeting, though it notes that markets are pricing roughly 26bps of tightening for September. For its EUR LVNAV liquidity strategy, it expects yields to rise by around 10bps from 17 June, with further gains as holdings are reinvested at higher rates.

Morgan Asset Management argues that gold's traditional reaction to real yields has broken down since 2022, with its R-squared falling from 85% to 16%, and that its recent behaviour is better explained by term premia, reflecting investor concern over fiscal credibility, policy uncertainty and central bank independence. The firm concludes that gold is now a less straightforward addition to fixed income portfolios, with less predictable diversification benefits, and advises investors to move beyond legacy frameworks and reassess the specific risks they wish to hedge.

PGIM expects borrowers in 2026 to keep seeking longer-dated, diversified and flexible capital, expects further growth in direct lending deployment and a more positive junior capital market, and identifies digital infrastructure and the energy transition as key real asset growth areas.

pieces.title: What is tranche thickness, and why does it matter for life insurers?
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that tranche thickness, the size of a CLO tranche relative to the overall capital structure, is becoming an important risk measure for life insurers, because two Baa3-rated tranches can carry very different modelled risk and capital charges as NAIC RBC treatment of CLOs is revisited. Citing the March 2026 NAIC and American Academy of Actuaries discussions, the firm notes that a 4% breakpoint was under consideration for tranches rated Baa3 or below, and it advises insurers to review structured credit exposures, manager reporting and capital frameworks now, without overreacting to a proposal still in development. Its explicit view is that ratings still matter but may not be sufficient on their own, and that regulators are moving towards a more risk-sensitive treatment in which structural features matter more.

Morgan Asset Management's global rates portfolio manager argues that UK inflation, driven more by government and regulatory policy than by domestic demand, should ease from April 2026, and that a weakening labour market should slow wage growth and services inflation. The firm says the Autumn Budget could move Gilts, and that a credible package of tax rises and spending cuts would support them. pieces.title: Three Market Risks Bolster the Case for Defensive Equities
Emerging Market Debt: Established resilience - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that emerging markets showed resilience in Q2 2026 despite Middle East conflict and energy-price shocks, with oil exporters such as the GCC benefiting from stronger fiscal revenues and oil importers such as India and Turkey facing higher inflation and import costs. It contends that, as broad returns tighten, country selection based on durable fundamentals, credible monetary policy and attractive real yields matters more, and it states that local currency EM debt "remains one of the more compelling areas of the asset class." The firm also warns that hard currency valuations have tightened, that inflation and a possible shift in Fed cuts could delay EM easing into 2027, and that US mid-term elections add uncertainty.

pieces.title: Beyond the Cash Rate | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that the RBA's pause on rate rises means Australian bond yields are likely to remain rangebound, making income rather than capital appreciation the primary return driver for bond investors. The asset manager contends that current yields of around 4.5-4.9 per cent on government bonds represent attractive compensation for investors waiting for the next policy move, and suggests that credit exposure through corporate bonds offers additional yield opportunities in this environment.

pieces.summary: BlackRock frames AI as a generational investment opportunity and argues that regulation should be adaptable, principles-based and focused on activities and risks rather than specific technologies, while building on existing financial services frameworks rather than creating parallel regimes. The firm states that AI adoption must be accompanied by appropriate accountability and governance to support its fiduciary obligations to clients, and identifies infrastructure, energy, labour and geopolitical implications as material to long-term investment outcomes.

pieces.summary: Apollo introduces AMAPS (Apollo Multi-Asset Prime Securities), a structured credit vehicle it presents as a successor to the CLO: roughly 85% investment-grade rated, with more diversified and higher-rated collateral, a thicker equity tranche, less structural leverage, a five-year term, and daily-priced, individually CUSIP-identified tranches. Apollo argues that spread compression in investment-grade CLOs, driven by heavy demand, pushed Athene to shrink its CLO holdings and seek safe yield elsewhere, and it expects the format to be replicated by third-party managers in time, much as CLOs were. The piece also flags a planned longer-duration variant, APADS, and is effectively a promotional statement of Apollo's view that AMAPS will become a meaningful high-grade market.

pieces.title: The Evolving Nature of Equity Quality in the Age of AI
So, Why Don’t You Own It? Understanding Underweights in Equities
Understanding the shifting risks of passive investing
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that passive investing no longer offers the simple, diversified market exposure it once did, because index composition has shifted sharply. Its S&P 500 returns are concentrated in technology (52% of the past decade's return), the US now dominates MSCI ACWI, and US Treasuries have grown to dominate the global aggregate bond index. Using a 60/40 example from 2008, it shows the portfolio drifting to 81% equities and 55% US exposure, and concludes that investors should be aware of these concentration risks, though it stops short of prescribing specific actions.

Economy: A path of moderation
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Chief Global Strategist expects 2027 to be a year of moderation for the US economy, with real GDP growth slowing to about 1.6% over the next four quarters from 2.5% in the year to Q4 2026. Its view is that AI-related capital spending and richer households will keep growth going, while weak job growth, falling real wages and a lack of fiscal support constrain lower- and middle-income consumers. It also forecasts payroll gains of roughly 50,000 a month (with unemployment falling below 4% as labour supply stays tight) and headline PCE inflation easing from 3.7% to 2.3% by Q4 2027, helped by a Middle East compromise, tariff reductions and a softening rental market.

pieces.title: Using ETFs to supplement income | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that more working-age Australians (particularly those aged 24–55) are using income-focused ETFs to supplement earnings, driven by cost-of-living pressures and changing work patterns. The firm argues that ETFs offer a simpler, more cost-efficient alternative to traditional income investing through individual shares or property, and that regular distributions from diversified portfolios can provide behavioural benefits during market volatility. BlackRock promotes its range of income-generating ETFs across different risk profiles as suitable vehicles for this investment trend.

The firm attributes the expected rebound to lower funding costs, US tax changes, AI demand, nearshoring and base effects, and says that if small caps regain their long-run growth advantage, a small-cap premium over large caps could return, though it stresses that forecasts are not guaranteed.

The firm says it is not bearish but sees complacency about volatility and elevated drawdown risk, and it suggests global healthcare, low volatility and EAFE income as defensive positions to hold alongside a strategically positive market exposure.

pieces.title: Multi-Asset: Boring is still beautiful for the second half of 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors warns that financial markets are exhibiting excessive speculation, driven by surging options trading and investor complacency about interest rates, and advocates that investors should instead favour "boring" assets such as dividend-paying stocks, non-U.S. equities and high-quality short-term bonds. The firm contends that strong nominal U.S. economic growth will prevent the Federal Reserve from cutting rates as markets expect and may force rate rises instead, which historically ends speculative periods and refocuses investors on fundamentals.

pieces.title: What does it take to 10x your money?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private equity and private market funds, which historically achieve around 15% annualised returns, can enable investors to grow their capital tenfold in 18 years through compounding, compared to 60 years at 4% returns from bonds or 31 years at 8% from public equities. The firm contends that long-term investors should adopt a "10x mindset" and consider diversified portfolios that include private market exposure to benefit from the compounding effect of higher returns over time.

pieces.title: Investing Insights from our Alpha Females: Season Round Up
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein's podcast round-up, "Investing Insights from our Alpha Females," appears to recap a season of episodes featuring its female investment professionals, but the text supplied contains only the standard disclaimers and no substantive commentary. It therefore sets out no specific market view, forecast or investment call, and it states that the podcast's views do not constitute research or investment advice and may change over time.

Factor rotation in changing markets | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that factor rotation—dynamically allocating across six equity style factors based on economic data, valuations and sentiment—can improve returns by timing exposure to whichever factor is likely to outperform in current market conditions. The firm reports that its US Factor Rotation Active ETF, recently launched in Australia, has outperformed both its benchmark and static multi-factor peers since inception in 2019. BlackRock suggests the strategy is particularly valuable given current uncertainty around US growth and supply shocks from Middle East conflicts.

pieces.title: Navigating market volatility: A comprehensive guide
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that volatility is a normal feature of markets, that markets have grown over time despite frequent pullbacks, and that they are forward-looking pricing mechanisms which often bottom during recessions rather than after them. The piece's explicit view is that staying invested is often the smartest long-term move, and that attempting to time dips risks missing the recovery. It adds that strategically managing around a decline can cushion the ride and make it easier to stay the course.

pieces.title: Compute as a new asset class | Insights
pieces.summary: Liontrust argues that compute (AI accelerator hardware such as Nvidia GPUs) is becoming a new asset class, because its cash flows can now be contracted and its value holds up better than the traditional "melting ice cube" depreciation view suggests: rental prices have risen, older chips such as the A100 still earn more than before, and software gains are raising output from existing hardware. It cites Nvidia and six large investors (Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR) setting up financing platforms targeting $500 billion for AI infrastructure, and says that financing, not chips or power, is the next constraint on the buildout. Liontrust's explicit view is that this financing machinery marks the birth of compute credit and that AI financing will approach $1 trillion of issuance this year, while acknowledging that the endurance of outside funding, rising loans against uncontracted clus

pieces.title: Bond Bulletin: Banks make the grade
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the fundamental case for owning credit remains sound, citing early bank earnings that suggest healthy consumer trends, resilient net interest income and benign credit costs. The firm states it remains comfortable with its bank holdings, given investment-grade yields near multi-year highs and supportive technical indicators. The piece identifies two key risks: potential spillovers between European sovereigns and banks, and a possible surge in bond issuance ahead of the mid-term elections.

pieces.title: Aviva Investors provides £175 million financing to The Arora Group
How do markets perform in midterm election years?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that investors should not change their portfolios in response to the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, citing evidence that politics should not override investment discipline. It points out that S&P 500 returns have been strong under both parties, that midterm-year returns have been weaker mainly because of rate hikes and other shocks rather than the vote itself, and that markets have tended to rally in the final weeks before elections. The firm concludes that economic fundamentals, such as monetary policy, labour markets, corporate profits and valuations, matter far more for returns than election outcomes.

pieces.title: UK Insurer Case Study: Portfolio Efficiency
pieces.summary: Schroders' case study examines how one UK general insurer, with a conservative portfolio concentrated in cash, short-dated credit and government bonds, could improve its strategic asset allocation by widening its investment universe to include public and private assets. Schroders reports two opportunities: first, a reallocation that raises expected return and diversification while cutting economic risk and leaving capital broadly unchanged; second, further return within a similar risk profile at the cost of higher capital consumption. Schroders' explicit view is that insurers should test whether established allocations are the only way to meet their liability, liquidity, risk and capital requirements, and that a purpose-led balance sheet (liquidity reserve, liability-matching and surplus portfolios) is a useful way to do so.

pieces.title: Comparing Large and Small Businesses Navigating AI Disruption
The Case for Securitised
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that securitised credit offers diversification from corporate bonds, given its consumer-driven and 'real economy' collateral, high-quality structures and typically better relative value than similarly rated corporates, which it says supports strong long-term risk-adjusted returns. It cites better spreads, historically lower default rates and higher Sharpe ratios, and says amortising structures and shorter durations can reduce credit and interest rate risk in core fixed income portfolios. The firm also stresses that the asset class is misunderstood and requires specialist expertise, but concludes that such misconceptions should not deter investment.

pieces.title: Insightful Investor Podcast: Cathy Marcus Discusses Investing Through Market Cycles
pieces.summary: PGIM's Cathy Marcus, Co-Head and Global COO of real estate, argues that investors navigating current market cycles should return to fundamental analysis rather than relying on broad sector trends. She contends that investment success increasingly depends on identifying specific opportunities suited to individual circumstances, a perspective informed by her decades of experience through multiple market cycles.

pieces.title: Asia Pacific Regional Spotlight
pieces.summary: PGIM expects Asia Pacific real estate returns to improve over five years driven by limited supply and resilient occupier demand, though near-term uncertainty is creating divergence across cities, with Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong underperforming whilst Japan and Australia benefit from defensive investor rotation. The firm anticipates that interest rate falls and constrained supply will support rental growth despite softening occupier demand, though tariffs pose the primary downside risk to the outlook.

Real Assets in 2026: The Year of Intelligent Infrastructure
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that real assets are shifting from static physical holdings into "intelligent operating platforms," where real estate, digital infrastructure and energy systems are tightly integrated, and that digital readiness, climate resilience and cyber capability are now core determinants of asset value. It explicitly urges investors and operators to embed AI, sustainability and data-driven decision-making into strategy now, before these factors become baseline market expectations, to secure lower costs, stronger income resilience and better capital access. The piece is a series preview that flags five forces to be explored in later instalments: AI, sustainability/climate/energy, blockchain and tokenisation, physical AI and robotics, and cybersecurity.

pieces.title: Key points from the 2022 Aladdin Wealth Executive Forum
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that wealth managers must adopt a new portfolio construction approach beyond the traditional 60/40 allocation, given unprecedented challenges including high inflation, geopolitical disruption and the simultaneous decline of stocks and bonds. The firm contends that its Aladdin Wealth platform provides the unified analytics and risk transparency necessary for advisors to navigate this environment, and calls on wealth managers to adopt forward-looking, holdings-based risk assessment and scenario analysis to better serve clients' long-term goals.

Private credit's overlooked opportunity: the case for non-sponsored direct lending
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that non-sponsored direct lending to family- and entrepreneur-owned European companies is an overlooked segment of private credit, since sponsored deals dominate the market while sponsored firms are under 10% of the corporate sector. It claims this segment offers lower leverage, less competition, stronger pricing (a 150-200bp premium over directly originated upper mid-market loans, per its own historical figures), tighter covenants and better borrower-lender alignment, and it presents its own lender, P Capital Partners, as well placed to exploit it. The piece also frames non-sponsored credit as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, sponsored direct lending.

The firm outlines its governance structures, trade association memberships, and political participation activities, disclosing that it does not contribute corporate funds to political candidates or committees but maintains a voluntary employee-funded PAC that makes bipartisan contributions aligned with its public policy goals.

pieces.title: On the Markets
pieces.summary: PGIM publishes regular market commentary covering macroeconomic conditions and trends across fixed income, equities, and real assets to support investment decisions. The firm's latest 2026 mid-year outlook identifies AI investment, interest rate dynamics and geopolitics as key market shapers, whilst noting that active fixed income managers must now focus on stock-picking ability rather than systematic risk premiums to generate returns.

pieces.title: AB Select US Equity Portfolio
Reflections on Our Global CIO Forum
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein reports on its Boston CIO forum, attended by 130 chief investment officers and senior asset allocators, where geopolitics and Federal Reserve independence dominated, and the mood was decisively pro-risk, though tempered by concern about market concentration and valuations. Attendees focused less on whether risk assets can deliver positive returns and more on which private assets to hold, with interest in active strategies as a counterweight to concentrated passive indices amid a low-return outlook; AI profitability ranked well down the agenda. The firm's stated view is that allocators are positioned for risk at the start of 2026, though it makes no explicit recommendation of its own.

BlackRock argues that Europe should simplify regulatory frameworks for asset managers, enhance pension system structures, and implement targeted financial market safeguards to support long-term growth and economic competitiveness.

pieces.title: JH Explorer in Bangkok: IMF highlights resilient EM but harder choices ahead
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through EMD portfolio manager Sorin Pirău, argues that the global economy has absorbed recent shocks but that emerging market resilience is now increasingly country-specific, with debt affordability and financing visibility mattering more than debt ratios alone. The firm contends that the easy phase of the EM recovery is largely over, so future credit improvement will depend on fiscal delivery, reform continuity and refinancing capacity, with reform announcements and IMF engagement proving useful only when backed by credible execution. It therefore favours selectivity, using interest payments as a share of government revenue as a clearer measure of near-term fiscal strain than headline debt-to-GDP.

pieces.summary: BlackRock's private equity division argues that its approach generates long-term value through active ownership that strengthens portfolio companies' operations and strategy, drives innovation including in AI and emerging technologies, and enables financial advisors to construct more resilient, long-term-focused portfolios through disciplined deal sourcing and structuring.

Balanced returns in 2026
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers expects 2026 to bring a normalisation of growth and inflation after a volatile 2025, with roughly 1.5% growth and 2% inflation in developed markets and 3.5% in emerging economies, producing moderate but positive returns of around 5% across many asset classes, driven by equity earnings growth and fixed-income carry. The firm explicitly favours convertible and emerging market bonds, expects rotation into under-owned equity segments, positions commodities and leveraged multi-asset strategies as hedges against sticky inflation or a tech valuation correction, and judges the traditional 50/50 portfolio likely to return below 5% in USD terms.

Underwriting Anchors Private Credit Success
pieces.summary: PGIM's Dianna Carr-Coletta argues that private credit retains strong risk-reward dynamics for investors working with disciplined, experienced managers, and that recent high-profile defaults look isolated, reflecting individual misconduct rather than systemic weakness. The piece warns that covenant erosion in the broadly syndicated loan market raises downside risk, and PGIM contends that a conservative underwriting approach (low entry leverage, high fixed charge ratios, low loan-to-value, limited payment-in-kind exposure and diversification) is what allows managers to preserve value through 2026 and beyond.

How to run on
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that UK defined benefit pension schemes can benefit from running on for the longer term, since this preserves flexibility while legislation and regulatory expectations remain unclear, and it points to the Stagecoach/Aberdeen transaction as an example of emerging innovation. The firm's explicit view is that schemes should secure liquidity for cashflow needs, hedge liability risks and grow any surplus, and that a core allocation to contractual assets such as high-quality corporate bonds, combined with a hedging overlay, provides a more resilient base from which to pursue surplus growth while reducing risk to members' retirement income.

2026 Mid-Year Outlook: U.S. Commercial Real Estate
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's 2026 Mid-Year Outlook for U.S. commercial real estate argues that the sector is set for a constructive period despite higher rates, citing a historical record of positive CRE returns in 85% of rising-rate periods since 1965 because rate rises usually accompany economic growth that lifts occupancy and rents. Its explicit views are that office is recovering, with quality the key differentiator, that retail, industrial (driven by reshoring) and rental housing offer durable demand, and that private CRE, with minimal direct AI exposure and negative correlations with stocks and bonds, is a useful diversifier against concentration risk in multi-asset portfolios.

pieces.title: Private Equity: Six Key Considerations for Investors
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that private equity's historical outperformance advantage over public equities remains valid, but only for investors who can access capable managers and commit capital long-term, as the industry has shifted from a benign environment of cheap leverage and multiple expansion to one where operational skill and disciplined underwriting drive returns. The firm contends that manager selection has become critical—returns now vary widely across the asset class—and that scale and platform infrastructure increasingly matter more than market segment, as larger, established managers with proprietary deal flow and operational expertise are better positioned to deliver the operational improvements necessary to hit return targets in a structurally higher-rate environment.

pieces.title: Why Track Record in Credit Underwriting is so Important
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that cross-cycle experience is the main way to tell credit managers apart, since returns look similar in healthy markets and real differences emerge during volatility and defaults. It presents its "pivot risk" framework, which prepares for rapid shifts in market expectations rather than attempting to predict the next crisis, and cites its private credit investing since 2002 through the GFC, COVID and the 2023 regional banking crisis. The piece's explicit view is that a manager with less than 17 years in private credit has not experienced the GFC, a point it presents as a key differentiator.

pieces.title: secondaries-roundtable-25
The Rewiring of Global Supply Chains
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that global supply chains are being reconfigured through geopolitical tensions, industrial policy and economic security concerns, but that this amounts to diversification and regionalisation rather than deglobalisation, with China still central and dependencies being redistributed. It contends that emerging markets' advantages now extend beyond labour and commodities to positions in AI-related infrastructure, and that the economies that benefit most will be those that build industrial capacity, supplier ecosystems and domestic value-added. Its explicit view is that rising cross-country and cross-sector dispersion strengthens the case for active country, sector and issuer selection over passive allocation.

pieces.title: Seizing the euro fixed income opportunity with flexibility and diversification - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that euro fixed income yields, at levels not seen in over a decade, offer both a larger buffer against rising rates and a better chance of stronger long-term returns, since historically higher starting yields have tended to coincide with higher subsequent three-year returns. It contends that the recent rate volatility, driven mainly by interest rates rather than spreads, is an opportunity for an active, agile duration strategy, and recommends a flexible allocation across credit, inflation-linked debt and sovereign bonds to diversify risk amid geopolitical and fiscal uncertainty. The firm's explicit view is that investors should not ignore the euro fixed income market's attractive yields, provided they are managed actively, flexibly and in a diversified way.

pieces.title: Why water risk management is becoming a key differentiator in copper mining
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that water risk has become a core economic and operational constraint in copper mining, affecting project viability, capital intensity and profitability, and that differences in water governance and execution between producers are emerging as a key source of differentiation. Drawing on engagement with seven major copper producers, the firm contends that copper supply growth may be more constrained than headline project pipelines suggest, and it calls on investors to assess water strategy, governance, delivery capability and decision-useful disclosure when evaluating producers' resilience and growth potential.

pieces.title: ares-infrastructure-debt-white-paper-jan-2024-0
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that infrastructure debt is an advantageous component of private credit portfolios, offering diversification, an illiquidity premium over public assets, attractive risk-adjusted returns and downside protection. It defines infrastructure as essential-service assets in high-barrier markets with stable, long-term, inflation-linked cash flows and high operating margins, and points to durable tailwinds such as digitalisation, mobility and decarbonisation, a public investment and bank-retrenchment funding gap, and a projected $5.5 trillion of private capital needed through 2035. Ares's explicit view is that the market will keep offering attractive opportunities for scaled, experienced infrastructure lenders.

The firm's explicit views are that US reindustrialisation is the biggest opportunity, that Europe's main risk is policymakers moving too slowly on the innovation gap and single-market integration, and that China is "the biggest opportunity" in 2026, while flagging risks such as a real-income squeeze on low-income US consumers, AI capex monetisation doubts, and a possible Fed-driven slowdown.

pieces.summary: Apollo argues that private market secondaries have evolved from a niche strategy into a core portfolio allocation, citing historical data showing median net IRRs of 12.6% with narrower outcome dispersion than other private market strategies and consistent outperformance during market shocks over the past two decades. The firm contends that whilst the structural advantages of secondaries remain intact, the recent shift towards GP-led deals has expanded the opportunity set but increased dispersion, making manager selection increasingly critical as the market reaches record volumes.

pieces.title: Use Structural Shifts in Credit Markets to Capitalise on VUCA
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that credit markets have structurally shifted since the Global Financial Crisis, with banks retreating from traditional corporate lending and institutional and retail investors filling the gap, a change that reduces systemic risk but raises asset-level risk. Its explicit view is that this shift, combined with the current VUCA (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous) environment, lets investors raise diversification and income by selectively allocating to higher-yielding segments of the credit market. The piece promotes a presentation by Samantha Milner, Partner and Portfolio Manager at Ares, delivered at the Portfolio Construction Forum Markets Summit 2020.

pieces.summary: KKR reports that December's U.S. jobs data showed modest payroll growth of 50,000 but a falling unemployment rate of 4.4%, driven largely by government and healthcare sectors whilst rate-sensitive areas contracted. The firm maintains its forecast for 2.3% GDP growth and two additional Fed rate cuts to 3.125% in 2026, arguing that accommodative financial conditions and productivity gains support continued U.S. economic expansion despite persistent wage pressures. KKR recommends portfolio upgrades towards quality, productivity-driven companies with pricing power, and a shift in private markets towards operational improvement and collateral-backed strategies.

pieces.title: Credit Quarterly: New terms
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management argues that elevated interest rates represent a permanent repricing of capital rather than a temporary phenomenon, creating attractive yields for credit investors (high yield bonds at 8%, broadly syndicated loans above 9%) whilst simultaneously pressuring highly leveraged borrowers whose cash flows were predicated on lower rates. The firm observes that expected rate cuts have repeatedly failed to materialise as the U.S. economy has proved resilient, and that this higher-for-longer rate environment is now a global phenomenon affecting bond yields across developed markets.

It also highlights that hyperscalers now make up about 5% of the USD IG index versus 1.2% in EUR, creating AI-related issuance as a distinct index and dispersion risk that investors should monitor. The piece does not offer a specific trade or allocation call; its explicit view is that AI supply should be treated as a separate technical factor across issuers, curves and benchmarks.

pieces.title: Portfolio Management Outlook: Positioned for a Bond-Friendly Environment
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that fixed income is well positioned in a supportive backdrop of solid growth, moderating inflation and Fed rate cuts, but that credit selection matters because spreads are near historic tights with little differentiation between high and low quality. Its explicit positioning is primarily defensive: it prefers higher-quality structured credit (non-Agency RMBS, senior CLO tranches, commercial ABS), investment grade financials, select industrial and utility credits, and defensive assets such as infrastructure and energy, while holding liquidity to exploit market overshoots. On duration, it expects the yield curve to steepen further, keeps the 10-year Treasury yield in a 3.75 to 4.75 per cent range, and favours positioning slightly further out the curve, including longer-dated TIPS, with tactical trading around the 10-year.

Is AI running out of compute?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that AI compute is unlikely to run out entirely, but that supply constraints across chips, power and data centre capacity will increasingly shape market conditions, with pricing power accruing to scarce-input providers and cost pressure eventually reaching end users. Its explicit view is that supply-constrained conditions will likely persist for at least several years, so power, materials and infrastructure providers remain well positioned, while hyperscalers' recent underperformance reflects zero-sum scepticism that may fade. It therefore suggests that investors heavily concentrated in lagging AI names consider rebalancing toward infrastructure providers and companies poised to benefit from broader AI adoption.

pieces.title: Retirement planning: Five tips to share with clients now
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that advisers should use portfolio reviews in 2026 to help clients keep retirement plans on track, citing five areas: running the numbers on income replacement and Social Security, planning for spending volatility (its research finds six in 10 retirees see a 20% or more annual shift in spending in their first three years), diversifying across taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free accounts, consolidating assets under a single adviser, and staying invested rather than market timing. The piece explicitly favours Roth conversions, suggesting that relatively low US tax rates make this a timely opportunity, and it advises clients to resist short-term urges to abandon long-term plans where their goals have not changed.

Morgan Asset Management argues that tokenized money market funds, which represent fund shares as digital tokens on a blockchain, can improve collateral management, speed up trading and settlement, and support 24/7 operations while keeping a familiar investor onboarding process. The firm reports that these funds hold roughly USD10 billion in assets (per RWA.xyz data as of 9 November 2025), a small fraction of the USD10 trillion traditional money market fund industry, but says momentum is building as regulatory frameworks in the U.S. and Europe mature. Its explicit view is that tokenized solutions are poised to play a central role in modern liquidity management, though it notes the trade-off between private blockchains, suited to regulated institutions, and public ones, which offer greater transparency but demand stronger wallet security.

pieces.title: Press Release: Ares Global Credit Income Fund achieves performance and rating milestones in first year
pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management, the joint venture between Ares Management and Fidante Partners, reports that its Ares Global Credit Income Fund returned 12.13% net of fees in its first year to 3 May 2021 and received a "Recommended" rating from Zenith Investment Partners. Ares argues that the "sweet spot of credit", combining high current income with low interest rate duration risk, offers Australian investors a solution for higher income and diversification, and that its senior, often secured, credit positions provide downside protection.

pieces.title: Ares Australia Management launches Ares Global Credit Income Fund
pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management, the joint venture between Ares Management Corporation and Fidante Partners, has launched the Ares Global Credit Income Fund, its first Australian product, which targets a 3% to 4% annual distribution paid monthly and invests across corporate bonds, bank loans and asset-backed securities. Ares argues that low rates and market volatility leave Australian investors seeking income without severe capital loss, and that the fund offers a more diversified alternative to the bank equity, hybrids and mortgage-backed exposure common in local portfolios, with capital preservation as its stated priority. The piece is promotional, so its claims of resilience and low historical default rates are Ares' own assertions rather than independently verified results.

pieces.title: The future of fixed income: Innovation, convergence and active opportunity
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that artificial intelligence and quantitative techniques are creating new opportunities to enhance returns in fixed income markets, while increasing market dispersion makes active security selection more important for outperformance. The firm encourages clients to broaden their mandates to include private credit alongside public markets, claiming this convergence offers additional yield of 80-200 basis points sometimes with lower associated risk.

Europe: Forging its own way - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's economic challenges (fossil fuel dependence, strained US trade ties, and Chinese competition in manufacturing) are driving a shift towards strategic autonomy, with more than €1.5 trillion proposed over the next decade for defence, infrastructure, renewables, energy replacement, raw materials and semiconductors. The firm sees this as creating long-term investment opportunities, particularly in defence, energy and technology, with equity and fixed income investors both positioned to benefit.

pieces.title: Quick View: NVIDIA signals agentic AI inflection point
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Richard Clode, argues that NVIDIA's latest earnings signal 2026 as an "agentic AI inflection point" that supports sustained AI capex, despite a share price that has stagnated and de-rated as investors question the durability of that spending. The firm views NVIDIA's strong revenue guidance, cash generation and competitive position as reasons to consider its strategic investments in AI leaders reasonable, while noting that China revenue is excluded from guidance. It concludes that harnessing AI opportunities requires an active investment approach.

pieces.title: The AI tide rolls on
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through portfolio manager Denny Fish, argues that demand for AI will outstrip supply of key inputs (chips, optics, electricity, labour and data-centre capacity) into 2028 and beyond, with supply bottlenecks acting as

pieces.title: Three minutes of insight into infrastructure with the CIO Infrastructure
pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors argues that infrastructure investment is being shaped by digitalisation and AI-driven data centre demand, alongside geopolitical pressure to secure domestic energy systems such as grids and battery storage, on top of the established energy transition. It says private credit is rotating towards infrastructure debt, which it presents as offering attractive risk-adjusted returns, with tangible asset backing, low default rates and strong recoveries, and it sees a healthy deal pipeline across debt and equity. The firm's explicit view is that the opportunity set is broadening across clean energy, networks, transport and digital infrastructure, and that long-term investors should find strong structural demand supporting it.

pieces.title: U.S. Housing Inflation: Stubbornly High to Stubbornly Low

Convexity in credit
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that convex, defensive credit strategies can protect capital in market stress, but that options carry persistent negative carry, so it proposes a three-pillar long/short relative value approach that pairs higher-quality, more liquid credits against lower-quality, less liquid ones and targets dislocations. Using proxies (IG cash versus CDX IG, and HY cash versus 2.5x CDX IG), the firm says its strategies have historically performed strongly as stress deepens, and it contends that credit spreads, still historically tight despite a 7-8% market fall in March 2026, enhance the potential convexity on offer. The piece explicitly notes that the proxies are not the firm's actual positions.

pieces.title: Is now the time to revisit biotech & healthcare?
Hedge funds finding opportunity | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that hedge funds are increasingly suitable for portfolio diversification in a volatile, uncertain macroeconomic environment, particularly multi-strategy funds constructed to have low correlation with equities and bonds. The piece contends that improved liquidity, fee alignment and access through local investment vehicles have made hedge funds more practical for Australian wealth clients, and positions them as an alternative to traditional bonds for portfolio ballast and uncorrelated returns.

pieces.title: Financing India’s e-mobility transition
pieces.summary: Macquarie Asset Management reports on Vertelo, a fleet electrification platform it launched in India in 2024 as a blended finance partnership with the Green Climate Fund, which it says has attracted $US405 million in commitments so far against a $US1.5 billion ten-year target and could deliver around 9.5 million tonnes of lifetime CO2 equivalent reductions. The firm argues that its blended structure, which combines commercial and catalytic capital to mitigate risk, offers "a practical and scalable model" for mobilising private investment in climate initiatives in emerging markets while still delivering attractive returns to investors.

What is quantum computing?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that quantum computing is entering a phase that bridges laboratory research, engineering scalability and commercial viability, but that practical success remains years away: current systems are unreliable, solve only narrow problems, and have yet to outperform classical computers on a real-world task. The firm sees quantum as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, classical computing, with near-term commercial need concentrated in quantum-resistant cybersecurity. It advises investors to approach early-stage quantum themes with caution, noting that listed quantum companies are largely pre-revenue and volatile, and suggesting that private venture capital may suit investors with longer horizons.

Feast to Famine: Municipal Credit in the Era of Fiscal Federalism
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that municipal credit, which benefited from a decade of rising federal funding (reaching $1.1 trillion in fiscal year 2024), now faces a headwind as 2025 brought federal spending cuts, policy reversals and more litigation, trends it expects to continue into 2026. It expects credit quality to diverge, with states better placed to absorb the shock than thinner-margined municipal issuers, and that smaller, disadvantaged issuers will need close bottom-up scrutiny. Its explicit calls are to sell issuers where credit deterioration is already evident and to selectively buy on spread widening driven by headlines, while noting that most municipal issuers still start from a position of strength with reserves near their highs.

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that 2026 will be defined by event-driven volatility and policy-driven surprises, which it attributes to the fragmentation of the global order, with policy announcements in the U.S. (on Venezuela, Greenland, credit card rates, Medicare and agency mortgage purchases) and Japan (a consumption tax cut) moving markets sharply. Its explicit calls are to be cautious on stretched U.S. equity valuations, watch for complacency in the VIX and MOVE indices, favour relative-value strategies, stay flexible across regions, and remain nimble and globally diversified across developed and emerging markets, since static positioning is "the greatest risk."

pieces.title: Private credit: Opportunity, risk and selectivity in a maturing market
pieces.summary: Robeco argues that private credit has matured into a multi-trillion-dollar asset class with structural tailwinds, but that concentrated risks have emerged in fast-growing segments, particularly software lending where AI disruption threatens loan valuations and borrower repayment capacity. The asset manager contends that selectivity and disciplined underwriting—particularly in less competitive segments such as Europe's lower mid-market—are increasingly critical to navigating the maturing market, though it believes private credit stress is unlikely to trigger a systemic crisis akin to 2008.

Finding opportunities in US high-yield amid uncertainty - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that, despite an uneven macro backdrop (resilient US growth, a weakening labour market, tariff and Iran-related inflation pressures, and unclear Fed rate-cut prospects), US high yield merits a place in flexible fixed-income portfolios for its attractive coupon income, lower duration and diversification. The firm contends that tight spreads partly reflect a structurally higher-quality index (BB-rated bonds at a record 59%, CCC down to 9%, and around a third now secured), so comparisons with pre-2008 spread averages may be misleading, and it expects a "mild slowdown" to be broadly supportive for issuers. The view is constructive but qualified: the firm expects the Iran-related energy impact to be limited if the conflict is short-lived, and flags a longer conflict as a material risk.

pieces.title: Midyear Fixed-Income Outlook: Tighter spreads, wider opportunities
pieces.summary: Columbia Threadneedle Investments argues that heightened policy and macroeconomic uncertainty, driven by persistent inflation, a stabilising labour market and a recalibrating US Federal Reserve, strengthens the case for selective, high-quality fixed income, with credit spreads near historically tight levels making security selection and dispersion more important. The firm's explicit view is that investors should keep income working by capturing today's higher yields, broaden their opportunity set deliberately, and lean into high-quality allocations across the curve, with select AAA non-agency structures cited as offering more attractive yields than lower-quality corporates. The piece is cut off before its full set of sector calls, which include leveraged loans.

pieces.title: Budget changes: time to prepare
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that changes from the November 2025 UK Budget, including frozen income tax thresholds, higher dividend and savings tax rates from April 2026, and a cut in the cash ISA limit from April 2027, will affect investors' finances and should prompt a review of how they save and invest. It presents tax wrappers such as ISAs and pensions as increasingly valuable, and promotes income-producing assets, particularly investment trusts with long records of dividend growth, as a way to build a tax-free income stream and add stability to a portfolio.

pieces.title: evaluating-evergreens
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that evergreen and drawdown funds can report similar IRRs yet produce very different dollar outcomes, because drawdown funds often hold uninvested capital and evergreens stay fully invested and compound continuously. It contends that comparing fund multiples on committed rather than invested capital gives a fairer picture, and that the choice between structures usually turns on investor profile, liquidity needs and structural fit rather than return potential. Ares also suggests the two can compl

pieces.title: What does the software sell-off mean for private markets?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the early-February 2026 software stock sell-off, triggered by advances in agentic AI, matters for private markets because technology is a large sector exposure in both private equity and private credit, and the S&P BDC index hit a 2026 low as investors trimmed private credit funds with software exposure. It contends that the true software concentration in private portfolios is hard to measure because lenders classify sector exposure differently, and that the bear case underestimates businesses whose defensibility lies in customer relationships, workflow integration and proprietary data rather than code alone. The piece's explicit view is that investors wary of AI disruption may find differentiated exposure to AI's growth through private infrastructure, which offers long-term contracted income and lower volatility, while venture capital is the route to direct exposure to AI's future leaders.

pieces.title: Understanding Triple Net Lease: An Inflation Hedge
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that triple net leases are an effective inflation hedge because their built-in rent escalators, whether fixed or linked to indices such as CPI, grow rental income over time, unlike the static coupons of bonds. It adds that exposure to the underlying real estate, which may appreciate, and the chance to re-lease at market rates on expiry further strengthen that protection. Fortress concludes that these features make triple net leases a natural hedge against persistent inflation, offering both income growth and capital preservation.

pieces.title: Insight Investment
Quick View: The good, the bad, and the (potentially) ugly of February’s inflation print
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Global Head of Securitised Products, John Kerschner, argues that February's US CPI print (headline 2.43% YoY, core 2.47%) was benign, with shelter disinflation evident in Owner's Equivalent Rent, but warns that Core PCE, the Fed's preferred gauge, is running above CPI and may exceed 3%, while a roughly 33% rise in oil since the start of the Iran War could feed into future inflation and constrain the Fed. The firm's explicit positioning call is to favour an overweight to the short end of the yield curve as a hedge against economic weakness or rising term premiums, while remaining bullish on credit spread risk, particularly in securitised sectors, given robust US growth.

pieces.title: U.S. Venezuela: limited risk to global markets
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that U.S. military action in Venezuela and President Maduro's capture underscore geopolitical fragmentation but pose limited risk to global markets, given Venezuela's minimal share of global oil production. The asset manager maintains its risk-on stance, remaining overweight U.S. equities and emerging market hard-currency bonds, and views the developments as consistent with its existing macro framework rather than a catalyst for portfolio repositioning.

pieces.title: What is a semi-liquid fund?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that semi-liquid funds (interval funds, tender offer funds, non-traded BDCs and non-traded REITs) widen individual investors' access to private markets by offering periodic subscriptions and quarterly redemptions, typically capped at around 5% of net asset value, and that the "semi" in the name deserves closer scrutiny after gates were imposed on redemptions in early 2026. The firm's explicit view is that investors should size allocations with the expectation that redemptions may be delayed in unsettled markets, and treat their capital as committed for the long term.

pieces.title: The Misconceptions Behind Asset Diversification
The growing global private debt opportunity
pieces.summary: Ares Management, which reports around US$360 billion in assets under management as of 31 March 2023, argues that private credit is filling a gap left by retreating banks and by public credit markets that have shifted towards larger issuers, with its own platform positioned to lend to strong middle-market companies on lender-friendly terms. It presents its Diversified Credit Strategy as a way to combine illiquid, self-originated private loans with liquid syndicated loans and high-yield bonds, and says its selective origination (declining about 96% of deals it sees), low historical default rates and low losses are how it aims to outperform, though it stresses that downside protection is not a guarantee against loss.

pieces.title: Future Shock: Reading Financial Signals in Natural Hazards
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein, working with the Columbia Climate School, argues that its county-level Natural Hazards Index, which covers 14 perils and now forecasts how wildfires, flooding, tornadoes and hurricanes will shift over time across more than 3,000 US counties, can give investors forward-looking geospatial insight into both risk and opportunity. Its speakers contend that natural hazards should not be treated as a mere environmental concern, citing utility wildfire exposure and grid hardening, and rebuilding and engineering demand after disasters, as examples where the data could inform equity analysis. They also suggest that because investors have historically relied on backward-looking data, a predictive tool of this kind is valuable for assessing company exposure that may not yet be reflected in financial analysis.

UK debt sustainability:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that concerns about UK debt sustainability are overblown: although UK debt and debt-to-GDP are expected to rise over the next few years, it sees default risk as extremely low, with the overall debt burden likely to stabilise. The piece flags a more pressing issue for defined benefit pension schemes: long-term gilt demand is uncertain as issuance shortens and pension scheme demand falls, so the market will increasingly rely on foreign investors and banks. Insight's stated view is that schemes can consider swaps, more corporate bonds or discretionary liability-hedging strategies to diversify away from gilts, while acknowledging that swaps carry trade-offs for funding and transaction costs.

pieces.title: Finding Hidden Gems In Asia
Growth and venture debt
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that growth and venture debt is an emerging private credit segment experiencing significant expansion, with US$35 billion in deals across the U.S. in 2024 and European markets growing over 25 year-on-year. The firm argues that this asset class offers attractive exposure to innovative tech and healthcare companies with lower risks than venture capital, particularly following 2023's regional banking disruption, which has created opportunities for established private debt managers to capture market share and favourable lending terms.

pieces.title: Staying risk on in our market outlook
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management stays risk-on in its market outlook, arguing that the Middle East conflict is a manageable energy shock rather than the start of a broader macro break, so growth should slow gradually and earnings and the AI investment cycle should keep supporting risk assets. It favours US equities, given AI-related stocks' weight in the S&P 500, and Asian semiconductor and memory producers, while remaining cautious on Chinese stocks because domestic demand is weak. It s

pieces.title: €STR oder Euribor?
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that €STR and Euribor measure different segments of the euro money market and should not be treated as interchangeable benchmarks. The piece contends that treasury teams should select between them based on their specific liquidity objectives—whether operational, reserve or strategic—and their investment horizon, as benchmark choice materially affects money market fund performance assessment.

pieces.title: Inside Alternatives
pieces.summary: BlackRock has launched Inside Alternatives, a digital resource centre designed to help investors navigate private markets and liquid alternatives with integrated portfolio perspectives. The firm argues that investors increasingly demand greater transparency, easier access, better analytics and a whole-portfolio approach where private and public markets operate seamlessly together. BlackRock positions alternatives—including private equity, private credit, real estate and liquid strategies—as essential tools for diversification and resilience in an increasingly complex market environment.

pieces.title: Project Glasswing and Mythos: Redefining the cybersecurity landscape
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Anthropic's Project Glasswing and its Mythos model, which gave launch partners such as Apple, CrowdStrike, Microsoft and Palo Alto Networks access to a non-public model for finding software vulnerabilities, show AI accelerating both the discovery of vulnerabilities and the complexity of enterprise security. The firm's portfolio managers, Ana Chkhikvadze and Richard Clode, contend this confirms cybersecurity as critical AI infrastructure, with likely gains in security spending across network, zero trust, endpoint, identity and observability products, and more stock-selection opportunities as competitive dynamics shift. They also say Anthropic is a potentially key partner for cybersecurity firms, while stressing the need for safe deployment of advanced AI, and state that they will monitor model capabilities and assess vendors' AI-infused products as they develop

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that AI infrastructure financing currently moves as one credit trade, with spread dispersion across the financing chain limited despite large differences in underlying risk, in contrast to increasingly differentiated equity performance. It expects the funding gap to persist and debt issuance to widen across issuers, structures and risk exposures, creating more room for differentiation over time. Its explicit view is that, because credit investors capture little of the upside, downside mitigation matters more than picking winners, and that hyperscaler cred

pieces.title: AI is becoming a credit-cycle story, not just a technology story
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors argues that AI's near-term impact on credit is driven less by technological disruption than by the capital spending needed to build AI infrastructure, which is increasingly financed through debt markets. The piece says the market is pricing future disruption faster than current fundamentals justify, and that credit investors should focus on financing details, cash-flow conversion and credit resilience. It takes an explicit view that hyperscaler issuers are raising their share of high-quality IG index supply, and that some of the more attractive credit opportunities may lie in businesses enabling AI, such as infrastructure, utilities and structured-credit exposures backed by data-centre leases.

pieces.title: GCC Project Bonds: Opportunities in the Post-War Infrastructure Buildout
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that post-war reconstruction and the Gulf states' push to bypass the Strait of Hormuz create a growing opportunity in GCC project bonds, which give governments a way to release capital tied up in strategic assets while offering investors secured, long-duration income at a spread premium to comparable unsecured corporate debt. It traces the asset class from RasGas and Nakilat in the 2000s through lease-and-leaseback and centralised-entity structures, and it says pipeline bonds, backed by offtaker payments regardless of throughput, are the strongest credit, currently yielding roughly 6.1–6.4%. The piece's explicit view is that this combination of structural protection and reconstruction-driven supply makes GCC project bonds a compelling asset class for both issuers and investors.

pieces.title: How Machine Learning is Enhancing Macro Investing
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that machine learning has underperformed in macro investing because traditional techniques tend to overfit to dominant factors, but that purpose-built applications can unlock alpha by pooling data across assets and markets to strengthen forecasting models, translating macroeconomic signals into tradeable exposures, and deploying specialised learning techniques within relative value frameworks. The firm contends that reframing machine learning away from direct return prediction toward these structural solutions can help macro strategies adapt to regime shifts and extract value from sparse, complex data.

Infrastructure and Structured Credit 2025 Mid-Year Review
pieces.summary: PGIM's Infrastructure and Structured Credit Group reports deploying $893 million across 13 transactions in the first half of 2025, split between seven new borrower relationships (over $504 million) and follow-on financing for existing clients ($389 million), spanning North America, the UK, Europe and Latin America in five currencies. The use of proceeds was broad, covering refinancings, growth capex and HoldCo or sponsor back-leverage, with ticket sizes from about $20 million to roughly $140 million. The piece makes no explicit market view or call; its emphasis is on PGIM's global origination reach and its ability to deliver bespoke financing across investment grade and high yield.

pieces.title: Can a Systematic Strategy Sharpen Stock Selection for Investors?
3 investing principles and why they signal international markets for 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that three fundamental investing principles—earnings growth drives equity returns, capital scarcity generates superior returns, and last cycle's winners rarely lead the next cycle—point to international equities taking market leadership in 2026. The firm contends that improving earnings momentum outside the U.S., extreme underallocation to international markets relative to their global weight, and a macro environment that no longer favours the mega-cap growth and private assets that dominated the previous cycle all support this shift. Janus Henderson calls for positioning in developed international equities, selective emerging markets, and cyclically oriented exposures consistent with this predicted rotation.

pieces.title: Concentration issues: The problem with indexing bonds in an AI world
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the AI infrastructure build-out, financed largely through investment grade credit, is pushing bond indices towards the same concentration seen in equities. Sixth Street’s Architecture

It contends that flexibility is now a requirement, and that its multi-strategy platform, smaller focus strategies and one-team culture of more than 750 people let it shift capital across themes and limit exposure to oversupplied areas. pieces.title: Corporate Credit
Multi-Asset Investments Views: Midnight oil - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's multi-asset team, led by Clément Dupire, keeps an overweight stance on global equities, citing the early-June pullback, supportive quantitative signals and strong earnings momentum, with Q1 S&P 500 earnings up around 28% year on year. It argues that the AI and semiconductor rally is increasingly driven by leverage and positioning flows, with SpaceX's $1.8 trillion IPO a sign of late-cycle excess, so it has taken profits in emerging market equities. The team also took profits on its long position in five-year German Bunds, and it is more positive on the dollar, which it sees as fundamentally undervalued.

Global climate and nature conferences
Five things the new Fed Chair should know…but might not
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that deglobalization and rising inflation represent a structural shift requiring a reconsideration of the Federal Reserve's existing policy framework, including its 2% inflation target. The firm contends that current economic conditions more closely parallel the 1960s "Guns & Butter" period of concurrent defence and social spending than the 1970s oil shock consensus, and that the Taylor Rule suggests rate increases rather than cuts are warranted given productivity uncertainty and labour market strength. Janus Henderson identifies opportunities in shorter-duration, pro-inflation assets for investors adapting to this shifted backdrop.

pieces.title: Prospects for geothermal energy are heating up
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that next-generation geothermal, enabled by enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) and closed-loop designs, is shifting from a geographically constrained niche into a potentially scalable source of 24-hour baseload power that complements intermittent wind and solar, with the oil and gas sector's drilling and subsurface skills a key enabler. It judges that costs could become competitive with nuclear, hydropower and gas-fired generation by the mid-2030s, while noting risks around water use and induced seismicity that must be managed to sustain investor confidence. The firm favours an active, selective value-chain approach to investment, spanning oil and gas services, equipment and engineering providers.

pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that wealth advisors typically rely on historical returns-based analysis to assess portfolio risk, which is flawed because it reflects past positions rather than current holdings. The firm contends that forward-looking risk measures based on today's portfolio constituents provide more accurate insights for decision-making, illustrating this with a hypothetical scenario where applying current S&P 500 weights to the 2007–2008 credit crisis yields a 1% loss rather than the 15% suggested by historical analysis. BlackRock promotes its Aladdin Wealth technology as the solution for advisors to adopt this more robust, forward-looking approach.

pieces.title: Overnight ETFs: A potentially lower-risk cash management solution - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Overnight ETFs can offer a liquid, stable and potentially lower-risk way to manage cash, tracking very short-term rates such as the €STR through synthetic replication via equity swaps. It says these funds may outperform their underlying index through positive margins paid by banks, and it explicitly presents them as a potentially valuable component of a diversified portfolio for investors seeking liquidity, stability and predictable returns. The piece also acknowledges counterparty risk, noting that swaps are collateralised daily and capped at 10% of net asset value.
