pieces.title: Election boosts Costa Rica’s “rising star” path toward investment grade
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Laura Fernández Delgado's first-round presidential win, and her party's simple majority of 31 of 57 congressional seats, reduce governance and execution risk in Costa Rica without changing its already sound macroeconomic framework. It expects faster policy delivery, including likely Eurobond authorisation and smoother external financing, and says this strengthens Costa Rica's medium-term path toward investment grade. The firm has

pieces.title: Investment perspectives
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that supply-side forces such as artificial intelligence and geopolitical fragmentation, rather than traditional business cycles, are now the primary market drivers, whilst U.S. policy shifts—particularly on trade, immigration and fiscal matters—risk destabilizing financial markets. The firm projects the average U.S. effective tariff rate will reach approximately 10%, expects fiscal deficits to remain above 5% through 2030, and forecasts long-term bond yields to stay elevated; it recommends staying pro-risk in equities but being selective, anticipating that as policy uncertainty dissipates, U.S. equities could resume global leadership.

pieces.title: How Katlyn Gao’s Vision for Women’s Volleyball is Paving the Way for Future Generations
European farmland as a strategic sustainable investment - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that rising global food demand, set against limited arable land, soil and freshwater, makes agriculture a resilient sector that needs investment, and that European farmland is a compelling sustainable asset with stable income, diversification, inflation-hedging and attractive long-term returns. It explicitly calls farmland a strategic opportunity for (institutional) investors to align financial returns with environmental and social benefits, and expects private capital to play a key role as generational turnover in European farm ownership brings parcels to market for consolidation.

pieces.title: Solar Energy Market Update
European defence: Strategic autonomy drives long-term investment potential - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's push for strategic autonomy is driving a structural rise in defence spending, with EU defence spending projected to reach €454 billion in 2026 from €418 billion in 2025, citing European Defence Agency data, and it sees this creating long-term investment opportunities across advanced manufacturing, technology and domestic supply chains. The firm's explicit view is that greater defence expenditure, rising budget allocations, technological integration and government procurement contracts make a "compelling, and long-term, structural investment case" for defence companies and their wider supply chains, which it considers "well-positioned for sustained growth." The piece is promotional in tone, leaning on third-party forecasts (including a 29% annual growth estimate for the European defence market to 2030) and linking to its own ETF product materials.

pieces.title: How might mega-cap IPOs affect markets?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that mega-cap IPOs, such as the roughly 800 private companies valued above $1 billion and a handful near $1 trillion, need not be market-moving events on day one, since IPOs typically float only a small fraction of shares and lock-ups often last six months or more. It notes that the Nasdaq 100 and Russell 1000 index providers plan to fast-track inclusion, whereas the S&P 500 keeps its existing rules, and that funds with inflows can buy new shares without selling holdings, though some short-term volatility from rebalancing is likely. The authors also suggest that active strategies may manage this volatility better than passive ones, while stressing that post-listing fundamentals, not listing-day excitement, will ultimately determine where prices settle.

pieces.title: Discover the opportunity in European private credit
Agriculture Landscape: July 2026
pieces.summary: PGIM's July 2026 Agriculture Landscape report identifies three key pressures on the farm sector: persistent food price inflation above pre-COVID levels, ongoing trade policy uncertainty from USMCA renegotiations and U.S.-China discussions, and legislative developments including proposed changes to the H-2A guestworker programme and a contested new Farm Bill. The report notes that the current administration is seeking a financial aid package for farmers, with disagreements over the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program emerging as the primary obstacle to Senate passage of the updated Farm Bill.

pieces.title: Intro to Private Markets
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that private markets are becoming central to client portfolios rather than niche allocations, driven by three trends: improved accessibility through new investment structures, greater integration with public markets (shifting traditional 60/40 portfolios towards 50/30/20 allocations), and enhanced transparency around general partners and assets. The asset manager presents these developments as creating opportunities for wealth investors to access alternatives more easily and construct more diversified portfolios.

pieces.title: Quick View: The Fed chooses patience as productivity boosts growth
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75% to 4.00% in October, with two dissenters favouring a hike, because the coming weeks are "information rich", and that it may resume tightening in December. The firm reads Chairman Warsh's remarks as signalling that further hikes are effectively necessary, while jud

pieces.title: Private credit market update
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that private credit, now about $1.8 trillion in size, remains a compelling asset class despite recent headlines. It says that redemption gates at some non-traded BDCs reflect the orderly management of ill

pieces.title: Key Considerations for Investing in the Private Markets
Bryan McDonnell Commercial Observer 2025
pieces.summary: PGIM, through Bryan McDonnell, reports that commercial real estate lending has recovered from a cautious start to 2025, with improving capital flows and rising competition for new loans, though transaction volumes remain constrained by a shortage of core equity. The firm highlights growth in agency lending for multifamily assets and expects private credit to continue expanding, whilst identifying data centre financing and geopolitical risk as key market developments. PGIM favours supply-constrained multifamily markets in the Northeast and West Coast over the Sun Belt, citing better fundamentals from low vacancy rates and appeal to young professionals.

pieces.title: Private Real Estate
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that its private real estate investment activities serve three functions: providing critical infrastructure across social, industrial and digital sectors; enhancing built environments to meet tenants' evolving needs; and enabling long-term partnerships with communities and clients. The firm positions private real estate as a vehicle for delivering sustained returns whilst addressing infrastructure gaps and improving quality of life.

pieces.title: Harnessing tax-loss harvesting in volatile markets
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that volatile markets create tax-loss harvesting opportunities, and that a continuous, daily approach, ideally automated through direct indexing, captures more of them than a year-end review. The piece cites 2025 and early 2026 episodes, including stock-level volatility in Q1 2026, where a $1 million illustrative account harvested losses 14 times in 2025 and six times in Q1 2026. It concludes that advisers using such a systematic, rules-based process can help clients preserve after-tax returns and stay committed to their financial plans.

pieces.title: Quick View: The Fed wants 2%; the markets want a plan
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors reports that Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's July meeting statement, though hawkish in tone and voting breakdown, failed to provide a concrete plan for returning inflation to 2%, prompting markets to sell longer-dated Treasuries and reduce near-term rate-hike expectations. The firm argues that while Warsh's commitment to price stability is credible, the Fed's reliance on market-driven tightening without a detailed policy framework has undermined confidence in its operational roadmap, leaving investors in a "show me" posture ahead of September.

pieces.title: 2026 Credit Research Outlook
pieces.summary: State Street Global Advisors' 2026 Credit Research Outlook argues that credit markets are in a late-cycle phase, with elevated valuations, rising M&A and leveraged buyouts, and an uptick in corporate bankruptcies raising the risk of volatility, though it sees these as idiosyncratic events rather than signs of broader distress. It highlights the opacity and rapid growth of private credit (around $3 trillion in the US, per Morgan Stanley) and the growing bank exposure to non-bank financial institutions (over $1.1 trillion, per the FDIC), which it sees as a channel for systemic risk. Its explicit view is that, given strong bank capitalisation, stress testing and moderate private debt, the likely outcome is volatility ahead rather than systemic collapse, though it says it is monitoring bank and alternative manager interconnectedness closely.

pieces.title: Conviction amid complexity
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that rising bond yields, persistent energy-market volatility and geopolitical tensions, alongside AI-driven disruption, will likely rotate market leadership and make markets noisy, though not necessarily fall. Its managers for Murray International Trust have trimmed AI ex

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: July 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the Iran conflict's energy price shock first strengthened the US dollar, but that the outlook has now shifted: with spot crude about 40% below its recent peak, the global cycle should benefit, led by energy importers. On this basis, the firm sees the dollar moving to the middle of its "dollar smile" framework, weakening as capital flows into riskier, higher-return markets. It adds that a further tailwind would come if global ex-US equities outperform the US, which it suggests is more likely after the recent Magnificent Seven correction narrowed the gap, given the MSCI World ex-US Index's far lower technology weighting (10.5% versus 38.3% for the MSCI US Index).

pieces.title: RBA market commentary
Driving Value Creation and Unlocking Liquidity Through Private Equity and Secondaries
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private equity is entering a tighter, higher-rate phase in which returns depend more on operational value creation ("business building", or alpha) than on market tailwinds, and that LPs increasingly prioritise liquidity, such as returning more capital than is deployed over a three-year period. The piece presents private equity and secondaries, including GP-led continuation vehicles, as complementary tools for generating liquidity and extending ownership of high-conviction assets, and it backs this with a formal exit-readiness framework (an exit committee and AI-enabled planning). Its explicit view is that firms combining disciplined value creation with innovative liquidity solutions will be better placed in the current environment.

Private Credit’s Other Lanes Still Offer Value
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that concerns about private credit have focused too narrowly on corporate direct lending, and that asset-based finance and high-quality consumer and mortgage credit still offer better diversification and value. It expects direct lending to face a full

pieces.summary: PGIM argues that institutional investors, who are familiar with financing private real estate, concentrate on commercial property such as offices, apartments, retail, industrial and hotels, and may be overlooking agriculture finance as a

pieces.title: Insight Investment
pieces.summary: Insight Investment has established a Global Macro Research Editorial Committee, chaired by its Global CIO Adrian Grey, to review and commission research on long-term investment themes for publication to clients. The committee's work feeds into a monthly Economics meeting that synthesises macroeconomic forecasts and analysis from its seven-strong Global Rates and Macro Research team to identify economic cycles and market-moving trends, with findings then developed into external research papers. Insight does not articulate an explicit market call in this piece, instead describing its governance structure and process for producing macro research.

pieces.title: What Is Infrastructure?
pieces.summary: Ares Management presents infrastructure as the economy's essential backbone, spanning assets from highways and wind and solar projects to data centres and LNG terminals, and argues that ageing systems and surging demand, particularly from data growth, are driving a period of rapid industry expansion. It explicitly views this as an opportunity for investors willing to back the organisations meeting that need, describing the build-out as "something of a sprint that may also turn out to be a marathon."

pieces.title: Take Two: Markets reach fresh highs on peace hopes - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: The weekly roundup reports that global equities hit fresh highs on hopes of a US-Iran peace deal and strong AI-related demand, with oil retreating and eas

pieces.title: Infrastructure private debt provides resilience and returns - Generali Investments
Longevity hedging demystified: 12 key facts
The Different Types of Strategies in Private Infrastructure
pieces.summary: Ares Management's piece sets out six private infrastructure strategies along a risk-return spectrum: Core (stable operating assets such as regulated utilities, toll roads and cell towers), Core Plus (moderate growth through enhancing existing assets), Value Add (transformational repositioning requiring active management), Opportunistic (higher-risk greenfield development or emerging-market exposure), Distressed (turnarounds of troubled assets), and Debt (financing positioned higher in the capital structure than equity). The only explicit view is Ares's closing assertion that each strategy helps power economies, connect communities and shape tomorrow's infrastructure. The piece is primarily educational and includes extensive disclaimers, so it offers no specific recommendation or performance claim.

pieces.title: Q&A: Space investing after the SpaceX IPO
pieces.summary: In a Q&A, Janus Henderson Investors' research analysts David Chung and Taylor Portman argue that the three commercial space growth drivers (communications, defence and infrastructure) have strengthened since last year, with the SpaceX IPO reinforcing the communications case. Taylor Portman judges that 20% to 25% of global internet traffic could plausibly move through space, which he considers more realistic than bullish for

pieces.title: Quick View: Tokens=revenues
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors portfolio manager Richard Clode summarises NVIDIA's GTC 2026 event, arguing that agentic AI (led by the open-source OpenClaw agent), token-based monetisation and "extreme co-design" across chips, networking and software can support attractive, durable returns on AI capital spending. The firm explicitly endorses four takeaways: OpenClaw is a "Windows moment" for agentic AI, tokens equal revenues (illustrated by NVIDIA's claim that a US$100 billion, 1GW Vera Rubin data centre could generate up to US$150 billion), the co-design moat is defensible, and NVIDIA expects over US$1 trillion in Blackwell and Rubin revenue across 2025 to 2027. Note that these are NVIDIA's own projections, which Janus Henderson relays with a generally supportive tone rather than independently verifying.

pieces.title: The Three Building Blocks of Private Credit Resilience
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that private credit portfolio resilience rests on three pillars: sector and borrower diversification, underwriting that stress-tests each company's capital structure against a 40–50% fall in earnings across a full credit cycle, and structural protections (limits on additional debt, debt ranking first, and restrictions on cash leaving the company ahead of lenders) combined with experience gained over multiple cycles. Dianna Carr-Coletta, speaking for PGIM's Alternatives Direct Lending Group, makes the explicit case that cash flow sustainability matters more than loan-to-value, which can move sharply in private markets, and that a manager's track record should be measured in "decades" because "investing is an apprenticeship."

pieces.title: Time for Thoughtful Transactions
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that, with macroeconomic uncertainty keeping M&A volumes low, companies and owners should focus on "thoughtful" strategic transactions (acquisitions, market entry, recapitalisation with a new financing partner, or portfolio rebalancing) to create value and offset higher borrowing costs. It positions its patient capital, including interest-only junior debt with no pre-maturity amortisation, preferred and common equity, and a "one-stop" mix of revolver, senior term debt and junior capital, as a way to balance added leverage against growth and return. The piece is promotional in tone and makes no specific market forecast, but its explicit call is for firms to optimise their capital structures now, with PGIM as the financing partner.

pieces.title: Beyond traditional fixed income: what can ABS offer investors?
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that European asset-backed securities (ABS), backed by granular pools of mortgages, auto loans and consumer loans, can offer diversification, resilience and relative-value characteristics beyond traditional government and corporate bonds. The video, presented by Matt Wardle and Harry Bullamore, describes the firm's value-based, bottom-up approach and suggests that the growing size and variety of the European ABS market provides a supportive backdrop for its M&G Investment Grade ABS Credit Fund. The piece is promotional in nature, and it carries standard risk warnings that capital is at risk and past performance is not a guide to future returns.

pieces.title: The cost of being too liquid
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton argues that private markets (private equity, private credit and real estate) have historically earned an "illiquidity premium" over their public equivalents, citing Yale's endowment model and UBS data showing family offices allocating around 37% of portfolios to an illiquidity bucket. The firm explicitly urges advisers to consider building an illiquidity bucket for clients with long time horizons, while acknowledging that endowments differ from individual investors and that private markets will not outperform public markets in every period.

pieces.title: What is a Private Placement?
pieces.summary: PGIM's explainer defines a private placement as a non-public sale of debt or equity to a small number of accredited investors, which is exempt from SEC registration, and it argues the structure suits businesses seeking long-term, fixed-rate capital, funding diversification, confidentiality and quicker execution than a public bond. It presents the private placement market, mainly long-term fixed-rate senior debt, as a flexible option that can complement rather than compete with existing bank debt, and it states that such capital is best used for long-term initiatives rather than short-term working capital needs.

pieces.title: Unlocking green, social and sustainability bonds’ full potential - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the nearly $4 trillion green, social and sustainability (GSS) bond market deserves investor attention despite the green segment's maturity, and that an unconstrained, non-benchmarked approach could unlock its potential by allowing flexible duration management and investment across segments, including under-represented high-yield and emerging market debt. The firm explicitly contends that such an approach can help investors avoid trading off return, drawdown control and positive impact, and it favours a blended GSS allocation with a dominant green tilt for investors prioritising net zero, with social and sustainability bonds adding impact and opportunity.

pieces.title: Aviva Investors seeks to tokenise products on the XRP Ledger in collaboration with Ripple
Picks, shovels and deep value: A re-examination of emerging market equities - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that emerging market equities have become a technology and manufacturing-led asset class, with Taiwan and South Korea accounting for nearly half the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, and that Asian semiconductor and hardware suppliers are the main beneficiaries of a shift of cash flow from US hyperscalers' AI capital expenditure. Its explicit view is that this "migration of cash flow from the spenders to the enablers" forms the core case for allocating to EM equities now, citing strong earnings momentum and still-attractive valuations relative to developed market mega-cap tech, with the piece's author, Zhikai Chen, pointing to active stock selection as the way to exploit the opportunity.

pieces.title: Build vs Buy Framework for Asset Managers
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that asset managers should shift from building technology in-house to focusing engineering resources on capabilities that provide competitive advantage, whilst outsourcing infrastructure. The piece contends that this approach has become necessary due to AI complexity, data challenges, regulatory demands and constrained technology resources, and that the strategic question is no longer whether firms can build capabilities but whether they should.

pieces.title: Bridging the technology gap: How Europe is building its digital infrastructure - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is investing heavily in AI, semiconductors, cloud computing and critical raw materials to reduce its reliance on external powers and strengthen its digital infrastructure, competitiveness and resilience, with policy instruments such as the European Technological Sovereignty Package, the Chips Act 2.0 and the Critical Raw Materials Act providing a stable, long-term framework. The firm presents this structural shift as creating significant long-term investment opportunities across technology, energy, defence and the raw materials supply chain, though it does not make an explicit call on specific securities or sectors.

pieces.title: Purpose in Action
pieces.summary: Apollo reports that its Apollo Opportunity Foundation's "deal team" model—pairing grant funding with employee time and expertise to advise nonprofits—has deployed $24 million across 28 organisations and contributed over 10,400 hours since launch four years ago. An independent analysis by FSG found that 100% of grantee nonprofits reported strengthened mission delivery, whilst 95% of participating Apollo employees built new cross-functional connections and over 90% reported improved sense of purpose and professional development. Apollo presents the model as a blueprint for integrating skills-based volunteering into talent strategy whilst advancing social impact, midway through a ten-year $100 million commitment.

pieces.title: Who Should Own AI? An Open Letter
Direct Lending: Attractive Economics in a Shifting Environment
pieces.summary: HPS Investment Partners (BlackRock) argues that higher-for-longer rates and wider credit spreads have made direct lending more attractive in 2026, with gross asset yield expectations on new investments rising from about 8.5% at the start of the year to roughly 10%. It says this yield improvement comes from stronger market fundamentals and tighter underwriting rather than greater risk-taking, and it points to record institutional fundraising ($72 billion in Q2 2026, per Preqin) as evidence of durable institutional conviction, contrasted with redemption pressure in some non-traded BDCs. HPS concludes that the environment is "highly constructive" for direct lending and represents one of the most attractive vintage opportunities in recent years.

pieces.title: Advisor succession is a continuity plan, not an exit plan
2025 Oaktree Responsibility Report
Improving M&A Environment But Valuations Remain a Hurdle
Investing for Growth
pieces.summary: Fulcrum Asset Management, in a recap of its "Investing for Growth" conference, argues that financial outcomes and economic resilience are inseparable, so long-term investors should pursue both at once, using its Alternative Solutions process and its Long-Term Asset Fund (LTAF) as the vehicle. Its explicit view is that credit is "not broken" and that opportunities remain, particularly in "going concern" and distressed-value strategies kept away from the crowded upper middle market, while managers should be questioned on AI integration, interest coverage and their worst trades.

pieces.title: Putting AI to Work: Streamlining Data Collection
Real Reasons to Consider Core Fixed Income
pieces.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management argues that higher real yields across major developed bond markets have strengthened the income case for core fixed income, so investors need not rely on falling rates for positive returns. Its latest outlook favours a pro-income stance while cautioning against strong outright duration views, and it prefers securitised and selected corporate credit for carry over government bonds. It also argues that active allocation within core bonds, with issuer-level selection, matters as much as the decision to hold the asset class.

pieces.title: STS ABS: Opportunities and expectations for European insurance investment portfolios
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that STS-labelled asset-backed securities offer European insurers a high-quality, scalable way to diversify fixed income, with a yield premium, lower Solvency II spread capital charges than non-STS

pieces.title: Market GPS: Multi-Asset Quarterly Q1 2026
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Q1 2026 Market GPS Multi-Asset Quarterly argues that renewed fiscal stimulus helped drive markets in 2025 and that a convergence of resilient global growth and forthcoming fiscal support points to a sanguine 2026. The firm's explicit view is that this backdrop supports maintaining exposure to risk assets, while it flags slowing U.S. jobs growth and real income as the key risks to monitor, since a downturn in either could substantially raise recession risk.

pieces.title: Rate Reality: Who Wins, Who Loses as the High-Rate Era Persists
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that the current commercial real estate downturn stems from the rapid rise in interest rates after COVID, not from overbuilding, and that this has lowered valuations even for well-performing properties. It contends that private credit lenders now have an opening to originate loans at lower loan-to-value ratios on high-quality assets, because banks have pulled back from competing for such lending. Fortress says its experience across several credit cycles, and its focus on lower-leverage loans with stronger covenant protection, positions it to take advantage of this.

pieces.title: Is There an AI Bubble?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that there is no AI bubble in digital infrastructure, because demand for AI and cloud compute is outrunning available supply, and the sector is demand-driven and underpinned by long-term contracts with large, profitable companies. Its explicit view, put forward by Michael Steele, Partner and Head of Ares Digital Infrastructure, is that short-term speculative investing and occasional oversupply are avoidable outliers rather than the norm in tier 1 markets. The piece presents digital infrastructure as a source of inflation-protected cash flows and capital growth, while the accompanying disclaimer stresses that such claims are not guarantees against loss.

pieces.title: YouLend Secures Multi-Year Forward-Flow Facility from Värde Partners to Accelerate U.S. Growth
pieces.summary: Värde Partners, a credit-focused asset manager, has agreed a multi-year forward-flow facility with fintech lender YouLend, under which Värde may buy up to $225 million of receivables originated by YouLend in the United States. Värde frames the deal as attractive because it knows the market well, having financed several fintech payment processing platforms, and it says it looks forward to a long-term partnership as YouLend scales globally.

pieces.title: Gabriel Sacks on A Different Perspective podcast
Beyond the storm: What a super El Niño reveals about climate resilience
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that extreme weather events like a super El Niño expose existing vulnerabilities in energy systems, infrastructure and supply chains whilst stress-testing the assumption that operating conditions remain stable, shifting focus to physical climate risks that are often mispriced in markets. The asset manager contends that the investment opportunity extends beyond decarbonisation to resilience—backing businesses that help economies absorb shocks and operate under volatile conditions—with insurance and risk-transfer solutions particularly positioned to benefit as protection gaps become apparent.

pieces.title: Confirmation Watch: What a Kevin Warsh Federal Reserve Could Mean for Money Market Investors
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's piece argues that a Kevin Warsh-led Federal Reserve would still be bound by the FOMC, so any shift in rates, communications or the balance sheet would be debated, gradual and conditional on inflation being durably anchored. It sees three likely themes: less forward guidance (including de-emphasising the SEP and dot plot), a smaller steady-state balance sheet with QE reserved for crises, and a policy rate that could fall over time from the current 3.50%–3.75% corridor, which it expects would make short-term rates more sensitive to data and funding conditions. The firm also stresses that ample reserves and smooth repo market functioning would remain central to money market stability, and it explicitly flags that its material is not investment advice.

pieces.title: An evergreen future for emerging market private credit?
Unlocking the Whole Portfolio
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that private markets are becoming a more important part of the investment universe, offering differentiated growth, returns and diversification, and that public and private assets should be managed together as complementary parts of a single portfolio. It contends that more granular and standardised data, along with integrated analytics for stress testing, liquidity and concentration risk, can bridge the structural gaps between the two. It calls for continued innovation, investor education, vehicles that broaden access, and a supportive regulatory framework, while maintaining investor protections and market resilience.

pieces.title: Sharesify podcast with Abby Glennie
The Mispriced Debt Powering the AI Boom
pieces.summary: Man Group argues that data centre asset-backed securities (ABS), which are backed by data centre lease cash flows and real estate, offer a wider spread than unsecured corporate bonds from the same hyperscalers, with AA-rated ABS at 155 to 175 basis points against 45 to 70 basis points for unsecured paper of equal rating. In its view, much of this gap reflects a liquidity and complexity premium rather than fundamental credit risk, while technical downgrade risk, tenant concentration and faster hardware depreciation relative to 15-to-20-year lease assumptions need careful underwriting. Man Group therefore sees data centre ABS as a potentially rewarding opportunity for investors who rigorously assess tenant, technology and liquidity risks.

pieces.title: Inviting Opportunity through Emerging Markets
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece promotes an emerging markets total return strategy, arguing that fast-growing economies and less efficient markets can offer active managers wider credit spreads and potentially stronger risk-return profiles than developed market debt of comparable credit quality, along with diversification across geographies, currencies and credit environments. It explicitly invites readers to consider the role emerging markets debt can play in portfolios today and to look at differentiated income engines for enhancing portfolio resilience. The rest of the page is largely boilerplate, setting out risks including credit, currency, sovereign debt, custodial and emerging market political and economic instability.

pieces.title: From Information to Insight: Openness As Competitive Edge
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that its Direct Lending business gains a competitive edge from an "open architecture" in which deals are done in full view, information flows freely across the firm, and investment committee debates are visible to the whole team, a culture it frames as transparency and mutual accountability. It cites a claim that traditional bank lending contracted seven times over the past 25 years while private credit contracted only once, and presents private credit as the more reliable source of funding during the 2008 crisis and COVID-19. The piece is the first in a "Demystifying Private Credit" series and carries a disclaimer that its opinions and forward-looking statements should not be relied upon.

pieces.title: This asset class has been growing at 20% a year for the last 5 years
pieces.summary: Ares Management, in a Livewire interview published on 21 November 2024 (taped 31 October 2024), argues that COVID-19 and the steepest interest rate hiking cycle in more than four decades created an unusual environment for private equity secondaries. Its secondaries specialist, Barry Miller, says the slowdown in fundraising and distributions raised investors' need for liquidity, which they increasingly seek in the PE secondaries market. The piece itself is a promotional interview with no explicit investment call beyond highlighting secondaries as a source of liquidity; the headline's 20% annual growth figure is not substantiated in the text.

pieces.title: Monitoring the Middle Market
Seven Questions Before Hiring a Systematic Fixed-Income Manager
Resilient growth keeps MAS’s tightening stance alive
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's liquidity team argues that the Monetary Authority of Singapore's July 2026 move, a "very slight" increase in the S$NEER policy-band appreciation rate, is a further calibrated tightening that keeps an inflation-fighting stance intact, supported by stronger-than-expected growth led by AI-related investment and imported cost pressures. It holds that the S$NEER should stay supported, while SGD interest rates are likely to stay volatile, and recommends disciplined liquidity management, selective duration extension and diversification.

pieces.title: Monthly Market Views: Equity earnings boost and Asia’s move away from oil - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that equities tilt positive, citing strong second-quarter earnings (S&P 500 earnings up nearly 30% and 12% above forecast) and unusually positive corporate guidance, while it judges the downside from Middle East risks to be limited. It favours income over duration, pointing to US high yield, particularly the one-to-three-year segment yielding close to 7.5% with under two years' duration and about 90

pieces.title: Considerations for AI Related Debt Issuance in the High Yield Market
Investment Outlook 2026 – The shifting investment landscape - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Investment Outlook 2026 argues that the global economy has proved more resilient than expected despite geopolitical tensions, tariffs and policy shifts, with growth forecasts revised upwards but diverging across regions. It expects Europe to regain momentum, the US outlook to be clouded by uncertainty over Federal Reserve policy, and China to pivot towards medium-term gains as it moves away from investment-led growth. Its explicit views are that fixed income will benefit from central bank easing, that credit remains supportive despite rising sovereign yields, that technology-led equities will keep growing on AI-driven capital expenditure, and that emerging markets with strong tech sectors may gain from lower US yields and a weaker dollar, while export-heavy economies face headwinds; it concludes that flexibility and selectivity will be essential.

pieces.title: When a Gradualist Fed Collides with Hot Inflation
pieces.summary: PGIM's weekly view argues that the U.S. economy continues to show elevated inflation with little sign of easing, while Fed officials appear committed to a gradual tightening path, a combination PGIM believes will carry policy ramifications into 2027. The piece frames this against recent AI-related market jitters, interest-rate outperformance and geopolitical developments. Its explicit view is that the gradualist Fed stance is at odds with the persistence of inflation, though the excerpt provided does not spell out any specific asset-allocation call.

pieces.title: ERAFP selects LOIM for convertible bonds
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers reports that ERAFP, a EUR 53 billion French public pension scheme, has renewed its global SRI convertible bond mandate with LOIM, the second renewal since the relationship began in 2012. The EUR 1 billion total convertible allocation is split between LOIM and BNP Paribas Asset Management, with M&G Investments on standby, and the four-year mandate is aligned with ERAFP's Net Zero Asset Owner Alliance climate commitments. The firm presents the win as a validation of its SRI convertible capability, though the piece makes no explicit market call.

pieces.title: JH Explorer: Hong Kong is back! With property at the forefront
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Hong Kong's residential property market bottomed in mid-2025 and is now recovering, with secondary prices about 10% above the Q2 2025 trough, supported by rate cuts, equity-driven wealth effects, talent visa schemes, and falling supply. The firm states it remains constructive on Hong Kong residential developers, which it says still trade at a roughly 40% discount to NAV (against a 70% trough) and remain flat versus 2018, so further re-rating and earnings growth are possible, provided the drivers of stronger fundamentals stay on track.

pieces.title: Has the U.S. government broken the Aggregate Bond Index?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the U.S. Aggregate Bond Index has become structurally broken due to Treasury securities now comprising 46 per cent of the benchmark—double their 2001-2008 weighting—because massive federal deficit spending has crowded out other fixed income sectors and left investors overexposed to duration risk whilst forgoing spread-based returns available elsewhere. The firm contends that this concentration is particularly problematic given deteriorating U.S. fiscal dynamics, including interest payments now exceeding 18 per cent of federal revenues and expected to reach 26 per cent by 2036, risks that a passive Agg-tracking strategy fails to address. Janus Henderson proposes that investors adopt a more flexible, multi-sector approach to construct fixed income portfolios aligned with their specific risk and return objectives rather than defaulting to index-tracking strategies.

pieces.title: Perspective on Private Credit’s Relative Value
Virtual Investment Trust Conference: Insights from James Thom
Credit Standing Strong as AI Reshapes the Landscape
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments' Q2 2026 Corporate Credit Quarterly argues that credit has held up well despite the Iran conflict and oil shock, with spreads fully reversing their wartime widening and solid earnings anchoring a constructive view, though it flags AI-driven divergence: AI supports record corporate bond issuance while accelerating stress in leveraged loans and private credit, especially in software and tech-enabled services. Guggenheim expects default rates in floating-rate markets to rise over the next 12 months but considers the stress manageable, and its baseline has the US economy growing around 2 percent in 2026 with one more Federal Reserve cut, while it views market pricing of rate hikes as overdone. The firm names a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz as the main tail risk to its outlook.

pieces.title: ELTIFs: A Path to Private Markets
pieces.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management's explainer argues that ELTIFs (European Long-Term Investment Funds) give individual investors in Europe a route into private equity and private credit, which were historically hard for them to reach, with the ELTIF 2.0 rules of 2023 lowering minimum investments and improving liquidity. It acknowledges that these funds are illiquid, typically require holding periods of eight years or more, carry valuation difficulties and a real risk of capital loss, and that performance varies between managers, so it urges investors to research and choose a fund manager carefully. The firm's explicit view is that private markets can diversify portfolios and potentially improve risk-adjusted returns, though it qualifies this with the caveat that past performance does not predict future returns.

pieces.title: Unlocking growth: The AI investment opportunity
Staying in control
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that bonds deserve a continued place in diversified portfolios despite the appeal of equities and alternatives, citing their relative price stability, predictable coupon income, and role as safe havens in uncertain or recessionary periods. The firm states that bonds can be particularly suitable for risk-aware investors and those at or near retirement seeking to protect capital, and that higher-yielding existing bonds become especially attractive when interest rates are stable or falling. It also presents a table mapping bond strategies (absolute return, global aggregate, global credit, strategic bond, high yield, emerging markets) to goals such as total return, income, growth, and diversification.

The firm positions its HPS lending division as having played a role in scaling private credit into a key investor allocation over the past decade.

The piece lists quarterly "Reflections From the Path" sessions on LifePath portfolio performance, alongside specialised webinars on topics including fixed income positioning, private markets, and systematic investing approaches. BlackRock positions these events as providing actionable intelligence to help institutional investors navigate market complexity and stay informed on evolving asset-class themes.

pieces.title: The credit behind the compute
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments, through portfolio manager Steve Rolecek, argues that AI infrastructure spending is shifting toward sophisticated debt structures, some backed by credit support from highly rated hyperscalers, and could transform corporate credit markets. Using a Louisiana data centre financing as an example, where Alphabet guarantees lease obligations, the piece presents these deals as partially de-risked project financings rather than speculative bets. Fidelity's explicit view is that the next wave will centre on private chip-financing issuance, which falls outside benchmark indices, and that investors are only beginning to see the scale of the opportunity, so deal-level differentiation will be crucial.

pieces.title: Sixth Street's Approach to Direct Lending in Europe
A money and cycles perspective on the global economy
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Simon Ward argues that the global economy is entering a vulnerable phase, with the housing (Kuznets), business investment (Juglar) and stockbuilding (Kitchin) cycles all expected to be in downswings over the next one to three years, so a "Gulf War III" oil shock could tip it into recession, most likely a severe one if the cycle troughs coincide as they did in 1973-75. The firm's explicit view is that real money trends and central bank responses over coming months will determine whether weakness intensifies, with the squeeze from higher inflation and possible precautionary tightening or credit contraction the key risks, while modest global nominal money growth argues against a sustained inflation surge of the 1970s kind. The piece also rates US prospects as relatively improving before the shock, while Japan, the Eurozone and the UK look weak and China may hold up better.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that war typically drives inflation rather than deflation because resources are diverted from productive use, and warns that current conditions—including fiscal stimulus, trade deficits and reversing globalisation—create greater inflationary risks than during previous Middle East conflicts. The firm positions portfolios defensively by overweighting dividends and non-US equities in stocks, maintaining shorter-duration fixed-income holdings, and holding gold as a hedge against war-related uncertainty.

pieces.title: Same-day liquidity:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that for treasurers, liquidity is now as much about timing and operational delivery as about allocation, so same-day funds must be assessed against cut-off times, settlement timing and internal systems rather than treated as interchangeable with overnight cash. It recommends holding core intraday requirements in immediately or highly predictably accessible instruments, with same-day money market funds used as a complement only where their timelines are fully understood, and urges treasurers to split liquidity tiers into immediate, same-day and short-term. The piece also promotes Insight's own policy reviews, intraday liquidity mapping and scenario analysis as a way to test whether existing MMF allocations work under real operational conditions.

pieces.title: Global Fixed Income Outlook Q3 2026 – Bonds keep calm and carry on - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Q3 2026 Global Fixed Income Outlook argues that global bonds look well placed after resilient returns despite an energy shock and Middle East tensions, with yields still attractive, though the unresolved conflict remains a significant hurdle. Its sector views are broadly positive: it favours carry over capital appreciation in euro investment grade, sees robust fundamentals in US agency mortgage-backed securities and European high yield (with selectivity needed given tight incremental yields), and advises disciplined country selection in emerging-market debt, distinguishing oil exporters from vulnerable oil importers. On sovereigns, it warns that further rate hikes cannot be excluded if inflation persists, but suggests long-dated yields are unlikely to break out of their year-to-date range absent a major deterioration in the energy crisis.

Invesco explicitly favours this approach for UK and European insurers, citing an attractive risk-adjusted return, a strong return on capital under the Solvency regime, and diversification against fixed-rate bond holdings, with a majority of the allocation in private loans to capture the spread premium.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that advisory practices considering mergers should prioritise alignment on vision, culture and compatibility over financial terms and valuation structures. The asset manager contends that successful partnerships are determined by shared goals, clear communication about decision-making and accountability, and personal fit, rather than by the size of teams or attractiveness of economics. Janus Henderson recommends that advisors approach combinations as long-term relationships first and transactions second, answering three foundational questions about shared vision, cultural fit and working relationships before negotiating deal terms.

pieces.title: How exposed are CLOs to AI disruption?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that headline technology exposure in CLOs overstates AI disruption risk, since only about 11 per cent of U.S. CLO loans face direct AI threat compared with 22 per cent technology sector classification, with stressed loans representing just 3 per cent of the universe. The firm contends that active loan-level analysis and manager selection are critical to navigating this risk, and recommends higher-rated CLO tranches (AAA, AA, A) as offering superior structural protection against AI-related defaults.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Oil Supply Shocks Don’t Age Well
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that oil supply shocks matter for markets mainly when they persist, not at the initial price spike; comparing spot and six-month WTI moves with the 1990 Gulf War, 2000 OPEC cuts, and 2022 Russia–Ukraine episodes, it notes the current path closely resembles 1990, while bond yields remain elevated and spot crude sits near $100 a barrel. It also contends that the economy is becoming K-shaped, with subprime auto and card delinquencies near two-decade highs even as high-income households are cushioned by record household equity and property wealth, and that headline ABS spreads look stable but dispersion between prime and subprime collateral is widening beneath the surface. PIMCO's explicit recommendation is to stay higher up the capital structure in securitised credit and focus on quality.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: What BDC Redemptions and NAV Pressures Mean for Investors
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that redemption pressure in non-traded BDCs is not easing, with withdrawal requests still exceeding liquidity and managers relying on caps and prorations. Unlike private REITs in 2023, where appraisal-based marks move more gradually, BDC NAVs depend directly on borrowers' ability to service debt, and dispersion in manager-specific marks is widening, which PIMCO suggests points to valuations that may eventually converge through markdowns, wider secondary discounts or realised losses. PIMCO's explicit view is that private credit is not a monolith: stress is concentrated in direct lending's corporate exposure, while asset-based finance offers collateral-backed profiles, and that fundamentals are "not breaking, but not healing." Venezuela and Beyond: the Brave New World of Emerging Markets
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the U.S. intervention in Venezuela is part of a broader expansion of U.S. geopolitical influence across Latin America, including financial support for Argentina and a shift towards the political Right in the region, which it expects to drive EM sentiment and asset prices in 2026, notably around the Colombian and Brazilian elections. It views more orthodox economic policies as supportive for financial assets, and sees a clearer path to debt restructuring in defaulted and distressed EM sovereigns as offering upside, though, after 2025 sovereign returns of 13.2%, it advises selectivity by country rather than a broad overweight to high yield and careful position sizing given restructuring setbacks.

pieces.title: Why Do Evergreen Funds Exist?
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that evergreen funds address accessibility barriers in private markets by allowing investors to deploy capital immediately into existing portfolios and receive periodic redemptions, rather than committing to traditional drawdown funds with multi-year capital call schedules. The firm contends that because private assets remain illiquid regardless of their fund structure, evergreen managers must carefully balance investor liquidity needs against exposure to underlying private investments through portfolio construction and cash management. Ares presents evergreen funds as a simpler entry point for individual and smaller institutional investors seeking private market returns without the operational complexity of managing multiple drawdown commitments.

pieces.title: View from the Markets: Chips and oil - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chris Iggo argues that technology hardware, particularly semiconductors and the "picks and shovels" suppliers of AI infrastructure, remains the dominant equity theme in 2026, with Korea and Taiwan leading on the back of chip earnings. The firm's view is that the AI trade should survive the energy shortage caused by the Middle East conflict, but that markets are too optimistic about a quick settlement and that the risks, including a possible global recession, are underpriced. It stresses that a deal on the Strait of Hormuz is essential to restoring investor confidence.

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: January 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's January 2026 Chart of the Month argues that markets are not pricing a dovish Fed despite the upcoming leadership change, with consensus expecting only two 25 basis point cuts in 2026 amid steady growth and a gradually softening labour market. It attributes this restraint to the 2025 FOMC vote, in which fellow members did not dissent when Trump-nominated Stephen Miran called for 50 basis points of cuts, and to the fact that Lisa Cook remains on the committee. The firm expects the US 10-year Treasury yield to trade within a 3.75%–4.25% range in the coming months, with direction driven mainly by labour market data, while identifies a ruling in favour of Cook's removal as the main risk, which could bring additional dovish appointees, lower rates and higher bond volatility.

Its explicit calls are to favour U.S. and Japanese equities, on the back of AI-driven earnings strength; to lean into U.S. high yield for carry; and to hold a long duration position in Europe over the U.S., on the view that markets have overpriced the ECB's hiking path. The firm also expects three Fed hikes in total, including the one just delivered, and identifies an aggressive Fed tightening cycle or a significant equity sell-off as the two main risks to its outlook.

pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that liquid alternatives address three portfolio challenges: generating returns independent of market direction through alpha-generation techniques; providing defensive diversification as traditional bonds prove unreliable hedges against inflation; and expanding the investment opportunity set through strategies such as long/short investing. The asset manager positions liquid alternatives as a complementary tool to help financial advisors build more resilient portfolios in an environment of high equity concentration and diminished traditional diversification.

pieces.title: The $106 trillion infrastructure funding gap
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that infrastructure's traditional funding model of government budgets and bank lending can no longer meet a projected $106 trillion global investment need through 2040, so private lenders are becoming a necessary source of capital. The piece presents infrastructure debt as a mainstream institutional asset class with attractive return targets and lower historical default and loss rates than corporate debt, and it advises investors to focus on sourcing, structuring and monitoring discipline, since political, regulatory and obsolescence risks require careful underwriting.

pieces.summary: PGIM argues that borrower size is a meaningful starting point for evaluating a private credit strategy, since direct lending is not a uniform market and middle-market borrowers, with their more fragmented base, let lenders exert greater influence over pricing, entry leverage, covenants and monitoring than the more competitive large-cap segment. The piece makes an explicit case for PGIM's own disciplined middle-market focus, which it says is designed to support more resilient outcomes, though it offers this as a view rather than quantified evidence.

pieces.title: MOAR: The AI Rotation Reshaping Markets
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that, while many investors are focused on AI-related weakness such as falling compute demand, capex and earnings, the bigger story is a "Mother of All Rotations" (MOAR), in which capital moves between parts of the AI stack rather than leaving it. It contends that rising supply of certainty, including the expected profitability of AI model developers and a wave of roughly $200 billion in mega-IPOs (SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic), could widen the opportunity set, with knock-on effects for passive flows, index liquidity and regional markets. Aberdeen's explicit view is that emerging markets remain well placed, given their exposure to hardware and energy, stable domestic investor bases in Korea and Taiwan, and access to both Western and Chinese AI ecosystems, and that "MOAR doesn't mean AI fails – it's what happens if it succeeds."

pieces.title: The Big Question on Asia Investors Minds
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that current elevated yields present a rare opportunity to build high-quality, diversified portfolios without taking excessive risk, particularly through fixed income assets such as agency mortgages and emerging market bonds. Rick Rieder, the firm's Chief Investment Officer of Global Fixed Income, recommends locking in a substantial portion of allocations now, as he believes such yield levels will not recur for years given expected productivity-driven disinflation. BlackRock also emphasises its use of alternative data and machine learning across thousands of investment signals to identify income-generating opportunities in equities and systematically time dividend capture across global markets.

The firm reports that 2015–2020 vintage global senior direct lending funds generated a median KS-PME of 1.18x versus bank loan ETFs when properly cash-flow-matched, indicating genuine outperformance that persists even under conservative assumptions. Ares contends this benchmarking approach provides the economically relevant comparison for assessing whether private credit managers added value relative to public alternatives.

pieces.title: What Does the Interest-Rate Outlook Mean for Private Credit?
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that central banks have started cutting rates, with the ECB moving first in June, but that markets had been too optimistic about the pace. Sticky inflation and resilient economies have led policymakers to temper expectations, and PGIM contends that the ultra-low rates of 2009–2020 were an anomaly. It expects rates to settle nearer historical averages of around 4–5%, which it says changes the calculus between fixed- and floating-rate borrowing for private credit clients.

pieces.title: CLOs: When carry matters more than conviction
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson argues that collateralised loan obligations (CLOs) offer attractive risk-adjusted returns through carry income and structural safety features, making them particularly valuable in an uncertain macro environment where traditional fixed-income spreads are tight. The firm contends that CLOs' floating-rate characteristics, diversification benefits across 100-300 underlying loans, and historical resilience (with no AAA-rated European CLO tranche having defaulted in 30 years) make them a compelling complement to traditional bond allocations. Janus Henderson's implicit call is that investors should shift focus from directional market calls to harvesting carry through CLOs, where specialist active management in identifying quality deals and managers can generate returns with reduced dependence on capital appreciation.

pieces.title: Factor and Style Risk: Taming the Hidden Hazard to Core Equity Returns
Global IG credit: Demand for quality
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that global investment grade credit remains attractive despite spreads sitting near the tight end of their historical range (around 80-90bps in US and European markets), citing high starting yields (US IG corporate index above 5%), resilient demand from life insurers, retail funds and overseas investors, and improving corporate credit quality with upgrades outpacing downgrades. It flags geopolitical risk, rising AI-driven capex and supply (including an estimated USD 300bn of hyperscaler issuance over two years, with Oracle under closer scrutiny) as areas to monitor, and concludes that active security selection, capital structure positioning and a preference for high-quality mid-cycle issuers are the right approach.

2026 Infrastructure Summit
pieces.summary: BlackRock and its infrastructure investment arm Global Infrastructure Partners are hosting a summit to discuss how government and business can collaborate on US infrastructure development, particularly in electricity, artificial intelligence and modernised systems. The company argues that this infrastructure opportunity can accelerate economic growth and create skilled labour jobs. BlackRock's implicit position is that large-scale coordinated investment in infrastructure, coupled with workforce development, is essential to America's future competitiveness.

pieces.title: Water: The hidden constraint shaping the digital economy - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Environmental Strategies Group argues that water, not just electricity, is becoming a binding constraint on AI and the digital economy, through datacentre cooling, ultrapure water use in chip fabrication and the water footprint of fossil-fuel power, with many new sites and fabs located in water-stressed regions. It contends that water scarcity and tightening regulation create both risk and investment opportunity, and advises that tech firms embed water-risk assessments into capital decisions, adopt closed-loop cooling, hybrid systems, data-driven leak management and water reclamation, and warns that operators relying on high-withdrawal evaporative cooling or siting capacity without regard to local water availability face stranded assets and rising costs.

pieces.title: The evolution of infrastructure investing
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management argues that infrastructure investing has evolved significantly, encompassing broader sectors, risk profiles and investment structures driven by digitalization, decarbonization and deglobalization. The firm contends that many institutional investors' current allocations may not adequately capture this expanded opportunity set and calls on them to move beyond deciding whether to invest in infrastructure to instead constructing integrated portfolios tailored to specific objectives by selecting strategies based on return drivers, risk compensation and liquidity needs.

Technology outlook: Balancing rapid growth with long-term valuations - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Vincent Nichols argues that AI infrastructure spending has driven a sharp rally in technology stocks, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor index up 88% in a record quarter, and that investor focus is shifting from valuations to the trajectory of future earnings. The firm's explicit view is that AI adoption is not overhyped and is advancing much faster than in the dotcom era, but that the opportunity will move from hardware suppliers towards cloud providers and software over time, and that a period of disillusionment and a slowdown in computing spending are likely at some point. It also cautions that the hardware segment's valuations are cyclical and that the key question for investors is which companies can convert AI capacity into sustained margin expansion and profit growth.

pieces.title: boomers-next-gens-and-private-markets
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the Great Wealth Transfer, with around $84 trillion changing hands between generations, is shifting capital markets: older investors are moving towards income and capital preservation, while next-gen inheritors (ages 21–42) doubt that traditional stocks and bonds can deliver the returns they need. The firm's explicit view is that public equity, once the main route to broad ownership of the economy, is now a shrinking and more concentrated universe, so private markets should be incorporated thoughtfully alongside equity-centric public portfolios as "new portfolio construction tools" that can potentially match or beat public-market returns for similar or less risk.

pieces.title: Private Equity Opportunities in 2026: Value Creation in a Higher Rate World
pieces.summary: Apollo's 2026 Private Equity Outlook, by David Sambur and Matt Nord, argues that private equity's best opportunities lie in market blind spots created by index crowding, higher rates and extreme public valuations, with the Shiller CAPE near 40x and the S&P 500 price-to-sales around 3.3x, levels Apollo compares to the dot-com era. It identifies three opportun

pieces.title: Private credit: Opportunities amid market dislocation
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that recent negative headlines about private credit (high-profile defaults in the broadly syndicated loan market and redemption requests) overstate systemic distress, with risks largely isolated to large lenders and 2021-vintage loans, particularly those tied to software borrowers, where valuations and AI-related obsolescence risk are the main concerns. The firm contends that the resulting market dislocation could create a constructive setup for lenders over the next six to twelve months, with the lower- and core-middle-market segments supported by earnings growth, declining leverage and improving interest coverage. It therefore sees the current bifurcation between large-cap and smaller segments as an opportunity rather than a broad warning sign.

pieces.title: Värde Provides €100 Million Financing for German Property Developer PANDION AG
pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that an affiliate has provided €100 million in financing to PANDION AG, a German residential and commercial developer, secured on 13 projects in cities including Berlin, Munich and Cologne, with the deal closing alongside an extension of PANDION's corporate bond. Värde frames the transaction as a sign of its confidence in the German residential market and in its ability to offer tailored capital across European prime real estate, while PANDION's CEO describes it as the foundation for restructuring the company's corporate financing so it can focus on core development.

Investors Seek Diversification. Borrowers Seek Certainty
pieces.summary: Apollo's Chris Edson argues that its private credit origination platform, spanning corporate, asset-backed, leasing, trade and consumer finance, gives it direct borrower access and proprietary deal flow that matter more in today's market. He contends that investors now seek diversification and differentiated access, while borrowers prioritise funding certainty after shocks such as April 2025 and spring 2023, and that Apollo's willingness to act as a principal that buys and holds a meaningful share of deals, rather than as a transactional agent, offers that stability. Apollo presents its strict underwriting standards and a "no walls" structure as the basis for selecting from the trillions of dollars of opportunities it passes on each year.

pieces.title: Disruption decoded: How AI is rewriting the software playbook for private credit investors
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that AI is prompting a structural reassessment of software credit risk in private credit, where software is now one of the largest sector concentrations, and that managers able to separate genuinely vulnerable borrowers from those merely caught in indiscriminate de-rating will be best placed. Based on Q1 2026 meetings with direct lenders, sponsors, research providers, allocators and technology analysts, it identifies four transmission channels to credit impairment (revenue erosion, margin compression, valuation compression and refinancing seizure), and says that the type of software exposure matters more than its size, that traditional metrics are inadequate, and that disruption timing should be weighed against loan maturities. The firm presents a loan-level AI disruption scoring framework as an evidence-based tool for investors, to be updated as conditions evolve, though the piece does not make a specific market call.

pieces.title: Private Credit: Reality Check
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that concerns about private credit, including its rapid growth, relative illiquidity and a few high-profile corporate failures, are understandable but overdone, and that the sector is not new: insurers have made long-dated private loans for at least 150 years, and PGIM itself has been active in private credit for 75 years. The firm contends that direct lending, while growing in scale, investor base and borrower range, is a prosaic business of senior secured loans whose lenders prioritise getting their principal back, so the growth "deserves scrutiny, but not alarm."

Its explicit view, voiced by Zhikai Chen, is that EM is "too large and now too critical" for equity investors to be underexposed to, and that the concentration in technology is a feature of the regional indices rather than a flaw. The firm presents the current backdrop as a potentially rich hunting ground for active stock selection, while acknowledging that the returns on the wider AI investment remain an open question.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that exuberant markets, including a Q2 surge in momentum stocks and heavy inflows into leveraged and thematic ETFs, are being amplified by these products, which are designed as short-term trading tools and can magnify both gains and losses through daily rebalancing and compounding. It cites the rapid growth of the leveraged ETF universe, with about 75% of its assets in tech or tech-adjacent strategies, and notes that thematic ETF flows tend to chase performance, with several recent themes, including AI, nuclear and space, now down double digits from their peak inflows. The firm's explicit view is that long-term investors are better served by active ETFs with broader objectives grounded in fundamental analysis, rather than by high-conviction leveraged or thematic exposure.

pieces.title: Reducing Water and Waste Across European Data Centers

The company indicates that Data4 plans further water efficiency gains through recycled and alternative water sources, and has achieved zero-waste-to-landfill certification across four European countries.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that passive US equity investing is itself an active decision, one that adds concentration risk (the top 10 S&P 500 companies make up nearly 40% of the index, and 61% of the Russell 1000 Growth), leaves clients exposed to yesterday's winners, and, at a projected 6.7% annual return for US large caps over the next decade, is expected to deliver less than half the category's returns of the last ten years. Its explicit call is that investors should be deliberate in choosing an active manager, since alpha will matter more to returns, and it cites its own record of 89% of equity assets outperforming benchmarks over ten years, a figure the piece presents as evidence of its active advantage.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that monitoring year-end capital gains distribution estimates helps advisors avoid tax surprises, plan around key dates and hold more useful after-tax conversations with clients, particularly for funds held in taxable accounts. It promotes the capital gains view in its Heatmap Analysis tool, which it says covers estimates for about 5,000 investments and updates weekly in October, November and December, as a repeatable way to do this. The piece explicitly advises assessing position size alongside distribution size, checking record dates before trades, and distinguishing short-term from long-term gains, while noting that the content is for planning only and that client-specific tax questions should go to a tax adviser.

The firm presents Fleetwood as embodying its own values of disciplined performance, fierce determination and high ethical standards, and says it is "genuinely excited" to partner with someone committed to winning "in the right way." The piece is essentially brand marketing rather than market commentary, and it makes no investment claims or recommendations.

pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that AI-related funding needs could drive $400bn in credit issuance in 2026, potentially making it the largest year for investment grade issuance, though the firm remains cautious that supply could outpace demand and push spreads wider over successive funding waves. The asset manager positions itself cautiously to navigate both the opportunities and material risks presented by elevated AI-driven credit issuance over coming years.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that China's economy is proving more resilient than expected amid the global oil shock, citing energy substitution (EV uptake, rail travel), coal-to-chemicals switching and export restrictions as containing the drag, while exports, up 15.5% year-to-date, are supported by the AI and green-energy upcycle. It sees the Q2 slowdown in fiscal support as a pause rather than a change of direction, expecting fiscal support to ramp up in Q3 to keep the growth target on track. On markets, it maintains a range-trading view on Chinese rates (buying yield spikes and selling rallies) and expects gradual yuan appreciation against the US dollar, with the CFETS basket outcome dependent on broader dollar moves.

pieces.title: DB endgame: practical considerations for run-on and surplus release
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that a defined benefit scheme choosing to run on and release surplus needs a different operating model, with its primary aim being to pay pensions and build a resilient surplus rather than to pursue buy-out. It proposes a practical framework covering the purpose of running on, the scheme's ambitions for its surplus, the implications for the portfolio, and the governance needed to support the strategy. The piece's explicit view is that running on done properly means actively using financial strength productively while keeping member security at the core.

pieces.title: Unravelling the forces driving corporate credit’s resilience
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that corporate credit has absorbed recent Middle East and oil-price shocks with limited disruption, because spreads have moved broadly in line with rates and have not yet shown a material transmission into corporate fundamentals or economic data. It attributes this resilience to light investor positioning, front-loaded issuance, yield-sensitive buyers such as

Homeward bound - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's monthly multi-asset update says it has marginally trimmed its strong overweight in equities, citing increased uncertainty after a late year-end rally, a Federal Reserve rate cut that exposed a lack of policy consensus, and a cooling of investor appetite for AI-linked technology stocks. It still holds a significant equity overweight, remains neutral on credit and on interest rate sensitivity, and sees room for investors to add to equity positions barring a new shock, because discretionary investors have been underweight and may have to chase the market.

pieces.title: Cash at the crossroads: navigating rates, energy and AI
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that a Middle East energy shock has reignited inflation and pushed central banks towards a "higher for longer" stance, even as a US–Iran framework has reduced tail risks and AI-driven demand has kept risk appetite firm. It expects the ECB to deliver one more 25bp hike in September, taking the deposit rate to 2.25%, before a high bar for further tightening, while the BoE holds at 3.75% with a single hike possible if energy-driven second-round effects emerge and cuts returning in 2027. The firm is constructive on cash and short-duration assets, front-end euro yields and financials, while cautioning that markets may be too confident about early easing and that geopolitics remains the key swing factor for Europe.

pieces.title: Quick View: ECB rate shift puts focus on dispersion, not direction for credit investors
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the ECB's 0.25% hike to a 2.25% deposit rate is a credibility-driven response to re-accelerating inflation (3.2%, driven by the energy shock) rather than the start of a broad tightening cycle. It expects credit spreads to stay range-bound, supported by strong primary demand, with the main effect being rising dispersion between resilient issuers, such as European banks, and more leveraged, rate-sensitive ones like real estate. Its explicit call is that active management, focused on issuer and sector selection and relative value, should drive excess returns, while it remains constructive on European duration.

pieces.title: Opportunity or risk? Investing in AI capex
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that while equity investors face clear risks from a possible AI-driven bubble, fixed income investors can view the surge in AI capital expenditure as an opportunity, given that hyperscalers (such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle) have strong balance sheets and diversified cash flows, unlike dot-com-era firms. Citing JP Morgan forecasts of $1.5trn in high-grade issuance to 2030, the firm concedes that heavy supply has eroded hyperscalers' scarcity premium and widened their spreads, but it considers this a short-term concern. Its explicit view is that issuance will come in peaks and troughs, that demand has so far kept pace with supply, and that active managers should assess each deal individually to see whether investors are adequately compensated.

pieces.title: On the Ground, Around the World
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that a large, locally embedded real estate team gives it an edge in sourcing and underwriting deals, citing 740-plus professionals across 36 locations, a new Milan office opened in May 2025, and a portfolio of over 4,000 investments. It frames its "ground-level" model, combining local relationships, real-time market data and decades of market-cycle experience, as making it more competitive in local and global markets, with a stated commitment to highly localised investing in Europe. The piece contains no explicit investment call, and its disclaimers caution that its forward-looking statements are not reliable.

pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors reports that impact investing has grown from a niche strategy to mainstream adoption among major pension funds and asset owners seeking financial returns alongside social and environmental outcomes. The firm argues that its competitive advantage lies in a 10-year track record in blended finance and emerging markets, combined with an in-house impact team that collaborates directly with portfolio managers rather than relying on external consultants, enabling closer engagement with portfolio companies on impact measurement and strategy.

What does the Iran conflict mean for defense & security investing?
