Morgan Asset Management argues that the Iran conflict is driving near-term munitions replenishment demand for defense contractors, with the U.S. and Israel having used large volumes of precision weapons, including over 400 Patriot missiles, roughly two years' supply at current procurement pace. It notes that defence stocks have nonetheless lagged the S&P 500 year to date, as sector and European gains in 2025 had already priced in rising budgets. The piece's explicit view is that the longer-term opportunity lies in frontier technologies such as drones, electronic warfare and AI-assisted weapons, which are increasingly funded by venture capital and sit in private as well as public markets, so investors should be exposed to both.

pieces.title: Castlelake and Redwood Trust Announce Strategic Joint Venture to Purchase up to $8 Billion of Prime Jumbo Mortgage Loans
pieces.summary: Castlelake and Redwood Trust have formed a joint venture under which Castlelake will buy up to $8 billion of prime jumbo mortgage loans sourced, aggregated and diligenced by Redwood's Sequoia platform, with scope to scale up, including seasoned loans from bank balance sheets. Castlelake presents the deal as giving its investors access to high-quality, fully documented prime jumbo assets, which it describes as offering attractive, risk-adjusted outcomes, and as reflecting shared commitments to disciplined underwriting and institutional governance.

pieces.title: Europe’s path to strategic autonomy opens new horizons for bond investors - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's push for strategic autonomy in defence, energy, communications and technology, backed by an estimated €1.5 trillion to €2 trillion of investment by 2035 (the piece gives both figures), creates fixed income opportunities, particularly in private and state-linked companies. The firm's explicit view, put forward by Fadi Berbari, is that a selective, bottom-up approach is essential to capture the stability and visibility of these strategic European investments, and that the funding is not aimed at governments but at European industry.

PGIM states that it continued to offer tailored financing amid tighter lending conditions and global economic shifts, and says it remains committed to helping partners navigate the current environment and focus on their long-term goals, though it makes no explicit market call or forecast.

pieces.title: What are US Municipal Bonds? Case Studies
pieces.summary: Insight Investment's whitepaper introduces US municipal bonds, distinguishing general obligation bonds backed by tax revenues from revenue bonds backed by income from specific infrastructure assets, and notes their historically low default rates. The firm argues that the market's fragmentation offers considerable opportunities for active managers, but that exploiting them requires specialist, bond-by-bond credit analysis, particularly of the underlying assets for revenue bonds. The piece is illustrative rather than advisory, and its explicit view is that the municipal market is underappreciated by non-US investors.

Morgan Asset Management reports that ETF adoption has accelerated over 15 years, with active ETFs capturing disproportionate inflows relative to their asset base, particularly in technology and fixed income. The firm argues that the ETF structure's transparency, liquidity and tax efficiency are driving investor preference for this wrapper, whilst noting that ETFs have demonstrated utility during market stress. J.P. Morgan Asset Management presents this as a reference guide to help investors and advisers understand ETF market structure, flows and trading practices.

pieces.title: How U.S. middle market direct lending complements and enhances European portfolios
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that a complementary allocation to U.S. middle market direct lending can diversify and potentially enhance returns for European investors, since demand for private credit is outpacing supply in Europe, where banks still dominate middle-market lending. It contrasts the more investor-friendly U.S. terms (covenant headroom of roughly 25–35% versus 35–40% in Europe, more flexible equity cures, and super senior working capital facilities) with the European market's fragmented legal landscape, and presents the U.S. non-sponsored channel as a source of potential alpha. The firm concludes that U.S. direct lending offers a deeper investment universe, lower default levels (around 2% long-term), and stronger structural protections.

pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that early 2026 offers an attractive entry point into commercial real estate debt, citing healthy property income, high occupancy, limited new supply, and banks lending at reduced proceeds. It contends that private credit providers, particularly subordinate lenders, can benefit from favourable yields, stronger lender protections on reset property values at modest leverage, and flexible partnerships with senior lenders. Fidelity's explicit view is that these conditions, namely strong fundamentals, constrained bank capital and historically modest leverage, remain in place and make subordinate real estate debt a compelling opportunity.

PIMCO reads the decline in long-dated net issuance from non-AI firms as a maturity choice driven by higher long-end Treasury yields, not evidence of crowding out, and it concludes that the corporate-credit "crowding-out" story is not visible yet, though the view is explicitly provisional ("so far").

The firm states that the broad sector and macro effects of the Act are not yet fully priced into markets, and that portfolios including transition-linked investments are likely to generate returns as the transition accelerates, while cautioning that it will monitor for overpricing and remains open to traditional energy investments given sustained global energy demand.

In the words of CEO Marc Rowan and Asia Pacific head Eiji Ueda, Apollo sees its role as complementary to, not a substitute for, Japanese banks, which continue to provide advice, hedging, derivatives and M&A services. The firm's explicit view is that private finance should become "just another alternative" for CFOs and treasurers in Japan, as it already is in the US and Europe.

They cite returns from Latin America (36%), Asia (32%) and Europe (22%) against 9.8% for UK investors in the S&P 500, and a 5.1% dividend increase, as evidence. The piece takes an explicit stance that managers should concentrate on factors they can control, favour companies with tangible assets and visible cash flow, and prefer "greater degrees of certainty" over best guesses about AI disruption, oil shocks and tariffs.

pieces.title: The Key Inflation Signal for Investors
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the best guide to underlying U.S. inflation is unit labour costs (wages adjusted for productivity), which it says track medium-term price trends and are now running at about 1.5% over the past year and 2% on a four-year average, at or below the Fed's target. It contends that current above-target inflation stems from temporary factors such as energy, tariffs and AI-driven chip and electricity prices, and that the labour market is not a source of underlying pressure. PIMCO's view is that underlying unit cost inflation is likely to stay at or below 2%, helped by rising productivity from AI, so any Fed rate rise under Kevin Warsh would be to anchor expectations rather than to cool an overheated labour market.

pieces.title: Interval funds 101: How to diversify with private market investments
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers reports that interval funds—SEC-registered closed-end funds offering periodic rather than daily liquidity—have attracted $13.2 billion in net inflows in the second quarter of 2025 and now hold $215 billion in assets, as investors seek diversification and exposure to private market assets traditionally available only to institutions. The firm argues that interval funds provide a middle ground between illiquid private investments and daily-liquid mutual funds, offering professional management and potential return enhancement through access to private credit, real estate and infrastructure, whilst acknowledging risks including valuation complexity, limited redemption windows and higher fees than traditional funds.

pieces.title: Measuring risk in the private credit markets
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that middle market direct lenders must rely on proprietary credit analysis rather than external ratings, since most borrowers lack them, and describes its internal framework (PAC CreditIQ) which incorporates loan-to-value ratios, earnings volatility, and capital intensity as key risk determinants. The firm implicitly positions its 65 years of credit rating experience and empirical methodology as superior to traditional rating agency approaches, particularly in accounting for private market valuations and forward-looking business drivers. Principal does not make an explicit market call but presents internal ratings monitoring as providing portfolio transparency to investors over a loan's lifetime.

What could drive U.S. small cap returns in 2026?
pieces.summary: In a mid-2026 outlook, Janus Henderson Investors portfolio manager Jonathan Coleman argues that U.S. small caps can perform in 2026 without lower interest rates, pointing to reshoring, a pick-up in M&A (notably in biotech) and a recovering IPO market as drivers. pieces.title: pere-ares-oct2022
pieces.summary: Ares Management has closed Ares US Real Estate Fund X, its 10th US value-add fund, at $1.8 billion, a 75 percent increase on Fund IX, with over half of the capital from non-US investors, mainly in Asia and the Middle East. According to David Roth, Ares's co-head of US real estate, the larger fund will allow bigger, platform-style deals and a broader sector focus beyond multifamily and industrial, including life sciences, medical office and single-family rentals, and some deals will use structured positions such as preferred equity. Roth presents this structuring as a deliberate response to current market volatility, offering downside protection at the cost of limiting upside if values recover.

pieces.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Private Infrastructure
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private infrastructure, spanning data centres, fibre, renewable energy, electrified transport and essential utilities, is becoming central to the "New Economy" as rising demand for data, energy and connectivity meets a funding gap created by governments stepping back. The firm explicitly contends that private infrastructure offers allocators resilience, income and long-term growth in one asset class, and that its Wealth Management team, citing Raj Dhanda, believes it can enhance portfolio resilience. The piece is a promotional guide that markets Ares's global sourcing, disciplined approach and focus on structural trends, with disclaimers noting that "downside protection" and "risk-adjusted returns" are not guarantees against loss.

pieces.title: Livewire | Income is back
pieces.summary: Ares Management (via Teiki Benveniste, Head of Ares Australia) argues that income-focused investors are better served by spreading risk across sovereign bonds and corporate credit, mixing fixed-rate bonds with floating-rate loans to capture higher current yield while limiting interest rate duration risk. The firm says loans, with current yields of roughly 8-9%, carry mainly credit risk, whereas bonds carry both rate and credit risk and yield less (the Bloomberg-cited Global Agg index averages 2.9%, below cash rates). Ares positions its Global Credit Income Fund as a low-duration, benchmark-unaware vehicle with around 8% unhedged current yield, favouring asset-based BBB exposure such as CLO debt, and it expects rates to stay volatile and possibly higher for longer.

pieces.title: Reshaping infrastructure debt
pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors reports that infrastructure debt enjoyed record issuance in 2025 and argues the asset class is becoming increasingly attractive to institutional investors due to its stable returns, inflation protection and diversification benefits amid geopolitical uncertainty. The firm identifies digital infrastructure—particularly fibre networks and data centres—and energy transition assets as offering the most compelling opportunities, though it cautions that investors should maintain disciplined risk assessment and focus on credit fundamentals as competitive pressure and liquidity intensify the market.

pieces.title: Three questions at the center of the autonomous vehicle debate
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption is still negligible but accelerating, and that the industry is more likely to concentrate around early movers with data, scale and unit-cost advantages than to fragment. It frames three open questions: whether scale and data will decide winners, whether ridesharing platforms will become essential partners or be disintermediated, and whether AVs can become safe and cheap enough. pieces.title: Authorised participants in ETF universe | iShares -BlackRock
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that its Australian iShares ETFs are supported by a diverse base of authorised participants (APs), with an average of ten contracted and six active APs per fund, and argues this breadth mitigates concentration risk and ensures competition in creation and redemption services. The firm notes that creation and redemption activity is spread across eight APs with no single participant dominating, and that secondary market trading substantially exceeds primary market activity, which it suggests benefits investors through tighter spreads.

pieces.title: Quarterly fixed income review and outlook
Inside the Loomis Sayles Private Credit Team
pieces.summary: Loomis Sayles presents a video profile of its private credit team, describing the disciplined, collaborative process the team uses to evaluate private credit opportunities and structure solutions for issuers. The piece is promotional and makes no explicit market view, forecast or investment call. Its disclosures state that it is for information only and not investment advice.

pieces.title: Japan Stewardship Code
pieces.summary: LOIM reaffirms its formal acceptance of Japan's Stewardship Code (dated 26 June 2025), stating that active engagement and voting are central to its fiduciary duty to clients, beneficiaries and investee companies. The firm argues that stewardship protects and enhances long-term value and that engagement and voting help shape companies' governance and sustainability trajectories. The piece points readers to LOIM's 2025 commitment report, mapping its stewardship activities to the Code's eight principles, and to supporting documents such as its engagement and proxy voting policies and its 2024 Stewardship Report.

pieces.title: What might change under a Warsh-led Federal Reserve?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Jordan Jackson reports that the FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.50%-3.75% at its April meeting, Jerome Powell's last as Chair, with four dissents (Miran favouring a cut; Hammack, Kashkari and Logan opposing the easing bias). Powell will stay on as a governor after his chair term ends on 15 May, and the piece argues that Kevin Warsh's influence on policy will be limited in the near term, though his proposed changes to communication, the balance sheet and regulation could alter how markets price the Fed. JPMAM expects the Fed to stay on hold, retains its support for the easing bias on the view that supply shocks are short-lived, and recommends diversifying across high-quality fixed income, resilient-earnings stocks, international assets and commodities and real assets.

pieces.title: Quick view: Energy price sensitivity could drive EM differentiation amid Iran conflict
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the market reaction to the Middle East conflict has so far been driven by energy supply and shipping risks, with oil prices carrying a temporary risk premium rather than a confirmed permanent loss of supply, and that duration rather than headlines will determine whether the shock becomes macro-relevant for emerging markets. The firm's view is that sustained high energy prices would widen differentiation across EMs, benefiting oil exporters while pressuring importers through weaker trade balances, inflation pass-through and wider sovereign spreads, though market reactions remain orderly and contained for now. Janus Henderson says it is monitoring energy-driven pressures and sovereign bond responses, but it makes no explicit portfolio call beyond identifying vulnerabilities should a persistent shock materialise.

pieces.title: Commercial Real Estate: A Reset, Not a Replay
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the recent rise in real yields has revalued commercial real estate, pushing down public REIT prices, but that this is a valuation reset rather than a repeat of the 2023 credit stress. It notes that cap-rate spreads over real Treasury yields sit near the low end of their historical range in most sectors (office excepted), leaving valuations exposed to further rate rises even without weaker fundamentals, while REIT bond spreads, CMBS spreads and issuance markets have stayed resilient. PIMCO's explicit view is that "this time is different" because borrowing costs start from a higher base, several years of tighter lending have produced lower leverage and stronger debt-service coverage, and credit remains available, though refinancing risk and dispersion across vintages, capital structures and property types will persist.

pieces.title: CIO Weekly: Europe’s Risk Premium Is Upside Down
Equities: Strong growth amid disruption
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Global Market Strategist team argues that U.S. equities enter 2027 with strong fundamentals: S&P 500 earnings growth expectations have risen from 15% to 33% for 2026, yet the index is up only 10.9% year-to-date because valuation multiples have contracted 17.4%. The piece sees AI capital spending as a continuing earnings driver, but it warns that returns will be uneven, with hyperscalers facing free cash flow pressure, costlier financing and disruption to legacy businesses. Its explicit view is that less demanding valuations and a strong earnings backdrop leave it "constructive on equities in 2027," while expecting dispersion and volatility as technological change reshapes earnings expectations.

pieces.title: Beyond Treasuries
Fixed income in 2026
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers' 2026 fixed income outlook sets a base case of a soft landing, while flagging risks such as rising unemployment, disappointing AI returns, a politicised Federal Reserve, fiscal easing, geopolitics and a market correction. Because bond returns will mostly come from income rather than falling policy rates, the firm favours carry, particularly from the belly of the sovereign curve, selectively adds credit spread exposure and likes emerging market bonds, while staying neutral on sovereigns overall and seeing tactical value in curve steepening, notably in Australia and the UK.

pieces.title: For new retirees: To Roth or not to Roth?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the rise in the RMD starting age (now 73, rising to 75 by 2033 under SECURE 2.0) makes Roth conversions a question for new retirees, but that the usual rule of thumb (convert if taxes will be lower in retirement) can be costly without detailed planning, since life events such as widowhood, inheritances, RMDs, Social Security taxation and Medicare IRMAA surcharges can push retirees into higher brackets. The firm's explicit view is that Roth conversions are "not a one-size-fits-all strategy": they should be sized carefully at household level, usually not for all traditional assets, and tested with retirement planning software in close consultation with clients' tax advisers.

pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that the sell-off in credit has made convexity attractive: bonds and loans trading below par offer "pull-to-par" upside and higher yields, with high-yield prices lower than now only about 5% of the time over the past decade. It expects default rates to rise modestly from below 1% but to stay below historical averages even in a recession, and it judges credit spreads to be at attractive entry points while warning of higher tail risk and dispersion. Its explicit call is that active, bottom-up credit selection, focused on avoiding marginal-quality issuers, is best placed to capture these opportunities, citing its Global Liquid and Alternative Credit platforms.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's piece argues that the 2026 midterm results point to voters favouring targeted tax measures over broad-based ones, with mixed but largely manageable credit implications for US municipal issuers. It expects state and local bond supply to stay structurally elevated over the medium term, citing ageing infrastructure, higher construction costs and population growth, and it judges California's defeated billionaire tax a net positive for the state's credit. The firm concludes that the evolving tax landscape will require active, bottom-up credit selection.

2025 Defined Contribution Plan Sponsor Survey Findings
A bond market built for active management
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers argues that higher Treasury yields, despite recent negative bond returns, have made the risk/reward for fixed income more favourable, with higher income and a bigger cushion against further rate rises, and that bonds have again acted as a safe haven during an equity sell-off. It highlights selective US opportunities in agency mortgage-backed securities (supported by sharply reduced net MBS supply), highly rated CLO tranches (floating-rate and structurally protected), and high-quality investment-grade credits in AI-linked and data-centre names where spreads have widened. It also sees value in emerging-market bonds, particularly commodity and energy-related corporates and local-currency sovereigns offering attractive real yields, and it presents Loomis Sayles' Rick Raczkowski's view that selectivity is becoming increasingly important.

pieces.title: Bank Loans: Opportunities Are Knocking
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that bank loans offer strong relative value in 2021, combining short duration, stable floating-rate income and low expected defaults, with a full-year return forecast of 4-6%. It supports this with a favourable technical backdrop (CLO issuance of roughly $100-110 billion, strong retail inflows and limited new supply) and a view that default rates, which peaked at 4.3% in 2020, will fall to about 3.5%. Ares expects returns to be increasingly driven by security selection as the recovery proves uneven, warning of zombie credits in COVID-hit sectors.

pieces.title: Gemcast Episode 8: Staying Original
pieces.summary: Gemcorp Capital's Co-Founder and Head of Origination, Selim Basak, discusses deal sourcing in emerging markets, contrasting the challenges there with those in developed markets. The episode argues that a manager's network is central to sourcing deals, and Gemcorp states that it deliberately takes the time to work with and listen to its borrowers.

pieces.title: Venezuela: Focus on stability rather than regime change for now
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (portfolio manager Thomas Haugaard) argues that Washington's removal of Nicolás Maduro points toward stability and transactional engagement rather than rapid democratisation, with the Chavista system and figures such as Delcy Rodríguez remaining in place and Rodríguez likely leading a caretaker government for 12–18 months. The firm expects gradual, conditional sanctions relief, slow oil production recovery, near-term oil price softness and lower inflation, and limited geopolitical spillover, while advising investors to watch US-Venezuela negotiations on oil access and migration and to rely on diversification and discipline in emerging markets.

pieces.title: Private Markets Study 2026
Financing the AI buildout and its implications for credit markets
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that AI infrastructure spending is beginning to outrun the internal cash flow available to fund it, leaving an estimated USD 1.1 trillion external financing requirement for five major US technology companies (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle). It sees this as an expanding opportunity for credit investors, with computing infrastructure providers well placed to capture AI revenues, provided demand, pricing discipline and capital investment timing hold up, although the added borrowing will raise leverage. The firm favours senior unsecured hyperscaler bonds, data centre and AI chip-backed financing, and utility hybrids, while stressing that rigorous security selection is needed as financing structures grow more complex.

pieces.title: AI and Private Credit: Assessing Risk and Finding Opportunity
pieces.summary: HPS Investment Partners (BlackRock) argues that AI's credit impact varies widely by company, industry and business model, so investors should take a bottom-up approach rather than rely on broad themes. It sees software as likely to produce both winners and losers, with lenders increasingly prioritising cash flow to service debt and expecting the market to bifurcate into lower-risk borrowers that retain favourable terms and higher-risk ones facing tighter structures. HPS also flags legal services, business process outsourcing and B2B service providers as exposed to repeatable-task disruption, while describing AI infrastructure financing as supported by strong counterparties (hyperscalers and investment-grade borrowers) and contending that uncertainty itself creates opportunity, so discipline and diversification matter most.

pieces.title: Inside the Practice: HNW & Growth Strategies
Iberia
pieces.summary: PGIM's Madrid private credit team reviews its 2025 Iberian activity, which spanned investment-grade and below-investment-grade private placements, direct lending, and real assets, with notable sports financings for Spanish and Portuguese football clubs. Looking ahead, PGIM says it expects shelf facilities and direct lending to remain attractive to borrowers, sees further room for growth in real assets (particularly digital infrastructure and energy transition), and anticipates more hybrid structures with local banks, citing Spain's economic resilience as support for its portfolio.

pieces.title: Beyond the US – Diversification, valuation and dividend growth drive the case for international equities
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that international equities offer diversification, attractive valuations and higher income, with broad sector participation (technology, financials and energy) providing multiple sources of return rather than reliance on a single AI theme. The firm's Head of Global Equity Income, Ben Lofthouse, sees opportunity in banks benefiting from higher rates, in defensive sectors whose valuations have fallen, and in companies that can use AI to raise productivity, while noting that international indices have less exposure to AI-disrupted software and online services. It also flags risks from concentrated AI spending and geopolitical conflict, and stresses the importance of balance-sheet strength and diversification.

pieces.title: Active ETFs in Modern Portfolio Construction
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that active ETFs are becoming central to portfolio construction, citing their growth to roughly $2.0 trillion across 3,200+ funds and their share of 37% of year-to-date flows, alongside structural advantages such as daily transparency, low spreads and tax efficiency. It makes an explicit case for using active fixed income (ultra short, AAA CLOs, core-plus), and buffer ETFs as ways to put record money market cash to work and stay invested given stretched S&P 500 valuations (27.2x against a 19.5x average). The piece is promotional in intent, promoting PGIM's own funds (PULS, PAAA and its buffer suite) and a webinar, with its performance claims resting on selected Morningstar category comparisons.

pieces.title: House of Cards
October Economic Outlook and Key Themes
Global megatrends: the themes driving long-term equity performance - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that four structural megatrends (demographics, innovation, environment and geopolitics), which it says will drive markets and asset prices over the long term, offer investable opportunities across seven categories, including clean energy, digital transformation and healthcare innovation. It explicitly states that its global megatrends strategy selects quality companies with improving business momentum and attractive valuations, using a behavioural finance approach to exploit investor biases, and that it believes such quality companies tend to outperform over the long term. The piece is largely promotional, and its key claims rest on the firm's own belief rather than on evidence beyond a few cited forecasts.

pieces.title: Buffer ETFs Explained
pieces.summary: PGIM's short explainer argues that buffer ETFs let investors keep participation in market gains while limiting exposure to losses, and that they can help manage volatility within a portfolio. The piece is a promotional video page with little substantive detail: it makes no specific return or risk claims, and its only explicit recommendation is that buffer ETFs can be positioned within investor portfolios, with the mechanics left to the accompanying video. The surrounding text is mostly regional navigation and cookie and terms notices.

pieces.title: How Capital Solutions Looks Beyond Traditional Lending Parameters
pieces.summary: Barings argues that direct lending has converged towards syndicated loan and high-yield standards, leaving many sound companies outside its scope, and that capital solutions, with bespoke structures, can serve them. It contends that companies increasingly accept a modest premium over the lowest cost of capital for structures that better support long-term value creation. The piece is a Q&A with Michael Searles in Private Debt Investor, and the excerpt provided is truncated, so its fuller arguments are not visible here.

pieces.title: Inflation Defense: A Two-Pronged Approach
Investing in Europe’s defence: Why an ETF could make sense - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is rapidly rebuilding its military capacity amid geopolitical uncertainty and reduced confidence in US protection, creating a long-term structural growth opportunity. It cites EU defence spending rising to €343bn in 2024 and an expected €381bn in 2025, with defence investment growing faster still, and it argues that the spending will remain elevated, extending beyond traditional defence contractors into semiconductors, sensors, cyber and industrial technology. The firm's explicit view is that a diversified, passive ETF tracking a customised index such as the Bloomberg Europe Defense Select index could be an effective way for investors to capture this broad ecosystem and its multi-year trend.

pieces.title: Insight Investment
Target Net Zero Japan and US
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers (LOIM) announces two new strategies, TNZ US Equity (benchmarked to the MSCI USA, holding 300 to 350 companies) and TNZ Japan Equity (benchmarked to the MSCI Japan, holding 100 to 150 companies), expanding its TargetNetZero franchise, which now has over USD 6.8 billion in assets across 11 pooled funds on its fifth anniversary. LOIM argues that the transition to net zero will be driven by directing capital towards credibly transforming companies rather than by exclusions, and that its benchmark-aware, low-tracking-error portfolios, which it says keep temperature alignment below 2°C while materially reducing emissions relative to the benchmark, can serve as core allocations for investors.

pieces.summary: PGIM argues that grid capacity has become a material driver of development timing, capital expenditure and asset liquidity across European real estate, as electricity demand outpaces network investment and European permitting tim

pieces.title: Infrastructure private credit — a distinct and growing sleeve within private credit
US-Iran Update—The Map Is Expanding
pieces.summary: Franklin Templeton argues that the US-Iran confrontation has widened into a regional conflict involving Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz chokepoints, so markets must reassess assumptions formed when tensions seemed to be easing. It says this raises the case for diversification and flexible positioning rather than anchoring portfolios to a single outcome. It also notes that US Treasury yields have risen since the conflict began, with longer maturities up more, and that agency MBS now offer more attractive yields; it suggests yield-curve steepeners may merit renewed consideration where appropriate.

pieces.title: Infrastructure: Today’s “Generational” Investment Opportunity
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that infrastructure represents a $75+ trillion investment opportunity over the next decade, with investment need accelerating faster than available capital. The firm contends that structural shifts—deglobalization, ageing demographics and energy transition—have created an inflationary environment where long-lived physical assets with contracted revenues and inflation escalators offer both defensive and offensive return potential. Apollo positions itself as a major player in the space through its 35-year history and $150 billion in recent originations, emphasizing that infrastructure provides stable cash flows, inflation protection and low correlation to public markets as portfolio diversifiers.

pieces.title: Three Reasons to Stick with Growth Stocks in Rotating Markets
Global Slavery and Human Trafficking Statement and Report
Private Equity Returns to Its Roots
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that private equity must abandon the strategy of relying on cheap debt and multiple expansion that dominated 2010–2022, and return instead to fundamental value creation through disciplined acquisition, operational improvement and clear exit planning. The firm contends that structural changes in public markets—including index-driven crowding and the halving of publicly listed companies—make this operational focus essential for outperformance in a higher-rate environment. Apollo positions managers who can demonstrate genuine operational value creation, rather than those dependent on favourable financing conditions, as best placed to succeed in the coming decade.

pieces.title: Gold rush 2.0 | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that gold rose over 50% in 2025 and a further 15% in early 2026, driven by geopolitical uncertainty and eroding confidence in traditional safe-haven assets like government bonds as debt levels surge globally. The asset manager argues that despite media narratives of overcrowding, investor positioning in gold has actually declined year-on-year and remains modest among retail investors, suggesting room for further price appreciation. BlackRock contends that gold's low correlation with traditional assets makes it a useful portfolio diversifier and promotes its iShares gold ETFs as a convenient vehicle for exposure.

pieces.title: Private equity in the age of AI: Why manager selection matters
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that manager selection is becoming more important in private equity, as wide return dispersion and rapid AI-driven change raise the premium on disciplined underwriting and operational execution. It presents its Private Equity Group's small and middle-market focus, long-tenured team and bottom-up approach as the basis for value creation, citing its Medicus Healthcare Solutions investment as an example of AI being used to improve portfolio company operations. The piece explicitly contends that the question is no longer whether to invest in private equity but how to identify managers who can deliver resilient value creation and liquidity, and it sees AI-related "picks and shovels" businesses as a promising source of opportunity.

pieces.title: The wrong question about retirement
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that retirement planning asks the wrong question: rather than focusing on the size of a retiree's pot, it should focus on the sustainable income that pot can deliver, and it identifies three core retiree regrets (running out of money, dying with unspent wealth, and forced income cuts). The firm's explicit view is that a good retirement income solution should be lifetime, flexible and stable, that individuals cannot achieve this alone, and that institutional defined benefit techniques should be translated into retail products, such as a managed account in early retirement combined with later annuitisation. It concludes that the main obstacle is product development, slowed by regulation, distribution economics and investor behaviour rather than by a lack of tools.

pieces.title: What Should Investors Expect an Active Fixed Income Manager to Deliver?
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that active fixed income management can add value beyond the starting yield, which it says has restored bonds' income role, through security selection, maturity positioning, sector allocation and relative-value decisions. It organises alpha into structural, thematic and opportunistic layers, and says that its aim is excess return that is consistent, diversified and repeatable, grounded in valuation rather than a predetermined sector allocation. The piece explicitly highlights current opportunities in credit (dispersion across issuers and structures, amid AI-related investment), European sovereigns following French fiscal developments, and mortgages, while acknowledging that not every position will work.

pieces.title: China: The growing “news” and receding “olds”
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that China's growth is shifting from the "olds" (housing and exports) toward the "news" (AI), but the new drivers are too small yet to offset the old ones: AI's economy is about 0.8% of GDP in 2025, rising to roughly 1% in 2026, while housing remains weak and export contributions fade. The firm expects GDP growth to moderate to 4.5% in 2026, with fiscal support focused on investment and consumption, only a 10–20bp policy rate cut, and a possible 50bp RRR cut. Its explicit rates view is that China Government Bond yields will trade in a range in 2026, with investors advised to "use spikes in yield to receive."

pieces.title: Mid-Year Outlook for 2025: Make Your Own Luck
pieces.summary: KKR argues that despite geopolitical and economic turbulence in the first half of 2025, financial markets remain well-supported by easing monetary policy, productivity gains and favourable technical conditions, and therefore expect the cycle to extend further than consensus expects. The firm advocates tilting portfolios towards alternatives such as private equity control positions, senior credit tranches and real assets with inflation-linked contracts that offer operational leverage and protection against market dislocations. KKR also takes contrarian positions against consensus on several fronts, including expecting oil prices to decline to $60 per barrel, betting on US dollar weakness over Treasury yield rises, and predicting outperformance from European equities and private equity.

pieces.title: Beyond Capital: The Next Phase of Direct Lending
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that direct lending's next phase will be defined less by capital, which is now abundant, and more by access to opportunities, with origination networks, local presence, counterparty trust and active portfolio management separating winners from laggards. It contends that sponsored and non-sponsored deals can deliver comparable risk-return outcomes through structural discipline and downside protection, and that diversifying across both channels reduces thesis overlap only if underwriting standards hold consistently. The piece makes an explicit case that success will depend as much on avoiding losses as on capturing return.

pieces.title: Navigating a Changing Macro Landscape
Lipper award winners
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers (LOIM) reports that its Asia Value Bond and Swiss Franc Credit Bond (Foreign) strategies won five Lipper Fund Awards, with Asia Value Bond recognised for three- and 10-year performance in Bond Asia Pacific Hard Currency (its third consecutive 10-year award) and the Swiss Franc Credit Bond for three-, five- and 10-year results in Bond Global CHF. LOIM attributes these results to consistent, risk-adjusted performance and argues that Asia credit has emerged as a distinct growth market offering attractive value relative to global credit.

pieces.title: Portfolio Management Outlook: Staying Focused Amid Geopolitical Uncertainty
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments, in its Q2 2026 Fixed-Income Sector Views, holds its baseline US

pieces.title: High-Conviction Views: The return of pricing power
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that deglobalisation, higher structural inflation, and capital scarcity are restoring corporate pricing power, which will become increasingly important for investment returns. The firm contends that this inflationary regime change favours companies able to raise prices and resilient borrowers with strong cash flows, and that active fundamental analysis is essential to distinguish durable winners from temporary beneficiaries. The paper positions this view as part of a broader thesis on deglobalisation producing a more inflationary environment, following the firm's earlier call on short-duration bonds.

pieces.title: Cycle, Structure, Selection: Private Equity Portfolios for Today’s Market
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that private equity deal activity has rebounded in 2026 but remains challenging, with success now requiring deeper resources and value creation capabilities rather than relying on multiple expansion. The firm contends that the earnings multiple spread between private and public markets has widened to historic levels, positioning private equity for potential material outperformance if multiples normalise, whilst emphasising that sophisticated allocators should focus on vintage year risk rather than market timing.

pieces.title: Warsh at the Fed
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that Kevin Warsh, despite being seen as a political appointee, is acting as an independently minded central banker, with continuity on monetary policy amid a high growth, high inflation backdrop. Its first FOMC meeting as Chair brought a shorter policy statement, the removal of forward guidance, a plan to shrink the Fed balance sheet, and task forces reviewing key areas of Fed practice. Lombard Odier's explicit view is that it remains broadly risk-on, is overweight emerging market hard-currency corporate and sovereign bonds, and prefers European sovereign bonds to US Treasuries.

pieces.title: AI Hurtles Ahead
Top five trends in exchange-traded funds in Europe for 2026 - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Multi-Asset Investments Views: Don’t look back in anger - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's multi-asset team, led by Clément Dupire, argues that the Iran conflict resembles past geopolitical shocks: a brief sell-off followed by a near-complete recovery, with the equity rally driven by discretionary flows and systematic strategies. The firm says it remains significantly overweight global equities, having taken some profits and rotated from hard-hit markets (emerging markets, Japan and Europe) into US technology, and it keeps a long position in euro five-year German bonds on the view that ECB tightening is overpriced given fragile eurozone growth. It also holds a neutral stance on credit and a neutral position on US Treasuries, and expects oil to keep a residual risk premium until a definitive peace agreement with Iran is reached.

pieces.title: Non-Sponsor vs Sponsor-Backed: a Different Approach to Deal Selection
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that its private credit business deliberately favours non-sponsor-backed loans over sponsor deals, which are more crowded across managers, because the extra origination effort, due diligence and direct management relationships yield a more differentiated portfolio and a deeper view of business fundamentals. The piece, presented through Global Head of Origination Andy Frank, states that Fortress is actively increasing its share of non-sponsored transactions and advises investors to ask managers about their sponsor versus non-sponsored mix and the reasons behind it, since that mix shapes both the opportunities a manager sees and the risks it takes.

pieces.title: The new realities of investing
World Bank lifts global GDP forecast; US inflation holds steady - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Why CLOs stand out in today’s fixed income environment
pieces.summary: Fidelity Investments argues that collateralised loan obligation (CLO) tranches stand out in the current fixed income environment, citing floating-rate coupons that can cushion against interest-rate volatility, multiple layers of protection (seniority, diversification, and limits on lower-quality holdings) that it says have kept default and impairment rates historically low, and a decade of competitive returns versus similarly rated corporate credit. Fidelity cautions, however, that outcomes still depend heavily on manager skill, tranche selection, and an understanding of liquidity, credit-cycle and structural risks, and it promotes its own investment-grade fixed income, active ETF and asset allocation research offerings.

Connecting the Dots: A Holistic Approach for Insurers
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that insurers' asset management is entering an "insurance renaissance," driven by innovation in credit, equity and structured, securitised and private assets, and that holistic management across public and private markets is needed. It describes the firm's "dot plot" approach, which places risk estimates (defaults, rating migration, cash flow variability, liquidity and headline risk) across asset classes and sub-classes, combined with analysis of historical relationships and current spread pickups between asset classes. The piece's explicit view is that cash flow variability is becoming a growing risk insurers must get comfortable with, and that "connecting the dots" across public and private assets is the right way to manage insurance portfolios.

Chart to Watch: Growth stocks fell in Q1
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that defensive and value stocks outperformed large-cap growth in Q1 2026 amid geopolitical uncertainty, even though growth sectors saw upward earnings revisions while defensives saw downward ones. It reports that the Russell 1000 Value Index beat the Russell 1000 Growth Index by 11.8% year to date, a gap it attributes mainly to multiple contraction rather than earnings, and it calls this rotation overextended. The firm's explicit view is that this disconnect is an opportunity for patient, long-term investors to add exposure to secular growth companies, which it now sees as more attractively valued.

pieces.title: What is happening in private credit?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that media alarm about private credit outpaces the underlying data: isolated bankruptcies and fears of AI-driven disruption to software borrowers have unsettled investors, yet the default rate (about 2%, similar to high-yield bonds) and returns (still above public high yield) show no significant deterioration as of 4Q 2025. The firm cautions that semi-liquid funds, which hold roughly $250bn of the $2tn market, may gate redemptions, so private credit should be treated as a long-term allocation. Its explicit view is that private credit remains compelling versus public high yield for long-term investors without immediate liquidity needs, provided managers are selected with heightened diligence on sector-specific risks.

pieces.summary: Invesco argues that senior AAA CLOs may help insurers add floating-rate income, structural protection and diversification without materially increasing capital consumption, and that EU regulatory changes

Flash Macro: Tariff Update February 2026
pieces.summary: KKR reports that the Supreme Court's 6-3 decision overturning President Trump's IEEPA tariffs, combined with weaker-than-expected 4Q25 GDP growth of 1.4%, is consistent with its "Regime Change" framework of higher deficits and nominal growth. The firm slightly lowered its 2026 CPI forecast to 2.6 per cent (from 2.7 per cent) due to lower core goods inflation assumptions, whilst modestly upgrading its 2026 GDP forecast to 2.5 per cent (from 2.3 per cent) based on strength in tech capital expenditure and consumer services spending, maintaining its expectation of two additional Fed rate cuts in 2026.

pieces.title: How will energy companies react to higher oil prices?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that higher oil prices, driven by the war, are unlikely to spark a significant energy investment cycle, because companies are prioritising profits over production after years of uneven earnings. With refiners' crack spreads near $50/bbl (roughly triple the long-term average) and WTI

The Making of Strong Technology Partnerships
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that effective technology partnerships with wealth managers require rapid responses to market events, personalised analytical support tailored to specific client needs, and real-time education on best practices. The company contends that combining sophisticated platforms—such as its Aladdin Wealth offering with 3,000 risk factors—with expert human guidance and contextual insights enables wealth managers to serve clients more effectively during periods of market stress and uncertainty.

pieces.title: Three asset classes for European insurers to watch in 2026
pieces.summary: M&G Investments argues that 2026 conditions (steeper sovereign curves, near-record-tight credit spreads, persistent inflation uncertainty and elevated equity valuations) make broad allocations unattractive for European insurers, so value is more likely in targeted segments. It names three: STS ABS, for attractive spreads and favourable Solvency II treatment (with spread charges expected to fall from January 2027); flexible total return credit, such as M&G's own Total Return Credit strategy, to manage tight spreads; and defensive European direct lending in non-sponsored and senior mid-market segments, which M&G says offer better terms than competitive unitranche deals. The piece, which is promotional in tone, explicitly says these are "particularly attractive" for insurers in 2026 "in our opinion," and it adds a life-versus-P&C liability framing that favours long-dated private credit and IG credit for life insurers.

Quick View: Kevin Warsh’s nomination and the next era of U.S. monetary policy
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson's Daniel Siluk argues that Kevin Warsh's nomination as Fed chair marks a genuine shift in post-crisis monetary policy: a blend of hawkish instincts and willingness to rethink the Fed's tools, with a smaller balance sheet linked to lower policy rates, less forward guidance, and an AI-driven productivity narrative. Janus Henderson's explicit view is that markets should prepare for a Fed that is "simultaneously more unpredictable and more orthodox," with front-end yields having drifted lower on expectations of earlier cuts, longer-dated yields having risen (a bear steepening) as less balance-sheet support for term premiums is anticipated, and rate volatility likely to increase.

pieces.title: Diverse opportunities in equity markets - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that equity markets are becoming more dispersed across regions, sectors and companies, driven by AI, geopolitical fragmentation, fiscal expansion and divergent monetary policy, and that this favours active, conviction-led management. It flags AI-related volatility and valuation concerns in technology, while pointing to Europe (lower valuations and fiscal tailwinds), Japan and emerging markets (notably semiconductor and AI hardware supply chains) as areas that merit dedicated exposure. The firm also cautions that geopolitical second-order effects on commodities, supply chains and central bank policy could affect future returns, so investors should prioritise earnings quality, pricing power and balance sheet strength.

Its explicit calls are to favour BB-rated corporates, securitised credit, emerging market debt

pieces.title: Global Fixed Income’s Top 5 Investment Ideas for 2026: Mid-Year Outlook
pieces.summary: New York Life Investments, via its MacKay Shields Global Fixed Income team, argues in this mid-year 2026 update that bond yields remain attractive in real terms, so the year is better viewed as an income story than a capital gain trade, with duration, fiscal and idiosyncratic credit risks needing close attention in the second half. Its stated positions are a hawkish Fed and flatter curve, little margin for error in credit spreads, caution in CMBS conduits alongside opportunities in SASB, carry as the main driver in leveraged credit but with caution warranted, and emerging markets as a bright spot that is country-specific.

pieces.title: Tokenization of Money Market Funds
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that tokenised money market funds combine the liquidity and resilience of traditional MMFs with the speed, programmability and transparency of digital assets, and says they may offer benefits in portfolio management, settlement and collateral use. It highlights faster settlement via atomic delivery-versus-payment, smart-contract automation of processes such as dividend distribution and interest accrual, and improved collateral efficiency. The piece takes a clearly promotional stance, urging institutional investors to rethink cash management and explicitly encouraging readers to explore the full whitepaper.

pieces.title: deglobalization-and-the-rise-of-mexico-in-todays-supply-chain
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that U.S.-China decoupling is reshaping supply chains and that Mexico is the main beneficiary, citing its skilled labour, competitive wages, proximity to the U.S. and the renegotiated USMCA. It estimates that nearly a fifth of U.S. imports diverted from China have moved to Mexico, that nearshoring has already absorbed 52 million square feet of industrial space since 2019, and that it could add a further 50 to 65 million square feet over the next five years. The firm presents this as an early-stage structural shift, driven by rising Chinese production costs (Chinese GDP per capita now 118% of Mexico's) and supply-chain disruption, though the excerpt shown is cut off before its full conclusions.

Solving the Core Fixed-Income Conundrum
pieces.summary: Guggenheim Investments argues that the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index (Agg) has become misaligned with today's fixed-income opportunity set: it covers less than half of the $62.3 trillion U.S. fixed-income universe, is concentrated in Treasurys, and offers tight credit spreads that provide little cushion. The firm's explicit view is that investors should move beyond benchmark-constrained core strategies towards an active, diversified approach that combines management within the index with selective allocations to non-benchmark sectors such as structured credit, private lending and commercial mortgage loans, while avoiding simply swapping one concentration for another through an overweight to investment-grade corporates.

pieces.title: Investment Directions
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that while AI stocks face elevated volatility driven by leverage concerns and uncertain capital expenditure returns, the long-term opportunity remains compelling as the AI economy broadens beyond concentrated mega-cap stocks. The firm advocates for diversifying AI exposure through dividend-paying stocks and quality strategies, favours emerging markets (particularly Asia) over developed markets, and recommends supplementing traditional equity and bond allocations with alternatives to counteract rising correlation between asset classes as AI financing becomes increasingly important to fixed income markets.

pieces.title: Sovereign Bond Liquidity Dynamics on Aladdin®
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that sovereign bond markets, particularly UK gilts, experienced significant liquidity deterioration in autumn 2022, with bid-ask spreads and volatility nearly doubling despite recovery in trading volumes. The company demonstrates how its Aladdin platform can quantify the impact of these changes on portfolio liquidity, using a stress-test example showing that liquidating 25% of a gilt portfolio would cost 2.5 basis points over five days under stressed conditions versus 1.4 basis points previously. BlackRock implicitly advocates for institutional investors to use Aladdin's liquidity assessment and stress-testing tools to better understand their exposure to market liquidity shocks.

pieces.title: Castlelake Appoints Luke Jackson and Betsy Sylvester to Partnership Group
pieces.summary: Castlelake has promoted Luke Jackson, who leads its Residential Mortgage Finance investment activities, and Betsy Sylvester, who heads Client Management, to Partner. The firm presents the appointments as reflecting its commitment to long-term leadership, deeper client partnerships and expanding its asset-based investment capabilities, and says the partnership route is "a robust and rewarding way to ensure our firm's future."

pieces.title: Why longevity is the No.1 retirement planning challenge
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that longevity is the central retirement planning challenge and should be addressed well before retirement, since it affects nearly every decision, from how long income must last to how costs and care needs may evolve. It cites research linking greater wealth to longer life and highlights rising health care and long-term care costs, urging advisers and plan sponsors to use planning tools that model outcomes to age 95 or beyond and to integrate investing, Social Security, income and care decisions. Its explicit call is for planning for a longer life to preserve purchasing power and keep options open, rather than for any specific product or investment.

pieces.title: Tackling volatility with public debt money market funds - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that public debt constant net asset value (CNAV) money market funds, which invest at least 99.5% of assets in sovereign, supranational and agency securities, are an attractive option for investors seeking high quality, a stable net asset value and strong liquidity, with no exposure to financials or other corporates. The firm contends that the market has become viable because positive sovereign spreads now make these funds competitive with euro overnight rates, and it expects their performance gap with traditional money market funds to narrow as the ECB's balance sheet shrinks.

Chart to Watch: How well have AAA CLOs handled interest rate volatility?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson argues that markets have moved from the zero-rate era into a more volatile rate regime, with the Fed now expected to hike later in 2026, and that AAA-rated CLOs have held near par through this period because of their strong credit quality, low duration and floating-rate structure. The firm's explicit view is that investors should stay up in credit quality, limit interest rate risk, and add floating-rate CLOs to their fixed income allocation, which it considers essential for navigating the new regime.

pieces.title: Putting Private Credit Concerns in Perspective
pieces.summary: HPS Investment Partners (BlackRock) argues that recent high-profile defaults in private and liquid credit reflect heightened dispersion rather than broad-based stress, citing Cliffwater non-accrual data that sits below 10-year averages and Lincoln International data showing positive EBITDA growth for most borrower size cohorts. The firm's explicit view is that defaults are concentrated in the smallest borrowers (under $25 million EBITDA), which supports its position that experienced managers with scale investing in larger companies are best placed in challenging conditions. It also contends that private credit's growth has been measured, given that dry powder has compounded at a rate similar to private equity's, though from a much lower base.

pieces.title: A layman thinks about AI
View from the markets: A critical earnings season approaches - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, argues that Q3 earnings season is a critical test given sharp rises in bond yields and high expectations, with tech hardware expected to account for nearly two-thirds of global earnings growth and energy about 20%, leaving other sectors' median growth at a modest 7%, which makes the market vulnerable to any tech disappointment. The firm is nonetheless positive on the medium-term outlook, expecting AI investment to broaden into other sectors, notably in the US, and forecasting that non-tech earnings growth rises to 12% in 2027, which it sees as sufficient to support ongoing market appreciation, while expecting above-average, trending volatility in tech.

pieces.title: What does the situation in Iran mean for markets?
From AI to international markets: Finding opportunities where capital is scarce
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that while artificial intelligence remains an important investment theme, investors should diversify exposure beyond concentrated technology markets as earnings growth broadens across regions and sectors. The firm contends that international ex-US markets appear undervalued relative to opportunities presented by improving earnings and scarce capital, and recommends maintaining a diversified, long-term approach focused on earnings and profit cycles rather than responding to geopolitical noise.

Morgan Asset Management's chief global strategist expects the Federal Reserve to cut rates at its final meeting of the year, with futures pricing an 86% probability of a December cut, though the piece warns that the FOMC is divided and several members could dissent. It also reports that its 10-year equity forecasts have fallen across regions, because recent gains have made valuations less favour

pieces.title: Private Credit Outlook 2026: Growth and Maturity
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that private corporate credit enters 2026 from a position of strength, citing double-digit annualised earnings growth in its U.S. portfolio companies despite sticky inflation, a softening labour market and tariff uncertainty, and it contends that falling rates do not erode the asset class's premium over liquid credit, which it puts at 200 to 400 basis points through spreads, fees and call protection. The firm also presents the industry as mature and cycle-tested, with private credit now a mainstream asset class that has grown from filling the gap left by retreating banks after 2008, and it highlights a rise in individual investor participation through semi-liquid vehicles.

pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Global Property Equities Team reports that US REITs returned 18% year-to-date to 12 June 2026, roughly double the S&P 500, despite the 10-year Treasury yield rising from 3.9% to 4.7%, which it argues shows REITs are more than a simple rates trade. Citing deeply discounted starting valuations, record M&A activity, projected 6.3% earnings growth, low leverage (average loan-to-value around 30%) and low correlation with tech, the team concludes the backdrop for listed real estate is "more constructive than many appreciate" and that REITs offer recovery potential, income and diversification.

pieces.title: Senior Loan Talking Points
pieces.summary: Voya Investment Management reports that the U.S. leveraged loan market experienced modest price weakness in the week ending 8 October, with primary market issuance rebounding to $12.1 billion and investor demand remaining positive, particularly from CLO issuance. The asset manager notes that credit spread compression has stalled, with performance diverging between higher-rated and lower-rated segments, particularly weakness in CCC-rated loans. Voya observes that retail loan fund inflows have remained consistent over six consecutive weeks, totalling $1.38 billion.

The Credit Market Lens: A Higher Bar for Earnings Season
pieces.summary: PIMCO reports that analyst earnings expectations have risen sharply into Q2 earnings season: one-year EBITDA growth forecasts for USD investment grade non-financial issuers have quadrupled since January, from about 5% to over 20%, with margin expectations (24%) now above the 2015–2025 median of 21%. The firm argues that the AI hyperscalers (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle) are the key swing factor, since they account for about a third of IG capex and are expected to reach 54% of it by 2027, making their forward capex guidance the critical signal to watch. PIMCO also notes that high yield forecasts have risen from under 4% to over 14% with stable margins, a setup it describes as leaving "little room for disappointment," and it treats the earnings outlook as a test of whether this optimism is warranted.

Chart to Watch: AA and A rated CLOs have offered compelling risk-adjusted returns
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that A rated collateralised loan obligation (CLO) tranches have delivered compelling risk-adjusted returns, returning 5.9% a year over the five years to 31 December 2025, against 3.0% a year for a 75% 1-3 Year U.S. Credit / 25% U.S. High Yield portfolio of similar volatility. The firm's explicit view is that AAA CLOs suit investors prioritising low volatility, while AA and A tranches may appeal to those seeking more return with a slightly higher risk profile, and that BBB tranches are better suited to more aggressive investors. It attributes the low volatility of AA and A tranches to their minimal interest-rate risk, structural credit enhancement and strong credit ratings.

pieces.title: Private credit: Why fundamentals beat headlines
pieces.summary: Vanguard's Global Chief Economist, Joe Davis, argues in a short video clip that investors should look past private credit headlines and focus on fundamentals, noting that periods of stress and company failures also occur in public markets. Vanguard's explicit view is that investors should revisit the role private credit is meant to play in their portfolio and weigh expected net-of-fee returns against the risks, applying that discipline consistently rather than reacting to short-term news.

pieces.title: The Credit Market Lens: Sharpe Is Back in Emerging Markets
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that emerging market fixed income's risk-adjusted profile has meaningfully improved, with EM credit among the strongest fixed income performers over the past two years and outperforming a ratings-matched, duration-stripped USD high yield benchmark year-to-date. It contends that EM still merits a place in multi-asset portfolios, citing structural improvements such as deeper local rates markets and more credible central banks, but that as index-level valuations look less compelling, the next phase will be more selective, favouring issuer and curve dispersion. Explicitly, PIMCO prefers restrictive-policy markets such as South Africa and Mexico, where inflation appears nearer its peak, over accommodative Asian markets where inflation is still rising.

It cites a 15 basis point expense ratio, a 4.14% 30-day distribution yield (ahead of the passive ETF average but behind the active ETF and mutual fund averages), a fully investment-grade portfolio, and a 4-star overall Morningstar rating. The piece is marketing material aimed at financial professionals, and its central view, that PULS suits investors looking to upgrade cash management, is PGIM's own.

pieces.title: Transport: The rewiring of global trade
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management argues that supply chain diversification and geopolitical disruptions are increasing transportation requirements without necessarily raising trade volumes, because goods now travel longer routes through more dispersed networks. The firm contends that concurrent investment in AI, power and advanced manufacturing creates additional demand for transport infrastructure to build and operate new facilities. Brookfield identifies an opportunity for infrastructure investors to capture value from utilization of existing assets and capital deployment at attractive returns, particularly as industrial companies divest transport infrastructure to redeploy capital towards core operations.

pieces.title: Reviving "Guns & Butter"?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that current US fiscal policy—combining substantial tax cuts with increased defence spending—mirrors the 1960s "Guns & Butter" period and risks higher-than-expected inflation and budget deficits. The firm observes that investor positioning appears misaligned with historical precedent, noting that shorter-duration assets and cash outperformed during the original Guns & Butter era, yet investors currently remain underweight cash and indifferent towards small-cap value stocks. Janus Henderson suggests this environment may present investment opportunities in pro-inflation, shorter-duration assets.

pieces.title: Multi-Sector Credit Asset Allocation Perspectives: Defensive carry amid asymmetric risks
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the Middle East conflict has repriced markets, first through rates and more recently through credit spreads, with moves so far orderly but carrying escalation risk. Its explicit view is to favour high-quality securitised credit, particularly RMBS and ABS, for their short-duration carry, while staying cautious about adding corporate credit risk until greater clarity emerges. It also prioritises selectivity and security selection over macro calls or broad beta exposure.

Asia private credit opportunity
pieces.summary: Allianz Global Investors argues that Asia's private credit market, which it puts at USD 120 billion in AUM for 2024 (11–12% of global allocations), is supported by structural rather than cyclical demand, chiefly infrastructure, energy transition, digitalisation and essential services, and that persistent bank and capital markets funding gaps leave room for private lenders. It identifies concentrated opportunities in renewable-linked infrastructure, digital infrastructure, supply-chain resilience and domestic essential services, and stresses that long-term success depends on disciplined underwriting, conservative structures and regional expertise. The firm's explicit call is that the asset class can offer long-term investors access to resilient cash flows, provided they maintain a strong focus on risk management.

pieces.title: Beyond the headlines: Navigating today’s private credit landscape in Europe
How AI Drives Financial Advisor Growth Today
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that artificial intelligence enables financial advisors to enhance client relationships and grow assets under management by automating routine tasks like information gathering, allowing advisors to focus on high-value advisory work. The company contends that AI tools operating continuously can personalise services at scale, reduce client acquisition costs and convert business opportunities into AUM growth, whilst human advisors remain essential to relationship-building rather than being replaced.

pieces.title: Combining perspectives to navigate volatility - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that structural shifts (fragmentation of the global order, demographics, AI-driven innovation and climate) are adding volatility while creating investment opportunities, and that investors must look beyond traditional growth, inflation and policy data. It expects the world economy to prove resilient and inflation to ease, though not to return to the low-inflation regime of the last decade, with the US, Europe and China diverging in their paths. Its explicit stance is that the speed and regional pattern of inflation normalisation matter more than where it settles, and that flexibility and selectivity will be essential in a fragmented market.

pieces.title: Asset Based Finance Steps Into the Spotlight
pieces.summary: Barings argues that asset-based finance (ABF) is a broad, expansive market that can complement traditional private credit, though its boundaries are defined differently by different managers and investors. It distinguishes hard assets, such as equipment, digital infrastructure, aviation and mortg

pieces.title: Renewable energy in focus amid the energy shock - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Rethinking food: The shift from ultra-processed to health-conscious choices
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that rising GLP-1 drug use, scrutiny of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and mounting obesity costs (potentially 3–5% of global GDP by 2060) are pushing governments and food companies towards health-focused formulations, greater ingredient transparency and strategic change, with the UK's Healthy Food Standard and US MAHA-driven FDA reviews cited as evidence that policy has moved from debate to design. The authors explicitly call the current moment different from earlier cycles and say the shift is a systemic response that industry needs to act on, rather than a passing trend.

Smarter Hedge Fund Allocations
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that global macro hedge funds warrant increased portfolio allocation due to distinctive diversification properties often overlooked by traditional performance metrics. The firm identifies three key advantages: low correlation with other hedge fund strategies (particularly during drawdowns), positive skewness and near-zero excess kurtosis that offer defensive characteristics, and mean-reverting behaviour that typically produces positive returns following periods of losses. BlackRock contends that these attributes make macro funds valuable for constructing resilient, well-diversified hedge fund portfolios, especially in volatile macroeconomic environments.

How extreme is market concentration?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that market concentration in the S&P 500 is at an extreme level and poses a persistent portfolio risk, with the top ten stocks accounting for 40.8% of the index (above the 26.6% tech bubble peak) and trading at about 26x earnings, roughly 25% above their long-term average. The firm notes that these stocks also generate just over a third of index earnings, so their exposure is justified to a degree, but it contends that the biggest names are not reliably the best performers and that benchmark ownership, along with hidden overlap between growth and value funds, can leave portfolios over-concentrated. Its explicit call is that concentration requires regular review, rebalancing and active stock selection, supported by its new Top 10 Underlying Equities tool for identifying duplicated holdings across managers.

pieces.title: Fixed income balancing act
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' fixed income portfolio managers, Tom Ross and Tim Winstone, argue that higher government bond yields, driven by inflation concerns linked to the Strait of Hormuz disruption, have lifted corporate bond yields to attractive absolute levels, particularly in investment grade. However, credit spreads are near historical tights (high yield at the 5th percentile and investment grade at the 8th), so investors receive limited

pieces.title: Systematic Fixed Income: A New Approach to Bond Investing
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that systematic fixed income is a distinct, still early-stage way to seek active bond returns: a multi-factor quantitative model scores and ranks every bond in the benchmark, and its returns should differ from, and complement, traditional discretionary strategies that rely mainly on interest-rate, credit and sector bets. It presents the approach's success as depending on extensive clean data, dynamically weighted and wide-ranging factors, embedded liquidity analysis, and integration of quantitative experts within a broader fixed-income team, and it offers a checklist of questions for investors to put to prospective managers. The firm's explicit view is that systematic strategies using many dynamically weighted factors are "positioned to deliver better outcomes" than those using fewer factors and static weights, though the piece gives no performance evidence to support this claim.

pieces.title: Värde Partners Leads $1.7 Billion SRT Transaction with Klarna
pieces.summary: Värde Partners reports that a consortium it leads has agreed a three-year, $1.7 billion Significant Risk Transfer with Klarna, covering more than $40 billion of euro-denominated loans and freeing capital to support Klarna's growth. Värde's Global Head of Asset-Based Finance, Missy Dolski, presents the deal as evidence of the firm's commitment to structured capital solutions with leading financial institutions. The release is promotional in tone,

pieces.title: ETF transparency lets you know what you own
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that daily full-holdings disclosure gives ETF investors a clear advantage over mutual funds, which disclose holdings with a lag, aiding risk management and improving

pieces.title: Fed Holds Steady and Signals Longer-Term Easing Bias
pieces.summary: PIMCO reads the Fed's January hold (rates at 3.50–3.75% after 75bp of cuts over the prior three meetings) as a pause rather than a pivot. It argues that forward guidance signals eventual easing without urgency, and that the Fed will stay on hold until later in 2026, when cuts are likely to resume. PIMCO's case rests on disinflation drivers: AI-led productivity gains holding unit labour costs down, tariff price effects having largely run their course, and softer rental inflation, with core inflation still around 3% and gradual, measured easing expected unless growth weakens materially or inflation reaccelerates.

pieces.title: Quick View: What U.S. strikes in Iran mean for markets
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' Adam Hetts argues that the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, and Iran's regional retaliation, have so far pushed oil above US$70 but at levels consistent with a short-lived conflict rather than a sustained energy shock, with wider market effects depending on whether the uncertainty proves prolonged. The firm's explicit view is that a long-running escalation is not its base case, and it advises investors to stay diversified, keep high-quality safe-haven assets, avoid reacting to near-term headline volatility, and maintain exposure to long-term secular growth trends.
