pieces.summary: Insight Investment reports that US headline CPI was 2.4% year-on-year in February and core CPI 2.5%, with shelter contained, but warns that the Iran conflict has pushed US gasoline from about $3 to $3.60 a gallon since early March, which will likely lift energy inflation if oil prices persist. Its base case is that the Fed will "look through" the oil shock, as past energy shocks have had relatively contained effects on core inflation and activity, though it is watching for second-round effects or unanchored long-term expectations. It concludes that fixed income "contin

pieces.title: Boring remains beautiful
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that excessive speculation in financial markets—evidenced by surging options trading volumes—has created mispricing opportunities as investors chase momentum over fundamentals. The firm contends that stronger-than-expected US nominal economic growth will prevent the Federal Reserve from cutting interest rates as aggressively as markets anticipate, potentially forcing rate rises instead. On this basis, Janus Henderson favours "boring" dividend-paying equities, non-US stocks and higher-quality shorter-duration fixed income as more attractive investments than current market favourites such as technology stocks and high-yield bonds.

pieces.title: Why it’s time to look to the market for retirement savings
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that the 2025 Budget, which cuts the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 from April 2027 and raises tax on savings interest and dividends, makes it time for long-term savers to look beyond cash towards the stock market. It explicitly urges investors with a horizon of at least three years to consider UK equity income, citing the FTSE 100's 2025 rally, relatively low valuations and the roughly 6% yield on its own flagship, the Aberdeen Equity Income Trust (AEI), as support for that view.

pieces.title: The winds of change: China, technology and the energy transition
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that China is leading the energy transition by embracing change, driven by a strategic push in technology, the use of green finance and environmental credentials as soft power, and a manufacturing base that cuts costs in solar and wind. Aberdeen contends that investors who dismiss China on fossil fuel use and ESG shortcomings are overlooking its renewables strength, and that the US is the one "building walls". Its explicit call is to "look East", backing smaller Chinese "enablers" such as CATL and Zhejiang Shuanghuan Driveline, and it argues this search rewards on-the-ground research and direct engagement.

pieces.title: The 50/50 Portfolio: The next phase of asset allocation
Public and private credit: An introduction
pieces.summary: Natixis Investment Managers presents public and private credit as a broad, converging universe of financing, noting that public fixed-income markets exceed $145 trillion outstanding while private credit offers extra compensation for complexity and illiquidity. The piece argues that growing private credit, driven by corporate borrowers turning to nonbank lenders and the expansion of business development companies, is moving towards convergence with public debt markets. Its explicit view is that a blended approach across both markets can help investors maximise income and identify the best-value opportunities, with Loomis Sayles' Credit Research Team cited as the source of the comparisons.

pieces.title: France & Benelux: Year in Review & Outlook
pieces.summary: PGIM's Paris private credit team reports that its France and Benelux business closed 15 deals in 2025 despite a slower year for debt issuance, with activity accelerating from September and over half the region's deals closing in Q4. Across private placements, direct lending and real assets, it highlights refinancing-led issuance, sponsor-driven demand for flexible unitranche lending, and steady opportunities in renewables, digital infrastructure and water utilities. PGIM takes a "cautiously optimistic" view for 2026, expecting M&A to pick up as sponsors face pressure to divest and issuers accept market uncertainty as the new normal.

pieces.title: NAV Loans: From Fund Finance to Investment Opportunity
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that NAV loans, which are loans to a private equity fund secured against the value of its underlying investments, give managers flexibility to hold assets, fund add-on acquisitions, or generate liquidity across a fund's lifecycle. The firm's explicit view is that well-structured NAV loans offer strong risk-adjusted returns, citing low loan-to-value ratios and diversification, and that IG-rated (BBB) NAV loans yield around 350 basis points over IG corporate credit, making them attractive to insurers. It expects the NAV lending market to grow substantially over the next couple of years, driven by the scale of private equity assets under management and growing sponsor adoption.

pieces.title: Investing In Your Decade
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece, part of its "Investing In Your Decade" retirement series, argues that savers should start early, keep contributing through competing financial priorities, and step up saving in their 40s and 50s, using catch-up provisions where available. It explicitly frames time as the young investor's greatest advantage and urges staying invested, continuing workplace 401(k) contributions, and making full use of employer benefits. The page is largely a set of signposts to further articles on retirement education, savings milestones and envisioning future needs, rather than a detailed analysis.

pieces.title: Income Strategy Update: Managing Risk While Locking In Yield
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that fixed income offers compelling income, with starting yields providing a cushion even if inflation stays elevated and policy paths diverge. It recommends managing risk through an up-in-quality, up-in-liquidity bias, broad global diversification, and flexibility to act on dislocations. Specifically, PI

pieces.title: What does an oil shock mean for the dollar, gold and Bitcoin?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the Strait of Hormuz disruption, which has pushed WTI above $100 a barrel, has driven investors towards the dollar, gold and Bitcoin, but that their "safe haven" credentials are mixed. It sees the dollar's rally as partly a fear trade, gold's near-term path as choppy because rising yields raise its opportunity cost, and Bitcoin's recent rebound as fragile given its positive correlation with equities. The firm's explicit call is that, with the outlook for growth,

pieces.title: The Outlook for Autos
June 2020
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that macroeconomic policymakers have fundamentally transformed policy frameworks by directly injecting liquidity to households and businesses whilst blurring fiscal and monetary policy, a shift it argues was necessary but risks uncontrolled deficit spending and inflation without clear exit strategies. The firm calls for a Standing Emergency Financing Facility with explicit governance frameworks to manage the exit from this unprecedented policy coordination, warning that the longer such measures persist, the greater the risk of financial market distortions and de-anchored inflation expectations. BlackRock contends that this policy revolution, whilst essential to prevent financial crisis in the near term, is unlikely to fuel a sustained bull market for risk assets as the traditional post-2008 playbook no longer applies.

pieces.title: Asset Managers and Investors Queue Up for Solutions
pieces.summary: Barings presents portfolio finance as an increasingly important tool for investors and asset managers seeking more flexibility over liquidity and capital efficiency. In this Q&A, Matt Hansford argues that tailored solutions can help investors meet diverse risk and return objectives.

pieces.summary: PGIM Real Estate reports on recent agricultural sector developments, noting stable food price inflation, uncertain impacts from potential US tariffs, benefits from the One Big Beautiful Bill safety net funding, and labour shortages from deportation concerns. The firm implicitly argues that asset managers lacking farmland investment capacity may pursue acquisitions of agricultural investment managers, and positions itself as uniquely placed to serve institutional investors seeking farmland diversification.

pieces.title: How US Dollar Weakness Could Buoy Emerging Markets
Higher Rates Have Reset the Economics of Lending
pieces.summary: Apollo's Jim Vanek argues that the shift from near-zero to higher base rates has structurally reset credit economics, with 2022–2024 vintages offering better returns, lower leverage and more subordinated capital beneath the lender, whereas 2025 saw Apollo pass on much of its opportunity set as yield-seeking demand eroded those protections. Apollo's explicit view is that the cost of capital has now reset, creating a more attractive forward opportunity to lend at wider spreads with tighter documentation, and that it will invest most when returns are wide, documentation tight and leverage low, while demanding stronger structures in disruption-exposed sectors such as service-based companies. It also positions its funds as designed to perform in less stable markets rather than to outperform in the best conditions, which it presents as a key differentiator from peers.

pieces.title: private-credit-opportunities-in-asia-pacific
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that Asia Pacific has a sizeable private credit funding gap, as banks, which supply about 77% of regional credit, retrench under non-performing exposures, policy-directed lending, government-funded recapitalisations and tighter regulation, while demand grows with regional GDP, expected to reach 52% of global output by 2030. The firm's explicit view is that this dynamic favours alternative capital providers, particularly managers with local origination platforms, flexible capital and scale, who can earn superior economics (cash and accrual interest, fees, non-call premiums and equity upside) with strong covenants and collateral, often around 50% loan-to-value. It further contends that higher regional entry barriers limit competition and that Asia Pacific private credit offers low correlation with developed-market returns, though it notes diversification does not assure profit or protect against loss.

pieces.title: What Can Structured Finance Do for Your Portfolio?
pieces.summary: Loomis Sayles argues that securitised markets, at roughly $17 trillion, are important to global financing yet under-represented in client portfolios, and that the sector has matured and become more resilient in the nearly two decades since the Global Financial Crisis. The firm contends that securitised credit offers diversified fundamentals, low rate sensitivity and lower correlation with traditional corporate allocations, with attractive risk-adjusted yields relative to corporate bonds, while cautioning that the source of the additional yield must be properly understood. Its explicit view is that agency mortgage-backed securities offer a yield pickup over US Treasuries together with enhanced liquidity.

pieces.title: The Fortress Partnership Model: Reputation Matters
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group argues that a manager's reputation is best judged by whether investors and borrowers keep coming back, not by its own claims, and it cites its repeat borrowers in real estate credit as evidence of how it operates. The piece makes an explicit case for a "partnership-focused" lending model, in which Fortress stays involved with borrowers throughout a loan through regular contact, property monitoring and early problem-solving, which it says leads borrowers to bring it deals before they reach the market. Its co-CEOs, Drew McKnight and Jack Neumark, present this model as the kind of partner investors should want when allocating to private real estate credit.

pieces.title: 2026 Private Markets Outlook
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that private markets are expanding beyond institutional investors to retail wealth and retirement clients through more liquid fund structures, and that this shift is accompanied by evolving dynamics across asset classes: private credit is absorbing more lending activity, infrastructure offers generational opportunities driven by AI, energy transition and demographic change, and real estate is being reshaped by demand for residential, industrial and specialized properties. BlackRock's view is that private markets, when integrated into whole-portfolio strategies with attention to liquidity and diversification, can deliver higher returns with lower volatility than traditional allocations.

pieces.title: Oil-shock: US, Europe, Asia
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the Iran-driven oil and gas shock will hit the US, Europe and Asia differently, based on each region's energy-import and fossil-fuel dependency: strong US domestic production should insulate its industry, though inflation risks remain, while Europe's gas reliance and uneven inflation across the bloc raise price pressures. The firm views Asia's fossil-fuel imports as offset by diversified supply, and considers the region's structural growth drivers and abundant liquidity likely to sustain its long-term trajectory.

pieces.title: A Short Insight on Opportunities in Alternative Credit
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that Alternative Credit, particularly collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), offers relative value over similarly rated corporate fixed income, with downside protection from credit enhancement and robust covenants. Its central claim is that CLOs have largely avoided the year's defaults: Ares puts their exposure to defaulted loans at 13.3% (rising to 25% looking back), well below their roughly 59% share of outstanding corporate loans, which it attributes to credit strategy and investment criteria rather than luck, though it notes this varies across managers.

The piece emphasises PGIM's real estate platform capabilities across Asia Pacific markets but does not articulate a specific investment call or explicit market view.

Social Security’s 2026 Trustee Report: Context, Clarity and the Path Ahead
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report shows a materially worse long-term financing position, even though the combined OASDI depletion date is unchanged at 2034 and the OASI date has moved one quarter earlier to Q4 2032. The 75-year shortfall rose from 3.82% to 4.42% of taxable payroll, driven mainly by demographics and lower fertility and immigration assumptions, and the firm says that Congress will probably act to protect existing and near-retirees from large cuts, so clients should not claim early out of fear of reductions. It views Social Security as remaining a foundational part of retirement planning, while expecting that the program will evolve through revenue or benefit changes, and that the longer policymakers wait, the larger the eventual adjustments.

pieces.title: AI Boom or Credit Risk?
From accumulation to decumulation: Why participant education must evolve
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the retirement industry has successfully addressed savings accumulation but must now focus on helping participants manage decumulation, as many arrive at retirement with substantial balances but lack understanding of sustainable withdrawal strategies. The firm cites research showing that fewer than one-third of pre-retirees have a withdrawal strategy in place, and contends that retirement income education should begin years before retirement rather than shortly before it. Janus Henderson calls for plan sponsors to evolve participant education to include decumulation concepts such as withdrawal strategies, guaranteed income solutions and longevity risk management.

pieces.title: Leslie Mapondera Discusses Apollo’s $6.5 Billion Commitment to Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 and More on Bloomberg
pieces.summary: Apollo announces a $6.5 billion commitment to finance Ørsted's Hornsea 3 offshore wind project, the world's largest, which will supply electricity to over 3 million UK homes. Apollo positions this investment as part of its strategy to provide long-term, flexible capital for European energy infrastructure, framing the commitment as central to financing the "European Industrial Renaissance" and supporting UK energy security and net zero objectives.

pieces.title: Multi-sector fixed income: Bullish on spread carry
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (Global Head of Multi-Sector Credit John Lloyd) argues that multi-sector fixed income is well placed for continued strong performance in 2026, citing U.S. GDP growth of about 2%, inflation staying in a 2.6%–3.0% range, and markets pricing at least three Federal Reserve rate cuts by end-2026. The firm's explicit call is "bullish on credit spread carry": it sees current yields as an attractive entry point, with securitised sectors and real Treasury yields above 1.25% supporting the case, and it favours short-dated positioning to benefit from expected curve steepening.

pieces.title: Bloomberg Spotlights Barings’ Growth Ambitions
pieces.summary: Barings, marking its tenth year as a global alternatives manager, reports through a Bloomberg spotlight that it plans to grow by acquisition. Co-head of global investments Martin Horne states that Barings has no private equity business and argues that such businesses cannot be built organically, so they must be bought. The excerpt is truncated behind a paywall, so the wider detail of the interview is not available

pieces.title: Europe’s strategic autonomy: what we know and what is forecasted - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe's push for strategic autonomy, meaning reduced dependence on other countries across food, health, energy, industry, technology and defence, is a long-term structural theme creating attractive investment opportunities, with roughly €1.5 trillion expected to be deployed by 2035 through initiatives such as Readiness 2030, clean energy investment and the European Chips Act. The firm acknowledges uneven progress, including slow EU decision-making and coordination disputes over joint defence projects, but its explicit view is that Europe is moving in the right direction, though the pace may need to accelerate.

pieces.title: Insight Investment
Beyond Traditional Income: Exploring the Derivative Income Landscape
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors promotes a webcast on derivative income, arguing that higher yields, elevated volatility and shifting rate expectations are prompting investors to look beyond traditional income sources. It contends that option-based strategies may help generate income, manage uncertainty and complement core fixed income and equity holdings, while noting that the tradeoffs must be weighed. The piece is primarily promotional, presenting the approach as worth exploring rather than issuing a specific trade or allocation call, and it carries standard risk warnings on options and derivatives.

pieces.title: Material Matters: Digging into Commodities
View from the Markets: Not bear feeding time just yet - BNP Paribas Asset Management
Chart of the Month: October 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's October 2026 Chart of the Month argues that emerging market debt enters the final quarter of 2026 with a supportive backdrop: resilient growth (4.1% expected in 2026, rising to 4.3% in 2027), stabilising inflation, and fundamentals that are stronger than in 2022, including narrower fiscal deficits, lower debt and healthier current-account positions. It contends that EM central banks are more likely to calibrate policy than launch full hiking cycles, and that EM real yields remain significantly higher than in developed markets, which it characterises as facing greater policy uncertainty and heavier bond-supply pressure. The firm's explicit view is that this backdrop offers EMD investors attractive return prospects, relative value opportunities and a potential buffer against economic shocks.

pieces.title: The Investment Implications of Shrinking the Fed’s Balance Sheet
The case for floating rate credit
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that floating rate credit can offer "cash-plus" income with limited duration risk, citing yields that are high relative to prevailing cash deposit rates, lower return volatility than long-dated high yield, and healthy corporate balance sheets that help contain default risk, particularly in sub-investment grade issuers. The firm's explicit view is that there are "strong reasons to consider investing in floating rate credit," though the piece is brief and includes no quantified yield or default figures beyond a chart caption.

pieces.title: Small-Cap Stocks Are Stirring on Policy Shifts, Earnings Edge
Financial Advisor Trends Survey
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that financial advisors managing high-net-worth clients increasingly use model portfolios incorporating separately managed accounts, private markets and liquid alternatives, whilst noting a significant gap between demand for tax guidance (92% of advisors fielding such requests) and its integration into portfolio strategy (only 17% prioritising after-tax returns). The firm highlights that millennial advisors are driving growth by offering sophisticated services aligned with wealthy clients' needs, including concentrated stock strategies, direct indexing with tax overlays and private market access.

pieces.title: Blackstone - 2026 Investment Perspectives: Mid-Year Update
pieces.summary: Blackstone's mid-year 2026 update says its January themes remain intact, with AI as the "Main Thing" driving a multi-year capex cycle in data centres and power, and private markets well placed to fund the gap between surging demand and constrained supply. It argues the US economy is resilient despite repeated geopolitical and macro shocks, with growth solid, labour markets balanced, and inflation pressures near term but cooling over time, helped by falling rents and AI-led productivity gains. Blackstone explicitly frames recent volatility as an opportunity for investors to "lean in, not retreat," and cites its QTS data centre investment, whose leased capacity is 15 times larger than at acquisition, as evidence of its data advantage.

pieces.title: Private credit defaults 101: The fundamentals
Are stocks repeating last year’s rally?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Meera Pandit argues that 2026 is tracking 2025's pattern: markets shrugged off early AI-related anxieties and geopolitical shocks (the Iran war this year, tariffs last year), with the S&P 500 up 13% a month off its low, and that peak uncertainty is probably behind us. Stronger fundamentals than in 2025 are cited, notably 2026 S&P 500 earnings growth estimates of 18.7% against 14.9% at the start of the year, though the piece cautions that the rally's sustainability depends on sentiment swings and multiple contraction. It also notes that sector leadership has rotated sharply, with growth stocks now leading since the market bottom, while value has outperformed on breadth and semiconductors have surged.

pieces.title: What Are Investors Really Getting from Private Markets?
Recognize and catch the drift
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that advisors should actively monitor portfolio drift—the deviation of asset allocations from target benchmarks caused by market volatility—rather than relying solely on fixed rebalancing schedules, as significant market moves can quickly push portfolios off course from client goals. The company positions its Aladdin Wealth platform as a solution that alerts advisors to drift across their client base, enabling timely rebalancing, improved client communication, and potential revenue growth.

pieces.title: The People versus Inflation
Global Perspectives: Navigating AI transformation and rate uncertainty
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' podcast, hosted by Lara Castleton with portfolio managers Jeremiah Buckley and Greg Wilensky, argues that AI is broadening its influence across equity sectors through infrastructure spending and productivity gains, with earnings growth also spreading to areas such as commercial aerospace, travel and medical technology. On fixed income, the firm says absolute yields are attractive but recommends a cautious duration stance given uncertainty over the Federal

How Fortress Helps You Serve Sophisticated Clients
pieces.summary: Fortress Investment Group's Private Wealth Solutions arm presents itself as a long-term partner to RIAs and financial advisers, offering market insight, portfolio construction tools, education on private market concepts, due diligence materials and direct access to its investment teams. The piece explicitly argues that advisers need such support to add alternative investments to client portfolios, and that Fortress's teams, with over 20 years of experience through market cycles, help advisers serve sophisticated clients from a position of strength.

pieces.title: How to attract and retain high-net-worth clients ꟾ BlackRock
Private Assets in Portfolios: Reassessing the Strategic Case
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that recent scepticism toward private credit reflects a mismatch between investor liquidity expectations and the asset's underlying illiquidity, rather than an actual credit event, and that the wider private asset case should be reassessed against lacklustre public alternatives. It maintains a strategic low-return view for the asset class (though not a bearish one), expects defaults to rise, and concludes that private credit still offers an observable ex ante illiquidity premium and diversification value for institutional investors, with outcomes depending on underwriting, structuring and manager selection rather than on the asset class as a whole.

pieces.title: The evolving AI opportunity
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that the US-China contest for AI supremacy is creating investment opportunities across critical AI infrastructure (semiconductors, data centres, power and cloud), while the ultimate winners may be the countries and companies best able to turn AI breakthroughs into a functioning ecosystem for widespread adoption. The firm notes that the US leads on frontier models, chips and cloud, while China is closing the gap through cost-efficient open-source models and state-backed self-sufficiency, and it positions its own strategies (global convertible bonds, Asia equities, private infrastructure) as diversified exposure to AI build-out and adoption.

pieces.title: eli-appelbaum-feature
pieces.summary: Ares Management's Eli Appelbaum, speaking to Debt Business Magazine, describes the Alternative Credit strategy's focus on asset-based lending across the capital structure, citing its roughly $21 billion of assets under management and the Pathfinder fund's pledge to donate at least 10% of its carried interest to global health and education charities. He argues that the rate and inflation environment is driving capital-market dislocation and a likely rise in defaults, which Ares sees as an opportunity to act as a preferred counterparty for borrowers and to deploy capital in specialty finance, real estate and GP solutions. Ares also says it expects attractive returns across its funds' risk-return range, though the piece gives no return targets.

pieces.title: Measuring what matters: Impact reporting in listed equities - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Environmental Strategies Group has published the inaugural impact report for its Clean Energy Solutions strategy, its first listed equity strategy aligned with the Operating Principles for Impact Management. The firm argues that measurement matters but is not the whole story, and it calls for measuring what can be measured while acknowledging what cannot, without letting imperfect data become a reason for inaction. It also argues that listed equities, as the most widely used public-market impact instrument, can help close the gap between impact capital and the estimated $4 trillion a year needed for the SDGs, provided reporting standards for the asset class keep developing.

It identifies Independent Power Producers as early beneficiaries because data centres are driving up power demand and prices, and points to Bitcoin miners pivoting to AI, ne

pieces.title: The Cost of Liquidity
US small-cap equities: tailwinds set to drive performance - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that US small-cap stocks are in a genuine recovery, driven by an earnings rebound supported by Fed rate cuts, a resilient economy and the domestic revenue focus that insulates them from trade policy. It sees the persistent valuation discount to large caps, combined with improving fundamentals and the broadening of AI-related demand beyond mega-cap technology, as a compelling entry point, while stressing that selectivity is essential given the sector's breadth and the risks from AI disruption, Middle East-driven oil prices and a stalled rate-cut path.

pieces.title: Who bears the cost? The evolving economics of climate change
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that climate damage's economic impact is systematically underestimated because it erodes wealth and assets rather than directly reducing GDP, a flow measure that only captures rebuilding activity. The piece contends this accounting mismatch weakens government incentives to invest in climate mitigation, and advocates reframing climate economics at firm and sector levels rather than applying a single GDP reduction, whilst identifying industrial strategy alignment as key to addressing the challenge across regions.

pieces.title: Benchmark concentration and active portfolios
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that rising equity benchmark concentration reduces diversification and increases volatility for passive investors, and reports that active managers can mitigate this concentration risk through partial long-short strategies (130/30 portfolios) or portable alpha approaches. The firm contends that long-only investors who cannot adopt these strategies should reduce active risk levels to maintain consistent risk-adjusted returns as concentration increases.

pieces.title: More US Stocks Are Marching to a Different Beat
What Will Shape the Next Phase of Emerging-Market Equities?
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein, in an interview with portfolio manager Sammy Suzuki, argues that emerging-market equities are likely to keep outperforming developed markets, driven mainly by an expected continued weakening of the US dollar, which the firm expects to support EM for five to 10 years. It points to AI-linked opportunities in Asian component makers and energy-value-chain firms, to selective Chinese growth companies and governance-reformed state-owned enterprises, and to cheap valuations after a decade of weak returns. The firm explicitly advises against concentrating in a handful of large stocks given AI-bubble risk, and it presents the current moment as a favourable entry point for EM equity investors.

pieces.title: 2026 in Numbers!🎆
JH Explorer in Kenya: Into a lighter patch of trees, not out of the forest
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors' emerging markets debt team, led by portfolio manager Sorin Pirău, reports that Kenya's external position has clearly strengthened, with FX reserves up to US$12.5 billion and successful liability management, but that fiscal weakness remains the binding constraint on the credit story. The firm points to an elusive IMF re-engagement, a 2026 deficit estimate of 6% of GDP against a 4.7% target, and growing use of securitisations and PPP-style structures that the IMF and World Bank view as public debt. Its explicit call is that investors should look through near-term macro gains and anchor their views on evidence of durable structural reform, particularly on revenue, spending discipline and institutional follow-through.

pieces.title: A New Dawn for Non-US Stocks? Rethinking Global Equity Allocations
Northeast
pieces.summary: PGIM's New York office reviews 2025 in the Northeast as a year of slow activity after April's tariff announcements, followed by a stronger pipeline from September, with private placements skewed to existing issuers, Shelf Facilities supporting M&A, and direct lending dominated by sponsored repricings and refinancings. For 2026, PGIM says it is "optimistic" about opportunities, citing significant maturities from 2021–2022 deals that need refinancing, but flags macro risks and expects borrowers to adjust to structurally higher rates than in the pre-COVID era.

pieces.title: Modern Financial Markets Need Pressure Valves
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that post-2008 financial regulations have made the system safer but shifted risk from solvency to liquidity stress, whereby solvent institutions struggle to access cash quickly when margin demands surge synchronously across markets. The firm contends that traditional shock absorbers—banks—are now constrained by regulation and unable to supply liquidity when demand peaks, creating a dangerous mismatch. BlackRock proposes "pressure valves": targeted reforms to improve collateral mobility, strengthen repo markets, and upgrade infrastructure to ensure liquidity flows smoothly during stress without rolling back post-crisis safeguards.

pieces.title: Déjà vu: Parallels between the dotcom era and the AI surge - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that today's AI surge shares several features with the 1996–2000 dotcom bubble, notably high S&P 500 valuations near pre-2000 levels, though it notes that today's leaders are profitable, unlike many dotcom-era firms, and that the macro backdrop (higher inflation, a larger fiscal deficit) is arguably weaker. Its explicit view is that valuation discipline matters for managing risk: it says investors should be cautious at extreme valuation highs, and that historically value stocks (low P/E) outperformed after the 2000 crash, so a selective, valuation-focused approach looks prudent.

pieces.title: Rated by Kepler
pieces.summary: Aberdeen publishes a 46-minute webinar video, part of Kepler's 2026 "Rated by Kepler" series, in which Lead Manager Gabriel Sacks presents Aberdeen Asia Focus, a trust investing in high-quality smaller companies across Asia-Pacific, and discusses themes including AI supply chains, domestic consumption, the energy transition, Vietnam and India. The piece makes no explicit investment call of its own; its main claim, attributed to Sacks and Aberdeen, is that Asian smaller companies merit investor attention, and the trust's Kepler rating is presented as the reason for the featured appearance.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that human health is inseparable from animal and environmental health, and that the One Health framing, assessed through its geopolitics, innovation, demographics and environment megatrends, helps long-term investors spot health-related earnings, sovereign credit and labour-market risks the market may be underpricing. It explicitly cautions against treating every social or environmental issue as a health issue, urging instead that analysis identify where health determinants are financially material and through which channels. The firm's stated view is that a disciplined One Health approach should sharpen rather than dilute investment analysis.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that the dollar's decline is orderly rather than extreme, and that it has been damaging for unhedged non-US investors in US assets, with US stocks and bonds trailing European assets by 2%-3% in euro terms. It sees short-term dollar momentum as negative but notes the dollar is only 7.4% below its decade peak, while strong US earnings growth (19% in the fourth-quarter season so far) supports equities and may make a weaker dollar and lower valuations worth considering over time. The firm also judges Japanese government bonds to be cheap, with a 10-year yield of 2.25%-2.75% possibly representing fundamental equilibrium, though it flags Bank of Japan intervention as a risk to bearish yen positions.

The firm states that it "believes strongly that a diverse workforce is the key to better decision-

Treasury moves to accelerate Trump Account creation
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that the US Treasury has replaced opt-in Trump Account establishment with automatic account creation effective October 2026, estimated to create accounts for over 60 million children. The asset manager emphasises that automatic account creation does not equal automatic funding, as the $1,000 federal pilot contribution and family or employer contributions still require separate affirmative elections. J.P. Morgan Asset Management highlights that the removal of family action requirements for qualified general contributions from governments and charitable organisations may be the most significant practical benefit of the new structure.

pieces.title: The expanding role of investment grade private credit in institutional portfolios
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management reports that US investment grade private credit issuance has surged to record levels, driven by life insurers reallocating from public bonds to higher-yielding private placements, and argues this represents a constructive entry point for institutional investors given elevated yields without requiring downgrade risk and broadening borrower demand across sectors. The firm contends that the asset class offers institutional investors a middle ground between public bonds and private loans, combining standardised underwriting with negotiated protections, though emphasises the importance of manager selection, liquidity considerations, and appropriate portfolio sizing.

Innovating with liquid alternative and buffer ETFs - Australia Institutional
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that long-only investors overly dependent on equities and bonds should consider diversifying into alternative risk premia, which are long/short, systematic return sources driven by behaviour and market structure rather than traditional market beta. The piece introduces its four ETF strategies, grouped into absolute return funds (such as a managed futures and a global equity long/short fund) and defined-outcome, or buffer, ETFs, which seek to limit losses while capping gains over a set period. It presents both as potential sources of diversification and risk management, while noting their drawbacks, without making any explicit recommendation to buy.

pieces.title: How Private and Public Markets Are Combining to Fund the AI Buildout
Europe’s strategic buildout
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that Europe faces converging pressures—geopolitical fragmentation, AI infrastructure demands and energy constraints—requiring strategic investment in security, energy and technology, with the Netherlands illustrating both Europe's technological strengths and physical bottlenecks. The firm calls for more European savings to flow into equity and growth financing to expand capacity, and identifies near-term investment opportunities in defence technology, cyber, grids and infrastructure, whilst longer-term opportunities in semiconductors and advanced manufacturing depend on successful policy reform.

pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's 2027 macro outlook argues that the eurozone enters 2027 with renewed industrial momentum, led by Germany's fiscal-driven recovery, though French and other elections pose political risk. It expects US growth to exceed 2% for a fifth consecutive year, with inflation easing toward roughly 2.5% and the Federal Reserve on hold, while China's recovery fades into 2027 despite stimulus. The firm explicitly rejects consensus expectations of a consumption-led pivot in China, forecasting growth of barely above 3% on its in-house measure, and sees limited scope for broad synchronised emerging-market rate cuts.

Who benefits as open models make AI cheaper to run?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that rising enterprise adoption of lower-cost open AI models could expand overall AI usage, lifting demand for infrastructure across compute, networking, storage and memory, while hyperscalers can gain as gatekeepers hosting and routing workloads across models. The firm holds that AI labs face limited pricing pressure, since closed frontier models still generate most token revenue, and that the model layer will not commoditise or become winner-takes-all, with sophisticated workflows staying with frontier models and basic tasks moving to open ones. Its stated view is that open and closed models will both play a key role, and investors should monitor how the mix between them shifts and where value is created across the ecosystem.

Emerging Markets: Beyond the Benchmark
pieces.summary: PGIM's series "Emerging Markets: Beyond the Benchmark" argues that emerging markets should be viewed as a broader, more differentiated and more resilient opportunity set than benchmark-based or cyclical framing suggests, opening with the observation that the U.S. could soon spend as much of its budget on debt servicing as a median high-yield emerging market country. PGIM frames the series as a guide to a multipolar world, covering supply chains, debt, equities, private markets, sustainability and portfolio construction, with outcomes depending more on active discernment and informed allocation across segments than on broad exposure. A linked piece on quantitative equity research asks whether alpha in a dispersed EM landscape comes from country or stock selection, though the excerpt provided does not state its answer.

pieces.title: Global Credit Outlook
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that credit markets face heightened dispersion across managers and assets rather than systemic disruption in early 2026, with macroeconomic headwinds receding and growth returning to trend pace. The firm maintains that liquid credit valuations remain tight but offers compelling income yields, while private credit's structural growth drivers persist despite widening performance gaps between managers and vintages. BlackRock identifies sharp global growth downturns and corporate profit margin deterioration as principal risks to this outlook.

pieces.title: Four Reasons to Blend REITs and Private Real Estate
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that REITs and private real estate are not competing asset classes but two access points to the same market, and that investors should blend them, with a strategic allocation of roughly 30% REITs and 70% private real estate, which it says is market-representative and optimises risk-adjusted returns. The piece sets out four supporting reasons: REITs give access to alternative sectors such as data centres, towers and healthcare; higher return dispersion rewards active management; a blended portfolio, rebalanced annually, lowers volatility and reduces drawdown severity; and listed holdings provide liquidity that private assets cannot. PGIM explicitly advises that investment policy should evaluate public and private real estate jointly rather than in isolation.

pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that the UK Budget gave the government "breathing space" rather than markets a major shift: fiscal headroom of £15 billion matters less to markets than the near-term deficit path, and the plan has slipped as borrowing was revised higher, with further slippage likely before the Spending Review. It sees the gilt yield level as driven mainly by Bank of England policy (markets pricing four to five more hikes), which it considers an overpricing of tightening, and PIMCO explicitly says it continues to find gilts attractive as part of a diversified global fixed income portfolio.

GLAF at 3: Smarter diversification
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that its Global Liquid Alternatives Fund has outperformed global bonds since launch in September 2023 by combining multiple hedge fund strategies, arguing that recent market dispersion has created favourable conditions for such diversified approaches. The firm contends that investor demand for hedge funds has shifted away from the post-financial crisis preference for simple strategies towards funds offering genuine daily liquidity, consistent performance and reliable redemption terms. BlackRock argues against attempting to time individual hedge fund styles and instead advocates for balanced multi-strategy exposure to navigate varied market environments.

pieces.title: Stable income from backbone assets: An institutional investor’s introduction to infrastructure debt
Unlocking Value Through Sustainability and Innovation
pieces.summary: KKR argues that sustainability integrated into core business strategy—rather than treated as a separate initiative—can strengthen financial performance by mitigating risk, enhancing resilience and efficiency, and enabling sustained growth. The firm illustrates this thesis through three portfolio company examples: ContourGlobal's decarbonisation strategy reducing fuel-price volatility and opening access to sustainable finance; Charter Next Generation's circular economy approach improving competitive positioning; and Potter Global Technologies' investment in employees driving business results. KKR implicitly calls for asset managers and portfolio companies to embed sustainability into capital allocation and operational priorities as a value-creation lever.

pieces.title: Two bond markets at once
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (Jenna Barnard, Head of Global Bonds) argues that bond markets are splitting in two: short-dated bonds remain tied to near-term monetary policy, while bonds maturing in 10 years or more have decoupled from policy rates and stayed range-bound despite rate cuts, including the first US 10-year Treasury yield failure to fall during an easing cycle since the 1960s. The piece attributes this to structural forces, namely heavy government borrowing, reduced buying from price-insensitive investors such as central banks, lingering inflation concerns, and the shift of traditionally low-yielding anchors Japan and Germany towards higher yields. Janus Henderson's explicit view is that this two-market dynamic is set to continue into 2026, as structurally higher bond supply and weaker demand make the long end less responsive to policy.

Engineering the Future of Fixed Income
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein uses the story of Brunelleschi's dome in Florence to argue that investment problems, like engineering ones, have interlocking constraints that must be solved together rather than by optimising for the most obvious one. It presents its systematic fixed-income approach as that kind of integrated "engine": over 300 predictive factors, combined with research, dynamic models, portfolio construction and management of risk, liquidity, trading costs and execution, to deliver repeatable alpha. The piece's explicit view is that this engineered, systems-based approach is what can expand what is achievable in fixed income.

pieces.title: Net zero emerging markets
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that emerging markets are central to limiting global warming, since rising emissions are increasingly driven by China, India and other developing economies, and that decarbonisation should be treated as an economy-wide transformation rather than a narrow clean-tech theme. It acknowledges that EM climate ambition is currently weaker than in developed markets (22% of the MSCI EM Index has an SBTi target versus 56% of MSCI World, with an implied temperature rise of 3.0°C against 2.4°C), but it contends that many EM economies are leapfrogging legacy infrastructure with scalable low-carbon solutions. The firm's explicit call is to invest in EM equities through its TargetNetZero EM strategy, which targets an implied temperature rise of 2.5°C or below and favours engaging with transition leaders over exclusion.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that resilient, above-trend global growth and easing inflation set up a divergence in central bank policy for 2026, which it expects to create cross-market volatility and relative value opportunities in government bonds. Its explicit positioning is to stay constructive on duration, favouring the five- to 10-year sectors, keep a steepener bias in the eurozone, and prefer UK duration (where it is most constructive, expecting gradual BoE cuts) over Japan, where it is cautious given likely BoJ tightening and fiscal and supply risks. It also favours Spain and Italy over Germany and France within European spreads.

Emerging Markets: Pillars of Opportunity and Potential
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that emerging market equities, after years of lagging developed markets, are undervalued and offer a compelling entry point for 2026, resting on three pillars: a supportive macro backdrop (a weakening dollar and easing monetary policy), historically wide valuation discounts relative to developed markets, and corporate governance and policy reforms that are beginning to convert EM GDP growth into earnings. The firm also makes the case for active quantitative management in EM, citing higher stock return dispersion and stronger long-run factor returns (such as Value, Momentum and Earnings Revisions) relative to developed markets, and suggests passive index exposure may leave return unclaimed and add unrewarded risk. The piece is truncated before its final points, so its full set of arguments is not visible here.

pieces.title: Could rising AI debt derail the investment boom?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that rising debt financing poses real risks to the AI infrastructure buildout, particularly for leveraged "neocloud" providers such as CoreWeave, whose credit spreads have widened sharply, while the hyperscalers' strong balance sheets and robust demand for compute leave the broader investment cycle intact. The firm's explicit view is that the expanding market for AI compute still supports the wider buildout, though profitability will be harder for individual operators, and it names weakening utilisation, pricing or customer commitments as the key warning signs to watch.

Constrained Supply, Durable Demand: The Case for Investing in Manufactured Housing Communities
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that manufactured housing communities represent an attractive investment opportunity due to constrained supply of manufactured homes and persistent demand for affordable housing in the United States. The asset manager contends that these properties generate stable, recession-resistant cash flows with low capital expenditure requirements, positioning them to deliver strong net operating income growth. PGIM suggests that institutional investors should increase their allocation to this sector to enhance their real estate portfolio risk-return profiles.

pieces.title: Emerging market income equity: can MediaTek turn innovation into income?
pieces.summary: Aberdeen argues that MediaTek, a Taiwan-based chip designer that has grown from a mobile-chip challenger into a global leader, can combine AI and automotive growth exposure with resilient dividends, citing its rising share in higher-end smartphone chipsets, strong R&D, capital-light model, low debt and high cash conversion. The firm explicitly presents MediaTek as an important contributor to an emerging markets equity income strategy, though it notes the company is illustrative only and not a investment recommendation.

Mexico Regional Spotlight
pieces.summary: PGIM argues that Mexico's industrial real estate market represents a relative outperformer despite near-term policy headwinds, citing strong fundamentals including tight supply, low vacancy and projected annual rental growth of 5%—favourably comparing to the United States. The firm maintains conviction in Mexico's long-term investment case based on integrated North American supply chains, available skilled labour and proximity to the U.S. market, forecasting elevated returns driven by rent growth and yields around 7%.

pieces.title: Bridging the technology gap: How Europe is building its digital infrastructure - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that Europe is investing in AI, semiconductors and cloud computing to reduce reliance on external powers and strengthen its digital infrastructure, citing the European Technological Sovereignty Package, the Chips Act 2.0 and the Critical Raw Materials Act as a stable, long-term policy framework. It presents this structural shift as creating significant long-term investment opportunities across technology, energy, defence and raw materials, though it stops short of recommending specific investments.

pieces.title: Hedge Funds Quarterly Outlook Q4 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Q4 2026 hedge fund outlook reports that Q3 2026 produced sharply divergent results: quantitative strategies led on the back of high single-stock dispersion, while equity long/short struggled after reversals in AI-linked hardware, memory and momentum names, with activism in Japan a bright spot. The firm argues that higher cash rates and a higher cost of capital enhance hedge fund opportunities, and names relative value and opportunistic/macro as its highest-conviction areas for Q4, with selective equity exposure to activism and corporate change. It concludes that manager selection, portfolio construction and adaptability to shifting regimes will be critical through year-end.

pieces.title: Waiting for the clouds to part
pieces.summary: Aberdeen's Asia Focus manager Gabriel Sacks argues that long-term investors should stay calm through the current market turbulence caused by the Middle East conflict, which has hit Asian markets hard, and wait for conditions to improve. He points to three reasons for measured optimism: small companies, particularly domestic emerging-market firms, can be less exposed to the global backdrop; specialist, on-the-ground research can still uncover opportunities among under-followed smaller companies; and the case for China is strengthening, given its 4.5-5% growth target for 2026 and its relative resilience amid the conflict. The explicit call is to stay composed and keep a close watch for silver linings rather than react to short-term headlines.

pieces.title: Gulf Coast
pieces.summary: PGIM's Dallas office reviews its 2025 Gulf Coast private credit activity, reporting that 85% of originations were direct, relationship-based loans, with private placements driven entirely by shelf facilities and sponsor-led LBO activity described as soft. The piece attributes stronger regional demand to data centre and digital infrastructure buildout, and states that PGIM expects positive borrower sentiment in 2026, supported by reduced tariff uncertainty and attractive long-term rates and spreads that may encourage further shelf activity and issuance.

The firm forecasts improved returns in 2025 driven by rising rents and falling borrowing costs, with a shift toward income and rental growth rather than yield compression as the primary return driver.

pieces.title: The Role of Credit Secondaries in BDC Market Volatility
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues that BDCs, now about $560bn of AUM and roughly 30% of the $1.9trn private credit market, face volatility in Q4 2025 and H1 2026 from private credit sentiment, valuation scrutiny, AI disruption risk among software borrowers and high-profile restructurings, which has produced net outflows at non-traded perpetual BDCs. Ares contends that managers are increasingly using secondary sales, continuation vehicles and structured solutions to manage liquidity and portfolio construction, and that the resulting dislocation, which it views as affecting strong portfolios indiscriminately, creates attractive entry points for experienced credit secondaries investors. pieces.summary: PGIM argues that U.S. farmland represents an attractive investment for institutional portfolios, citing strong historical performance, diversification benefits, and structural advantages including superior infrastructure and geography. The firm identifies tailwinds including technological advancement, rising global demand, and growing institutional capital deployment in the sector. PGIM implicitly advocates for increased institutional allocation to agricultural assets, though the piece does not explicitly state a specific allocation recommendation.

pieces.title: Megatrends through a sustainability lens: the forces shaping responsible investment - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that four megatrends (environmental change, geopolitical fragmentation, technological innovation and demographic shifts) are reshaping long-term value and risk, and that a sustainability lens helps investors navigate them. It presents responsible investing not as a standalone theme but as the connecting thread between these forces, cautioning that analysing any one in isolation risks missing the bigger picture. The firm is explicit that innovation's promised sustainability gains are not guaranteed and require sound governance and risk management, and it cites IEA and press data on AI-driven power demand to illustrate that energy intensity is now a genuine investor issue.

pieces.title: Merger Arbitrage: Riding the Wave Into 2026
EU Securitisation Political Agreement: A Better Framework, But Not Yet a Market Reset
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece welcomes the provisional EU political agreement on the Securitisation Regulation as a better framework that should lift EU issuance and modestly widen investor access to global securitised markets, but it argues this falls short of the market reset needed. It highlights the removal of the strict ESMA template requirement for non-EU issuers, the rise in the UCITS single-deal limit from 10% to 25%, a more proportionate investor sanctions regime, a targeted cut of at least 35% in reporting fields, and lower bank capital requirements on STS senior positions. PGIM's explicit view is that key details remain subject to technical work and that the EU framework remains significantly stricter than other global jurisdictions, so meaningful relief will depend on the forthcoming Level 2 standards.

pieces.title: The next AI bottleneck: Power, permits and public support
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the AI infrastructure buildout is constrained less by capital and chips than by power access, water, permitting, regulation and community support, and that responsible development is therefore part of the investment case rather than separate from it. The piece notes that headline capacity figures overstate what will come online, citing over 120 US projects worth about $200 billion reportedly blocked or delayed in the first half of 2026, and that more than 300 state and local bans have been passed since 2023. Its explicit view is that social licence is becoming "hard project infrastructure", that companies with credible resource strategies, strong balance sheets and established community relationships may be better positioned, and that a diversified, phased energy portfolio is likely to prove more practical than any single power source.

pieces.title: The Long Game
pieces.summary: Ares Management argues, through CEO Mike Arougheti, that baseball's long 162-game season and institutional investing both reward sustained, collective resilience over flashes of brilliance, with teamwork proven during slumps and downturns rather than in moments of triumph. The firm's explicit view is that success in both fields rests on repeated collaboration and shared goals, which it frames as its "In Teamwork We Trust" theme. The piece makes no specific investment call; its disclaimer warns readers not to rely on its opinions or forward-looking statements.

pieces.title: Opportunities beyond Swiss bonds:
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that Swiss investors, facing some of the lowest bond yields in global fixed income, should look beyond the domestic market and consider a globally diversified, actively managed investment-grade credit strategy hedged back into Swiss francs. The paper contends that this approach keeps Swiss-franc stability while widening the investment universe, improving diversification and income potential, and reducing reliance on a concentrated home market. It also argues that past home-bias returns may not persist, and points to AI infrastructure financing, power networks, data centres and European securitisation reform as opportunities largely absent from Swiss bond indices.

pieces.title: The Instruments Of Change: empowering scalability & growth
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that investment managers must use technology as the primary instrument to achieve scalable growth and navigate market uncertainty, emphasising that fragmented legacy systems are inefficient and costly to end investors. The company positions its Aladdin platform—an open-architecture system supporting the full investment process through integrations with ecosystem partners—as the solution, and calls on industry leaders to adopt a common data language and consolidated platforms to drive profitable, coordinated growth across asset management.

Morgan Asset Management argues that Middle East military action will cause a temporary oil-price shock whose inflationary and growth effects persist for several quarters, and that the Federal Reserve's next move is likely to be a single, delayed rate cut rather than several. It concludes that U.S. money market funds should keep attracting inflows, since outflows are driven by severely negative real rates, which it does not expect in 2026. Its explicit guidance is to extend duration in Treasuries (two- and three-year yields sit slightly above overnight rates) or take selective high-quality credit risk, but not both at once, as combining them adds unnecessary volatility.

The firm emphasises that it acts as an engaged shareholder on clients' behalf within legally required standards, does not pursue activist strategies, and maintains transparent, publicly available voting records. BlackRock contends that politicising pension fund management undermines the interests of the millions of Americans who rely on these funds for retirement.

pieces.title: What are the tax advantages of real estate funds?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that real estate investments, including public REITs, non-traded REITs and other private vehicles, can carry tax attributes that should be weighed when comparing after-tax returns with other asset classes. It highlights deductible property taxes and expenses, depreciation that can reduce taxable income even when properties perform well, the 20% deduction for qualified REIT dividends, and return of capital distributions that defer rather than eliminate tax. The piece takes no explicit investment call, stressing that outcomes are complex and fund-specific and advising investors to consult tax and financial advisers.

pieces.title: Private credit: Looking beyond the headlines
pieces.summary: Principal Asset Management argues that recent private credit headlines overstate the problem: stress is concentrated among large lenders, software-heavy portfolios and 2021-vintage loans, while default rates sit below long-term averages and borrower fundamentals, leverage and underwriting standards elsewhere look sound. It takes an explicit constructive view that wider spreads and greater dispersion are creating attractive opportunities for selective lenders, particularly in the lower- and core-middle-market segments, where leverage is lower and investor protections are stronger.

The firm argues the RBA is shifting from a "wait and see" stance to a more proactive one, with further tightening possible if inflation stays above target, though the hike could prove a one-off if price pressures ease. Its explicit view is that the move is welcome for AUD cash investors, who benefit from higher yields and a steeper curve, but that ongoing uncertainty makes diversification across maturities and instruments essential.

It adds that long lease terms, creditworthy tenants and contractual rent escalators make these income streams reliable and offer some protection against inflation. The firm concludes that triple net leases are a compelling strategy for long-term, predictable returns.

pieces.title: Case for Collateralised Loan Obligations (CLOs)
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that CLOs, portfolios of securitised sub-investment-grade corporate loans, offer diversification and defensive, floating-rate income, and that the sector warrants an active, deal-by-deal approach given the variety of managers and structures. The firm's explicit view is that relative value favours AAA and BBB-rated CLOs, which it says offer more spread than investment-grade and high-yield corporate credit respectively, and that IG CLOs have historically delivered better long-term returns than other traditional fixed income. The piece also notes that Europe's roughly 70 managers and the US's 150-plus across hundreds of deals make manager and collateral selection essential.

pieces.summary: UBS Asset Management argues that active ETFs are gaining traction as investors seek the flexibility of discretionary management within the transparent, liquid ETF wrapper, with Europe lagging the US (7% of net flows versus 26% in 2024) but gradually expanding. Using CLOs as an example, it says active management can help investors respond to spread and credit changes, while cautioning that these are complex instruments unsuitable for all investors. UBS AM presents its first active ETF, with fixed income as the initial focus and possible equity strategies under development, as a strategic step, and says it sees active ETFs becoming an important component of portfolios, particularly for investors seeking flexibility and professional oversight.

pieces.title: Monthly Market Views: Fixed income resilience and equity market divergence - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's monthly outlook argues that fixed income has performed inversely to duration since the Middle East conflict began, with US bonds, high yield and inflation-linked exposure leading, and that US equities are outperforming Europe on strong earnings growth. It makes explicit calls for overweights in UK gilts (+), Euro high yield, US high yield, EM local currency and inflation, with US and Eurozone equities also rated positive, while preferring short duration in US investment grade and seeing China's AI advantage in power, infrastructure and physical AI as a possible diversifier. The firm frames these as team views that are not asset allocation advice.

The firm introduces a "Time Above Trend" framework as a measure of positioning and proposes using it as a tactical signal within asset allocation, rather than as a binary market-timing call. PGIM suggests that de-risking proves most effective after extended periods of above-trend growth, when positioning has become genuinely stretched, to avoid repeated whipsaws from premature reduction in risk exposure.

It attributes continued price strength to a soft US labour market, AI as a secular theme, fiscal stimulus and steadying manufacturing, and states that sentiment and positioning indicators show capitulation-level drawdowns in several segments that "could therefore represent attractive entry points."

The page is a promotional overview that frames these as open questions and does not state an explicit view or investment call.

pieces.title: Energy outlook: Scaling power to meet relentless demand
pieces.summary: Brookfield Asset Management's 2026 energy outlook argues that electricity demand, driven by digitalisation (notably AI and data centres), electrification and industrialisation, is growing faster than supply, making power a strategic bottleneck for governments and corporates. It contends that no single technology will suffice and calls for an "any-and-all" approach combining renewables (the lowest-cost bulk power in most regions), battery storage, nuclear and natural gas, with global power investment reaching an estimated $3.3 trillion in 2025, over 60% of it directed to renewables, storage and grid optimisation. The firm presents this as an opportunity for players with the right mix of capabilities and access to capital, and states that the binding constraint is the speed of investment and development rather than the availability of technology.

pieces.title: pere-2022-logistics-report
pieces.summary: Ares Management, in a PERE interview with head of real estate Bill Benjamin and CIO of industrial Dave Fazekas, argues that tight supply and strong tenant demand mean the logistics sector's "golden age is far from over", citing US industrial vacancy of 3.5 percent, record net absorption in 2021, and longer development timelines. The firm contends that industrial remains a "high-conviction bet" on both sides of the Atlantic, with European markets above 92 percent occupancy historically associated with rental growth, though Central and Eastern Europe is an exception where supply and demand are roughly in balance.

pieces.title: Uncovering value in euro high yield bonds - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that euro high yield has solid fundamentals, with healthy corporate balance sheets, low default expectations and supportive technicals such as strong inflows and CLO demand, but that rising dispersion means issuer selection, not broad market allocation, is now the main driver of returns. It explicitly favours an active, flexible approach, highlighting opportunities in German fiscal beneficiaries and recovering European real estate while flagging AI disruption to software and tariff exposure in supply-chain-heavy sectors as risks. The firm sees spreads as tight with limited room to tighten further, so it expects income rather than spread compression to drive returns.

Morgan Asset Management argues that ETFs have modernised fixed income by improving liquidity, cost, tax efficiency and transparency, and that active fixed income ETFs, which took 36% of ETF flows this year despite holding 18% of assets, are well placed to become a cornerstone of asset allocation. It contends that passive bond products are constrained by narrow benchmarks such as the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index, which covers about half the U.S. public bond market, whereas active managers can exploit a wider universe and have beaten that index on average over three, five and ten years on a net-of-fees basis. The firm's explicit call is that manager selection matters, since returns vary widely between top- and bottom-decile managers, so investors should favour managers with established research philosophies and proven processes.

pieces.title: How to measure risk for structured products
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that financial advisors commonly use proxy models to analyse structured products in portfolios, but these oversimplify risk analysis by failing to capture non-linear features and hidden risks specific to complex instruments. The firm advocates instead for "full revaluation" analysis based on each security's complete terms and conditions, and promotes its Aladdin Wealth platform as a tool to enable this more detailed risk modelling.

pieces.title: Emerging market debt likely to keep basking in the sun - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that emerging market debt has performed strongly in 2025, with hard currency bonds returning about 10% and local currency bonds about 15% year to date, driven by sound fundamentals, credible central bank policy and resilient growth. It expects these supportive conditions to last into 2026, with local currency rates, where its conviction is highest, benefiting from further easing by emerging market central banks. pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that financial conditions loosened significantly in 2019 but growth underperformed expectations, a puzzle it attributes to elevated geopolitical risk and trade uncertainty rather than broken monetary transmission mechanisms. The firm assigns a one-in-four recession probability over 12 months, dismissing yield curve inversion signals as distorted by low term premiums, and positions itself cautiously optimistic by categorising the current macro regime as a slowdown with potential to shift towards a benign "goldilocks" outcome. BlackRock's 2020 tactical stance is overweight risk assets, particularly Japanese and emerging market equities and high-yield debt, whilst favouring inflation-linked bonds against upside inflation surprises.

pieces.summary: Ares Management executives Andy Pike and Keith Derman argue that climate infrastructure (renewables, storage, EV charging and energy efficiency) is the most compelling of the three infrastructure verticals Ares focuses on, alongside gas generation and energy transportation. Ares contends that cost declines in wind, solar and batteries, together with a sprint to meet US tax-credit deadlines, create opportunity, and says the firm favours late-stage development, where value-creation and risk-mitigation potential remain high and capital is deployed once the question is what the project looks like, not whether it proceeds.

pieces.title: The case for emerging markets debt hard currency

The firm contends that EM government bonds have historically offered higher yields and returns differentiated from developed markets, with modest correlation to global equities and bonds. It also holds that focused credit analysis, particularly country allocation and security selection, can be rewarded and is critical to generating alpha.

pieces.title: Supporting decarbonisation: Why transition and sustainability-linked bonds can and should co-exist - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that transition bonds and sustainability-linked bonds (SLBs) are complementary rather than competing instruments, and that both should co-exist to finance hard-to-abate sectors and broaden the sustainable debt market. It contends that transition bonds offer purpose-specific, use-of-proceeds financing with KPI-based reporting that suits investors seeking targeted action, while SLBs offer issuers flexibility, including for those with limited capex needs and step-up mechanisms that compensate investors if targets are missed. The firm's explicit view is that the market's apparent fragmentation is outweighed by these differences and by the benefits of diversification and innovation.

The firm concludes that skilled active managers, with stock selection driven by company fundamentals, could be crucial to achieving differentiated performance and portfolio resilience.

The firm argues that direct voting choice enhances corporate governance by broadening participation in shareholder democracy and that it intends to extend the capability to individual investors and expand the range of voting guidelines available.

The firm presents TSMC as a distinctive blend of growth and resilience, and so a valuable investment anchor for equity investors. The piece is truncated before its full investment conclusion.

pieces.title: Project Finance: How Private Capital Can Help Manage Risks
pieces.summary: PGIM's piece argues that project finance, typically non-recourse debt repaid from a project's future cash flows and often held off sponsors' balance sheets via special purpose vehicles, suits long-dated infrastructure and energy projects that traditional short- to medium-term finance does not fit. It contends that private lenders can offer more flexible, patient structures (including senior and subordinated debt, preferred equity and follow-on capital) and, citing its own work for Gas Transmission Northwest, can match funding to a project and potentially reduce costs relative to bank financing. PGIM also notes that sponsors should be aware of the risks involved, though the piece does not elaborate on them.

pieces.title: Q3 2026 Investment Update
Quick View: What do the UK Budget measures mean for investors?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the UK Budget, delivered after weeks of speculation, has removed much of the uncertainty weighing on businesses, consumers and markets, and that its main measures were broadly in line with expectations and met the firm's three tests: non-inflationary, non-discriminatory and fiscally credible. The firm's explicit view is that investors can now refocus on corporate fundamentals and the attractive valuations in the UK equity market, which it notes has risen almost 20% year to date, while cautioning that the full economic impact may take time to digest. It also highlights a favourable early reaction in gilts, with the Chancellor's headroom of £22 billion against shocks described as slim, and stable yields seen as key to lowering corporate financing costs.

pieces.title: UK equities: Income today, growth tomorrow?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (author Laura Foll, Investment Focus, Summer 2026) argues that UK equities are overlooked because the UK economy and its stock market differ, with many UK-listed companies earning much of their revenue overseas at discounted valuations, notably against the US. The firm's explicit view is that low valuations, dividend income and stock-specific turnaround and structural growth drivers, such as infrastructure and defence spending, make UK equities a compelling contrarian allocation, with investors "paid to wait" for growth to emerge. The piece is framed as a view rather than a call on any named security, and it includes a disclaimer that references to individual companies, including Zigup, Marks & Spencer and Babcock, are not recommendations.

pieces.title: Why Real Estate in 2026?
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that real estate valuations have largely reset after the rate-driven repricing that began in 2022, while property fundamentals have held up, so 2026 may be a favourable point to re-engage with private real estate. It cites normalised real estate spreads against corporate credit, constrained supply due to higher financing and construction costs and regulatory delays, and uneven projected NOI growth across sectors. Apollo's explicit view is that selectivity, asset quality and underwriting discipline will matter more than broad market exposure.
