pieces.title: TargetNetZero Credit : 5 years
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers reports that, five years on, its TargetNetZero Global IG and EUR Credit strategies have matched market-rate performance while achieving materially lower carbon footprints and faster decarbonisation than their benchmarks, with the Global IG strategy outperforming its index by 0.25% annualised and the EUR Credit strategy by 0.17%. The firm attributes most of this return to bottom-up security selection rather than to climate constraints, arguing that net-zero alignment came at negligible cost and that its approach, which uses its proprietary Implied Temperature Rise tool to back issuers best placed to adapt rather than excluding hard-to-abate sectors, shows decarbonisation need not sacrifice return potential. The piece also promotes the newly launched TargetNetZero Euro IG Short Duration strategy as a further way for investors to combine climate and investment objectives in core fix

pieces.title: What’s happening to stocks beneath the index?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that the S&P 500's calm index-level performance, with a maximum drawdown of just 7% so far this year, masks considerable beneath-the-surface dispersion across sectors and single stocks. It points to energy being up 35% year to date, financials, discretionary and tech being down high single digits, a single-stock volatility gauge (VIX EQ) at 40.5, and average pairwise correlation among S&P 500 stocks at 13%. The firm concludes that this environment is "ripe for stock picking and active management."

pieces.summary: Ares Australia Management's Teiki Benveniste, in a Livewire interview published on 22 April 2022, argues that credit investors should "get back to basics" and avoid mistakes amid rising rates, inflation and the war in Ukraine. He sees wider dispersion emerging across fixed- and floating-rate, liquid and illiqu

pieces.title: View from the Markets: Portfolio maintenance in turbulent times - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's Chris Iggo argues that, despite market losses so far, the Middle East conflict could still wipe out year-to-date gains, and that little of the market is genuinely cheap, with most valuations still above their 10-year averages. The firm's explicit tactical stance is defensive: patience and a preference for cash, short-duration and inflation-linked assets until the outlook clears. It highlights short-dated government bonds, short-duration investment-grade and high-yield credit, and floating-rate instruments as relatively attractive, while warning that risk premiums have not risen enough to compensate for the adverse scenarios.

pieces.title: NBXG | Neuberger Next Generation Connectivity Fund
At the Edge of Insurability: When Wildfire Risk Becomes Investment Risk
The New Frontier in Insurance Asset Management
pieces.summary: PGIM's Yi Yang argues that higher rates and continued private-markets growth are widening the investment opportunity set for insurers, but that the harder task is building portfolios insurers can own, govern and explain. The piece covers five areas: product breadth, jurisdictional alignment, structuring, reinsurance partnership and analytics/risk governance, and uses a hypothetical loan portfolio to show how the same assets can attract different capital charges across regulatory regimes and structures. Its explicit view is that structuring and governance capability, rather than access to assets alone, will define success for insurers.

pieces.title: Could 5% Treasury yields create demand rather than destroy it?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, in a piece by portfolio manager James Briggs, argues that US Treasury yields near 5%, the highest since the Global Financial Crisis, are more likely to attract fresh money into fixed income than to crowd out demand for Treasuries and investment grade credit. It points to a shift in

pieces.title: Heard on the Hill Webinar: Multifamily Market Outlook 2026
Beyond headline spreads: Hidden opportunities in high yield
Beyond net zero: Evaluating transition plans and climate commitments
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that a decarbonisation target is not a credible transition plan, and that investors should judge companies on whether committed capital, realistic pathways, executive incentives and falling absolute emissions stand behind their headline pledges. It presents its proprietary Climate Transition Assessment, which scores companies across ambitions, actions, accountability and achievements, and uses Microsoft and TotalEnergies as examples of why intensity gains, reported figures and abandoned goals need careful scrutiny. The firm's explicit view is that "follow the money, not the pledge" is the right test, and that credibility must be assessed against each business model rather than a single standard.

pieces.title: Credit convergence: A framework for public-private income solutions
Hidden growth opportunities across Asia
pieces.summary: Aberdeen's Gabriel Sacks, lead manager of Aberdeen Asia Focus, argues that the best growth opportunities in Asia lie in under-researched smaller companies that can compound earnings over many years, rather than in forecasting macroeconomic trends. He highlights "picks and shovels" suppliers exposed to themes such as biologics manufacturing, precision machine tools, semiconductor and battery materials, and power infrastructure, alongside wealth management in India and healthcare. Aberdeen's explicit view is that Asia is well placed to benefit from a new era of advanced industrialisation, while India, though rich in ideas, is expensive to access and opportunities are broadening across Korea, China and Vietnam.

pieces.title: Credit Opportunities in 2026: From a Seller’s Market to a Buyer’s Market
pieces.summary: Apollo argues that credit markets are shifting from a seller's market to a buyer's market in 2026, as AI-driven capex (which it estimates could require $300–400 billion a year of debt financing from the largest hyperscalers) and a revival in M&A and LBO activity add substantial new supply and loosen the technical support that defined 2025. Apollo's explicit view is that the year offers one of the broadest opportunity sets in a decade, with the most attractive areas including AI infrastructure financing, sponsor-led M&A and LBO issuance, cross-asset portfolio management, and uncorrelated niches such as sports franchise lending and European private credit. It advises investors to take a cross-asset approach, pursue uncorrelated returns, assess AI-related disruption risk, and maintain strict underwriting discipline.

Income, diversification and resilience through mortgage-backed securities
pieces.summary: GAM Investments argues that non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities, particularly legacy deals issued before the 2007-2009 financial crisis, can offer income, diversification and resilience that complement traditional fixed income allocations. It contends that spreads have held up despite 2026's rate volatility, that RMBS carry low correlation with conventional sectors because they depend on mortgage pools rather than corporate creditworthiness, and that fixed-rate US mortgages, rising borrower equity and the "lock-in" effect support credit quality even if house prices soften. GAM's explicit view is that legacy non-agency RMBS are "particularly attractive" on these grounds.

The five building blocks of asset-backed securities
pieces.summary: BNY Investments argues that asset-backed securities (ABS) can strengthen a fixed income portfolio in a volatile rate and inflation environment, citing credit quality from structural protections such as bankruptcy remoteness, reserves, excess spread and tranching; a historical yield premium over similarly rated corporate bonds, with AAA ABS offering spreads close to A and BBB corporates; shorter-dated, lower-duration profiles; and diversification from granular, asset-based collateral. The firm's explicit view is that thoughtfully chosen ABS can complement core bond holdings, though the piece's claims rest on its own estimates and historical comparisons rather than forward-looking guarantees.

pieces.title: Look beyond frontier models for compelling opportunities across China’s AI ecosystem
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that China's AI opportunity should be assessed across the full value chain (energy, chips, infrastructure, models and applications) rather than by frontier model leadership, where the US remains clearly ahead. Its head of Greater China Equities, Victoria Mio, contends that China's lower costs, power and manufacturing scale, and faster deployment give it a dist

Macro Markets Podcast Episode 87: The Complexity Premium in Structured Credit: The Opportunity Set Today (Part 2)
As the Playing Field Expands, Insurance Investors Must Stay Nimble
Income in an AI-driven world | iShares
pieces.summary: BlackRock argues that artificial intelligence-driven market concentration has reduced dividend yields in global equity indices, making traditional income strategies less effective for investors seeking both growth and cash flow. The firm reports rising demand for income among younger Australian investors facing cost-of-living pressures, and advocates for its iShares World Equity High Income ETF (WYNC) as a solution that combines active dividend selection with option premium income to balance growth exposure with supplementary cash flows.

pieces.title: Private Credit 2026 Outlook
pieces.summary: Barings presents its 2026 private credit outlook as a 45-minute webinar, arguing that the opportunity is widening as investors broaden allocations across strategies and asset classes, and covering direct lending, asset-based finance and portfolio finance. The page makes no explicit allocation call or forecast; its only stated position is that the

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that non-listed REITs offer several tax advantages: a 20% reduction in the individual rate on the ordinary income portion of distributions (under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, through the end of 2025), tax deferral on return of capital distributions, which

pieces.title: Public Equity Markets Have Changed—Why Do Portfolios Still Look the Same?
pieces.summary: Apollo's piece, a short video summary by Partner Eric Hanno, argues that public equity markets have structurally changed: fewer listed companies, greater index concentration, elevated valuations for the largest stocks, rising intra-market correlations and continued growth in passive strategies. It contends that these shifts may justify investors reconsidering traditional equity allocations and evaluating alternative approaches, specifically private market strategies offering more predictable or contractual cash flows and lower correlation to public equities. Apollo's explicit view is that portfolios may need rethinking in light of these changes, though the piece itself is promotional, linking to its own "Aligned Alternatives" strategies, and offers little quantitative evidence.

pieces.title: What Are the Different Types of Data Center Infrastructure?
pieces.summary: Ares Management's piece explains that hyperscale data centres come in two main forms: turnkey facilities, which the developer fully builds out including IT fitout and which are ready for immediate operation, and powered shells, where the customer completes much of the fitout and owns the associated equipment. It attributes the prevalence of each to market conditions, citing powered shells as more common in the US and turnkey products in markets with smaller land parcels and more vertical buildings, and notes that Ares's own portfolio spans both types worldwide. The piece makes no explicit investment recommendation, though it frames understanding these distinctions as important for developers and investors in digital infrastructure.

Private Markets Perspectives 2H 2026: Capitalizing on Concentration, Liquidity and AI
Can credit markets absorb the AI buildout?
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that AI data centre spending has shifted from being funded by hyperscalers' own cash flow to being funded by capital markets, with the full buildout potentially costing around $5 trillion through 2030, of which roughly $2 trillion may be financed in investment grade credit. It estimates hyperscaler bond issuance will reach $279 billion in 2026 and $220–300 billion in 2027, and that these names could approach 10% of the US IG market by 2030, while cautioning that index-based measures understate the exposure given 144A and private placement issuance. The firm does not see this as a credit crisis risk, but expects some indigestion, with tech spreads now wider than the IG benchmark and demand softening at the margin, and concludes that AI-related supply will keep a floor under tech spreads and that active security selection and curve positioning, rather than passive index replication, will be decisive.

pieces.title: When is duration worth owning again?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that higher yields alone do not make longer-duration bonds attractive. Adding duration should instead depend on several signals turning together, including the Fed, inflation, employment, oil prices, risk assets and growth, rather than a single yield level such as 6% on the 10-year Treasury. The firm says it currently favours a lower-duration stance that emphasises carry and limits drawdown risk, while staying ready to add duration if those signals change.

pieces.title: Lottomatica: Transforming a Leader in Italian Gaming
pieces.summary: Apollo reports that its acquisition of Italian gaming company Gamenet in 2019, subsequently rebranded as Lottomatica, achieved an 8x value increase through strategic acquisitions, a shift to online gaming, and operational improvements across marketing, product and technology. Apollo argues that its success demonstrates the value of combining private equity expertise with strong management teams and tailored sector knowledge, supported by its capital solutions team in executing an IPO and full exit in 25 months despite market volatility.

Digitale Assets werden Realität
pieces.summary: Insight Investment argues that digital assets are transitioning from experimental to institutional reality, with tokenised money market funds, stablecoins and on-chain representations of traditional assets now regulated and operational. The firm contends that tokenisation offers practical benefits to institutional investors including faster settlement, improved liquidity management and enhanced collateral efficiency, while emphasising that digital assets enhance rather than replace existing financial infrastructure. Insight Investment expects a hybrid on- and off-chain financial system to emerge as the most likely long-term outcome.

From conviction to capital
pieces.summary: Gemcorp Capital's second annual investor study, based on a survey of 250 investment decision-makers across 22 countries, reports that most respondents expect emerging market private credit to outperform developed market equivalents over the next five years, and that EM is the region where allocation plans are growing fastest. The firm argues that EM remains significantly underweight, with EM accounting for just 5.8% of private credit portfolios on average despite 60% of respondents already allocating to the asset class, and it explicitly frames this as a gap between conviction and actual capital commitments. Gemcorp presents this as evidence of a shift in how sophisticated allocators view geography, diversification and risk, though the piece's stated call is essentially that capital will follow the conviction already expressed.

pieces.title: 4Q25 Earnings: Not your parents' consumer
Sobering developments in developed world rates markets
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (Jenna Barnard, Head of Global Bonds) argues that developed-market rate expectations have turned hawkish: soft-landing rate cuts have ended in several economies, resilient data has led markets to price in possible hikes in Australia and Canada, and long-dated yields have failed to fall even during the cutting cycle. The firm explicitly favours a more defensive stance on interest rates, having cut portfolio duration from high single digits in December 2024 to 3-4 years by end October 2025, while increasing credit risk on valuation and corporate-

Whiteboarding: Institutional Investing in Pro Sports
pieces.summary: Sixth Street, an asset manager, argues that private capital is flowing into professional sports because the business has become a scalable, global operation that rewards execution as well as money. It cites 48 major U.S. teams with private investment, team valuations compounding at roughly 10% a year since 2012, a rise of more than 80% in global sports media rights since 2014, and over $20 billion of stadium builds in the pipeline. Its explicit view is that a "flywheel" of spending, fan engagement and reinvestment becomes "supercharged" with the right capital partner, and that Sixth Street is positioned to provide that capital and its flexible solutions to teams.

pieces.title: 2026 Private Credit Survey: LP & GP Views
pieces.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management's 2026 Global Alternatives Survey reports that private credit investors rank rising defaults as the top risk to their portfolios, ahead of macroeconomic shocks, spread compression and refinancing pressure, and are therefore prioritising borrower quality and underwriting discipline over chasing yield. The survey finds LPs feel under-allocated to the asset class, with asset-backed finance leading planned commitments and wealth channels and evergreen vehicles seen as reshaping fund structures, while manager selection is the leading LP challenge. The firm's explicit conclusion is that performance dispersion matters as much as market direction, so allocators should favour managers combining proven underwriting discipline with specialist expertise and differentiated origination.

pieces.title: Take Two: US GDP revised up - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's weekly "world of finance in two minutes" reports that US GDP growth for Q1 2026 was revised up to 2.1% annualised from 1.6%, with US and eurozone flash PMIs also showing modest improvement, and it notes that oil has fallen from a May peak of $114 to around $70-$75 per barrel following the US-Iran peace deal. The piece does not state an explicit investment view or call; it frames the oil price as unlikely to return quickly to pre-war lows, but suggests that a somewhat higher level, near the five-year average of about $80, may not pose a problem for the global economy.

pieces.title: Investment Outlook – Asset class views for 2026 - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management's 2026 outlook argues that investors will need to be flexible and selective as economic fragmentation grows, and it expects bonds to benefit from rate cuts in the US and Europe while remaining exposed to rising budget deficits. It is constructive on credit, citing a supportive economic and policy backdrop, and on tech equities, where it expects robust earnings growth driven by AI-led capital spending. It also sees strong tech sectors supporting selected emerging markets, helped by lower US bond yields and a weaker dollar. The traffic-light asset class ratings, which indicate expected three-to-six-month returns relative to long-term trends, are not included in the text provided.

pieces.title: Positioning for the disruption
pieces.summary: BlackRock reports that the US-Iran conflict has triggered a 60% rise in oil prices and significant equity market declines, creating a prolonged global supply chain shock with risks to growth and inflation. The asset manager recommends investors reduce exposure to broad equities and instead position portfolios toward low-volatility strategies, infrastructure, and defensive fixed income such as cash-plus funds and inflation-linked bonds to weather the disruption.

pieces.title: Real rates and equities
pieces.summary: Lombard Odier Investment Managers argues that markets now expect positive real interest rates to persist over the long term, a structural shift that is not confined to the US, though Japan's short-end real rates remain negative. The firm contends this environment erodes the historical small-cap premium in favour of large caps, and it notes that real rates are most supportive of small caps when the curve is upward-sloping but at low levels, as the current configuration is not. Its explicit view is that high real rates should revive interest in bonds, making the equity/bond combination more attractive for multi-asset portfolios into 2026, while warning of the macro risks of this scenario.

pieces.title: Investors seeking resilience should consider a quality bias
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management argues that, after higher-quality equities underperformed broad developed markets by 5 percentage points in 2025 (their worst relative year since 2003), the "dash for trash" was a mistake to ignore, since quality has historically added resilience in drawdowns and recovered sharply after lagging phases. It explicitly favours a quality-centric allocation to build portfolio resilience, noting that the valuation premium of quality stocks has more than halved since July 2024, and cautions that investors should check whether heavy tech and AI exposure in some quality strategies would actually be defensive.

pieces.title: CIO Weekly: The Benefits of a Buyer’s Market
Adding annuities and life insurance to the retirement planning toolkit
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that annuities and life insurance have moved out of separate silos and now belong in one holistic retirement planning conversation, with annuities offering guaranteed income to address the psychological as well as financial loss of a salary, and life insurance providing tax-free liquidity for estate and legacy goals. The firm's explicit view is that advisers should shift from product selection to outcome design, treating these tools as standard components that work alongside investments rather than as binary choices

pieces.title: Agriculture Landscape: January 2026
pieces.summary: PGIM's January 2026 Agriculture Landscape reports on recent sector developments including rising food price inflation, new farm aid payments for Midwest and Southern farmers, ongoing trade missions to expand market access, potential regulatory relaxation for agricultural producers, and resolution of U.S.-Mexico water disputes. The publication notes expectations for continued consolidation in the seed and fertiliser sectors. PGIM positions itself as serving institutional investors seeking farmland asset class exposure for portfolio diversification.

pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that front-end municipal rates were broadly range-bound in June, with the SIFMA Municipal Swap Index trading between about 2.14% and 2.89%, and that VRDN resets were well supported by balanced supply and demand. The firm notes that seasonal note issuance is starting to build, and it expects that rising reinvestment cash alongside shifting VRDN inventory could bring softer reset levels and less attractive pricing for short-term variable-rate instruments over the summer, while overall technicals remain balanced.

Quick View: An AI report card through the lens of Nvidia earnings
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that Nvidia's latest earnings demonstrate the AI investment cycle is accelerating beyond hyperscalers into enterprise and industrial sectors, with growth in the latter expanding at 31 per cent quarterly. The firm contends that the advent of AI agents, persistent computing capacity shortages, and the emergence of token-processing "AI factories" support a case for AI capital expenditure potentially tripling within five years. Janus Henderson views AI adoption across hundreds of thousands of companies as a major but underappreciated driver that could exceed earlier technology adoption cycles.

Quick View: Will the Fed’s patience be rewarded?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors, through Head of Global Short Duration and Liquidity Daniel Siluk, argues that the Fed's pause in rate cuts reflects a stabilising U.S. labour market and sticky inflation, with a second 25bp cut by year-end a possibility rather than a certainty. The firm sees upward pressure on longer-dated bonds from policy uncertainty, tariffs and federal debt, and its explicit view is that range-bound short- to mid-dated bonds offer attractive yields and a way to stay invested while avoiding much of that volatility.

pieces.title: Does your balanced fund have these three key essentials?
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that an effective balanced fund rests on three essentials: equities focused on high-quality companies with multi-year secular growth, such as AI innovation; a fixed income allocation that generates income while limiting drawdowns; and a flexible mandate that lets managers adjust the equity-to-bonds mix. The firm's explicit views for 2026 are that AI-driven capital spending has not yet plateaued, that shorter-duration bonds may hedge a faltering economy, and that higher-quality securitised credit offers attractive income and diversification relative to corporate bonds.

pieces.title: A Fresh Look at the Strategic Case for Private Assets
pieces.summary: AllianceBernstein argues that, despite the 2026 software-driven stress in private credit, private assets remain worth considering in strategic allocations, with private credit more attractive than private equity because it offers a yield advantage and diversification. The firm frames the recent turmoil as a liquidity-expectations problem rather than a credit event, and says investors should be selective about managers, structures and liquidity assumptions. It also argues that, as capital raising shifts towards private markets and public markets look fully valued, the case for private assets rests on long time horizons and tolerance for illiquidity.

pieces.title: Hiding in Plain Sight: The Public Credit Opportunity
pieces.summary: New York Life Investments argues that public credit now offers a stronger combination of income, liquidity, transparency and governance than private credit, as the illiquidity premium in private direct lending has compressed from about 400 basis points over broadly syndicated loans in 2022 to roughly 150–200 basis points today. Citing an industry estimate that illiquidity costs about 200 basis points a

pieces.title: The role of public and private strategies in real estate
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Strategic Investment Advisory Group argues that real estate should be a permanent ("evergreen") holding in diversified portfolios, and that investors should use both public (REIT) and private strategies, which differ in sector exposure, price volatility, leverage and liquidity. The firm's explicit illustration is a mix of roughly one-third REITs and two-thirds private core real estate, with REIT liquidity and volatility providing tactical flexibility, and sharp REIT price moves flagged as potential opportunities to tilt allocations.

A New Fed Chair, a New Tone – But Familiar Anchors
pieces.summary: PIMCO argues that Kevin Warsh's arrival as Fed chair will bring a thoughtful but distinctive approach, with changes that are evolutionary rather than revolutionary, against a backdrop of above-target inflation and crosscurrents for the dual mandate that could keep the Fed on hold possibly beyond 2026. The firm expects a shift toward a more rules-based framework, less forward guidance, and a gradual reduction and shortening of the balance sheet, but it doubts Warsh will actually scale back post-meeting press conferences and stresses that any change requires a committee majority, so Fed independence and consensus decision-making should hold.

Europe’s securitisation deal: the door is open, now the detail decides
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors (authors Ian Bettney and Nathan Fox) argue that the EU's provisional securitisation agreement of 21 October is the most credible reform attempt yet, removing barriers that have kept investors out, but that its impact will depend on technical standards still to be written. The firm reports that its advocacy succeeded on several fronts: the bespoke investor sanctions regime was dropped, the EU reporting template for non-EU deals was removed, and the UCITS single-securitisation limit rose from 10% to 25%, though it says the last could have gone further. Janus Henderson's stated view is that the detail will decide the outcome, particularly how "equivalent" third-country information is defined, and it calls for rules guided by outcomes over format, proportionality and measurement of results.

pieces.title: Chart of the Month: May 2026
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Chart of the Month (May 2026), written by its Emerging Markets Debt portfolio manager, argues that China's exports have proved resilient despite US tariffs, with January and February 2026 exports up 21.8% year-on-year, and that trade diversion to non-US markets has offset the tariff hit to direct US-bound shipments, pushing the 2025 trade surplus to a record USD 1.2 trillion. The piece expects exports to moderate later in 2026 but judges that they could again surprise to the upside, and it sees little appetite in Beijing for stronger stimulus, with markets pricing further rate cuts. It also concludes that Middle East tensions and oil volatility are unlikely to materially affect China's GDP, given diversified oil supply and tightly managed domestic fuel prices.

pieces.title: Buy Bonds and Carry On
pieces.summary: New York Life Investments argues that higher bond yields near two-decade highs present a compelling opportunity for investors, driven by strong economic growth and firm corporate fundamentals rather than credit stress. The firm recommends deploying cash into bonds with an emphasis on short-to-intermediate duration, blending floating and fixed-rate exposure, and favouring higher-quality securitised credit and investment-grade corporates over lower-rated alternatives.

Monetising AI: Driving innovation and multiple investment opportunities - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that AI has moved from experimentation to large-scale deployment and is becoming a tangible driver of cost savings and revenue across industries, supported by heavy infrastructure spending, with returns taking longer to emerge than for typical technology investments. The firm's explicit view is that AI will create winners and losers, so investors should favour resilient, adaptable companies able to integrate AI into their core strategies, with "mission critical" software providers likely to thrive, while legacy software and some semiconductor margins face pressure. It also judges that the coming decade offers significant long-term return potential if the opportunity is approached strategically and responsibly.

Castlelake Acquires Majority Stake in U.S. Residential Lending Platforms Eastview and Lendmarq
pieces.summary: Castlelake, a $36 billion asset-based private credit manager, reports that it has taken a majority stake in Resfin Partners, which owns mortgage correspondent Eastview and residential lender Lendmarq, to expand its in-house origination of residential loans for its funds, building on more than 4,000 senior loans (over $2 billion funded) previously acquired through these platforms. Castlelake presents the deal as part of its strategy of taking long-term ownership in high-quality sourcing platforms to improve access to deals, risk control and disciplined capital deployment, and says it expects to support the platforms' growth, with Lucas Jackson, its Head of North American Residential Mortgage Finance, stressing a shared focus on asset quality and value.

pieces.title: rethink stability
Market Review
pieces.summary: J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that despite geopolitical tensions and central bank rate rises in Q3 2026, global equities reached record highs supported by strong earnings growth and economic resilience, whilst bonds faced headwinds from rising yields driven by persistent inflation and heavy corporate and sovereign issuance. The firm argues that market expectations for further rate rises by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of England through June 2027 appear excessive.

pieces.title: Monthly Market Views: Strong US growth raises rate risks - BNP Paribas Asset Management
pieces.summary: BNP Paribas Asset Management argues that strong US growth and sticky inflation raise the risk of higher US government bond yields, with oil prices and AI-driven earnings as the key market drivers. It contends that euro and UK market pricing for policy rates looks overly aggressive relative to central banks' data-dependent stance, and expects expectations to adjust, potentially easing long-term yield volatility. It also views gold's medium-term risk-reward as skewed to the upside, supported by central bank and official buying, and favours flexible euro credit, short-dated inflation-linked bonds and short-duration strategies as implementation ideas.

Taking the punchbowl away from the party
pieces.summary: Janus Henderson Investors argues that the U.S. economy is significantly stronger than widely recognised, with nominal GDP growth of 7-8%, and that the Federal Reserve's recent rate increases are likely the start of a broader tightening cycle that will persist longer than investors expect because the Fed lags the economic cycle. The firm contends that deglobalization is creating persistent inflation and corporate pricing power that will constrain the Fed's policy flexibility, potentially forcing higher interest rates for an extended period and shifting investor focus from speculative to fundamentally-based strategies.
